News.title: Demands for stronger laws after autumn sees more than 100 foxes chased by hunts
News.content:
Demands for stronger laws after autumn sees more than 100 foxes chased by hunts

EXCLUSIVE: Cub hunting takes place between August and the end of October and sees hunts surrounding fox habitats and setting their hounds on them to train the dogs how to hunt and kill

View 2 Images More than 100 foxes were chased by hunts across England and Wales this autumn (Image: Stuart Brock/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Animal rights campaigners have demanded stronger laws after more than 100 foxes were chased by hunts across England and Wales this autumn.

‌



‌



Despite a ban on fox hunting, new figures reveal 104 foxes were chased by hunts during fox cub hunting season.

‌



Cub hunting takes place between August and the end of October and sees hunts surrounding fox habitats and setting their hounds on them to train the dogs how to hunt and kill.

‌



Compiled by animal welfare charity the League Against Cruel Sports, the figures come from incidents reported into its confidential Animal Crimewatch service, evidence obtained by its field operatives, and from reports by hunt saboteurs and hunt monitors.

View 2 Images The Government has been urged to go harder on the hunts (Image: Getty Images)

As well as the hunting of foxes, the data also showed 332 reports of hunts wreaking havoc with anti-social behaviour. The figures are only from hunts being monitored, meaning the true figure of foxes hunted could be even higher.

‌



Emma Slawinski, chief executive of the League Against Cruel Sports, said: “The brutal practice of cub hunting is still happening despite the fox hunting ban and we need stronger hunting laws to end it once and for all.

“We need the government to act upon its pledge to ban so-called trail hunting and finish the job by introducing legislation in the next parliamentary session at the latest that will consign fox hunting to the history books.

‌



“We also need an effective deterrent in the form of tougher penalties, the removal of all the loopholes in the Hunting Act, and the law changed so that hunts cannot claim their kills are ‘accidental’.”

Labour MP Ruth Jones added: “These new figures reveal that hunts are continuing to flout the law whilst at the same time claiming they can police and control their hunters and supporters. It is time to end these cruel and barbaric activities and this can only be done by closing the loopholes in the Hunting Act. It was a Labour Party commitment in the 2024 manifesto and we need to action it now”.

Article continues below

The Government also hit out at the hunts. A Defra spokesperson said: “We are committed to enacting a ban on trail hunting that truly protects our countryside, wildlife and rural communities.

“The nature of trail hunting makes it difficult to ensure that wild mammals such as foxes, deer and hares are not placed in danger of being injured or killed by dogs and this must stop."

News.title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.

Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.

Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic.

"It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said.

The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning.

Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.

Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away.

"It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment.

Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty."

The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.

They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.

The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency".

But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said.

"A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive."

News.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
News.content:
It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation.

The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis.

When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation.

A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making.

How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments.

The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming.

Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed,, external he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented."

But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted.

On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared with what is spent on support to help them get into work.

He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one.

He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts.

But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other.

And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee".

He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people.

News.title: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
News.content:
Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.

The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.

Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years".

"I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said.

"I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

"Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."

Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper.

"How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.

Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"

Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.

News.title: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
News.content:
Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.

The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.

The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".

News.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
News.content:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.

Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.

Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.

And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

News.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
News.content:
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.

The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.

And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.

"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.

Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?

Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.

News.title: The search to find a friend for Jojo the gorilla after a lifetime of being alone
News.content:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

News.title: Brand, Walliams and Married at First Sight: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
News.content:
This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.

On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.

By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.

Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.

These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.

So why is this all happening now?

In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.

All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.

"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.

In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.

Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.

It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".

News.title: Man dies after being stabbed by gang of masked men
News.content:
A murder investigation has been launched after a 27-year-old man was stabbed in Manchester.

Officers were called to Moss Bank in the Crumpsall area of the city shortly after 01:30 GMT following reports that a man had suffered several stab wounds. He later died from his injuries in an ambulance.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said initial inquiries suggested the victim had been attacked by "a number of males" all believed to have been wearing dark clothing and balaclavas.

The suspects are believed to have fled the scene in the direction of Ash Tree Road, said a force spokesperson who added that no arrests had been made and inquiries were continuing.

News.title: King jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
News.content:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

News.title: Burnham suggests Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister's strategy
News.content:
The prime minister has told members of his party that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat.

On Saturday morning Andy Burnham addressed the first Welsh Labour conference since May's Senedd election.

He suggested the previous Labour government did not do enough to pass powers down to communities, and said it was "hard" to accept the party was no longer in power after 27 years of running the Welsh government.

He spoke before a review into what went wrong concluded that former First Minister Eluned Morgan's political strategy of calling out Westminster played a role in the party losing power.

The report by Prof Anand Menon, of PF Global, said Morgan's calls for constitutional change like the devolution of policing and the Crown Estate did not get through to voters.

A source close to the former first minister said it was "ludicrous" to suggest that Morgan was focused on constitutional issues.

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has criticised his party for focusing too much on powers for the Senedd.

In a subdued speech, Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" where "everyone" was "signed up and on the same page."

He spoke ahead of the publication of a review of what went wrong at the election.

Since he became prime minister he has been lobbying the Welsh government to devolve more powers to local councils.

"Somewhere along the way perhaps we lost sight of some of the principles that drove devolution in the first place.

"We probably stopped listening as much as we should have, and actually stopped driving power down into every Welsh postcode which is what the vision to me really should always have been about - about people and places."

He said the party would accept its defeat and "come back stronger" with a "vision for a stronger Wales in a fairer United Kingdom."

Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" where the party is "pulling in the same direction".

"Where I'm pulling with you and not creating problems for you or going against what Ken or colleagues want to achieve.

"We will put forward a vision for communities up and down Wales, as well as giving Wales a stronger national voice."

News.title: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia
News.content:
Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.

She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.

Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.

When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.

Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.

What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.

He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.

This article contains upsetting details

Dolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.

A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.

The car did not stop.

As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.

News.title: Milder weather coming before more cold health alerts take effect
News.content:
Another round of cold health alerts is set to come into force on Sunday following a brief break from the weekend's subzero temperatures.

After readings dipped as low as minus 7C early on Saturday, most places on Sunday morning will be milder and free of frost.

Widespread rainfall is likely with hail and thunderstorms possible for parts of Wales and southern England.

Into the new week, the wintry chill is set to return with UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) cold-health alerts beginning for the north-east and north-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber from 21:00 GMT on Sunday.

News.title: Fifteen taken to hospital after deliberate fire at Glasgow flats
News.content:
Police are treating a fire at a block of flats in Glasgow as deliberate.

Four fire engines were sent to the four-storey building on Copland Road, in the Ibrox area, just after 17:00 on Friday after reports of a fire on the ground floor.

Firefighters and paramedics initially said they were dealing with "multiple casualties" and police have now confirmed 15 people were taken to hospital as a precaution.

The fire was extinguished and crews left the scene by 22:00.

News.title: 'I'm lucky to be alive': Woman's warning over black market weight-loss jabs
News.content:
A woman has described how she could not speak or stand before being rushed to hospital after taking an unlicensed weight-loss jab.

Kay Roscoe, 38, from Birkenhead, said she had used a substance sold as retatrutide, or "reta", for two months before falling seriously ill.

The experimental drug is not approved for general use and is available only through clinical trials. Products claiming to contain it are widely sold online, but it is not known whether Kay took genuine retatrutide.

She is now warning others about the risks. "I am the luckiest person to be alive. Honestly I can't say it enough, get off the pens," she said.

On the day of her collapse, Kay had been due to go out for a roast dinner with a friend.

When she failed to answer her phone, her friend went to check on her at home and found her unable to speak or stand.

"I was frothing at the mouth, not responsive at all," she said, recounting what her friend later told her. "My eyes were moving around, but I couldn't speak or move or do anything."

Kay, who has no memory of the episode, said her friends rang an ambulance and told paramedics she had been taking "reta" before she was rushed to hospital.

She said it took more than an hour for her to regain consciousness.

News.title: Bonnie Tyler remembers loved ones in posthumous Christmas single
News.content:
Bonnie Tyler sings of "love, light and peace" and remembers "the ones who still live on inside our hearts" on her posthumous Christmas single, which was released on Friday.

The popular Welsh powerhouse singer, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.

Fans were able to hear the Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's husky tones one more time on the festive track titled "Love, Light and Peace".

The last song Tyler recorded features sleigh bells and angels and an ad-libbed farewell: "To all, goodnight."

The lyrics about grief and loss take on new meaning following her death.

Tyler sings: "Blessed are the ones who still live on inside our hearts.

"Here's to the best of them."

The song was written by Chrissie Hammond and Grammy-winner Terry Britten, who played guitar on Tyler's debut album, The World Starts Tonight in 1977.

Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer for the last song she recorded.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors winner Sebastian Croft explains what gave him an advantage
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Being gay might give players an edge on the BBC reality game show, according to Celebrity Traitors winner Sebastian Croft.

The 24-year-old actor, known for his role in Heartstopper, explained to The Times that "there’s an element of not being sure whether you’re gonna be accepted as a queer person entering any room, lots of [gay] people become good at having coping mechanisms for getting to know people, or feeling like they’re not a threat".

Croft triumphed alongside comedian Romesh Ranganathan in a dramatic climax to the popular series. His win follows previous gay champions on the show, such as comedian Alan Carr from the debut celebrity spin-off, alongside civilian series winners Stephen Libby and Leanne Quigley.

Fronted by Claudia Winkleman, the hit game involves 21 famous faces attempting to uncover hidden traitors who "kill off" players in the middle of the night.

Speaking about his own experience coming out, Croft said that “on the whole, everyone was supportive” when it came to sharing his sexuality with his family.

Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian Croft have won The Celebrity Traitors (BBC/Studio Lambert/PA) ( BBC/Studio Lambert )

However, he added: “I’ve been emotionally and physically threatened because of my sexuality, had people reject me as a person.

“And that’s the good end of the spectrum. Which is why I’ve ended up wanting to champion queer refugees.”

After winning the £83,000 prize pot for their chosen charities, Croft donated his £41,500 share to the charity Choose Love and Ranganathan to the Refugee Council.

Choose Love, a global humanitarian organisation and movement, formerly known as Help Refugees, supports refugees and displaced people around the world through emergency aid and long-term support.

However, the pair received criticisms online for their chosen charities, with the BBC confirming it received complaints.

Croft began his acting career while still at school, making his television debut as young Ned Stark in Game of Thrones.

Croft said he was then “ostracised and bullied” over his sexuality and acting, eventually leaving school aged 16.

After leaving Heartstopper in 2023 he turned his attention to music and on Friday released his debut EP – The Great Forever – and announced his first European tour.

On Sunday night he will also make his debut television performance on Strictly Come Dancing, where he will sing his recent single Everything Always Now.

News.title: Steve Tandy proud of ‘phenomenal’ Wales players after famous win over All Blacks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Wales head coach Steve Tandy hailed his “phenomenal” players after they delivered a stunning performance to sink Nations Championship opponents New Zealand 35-28 in Cardiff.

It was the first time since 1953 that Wales could celebrate beating the All Blacks, ending a run of 34 successive defeats in one of world rugby’s historically most one-sided fixtures.

On three separate occasions Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors.

“I feel pride for the players, and to see what it means to the supporters,” Tandy said. “We have been wanting some positivity, and I think the players delivered that today.

“We knew it was going to be brutal on both sides of the ball, and I thought the intent from minute one was exceptional.

“You always have belief. They are a special group of people, and there will be lots of bumps along the road, but the boys can be super-proud today.

“The players were phenomenal. New Zealand threw everything at us, and it is just an amazing feeling. We have got to savour moments like this.

“This is a real good statement win for us, and we have got to enjoy it, but we have got to keep going and building performances. We have got a massive game against Australia next week.”

First-half tries from Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake and Archie Griffin – all converted by Sam Costelow – put Wales in charge, although New Zealand clawed it back to 21-21 as Cortez Ratima, Wallace Sititi and Fehi Fineanganofo all touched down, with Richie Mo’unga booting three conversions.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game, and such an approach ultimately backfired, with Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit adding further Wales scores that Costelow converted.

open image in gallery Wales’ Louis Rees-Zammit celebrates with fans (David Davies/PA) ( PA Wire )

New Zealand mustered a fourth touchdown from flanker Peter Lakai, yet try as they might, there was no further way over the Wales line as tackle after tackle kept them out.

Wales captain Dewi Lake added: “To put on the field what we did today, to make history, is tough to put into words, but it is nothing this group doesn’t deserve for the work they have put in.

“Sometimes we sit in front of the media and say we can beat them, and it is probably a passing comment for some people at home, but it’s not for us. You wouldn’t believe the work that goes on for this group to go out and succeed.

“The boys dug in hard, a lot of defensive sets, three or four hold-ups over the line. I think I stopped watching with one minute, 20 seconds left and just waited for the whistle! It is an amazing feeling.”

Three Wales players – Dafydd Jenkins, Jac Morgan and James Botham – each made more than 30 tackles, and New Zealand skipper Beauden Barrett conceded how tough it had been to break Wales down in the second half.

“It is a tough one to take, particularly when we were building a lot of pressure but couldn’t convert into points,” Barrett said.

“It felt like a brick wall at times, so you have to give Wales credit. We were a little bit indecisive, we had three hold-ups over the line, and we have got be better at converting those opportunities.”

open image in gallery New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie was left hugely disappointed (Joe Giddens/PA) ( PA Wire )

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie, meanwhile, said: “We are massively disappointed. We started both halves poorly and conceded 14 points quickly. We had plenty of territory, and we need to be a lot better than that.

“Credit to Wales. They were really clinical when they got their chances, and they defended for massive amounts and were the better side.

“We got a bit one-dimensional, and that’s decision-making under pressure. They ran hard on to the ball, and we struggled to slow it down.”

News.title: Savannah Guthrie, popular and enduring face of morning TV, renews NBC contract after 15 years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News, ensuring she will continue to greet viewers each morning on “Today” after more than 15 years at the network.

The move by one of morning television's most enduring and popular personalities was confirmed to The Associated Press by a person close to the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity because the news has not been made public. It was not clear for how long the contract was extended.

The extension also came during a year of personal pain and turmoil for Guthrie. Her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84, was last seen at her home just outside Tucson on Jan. 31 and was reported missing the following day. Authorities believe she was kidnapped, abducted or otherwise taken against her will. The case remains dogged by questions; no suspects have been arrested.

In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after Guthrie went missing. The first note, sent Feb. 2, said she was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped.

Guthrie and her family have shared their pain and pleaded for information in videos posted to social media. Most recently, Guthrie addressed the tragic situation on Instagram, posting an old drawing from her daughter, Vale, which she said “says so much about how I feel.”

The drawing depicted an umbrella amid falling raindrops, with an accompanying message: "I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”

“The world goes on, things appear 'normal,' ” Guthrie wrote in her post, “as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be.”

“We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” she wrote in the post, to which she also attached a smiling photo of her mother. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”

Guthrie, 54, became a main co-anchor of “Today” in 2012, after joining the show the previous year. She now co-hosts with Craig Melvin. She is also a primary anchor for NBC's election coverage, most recently for last week's midterm elections.

News.title: Trump blames US ground stop outage on ‘old broken stuff’ as Duffy points finger at contractor
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the massive air traffic control outage that grounded flights across the U.S. Friday night was linked to a contractor replacing the antiquated system’s old copper wire.

Duffy gave the update at a Saturday press conference, while President Donald Trump has yet to publicly address the meltdown that left thousands of Americans stranded. Trump said “old broken stuff” was to blame in reported remarks to Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy late Friday.

New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, officials said at the briefing.

Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system's old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload.

He said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause.

open image in gallery Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the massive air traffic control outage that grounded flights across the U.S. Friday night was linked to a contractor replacing the system’s old copper wire ( Reuters )

“Our contractor didn't meet the moment,” Duffy said.

The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, added. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins noted that the president was posting about reviving the entertainment industry on Truth Social as chaos was unfolding in airports across the nation. “Trump posts, not about the ground stop, but about reviving the entertainment industry in bipartisan fashion,” Collins said in a post on X.

Doocy relayed his conversation with the president on Friday’s The Ingraham Angle. “He said instead this seems to be a situation where there’s a bunch of old broken stuff in the infrastructure that the FAA relies on to keep planes in the sky,” Doocy said.

“He said there’s a bunch of – some of this is like 55-year-old equipment that needs to keep working, keep running, and that they have worked on it, they’ve talked to Congress about replacing, it just hasn’t gotten replaced yet. So that is the first information that we have from the president,” he added.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump blamed aging FAA equipment for a nationwide flight outage that grounded planes as Democrats criticized the airport chaos ( Reuters )

Democrats called for a closer examination of the communications failure and the outdated technology underpinning the nation's air traffic control system.

Rep. Ted Lieu, a California Democrat, called the FAA's communications failure completely unacceptable, telling the Los Angeles Times: “I urge the FAA and the Trump administration to make sure this never happens again.”

Lieu also called for congressional hearings to determine what caused the breakdown and what needs to be done to prevent another nationwide disruption.

“What just happened is enormously damaging to trust in our air system, and our air system is a vital component of our national economy,” he said.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Aviation, Space and Innovation Subcommittee, also called for a full investigation into the outage.

open image in gallery Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy attributed the ground stop to aging technology that became overwhelmed with data, disrupting communications between pilots and air traffic controllers ( Getty )

“The safety of our skies is built on redundancies,” she said in a statement. “Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation.”

Pete Buttigieg was in disbelief after watching a joint press conference with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, according to The New York Times.

“You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters,” he told the newspaper. “I have questions.”

The FAA ordered the hours-long nationwide ground stop Friday after a communications failure disrupted 22 regional air traffic control centers. The order temporarily halted departing flights while allowing planes already in the air to land, triggering widespread delays as officials worked to restore normal operations.

With reporting from agencies

News.title: How Sonia Bompastor’s ruthless changes inspired Chelsea’s win over Man City
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

On what ended up being an excellent day for Sonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager first had to accept that it started with a mistake. Kadeisha Buchanan, the centre-back, had been cleared to start by Chelsea’s medical team despite taking a knock to the head in training on Friday. Her assignment was to stop the world’s best striker, Khadija Shaw, who had arrived at Stamford Bridge having scored in nine Women’s Super League games in a row since the start of the season. But the way Chelsea set up in their top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City at first appeared designed to present Shaw with every opportunity to make it 10. For Bompastor, it soon became apparent that something was not right.

Buchanan, visibly struggling, was given a torrid opening 12 minutes, beaten for pace by Shaw twice on the outside and dragged into deeply uncomfortable positions as the striker roamed and bared her teeth. Aoba Fujino should have fired the champions in front after four minutes, but she placed Shaw’s cut-back horribly wide after Buchanan had been easily by-passed. Katie McCabe then had a narrow escape when she sliced Shaw’s cross past the post. Bracing herself on the touchline, Bompastor had to act.

The Chelsea back-line all looked up with the same blank expression as Veerle Buurman stood ready on the sideline; no one appeared to know the change that was coming. Buchanan, perhaps to hide her embarrassment, went straight down the tunnel. “Watching her from the beginning of the game, she was not 100 per cent,” Bompastor explained. “I know my player and she was not in the game. You have to be brave to make that change in the moment.”

open image in gallery Bompastor made three changes before the start of the second half, but they all strengthened Chelsea ( Reuters )

Changing her back-line that early, Bompastor said, was a “risk”, but it was the ruthless change Chelsea needed. Bompastor spent the first half tinkering and tweaking until they could feel as if they could go toe-to-toe with Andree Jeglertz’s side. By the start of the second half, Chelsea had already made three changes. Buchanan’s early withdrawal was followed by Melvine Malard being forced off with a hamstring injury.

Sandy Baltimore’s stunning strike ended up being the winner, a thunderbolt that even she did not seem to expect, judging by the forward’s nonchalant celebration, but it was also her final touch as she was replaced at the break, as Bompastor decided to make a half-time change instead of using up her only available substitute window early in the second half.

That paid off, too. All the changes helped as Bompastor’s side began to compete and match City in all departments. Buurman was outstanding against Shaw and was not daunted to face her one-on-one. Lucy Bronze was immense, too, continuing to impress at centre-back and relishing the bruising battles with Shaw and Lauren Hemp. “They are magic and they can’t stop scoring,” Bronze said before revealing inspiration from McCabe. “We had to be dogs.” Eventually, Chelsea found a balance where they could be ferocious. Ellie Carpenter and Alyssa Thompson pushed high and wide, their midfield clicked together and City’s threat became muted; after such a menacing start, Shaw finished the game without a shot on target. “We restricted her,” Bronze added.

It meant Chelsea could leapfrog City to lead the WSL after 10 games, handing the champions their first defeat of the season while remaining unbeaten themselves. Despite the absence of Lauren James and their struggles to consistently turn chances into goals, they have found a way to win. Emma Hayes, the former Chelsea boss, ended the afternoon punching the air from her seat in the stands next to England manager Sarina Wiegman. This was a throwback to the Chelsea team she left, or the side Bompastor picked up in her first season at Stamford Bridge. “We’re in a better place than we were last year,” said Keira Walsh.

open image in gallery Lucy Bronze relished her battle with Khadija Shaw, who was shut out at Stamford Bridge ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Sandy Baltimore was also replaced in another ruthless change, shortly after scoring the game’s only goal ( Reuters )

Jeglertz responded with his own changes and introducing the fit-again Vivianne Miedema and Laura Blindkilde-Brown almost turned the game in City’s favour. Hemp missed a sitter, inches away from the goal line, when the England winger failed to get a connection on Shaw’s lob. “We had a couple of great opportunities to score,” Jeglertz accepted. “We deserved more.” The second half had become breathless but City’s hopes were as good as over by the 75th minute when goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita was sent off for rushing off her line and clattering into Thompson after the winger had rounded her outside the box.

A City victory would have opened their lead in the title race to five points. For the first 10 minutes, the champions felt as if they would be leaving Stamford Bridge with a statement result. Instead, while London City Lionesses could enter the picture if they defeat Arsenal on Sunday, it is Chelsea who lead the way. Led by Bompastor’s example, their ruthlessness is back and they look up for the fight.

News.title: England v Japan LIVE: Rampant England thrashing hopeless visitors in Nations Championship rout
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

( PA )

A heavily-changed England are wary of the threat posed by a Japan side promising “unorthodox” rugby in their Nations Championship clash.

Steve Borthwick’s side made an excellent start to their November by sweeping aside Australia last weekend, but have since dealt with significant injury disruption. Borthwick uses this as a chance to rotate his team heavily, handing opportunities to a number of fringe figures and World Cup hopefuls looking to force their way more fully into the head coach’s thoughts.

They cannot afford to take their eye off the ball, though, against a Japan team coached by Eddie Jones. The former England boss has returned to Twickenham with the promise of throwing a few curveballs at his old employers, and there is plenty of talent within the Japanese ranks as they seek a first win over their hosts.

Follow all of the latest from the Nations Championship clash with our live blog below:

News.title: Watch: British Airways plane strikes tail on runway
News.content:
A British Airways plane’s tail struck the runway at Heathrow airport during a landing attempt on Thursday (12 November).

Footage captured of the landing by Big Jet TV appears to show flight BA431’s rear bump and scrape the runway after completing a trip from Amsterdam.

The BA airbus aborted the landing after the tail strike before attempting a second successful landing.

A British Airways spokesperson said: “The aircraft landed safely and we're assisting the AAIB with its investigation and are legally unable to comment further at this stage.”

News.title: How brilliant Wales shocked the rugby world with historic All Blacks win
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Wales spectacularly ended 73 years of hurt against New Zealand with a stunning 35-28 victory at the Principality Stadium that shredded world rugby’s form book.

The All Blacks had beaten Wales 34 times in succession since their last defeat in 1953, but Steve Tandy’s team gloriously achieved mission improbable after a Cardiff classic, thanks to a combination of clinical attacking prowess and brave defensive resilience.

Three times Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time in history they scored five tries against New Zealand. Ultimately, though, it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors.

open image in gallery Wales celebrated the unlikeliest of victories in Cardiff ( Reuters )

open image in gallery It was an emotional day for the brave Welsh team ( PA )

During an almost 20-minute spell in their own half, Wales clung to a seven-point lead, holding the All Blacks up over the line on multiple occasions and building a red wall that simply could not be broken down.

A crowd of 55,152 could scarcely believe what had unfolded, and there were incredible scenes of wild celebration with players in tears as Wales began taking in arguably the most famous win of their 145-year Test match history.

It was perhaps also the greatest rugby shock since Japan stunned South Africa at the 2015 World Cup, given the contrasting state of both countries heading into the clash.

open image in gallery The All Blacks were heavy favourites but Wales stunned the world ( Getty )

Wales lay down early marker

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie had made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game, and such an approach ultimately backfired spectacularly.

Wales made a stunning start, going ahead after just 80 seconds following Louis Rees-Zammit’s first touch of the ball. Receiving possession in space, he kicked over the top of New Zealand’s defence and Tomos Williams won the race to touch down before Sam Costelow converted to open up a 7-0 lead.

Four minutes later, Wales moved into dreamland territory, rocking the All Blacks further back on their heels when Dewi Lake crashed over from close range and Costelow’s conversion doubled an against-all-odds early advantage.

open image in gallery Dewi Lake helped Wales to a fast start ( PA )

An All Blacks response was inevitable, though, and it arrived in the 10th minute as Cortez Ratima sprinted over after New Zealand secured quality lineout possession, with Richie Mo’unga booting a conversion and cutting the deficit in half.

Wales continued to have their moments in attack, with Rees-Zammit proving a consistent threat. But it was raw forward power that generated their third try after 24 minutes as Archie Griffin went over following a lineout before Costelow’s conversion restored a 14-point gap.

New Zealand struggled for fluency, yet they kept themselves in touch courtesy of a Wallace Sititi try that Mo’unga converted nine minutes before half-time, giving the visitors momentum.

Wales desperately tried to hold on, but the All Blacks hauled themselves level through Fehi Fineanganofo’s well-worked try, converted by Mo’unga to end a scintillating first period tied at 21-21.

It was the first time since 2016 that Wales had not trailed their illustrious opponents halfway through the game but it seemed inevitable that the visitors would kick on in the second half and pull away from their much-maligned hosts.

open image in gallery The All Blacks were ultimately left bereft ( PA )

Second-half bravery

Instead, the home side went back in front only four minutes after the break, this time through the impressive Eddie James, who barrelled over the line, before his Scarlets colleague Costelow maintained a 100 per cent conversion rate.

Rees-Zammit then crossed unopposed and Wales were 14 points to the good once more when Costelow converted.

New Zealand once again needed a response, and it arrived from a Peter Lakai try and Mo’unga conversion in the 53rd minute, setting up a pulsating finale that the game so richly deserved.

open image in gallery Wales were clinical in attack and resilient in defence ( Getty )

The All Blacks laid siege, but they were held up over the line three times during an absolutely immense Welsh defensive rearguard.

The home side just would not relent, sending a nation into raptures with a result that will shake up the rugby world.

News.title: Wales beat the All Blacks for the first time since 1953 in historic upset
News.content:
The second half of Wales’ Nations Championship started with a hard-fought 28-21 bonus point victory over Japan last Saturday. Steve Tandy’s side sit fifth in the Northern Hemisphere table, but just five points separate them from second-place England, and they still have a tonne of pride to play for as they aim to finish as high as possible in the group.

Speaking ahead of the encounter, Tandy said: “We’re excited for the opportunity we have against New Zealand. It was good to get the win last Saturday, but some elements of our execution weren’t where we wanted.

“We have to go up another level this weekend and be more ruthless. We have one of the best teams in the world coming. We want to be better and put in an 80-minute performance.”

Meanwhile, New Zealand arrive in the Welsh capital in imperious form, having won their opening four Nations Championship matches and boasting a +73 points difference. South Africa’s defeat has opened the door for the resurgent All Blacks to pounce, and they’ll be brimming with confidence following their eye-catching 43-21 triumph against Scotland at Murrayfield a week ago.

As for the team news, Tandy has made four alterations to the starting XV that overcame Japan. Taine Basham is poised for his first international appearance since the 2024 Six Nations, while James Botham, Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Adam Beard also begin the contest. The influential Aaron Wainwright is out with a minor calf problem.

All Blacks Head Coach has ordered 10 changes to the 23-man squad that brushed Scotland aside. Forwards including George Bower, Asafo Aumua, Josh Lord, Anton Segner and backs such as Richie Mo’unga, Anton Lienert-Brown and Fehi Fineanganofo all start for the heavily rotated visitors. Full-back Beauden Barrett will captain New Zealand for the first time, in his 149th Test, while Will Jordan is unavailable because of a hamstring issue.

Kick-off is at 14:10, with team news following now.

News.title: France pull off one of their greatest wins as Erasmus mind games backfire
News.content:
Given Les Bleus’ injuries, only the 1999 World Cup semi-final victory over New Zealand can come close to this win over the back-to-back world champions, South Africa. The Nations Championship, with the Springboks previously unbeaten, has been blown wide open. Crikey, given these two could meet in a World Cup semi-final next year, rugby’s blue-riband event in Australia has been blown wide open.

And how lucky are we. France did not score a point in the second half and South Africa’s comeback befitted a champion side, but these audacious hosts regaled their Parisian audience with a rugby feast. Rassie Erasmus, the Springboks’ head coach, said that he was nervous before the game and so he should have been. Fabien Galthié, his counterpart, had promised some fun and games, but Erasmus could not help himself: not long before kick-off, he pulled the coup de théâtre, switching his starting and replacement front rows. Time will tell whether such a move was legal.

“We didn’t play well,” said Erasmus. “I can’t find a lot of excuses. They were on top of their game and we were a little bit off. It was one point here and there. They took their opportunities and we didn’t. We weren’t just outplayed, we were outsmarted.”

“I think we’ve killed our dreams for the Nations Championship with this result,” he added, suggesting he thinks New Zealand will beat England next week.

Demons were present for both sides, mainly France. South Africa lost Jasper Wiese to a 20-minute red card for a nasty ruck clear-out – just as Lood de Jager had received in the visitors’ win last year – and, at the end, there was a reverse of that utterly compelling World Cup quarter-final on the same turf. This time, it was South Africa desperately searching for victory, having dominated the scrum and scoring all three of their tries from close range or mauls.

News.title: England’s batting capitulates in defeat to lift Australia’s spirits
News.content:
“We weren’t quick enough to adapt to the conditions, we talked extensively leading into the game about the surface here at Optus,” Brendon McCullum, England’s coach, said. “It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline, there are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away.”

McCullum called for his team to scrap a bit more, and at least acknowledged this time that driving on the up was unwise.

“KP has got such a nice manner about him,” he said. “He sees his role to get the talent to perform on the world stage. His message will be measured but firm – adapting to conditions, what could we have done, trying to drive the ball on the up is not wise. Next time we hit a surface like this we have to try and work it better.”

After a quiet start, both openers fell tamely. Ben Duckett prodded Johnson to point, then Banton had a booming drive at Bartlett and was caught behind.

Enter Beardman. When he came on to bowl the 10th over of the innings, there was palpable excitement from his home crowd, who had watched another West Australian, Mike Hussey, present his ODI cap before the toss. Later in the day, Hussey was probably glad he rebuffed England’s recent approach to work with their Test batsmen.

Beardman, who is a mentee of Dennis Lillee and has a gorgeously rhythmical action that helped him touch 90mph, started with a maiden to Root, then found just another movement away from Brook to invite the edge. On the occasion of his 200th ODI, Root had been dropped badly on three off Bartlett, and his only boundary came when Beardman found his an inside edge and the ball flew past his stumps.

The pressure told, and Root edged a big drive behind, where Josh Inglis took the third of his five catches. That sparked a collapse of five for 10, with Jordan Cox edging behind prodding in defence, before Curran was caught on the fence hooking for nought. Beardman’s five-fer was completed when Liam Dawson – selected ahead of Adil Rashid again – skewed a flat-footed drive to backward point. Overton followed in the next over, leaving England 65 for eight, with their lowest ever ODI score, 86, inevitably recorded against Australia in 2001, appearing a distant possibility.

A stand of 37 from Will Jacks and Gus Atkinson averted that particular indignity, and the fear of being bowled out for double figures. But the total was never enough and, despite Atkinson bowling Head first ball, the chase was painfully routine thanks to Marsh’s early barrage.

News.title: Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

News.title: Experts hail a “milestone” as TB deaths fall by more than a third in 10 years
News.content:
The number of people dying from tuberculosis has dropped by more than a third over the last 10 years but progress against the disease is still too slow, according to the World Health Organization.

Figures from WHO’s annual TB report showed that the lung disease took the lives of an estimated 1.13 million people in 2025, down from 1.7m in 2015, a drop of 35 per cent.

While WHO hailed this as a major milestone in achieving global targets - albeit five years too late - it said that progress in wiping out TB was still too slow.

Africa and Europe have made the greatest progress in reducing deaths, with numbers halving on both continents over the 10-year period. India and China - countries that have high burdens of the disease - also cut deaths by 35 per cent.

The report also showed that an estimated 10.6million people contracted the disease in 2025, a reduction of just 75,000 since 2024.

TB - still the world’s leading infectious disease killer - is preventable and curable, and is caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is spread when infected people cough or sneeze.

The disease has been around for centuries, and has been described as the quintessential disease of poverty as it spreads in areas of low quality housing, among people with poor nutrition and immunity. It is a particular risk to people who are HIV positive.

Treatment requires a six-month long regimen of medication, and while treatments have become less toxic in recent years, they still take a heavy toll on patients and have a range of side effects, including at the most extreme deafness. Adherence to medication is also a problem.

News.title: Low-cost parenting app halves rates of sexual violence amongst teenagers in Tanzania
News.content:
A low cost parenting intervention has more than halved rates of sexual violence among teenage girls in Tanzania, a study has shown.

The ParentApp digital parenting programme for families is aimed at reducing rates of violence experienced by teenagers of both sexes.

Researchers found the programme helped bolster family relationships and enabled mothers and fathers to better communicate with their children at what is often a tricky stage of their development.

The programme, led by Oxford University and the University of Cape Town in partnership with the Tanzanian government, the World Health Organization and Unicef, combines in-person and mobile parenting support.

Parents have an introductory session with a facilitator and then undertake 12 weekly sessions online. They also join a WhatsApp group with other parents where they can discuss problems and support one another.

The randomized controlled trial, published in The Lancet, included 2,396 children aged 10–17 and 2,396 parents and carers across 80 urban and rural areas.

Families were randomly assigned to receive either ParentApp or a comparison app focused on safe water and hygiene. Researchers analysing the results did not know which app each family received.

At the 14-month follow-up, girls in families participating in the ParentApp initiative reported a 67% reduction in sexual violence; a 54% reduction in sexual exploitation and an improvement in parent-child relationships. The successes were less marked in boys, however.

Violence against children is widespread globally: Unicef data shows that around one in five girls and women and one in seven boys and men globally have experienced sexual violence as children.

Lucie Cluver, professor of child and family social work at Oxford University and one of the authors of the study, said the intervention was aimed at helping parents and children talk to one another and discuss situations before they arise.

In Tanzania, for example, teenage girls might get a motorbike taxi late at night, potentially putting them in a dangerous situation.

“What you’re doing is making plans and problem solving ahead of these risky situations that teenagers end up in. And you’re building trust and the relationship so you can have these difficult conversations,” said Prof Cluver.

She said she was surprised at how big an impact the intervention had on sexual violence: teenage girls reported that because the app helped improve communication with their parents and carers they did not feel the need to go out as much.

The programme cost around $6 per family but researchers calculated that it goes up to around $10 per family if 20% are given smartphones. A traditional in-person parenting intervention generally costs around $120 per family.

Engagement in the sessions was high - around 70 per cent of participants completed the course - and some parents kept in touch with one another after the programme.

However, the authors of the study stressed that while the app focused on families there remains a need to prevent violence against children in other settings, such as schools and religious institutions. There also needs to be a broader societal push to address the scourge.

“The app isn’t the answer to everything - it’s just one part of the puzzle,” said Prof Cluver.

Prof Cluver said she hoped future versions of the programme would include greater focus on digital harms and test whether parents could take the lead themselves.

The programme is being rolled out in other countries, including Mexico, Panama and South Africa, and is easily adaptable for different contexts.

“Tanzania only has 20% smartphone use and we thought if it works in one of the hardest places to do a digital intervention it could work anywhere,” she said.

She said the study showed how parenting was a universal experience, with the majority focused on what is best for their children.

“Parents feel powerless. We live in a world where our kids are facing risks and parents just want to help,” added Prof Cluver.
