Last Saturday, Tenerife fans and players gathered at the club’s stadium for a memorial and farewell to De Miguel. His funeral took place last Thursday and around 400 mourners attended, including the Spain head coach, Luis de la Fuente, and the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez.

Sports.title: Carlo Ancelotti and Raphinha see red: Security separate furious Brazil stars from officials after shock 3-2 defeat by Japan - with manager and captain sent off in bad-tempered friendly
Sports.content:
Carlo Ancelotti and Raphinha see red: Security separate furious Brazil stars from officials after shock 3-2 defeat by Japan - with manager and captain sent off in bad-tempered friendly

Carlo Ancelotti hit out at an 'inexperienced' referee after the Brazil boss and captain Raphinha were sent off in the closing stages of their shock 3-2 defeat by Japan.

Security staff were required to enter the pitch at full time to separate players from the officials, with Brazil having been left furious over the nature of Japan's stoppage time winner.

Ancelotti and Raphinha, who had been substituted, were among those to furiously protest following Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's late strike.

Singaporean referee Jansen Foo Chuan Hui had allowed play to continue after Takumi Minamino had made multiple challenges on Brazil midfielder Joao Gomes, before eventually coming away with the ball.

Amid Brazilian appeals for a foul, Japan launched a late attack with Sakamoto ultimately lifting the ball over goalkeeper Pedro Morisco.

Brazilian protests continued despite Japan's winner being confirmed by VAR, with Ancelotti and Raphinha being shown red cards by the referee for their reactions.

Security staff intervened after Brazil stars confronted the referee after their 3-2 defeat by Japan

Carlo Ancelotti was sent off as Brazil were beaten in stoppage time in their friendly in Singapore

Ancelotti criticised the 'inexperienced' referee following the match and revealed he had been told he had been sent off for failing to control his bench

🚨🚨| Raphinha and Carlo Ancelotti have been SENT OFF for Protesting. 🟥😳 pic.twitter.com/YoXrZW9N0U — Kalshi FC (@KalshiFC) November 14, 2026

'He gave me the red card because he said I was not able to control the bench, and that all the players were on the field, that is the reason,' Ancelotti said.

Ancelotti added: 'A pity the result, because we don't like to lose the game, but we have to look at what we did well. There are many things. Some players who played for the first time, who showed good quality. For 70 minutes, the team was good.

'The result, obviously, is conditioned by the attitude of the referee, who did not blow the whistle.

'But it's not his fault; it was a high-level match, and I think he didn't have the experience to manage this type of match.'

Barcelona star Raphinha claimed post-match that Brazil had also been angered over a potential handball in the build-up to Japan's opening goal, as well as seeing a penalty appeal waved away.

'First of all, I'd like to take this opportunity to apologise for my behaviour and for being sent off,' Raphinha told Globo.

'Sometimes it's hard to keep calm, especially after what I felt were so many refereeing errors during the match. I tried to speak to him several times, and not once did I feel he was open to discussion. I believe that he made many errors throughout the game, and that is unacceptable.

'In my view, their first goal involved a foul where the opponent took the ball off me with his hand. I think it's a foul, but I can understand why it wasn't given based on the current law.

Brazil captain Raphinha was also dismissed amid their protests over Japan's winning goal

Brazil had been convinced there had been a foul in the build-up to Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's winner

'Then there was the penalty in the first half, in my opinion it was a penalty, but he said no. Then, for their third goal, there was a clear foul on Joao Gomes. With the help of VAR, he eventually allowed the goal. It's very difficult not to talk about the refereeing.'

Brazil had fallen 2-0 down in the friendly with Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura scoring in the opening 20 minutes at Singapore's National Stadium.

Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr scored twice to level the match before Sakamoto's controversial late winner.

It is the second time Japan have beaten Brazil 3-2 in the past 18 months, but the five-time world champions did win 2-1 in their last-32 meeting at this summer's World Cup.

Sports.title: Sonia Bompastor's side show their teeth as Chelsea sink the reigning champions to reclaim top spot in WSL title race: Chelsea 1-0 Man City
Sports.content:
Chelsea secured a deserved 1-0 victory over Manchester City at Stamford Bridge to leapfrog their rivals and reclaim top spot in the WSL table.

Sandy Baltimore's first-half goal was enough to ensure Chelsea inflicted City's first defeat of the season and blow the title race wide open.

After keeping the reigning WSL champions at bay following an early barrage, Chelsea grew in confidence but still lacked the cutting edge that had seen them held to back-to-back draws in recent weeks.

A moment of magic from Baltimore in the fourth minute of stoppage time ensured history would not repeat itself.

City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita was sent off in the 75th minute for a rash challenge on Alyssa Thompson, a move which appeared to invigorate the visitors, but Chelsea held firm to see out all three points.

Daily Mail Sport's Tara Anson-Walsh and Samara Watts were at Stamford Bridge to bring you the things we learned...

Chelsea inflicted City's first defeat of the season and blew the title race wide open

City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita was sent off in the 75th minute for a rash challenge on Alyssa Thompson

Buchanan’s feeling the blues

Devastation for Kadeisha Buchanan, who was hooked after 11 minutes by Bompastor. The centre back has been one of Chelsea’s standout performers this season but had an unusually shaky start to this match as she looked out of her depth against Bunny Shaw, ever a precarious place to be against the league’s top striker.

Buchanan gave an early ball away to allow Shaw to race through towards the Chelsea goal, and a few minutes later was again outmuscled and outpaced by the Jamaican striker, although City failed to capitalise on both occasions.

The 31-year-old Canada international looked devastated when her number flashed up on the board after just 12 minutes and reluctantly welcomed a hug from her manager as she headed straight for the tunnel.

Her replacement, the 20-year-old Veerle Buurman, who was outstanding against Shaw in the two sides’ last meeting in the FA Cup, changed the game, giving Chelsea a more solid platform to build upon as they grew in confidence.

Confident to step out from the back line and build forward, Bompastor hinted at half-time that the move had, indeed, been tactical.

If so, it showed the lengths Bompastor is willing to go to reclaim this title. Whether it will serve her in the long term, though, remains to be seen, with one of her best players’ confidence now undoubtedly knocked.

The centre back has been one of Chelsea’s standout performers this season but had an unusually shaky start to this match and was hooked after just 11 minutes

Royalty in the building

Women’s football royalty Sarina Wiegman, Emma Hayes and Ian Wright braved the chilly climes of Stamford Bridge to witness the showdown between the WSL heavyweights on Saturday afternoon.

The freshly anointed honorary Dame Wiegman sat next to Hayes and the pair chatted warmly. This is a relationship that will no doubt drop in cordiality as the sand in the hourglass ahead of next summer’s World Cup continues to run down.

Wiegman had several England players on her watching brief, not least young Lexi Potter, whose stock has risen dramatically this season. The 20-year-old put in another assured performance against the reigning champions, continuing to demonstrate her maturity in the highest stakes, which will no doubt put her in a good position ahead of Tuesday’s squad announcement.

The Dutch coach will have been alarmed by the number of crunching tackles put in against her right back, Lucy Bronze, in this match. If there is one player that she will want to wrap up in cotton wool ahead of Brazil, it is the recently turned 35-year-old Bronze for her steadfast leadership and relentless athleticism.

Another player looking to make an impact ahead of Tuesday’s squad announcement was Aggie Beever-Jones, who has struggled this season and was left out of Sonia Bompastor’s starting line-up. An injury to Melvine Malard saw her gain more minutes than she would have expected, but she will have been disappointed not to have converted after once again finding herself in good positions.

Another player who finds herself in a race against time is Manchester United’s Ella Toone. Toone was left out of yet another of Eva Olid’s starting line-ups as Manchester United stormed to a 2-0 win over Crystal Palace, and the two-time Euros winner will be growing increasingly concerned with her situation as Brazil edges nearer.

The freshly anointed honorary dame Wiegman sat next to Hayes at the WSL showpiece at Stamford Bridge and the pair chatted warmly

Chelsea's Malard blow

Melvine Malard’s absence raises questions about who Chelsea’s main goalscorer will be this season. The squad has lacked a clinical edge without England striker Lauren James, who is out with a hamstring injury until the international break.

The French forward went off injured after 35 minutes with a suspected hamstring injury. Although she missed Chelsea’s opening games after picking up a knock in pre-season, she has been the Blues’ top scorer in the absence of Lauren James with six league goals so far.

Chelsea are averaging 24 shots per game, an unprecedented rate across a WSL campaign, but have recently struggled to convert their chances. They were held to a 0-0 draw against BK Hacken midweek in the UWCL and a 1-1 draw against Everton last weekend.

Malard leaving the pitch meant Chelsea struggled to find a creative spark up front. Her replacement Aggie Beever-Jones has been dealing with an ankle injury, and is still trying to find her feet with only one goal in the WSL.

Head coach Sonia Bompastor said: ‘The frustration sometimes comes from us not being ruthless and clinical.’

A moment of magic from Malard’s French International teammate Sandy Baltimore was enough to make it 1-0 just before half time with the team’s first shot on target. However, Baltimore was substituted at half time to manage her minutes, and Chelsea were unable to capitalize on any of their chances in the second half.

Bompastor said: ‘From the outside it seems like we have had a lot of injuries, but we have been playing every three days.’

‘I knew coming into the game we were not as fresh as we would like to be, but that’s our environment.

‘We want to play in every competition but the players are not robots,’

Melvine Malard’s injury could cause more problems for the Blues’ attack, as they registered just two shots on target today and scraped the three points.

Malard limped off in the first half and meant Chelsea struggled for a creative spark up front

Yamashita’s moment of madness

Stamford Bridge was in uproar as City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita rushed out of her box and took down Alyssa Thompson, who had a clear chance on goal in the 75th minute.

The Blues were mounting a rapid attack down the left hand side, with Thompson just outside the box when Yamashita missed the ball and brought her to the ground.

The Japanese goalkeeper was shown a straight red card and was sent off the pitch. This was City’s first red card in the WSL since November 2023, and a rare moment of madness from the usually-composed 31-year-old.

The referee allowed City three minutes to replace the Japanese goalkeeper, with Scotland’s number one Eartha Cumings coming on to replace forward Aoba Fujino.

Her first test arrived only a minute later, as Aggie Beever-Jones' right-footed shot from the resulting indirect free kick dropped dangerously, but she was saved by the crossbar.

The bigger question now is whether Yamashita's absence - which could amass to three games - will have a lasting impact on their title race.

In the short-term against Chelsea, City reacted well. Andree Jeglertz said at full time: ‘The players dealt with it in a good way, so even though we were one player down we had a couple of great opportunities to score a goal. Of course it affected the game but that is not why we lost.’

Stamford Bridge was in uproar as Manchester City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita rushed out of her box to take down Alyssa Thompson, who had a clear chance on goal

It's all up for grabs

Chelsea’s win at the Bridge blows the title race wide open, as they are now just one point ahead of City at the top of the WSL table.

Sonia Bompastor’s side ended City’s unbeaten streak, and they now have 24 league goals compared to City’s 16 after 10 games.

However, with seven shots and just one on target this game, Chelsea will need to look at their attacking options as they take on Liverpool and London City Lionesses before the international break.

Sonia Bompastor said: ‘It’s a nice feeling to be top of the table right now and to win against these top sides, but I know we still have a lot of work to be done and it’s early on in the season so many things can happen.’

City were unable to create opportunities in front of goal, with the WSL’s all-time leading goalscorer Vivianne Miedema’s return overshadowed by Ayaka Yamashita’s nightmare in goal.

City head coach Andree Jeglertz said: ‘They managed to score on their big chance and (it was a) great finish.

'We also had some great opportunities where we didn’t manage to score, but I think we deserve more than going away from here with no points.’

London City Lionesses face Arsenal tomorrow at the Emirates, and a win in north London could bring them four points behind the new WSL leaders, and really start to make things interesting.

Sports.title: From shambles to history-makers: Wales break 73-year hoodoo in astonishing 35-28 upset of New Zealand. Fans expected a massacre but witnessed a miracle, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI
Sports.content:
From shambles to history-makers: Wales break 73-year hoodoo in astonishing 35-28 upset of New Zealand. Fans expected a massacre but witnessed a miracle, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

It’s worth knowing there were almost 20,000 empty seats on the occasion of New Zealand’s latest visit to Wales. For those who decided to stay away, one can only hope it was for the sake of a wedding or a funeral, because they missed one of the most remarkable sporting upsets of recent times.

How to summarise the scale of this Welsh win? How to catalogue the sequence of unlikely events that made it possible? How to contextualise the sheer madness?

We should start with a statistic – this was the first time Wales have beaten the All Blacks since 1953. And then we must expand upon it, because there have been 34 matches and 34 New Zealand wins in those 73 years.

But let’s divert quickly to a wonderful, historic a quote from the world of tennis. When Vitas Gerulaitis finally got one over Jimmy Connors in 1980, he said: ‘Nobody beats Vitas Gerulaitis 17 times in a row!’

This was a bit of that and twice as large. It was extraordinary. New Zealand were No 1 in the world. Steve Tandy’s Wales? Since 2023, they have beaten Italy, Fiji and laboured their way past Japan last week.

Their fans, a patient bunch, had succumbed to apathy. Their governing union is a shambles, their regions are being cut, their identity a fading cloud in the modern landscape. And then this happened, supplying rugby’s most improbable result since Japan beat the Springboks at the World Cup 11 years ago.

Wales delivered an astonishing win over New Zealand to beat them for the first time since 1953

The All Blacks were stunned 35-28 in one of the biggest rugby shocks in recent memory

Adam Beard was a colossus at six. Louis Rees-Zammit a marauding force on the wing. Dewi Lake was immense. Jac Morgan, a wrecking ball. And James Botham, due to become a father next week, stopped a try during the course of a final 20 minutes that will be burned into permanent memory.

About those final stages. They were huge, of course. And nervy. For the first half, it was all about the Welsh quality with ball in hand – they were 14-0 up after seven minutes. But the second was about backs against the wall.

And my word, they were strong backs. This set of Welsh players were no one’s idea of history makers, but the team photo they posed for at the whistle will be reprinted for decades.

If the roof of the Principality Stadium wasn’t so well attached, those 55,152 souls who showed up might have blown it off. But it was like that from the off, even if the initial assumption was that many had come to see a haka and a massacre.

Let’s go straight to the second minute for the start of the correction. Rees-Zammit supplied the velvet by caressing a chip over the top and Tomos Williams was the iron fist that thumped down onto the bouncing ball. Only 88 seconds had been played and Wales were ahead.

A little false hope can be forgiven in these parts, but after Sam Costelow kicked the extras, the scenario quickly became daft. With six on the clock, Wales had a lineout, and the point to make here is that the set-piece has been one of the few areas of pride for Tandy. They do it well.

But not against Japan. Last week, it was a mess that shaped into a liability. Against the All Blacks in those initial stages of the dance? Well, that was different. Dafydd Jenkins plucked the ball from up high, Gabriel Hamer-Web and Jac Morgan carried hard and then up popped Dewi Lake to thunder through the wall, bouncing Wallace Sititi onto his backside. When Costelow converted, the lead was up to 14-0.

The All Blacks, in pole position for this championship after what happened to the Springboks in France, were in pieces. Handling errors, penalties, second in the collisions, turned over.

Eddie James is pictured scoring his side's fourth try as the Principality Stadium erupts with joy

They stirred when Wales made it easy at the lineout, opening a channel for Cortez Ratima to burst through, but that wasn’t the portent of doom it might have been. It wasn’t the trickle that became a flood. And that’s because it didn’t factor for Archie Griffin, the Bath tighthead, muscling his way to a second try in two games. With ball in hand, Wales were superb, but even then the All Blacks were odds-on to find a means to correct it.

Naturally, the dominant thought was that gravity would begin to pull. And it did. At 21-7, the Welsh looked tired. On the chase, at the breakdowns, the gaps they left were growing. More pertinently, the All Blacks cut out the errors. Elite teams do that.

First, Sititi took a bite out of that lead and then a sequence of offloads culminated in Fehi Fineanganofo going over, two minutes into /the red. Richie Mo’unga kicked for 21-21.

That was sickening for Tandy for two reasons – one being the gut punch of conceding with the last action of the half. The other being the play that shortly preceded the try, when Wales kicked for position when three points would have added some comfort. Ifs, buts and maybes, but you couldn’t fault the ambition.

At the break, it was easy to consider that these sides were close on the scores last year before New Zealand stormed clear. Some statistical boffin rated the chance of a New Zealand win at 96 per cent. Their calculator ought to be smashed.

That much became clear 43 minutes in, when it the 16th phases of a Welsh attack that went left and then right and then left again, Eddie James was presented with the tiniest pocket of space on the corner. He crossed.

Louis Rees-Zammit was immense and Wales were in desperate need of this lift

It was a day that will be remembered for a long time, the predicted massacre became a miracle

With the bonus point secured, a small item of history followed – the Welsh maul was too much for New Zealand and Rees-Zammit went over. It was the first time Wales have put five tries on the Kiwis; not for the first time, you had to wonder where this was all coming from.

But the All Blacks pushed again. Flanker Peter Lakai, so brilliant lately in the considerable task of filling the void caused by Ardie Savea’s absence, found a gap to get the score to 35-26.

After Mo'unga converted, the heat was on, but the Welsh were fighting for their lives. Taine Plumtree landed a huge turnover, for one. For another, see Gareth Thomas. Or Louie Hennessey. And then, top of the lot, Botham got his hand under the ball when the Kiwi thought they had grounded. The defence was sublime.

And it needed to be. For all the waves that followed, nothing got through, before finally the whistle blew on a magnificent piece of sporting theatre.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino's Man United SQUAD AUDIT: Axe EIGHT stars, new role for the attacker he's 'always liked' and who could be his new Dele Alli... now give YOUR player-by-player verdict
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino's Man United SQUAD AUDIT: Axe EIGHT stars, new role for the attacker he's 'always liked' and who could be his new Dele Alli... now give YOUR player-by-player verdict

Walking into a club in turmoil is nothing new for Mauricio Pochettino.

He arrived at Southampton with the Saints three points clear of the relegation zone. Tottenham Hotspur were crying out for some leadership after Andre Villas-Boas and Tim Sherwood's spells, while Chelsea picked up Pochettino in 2023 on the back of their lowest league finish for more than 25 years.

Now it's Manchester United that require what Victor Wanyama once described as Pochettino's 'magic touch' – and they need it quick as they sit in the relegation zone with ten games played. Pochettino remains weeks removed from the January transfer window and has a number of first-team regulars out with long-term injuries, so his reputation of improving the players at his disposal will be put to the test.

He has developed a reputation for placing faith in youth – while at Tottenham, Pochettino handed 12 debuts to players aged 21 or under, more than any other manager.

Money will be tight and United look almost certain to miss out on next season's Champions League, which will make squad development significantly harder, so Pochettino will have to make do and mend with a lot of the current underperforming crop of players.

With all that in mind, Daily Mail Sport runs the rule over the 36 players Pochettino will be inheriting when he walks through the door at Carrington next week.

And you can scroll to the end of the article to have your say on who should stay, and who should go...

Mauricio Pochettino will rapidly have to assess which Man United players to discard

GOALKEEPERS

Senne Lammens (Goalkeeper, 24)

Lammens won't be going anywhere. He is United's No 1 and despite a downturn in form this season, he's not become a bad goalkeeper overnight. Pochettino's trusted goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez will almost certainly replace Craig Mawson to bring some fresh ideas.

Jimenez focuses a lot on developing goalkeepers to be comfortable as sweepers and playing higher up. That is a sore spot in Lammens' game – recently exposed by Bournemouth striker Evanilson – but proper coaching should help develop Lammens, just like Jimenez developed Hugo Lloris.

VERDICT: Keep

Karl Darlow (Goalkeeper, 36)

A summer arrival from Leeds United as a back-up goalkeeper. Pochettino has more important issues than messing around with his No2.

VERDICT: Keep

Tom Heaton (Goalkeeper, 40)

Heaton is hugely popular at the club and while he doesn't play, he is viewed as a vital cog in the dressing room given his wealth of experience. He turns 41 later this season and has been busy preparing for life away from the pitch.

Heaton has completed courses on becoming a sporting director, as well as an executive leadership short course from Oxford University.

He also holds his goalkeeper coach B-Licence, A-Licence outfield, and a certificate of football management from UEFA.

Pochettino would be wise to keep Heaton in-house, even if not as a player. He is a respected figure who knows United inside out and that shouldn't be overlooked as Pochettino tries to build out a culture.

VERDICT: Find off-pitch role

Senne Lammens (right) has made a shaky start to the season but will be going nowhere

DEFENDERS

Diogo Dalot (Full back, 27)

Dalot is highly respected by every manager that works with him for the effort he puts in, something that can't always be said of some of his team-mates.

But he is woefully short of the required quality to take United forward and he is not a comfortable fit for Pochettino's ideals, either.

Pochettino gets width in his sides via the full backs and that requires a relentless runner – which Dalot is – having quality both defensively and in attack, which Dalot does not.

Malo Gusto, who is keen to leave Chelsea and could become a key target for United, spoke of how Pochettino developed his game in 2024 when he said: 'He helps us a lot. He has tried to show us the desire to win, to keep fighting against every team.

'He talks to us a lot about tactics, technique and everything. He is a good person as well. He tries to help us a lot on the pitch and off it. He is a good coach for this young team.

'He is here for this. He knows he has to wake up our mentality, to wake up our desire to win everything.'

United have neglected their back-line for years and it's time for a dramatic refresh, starting with shifting Dalot, who is under contract until 2028.

VERDICT: Replace

It is time for Man United to move on from Diogo Dalot - he is short of the quality required

Noussair Mazraoui (Full back, 28)

Another that should go.

Dalot has at least shown he has the engine to get up and down, which could offer a lifeline under Pochettino, but Mazraoui hasn't.

Full backs are essential to Pochettino's high-intensity, high press 4-2-3-1, and that's not a formula that suits Mazraoui's abilities.

Privately, sources close to the dressing room have suggested in recent weeks that Mazraoui, another under contract until 2028, is keen for a new challenge.

VERDICT: Replace

Matthijs de Ligt (centre back, 27)

Overhauling the defence is one of the main topics of conversation among agents and players right now but De Ligt's future is secure at Old Trafford.

He is under contract until 2029, with the option of a further year, and many figures behind the scenes believe he can bounce back from such a long period out with injury to be a success.

De Ligt's injury record, as well as the fact he isn't a natural fit for Pochettino's idea of the perfect, mobile centre back, makes him an intriguing prospect.

Strong in physical duels, he could become a key squad player.

VERDICT: Keep

Harry Maguire (centre back, 33)

Maguire has taken more criticism than most during his time at United and deserves credit for how he has overcome it.

His contract expires in the summer, with the option of a further year, and Maguire has described playing for United as the 'ultimate honour' so is unlikely to agitate to leave.

That being said, Pochettino puts a lot of emphasis on recovery pace given the high line he has favoured in the past and the Argentine's tactics have routinely exposed centre backs in transition, with speed essential to masking shortcomings.

Maguire would undoubtedly struggle in that department and while his physical profile would appeal, he said earlier this year that he does not want to be kept around for 'sentimental value'.

'I love this club. But it's got to be right for myself, it's got to be right for the club as well,' Maguire said in March before a one-year extension was triggered.

'I don't want to be staying on sentimental value. I want to be staying because I want to be there and the club want me to drive the club forward still, and they feel like I've got a big part to play in it.'

The prospect of a diminishing role, with United planning multiple defensive reinforcements, may see both sides agree it's time for a change.

VERDICT: Replace

After seven years it may be time for Harry Maguire to move on, with his contract expiring

Lisandro Martinez (centre back, 28)

A player that looks to have one foot out the door after calling out director of football Jason Wilcox following the defeat by Atletico Madrid.

It's funny, almost, given Pochettino's arrival should suit Martinez down to the ground. In theory, he is the exact type of player his compatriot would implore his bosses to recruit.

Pochettino puts huge emphasis on passing out from the back and Martinez is the best in that category among United's centre backs.

Pochettino is also incredibly intense, something Martinez has been for some time at United, sometimes to the group's benefit and sometimes to its detriment.

The Argentine's contract expires in the summer and while there is an option to trigger a further year to avoid a World Cup winner walking away for nothing, the expectation is that he won't agree to a new one and his time at United is more likely than not drawing to a close.

He holds a desire to play in Spain and that may not vanish overnight. But if anyone can connect with Martinez about a longer-term role, it's a fellow Argentine.

VERDICT: Keep (but expect to go!)

Patrick Dorgu (Full back/winger, 22)

Has the potential to be the biggest winner of the Pochettino appointment.

Pochettino's full-back-turned-winger style totally plays into Dorgu's hands given both his engine and his comfort playing higher up the pitch. Look at the development of Danny Rose – who played more games for Pochettino than any other player – and Kyle Walker, as well as Sergino Dest with the USA.

Dorgu has a lot of the attributes Pochettino craves while he also remains raw enough that intense, but targeted, coaching could improve him.

He should immediately become one of Pochettino's go-to men.

VERDICT: Keep

Leny Yoro (centre back, 21)

Where there are concerns around Maguire's ability to play in a system which squeezes everyone that bit higher up the pitch, Yoro should thrive.

He showed against Villa, with a chase down to deny Nicolas Jackson a run on goal, that he possesses the necessary recovery pace.

Pochettino's centre backs need to be strong passers and Yoro can improve in this area, although he has shown a willingness to dictate with long diagonals, as well as burst through lines as a ball-carrier.

United need five reliable centre backs in the squad moving forward and Yoro can establish himself as the No1.

Given Pochettino's track record with young players, he should be really excited at becoming a key piece of the puzzle under him.

VERDICT: Keep

Luke Shaw (Full back, 31)

A reunion… but one that may not last very long.

In a 2017 book about Pochettino, Shaw revealed his desire to work under him again and that wish has now come true.

'With Southampton he achieved the impossible,' said Shaw. 'We were one of the best footballing teams in the league... I do hope that I can play for him again one day. And I think he really wants me to play under him again.'

Pochettino used to call Shaw his 'son' and their relationship has stayed strong over the years.

But Pochettino is also a winner and will be acutely aware that Shaw cannot maintain the levels that Pochettino will require from his full backs after years of injury problems.

Sources close to the player have suggested the potential for a one-year extension given the relationship with Pochettino, even if those same sources believe the time is right for a fresh start.

A long servant but not one that can take United forward from this lowest of ebbs.

VERDICT: Replace

Luke Shaw and Pochettino enjoyed success together at Southampton but the reunion won't last long

Ayden Heaven (centre back, 20)

Arriving as an Ineos project, United aren't going to cut their losses on Heaven just yet.

His strong passing ability will appeal to Pochettino and his coaches and he's worth a season of proper coaching to see how high or low his ceiling is.

Heaven can be reckless, particularly in his approach to tackling, but he's got a good physical profile and those who have worked with him have praised his approach to training and willingness to listen to coaches.

United are likely to go out and sign two new centre backs in the summer – at least they hope to – but Heaven should get a shot at development as a bit-part player.

VERDICT: Keep

Harry Amass (Full back, 19)

Wholly ignored despite a left back crisis this season, Amass is widely expected to be out the door in January.

It is hard to blame him, either, given United's decision to keep him around has stunted his development.

Amass is a strong crosser of the ball and, in time, could develop into a full back in Pochettino's vision.

But neither Amass nor Pochettino will have time to wait and see. With a left back high on the shopping list, to go with Dorgu's expected ascension, this relationship shouldn't last too long.

VERDICT: Replace

Jaydan Kamason (Full back, 19)

An academy player to keep an eye on.

Kamason has played both at right back and right wing for United's Under 21s and that plays massively into his hands in a bid to try and catch the eye of his new manager.

The United youngster is a well-rounded full back that constantly looks to get forward, all while not neglecting his defensive responsibilities.

Kamason has trained regularly with the first team in recent months and that could be a sign of things to come under Pochettino, too.

VERDICT: Keep

Diego Leon (Full back, 19)

United rolled the dice on Leon a year ago in a deal worth an initial £3.3million – but the move has not worked out at all.

The 19-year-old hasn't come close to making a first-team appearance and his agent has even suggested they are getting itchy feet despite sub-par performances for United's Under 21s.

'If there isn't a plan to break into the first team between December and January, we'll look for a way out for him,' Leon's representative Renato Bittar admitted. 'A loan somewhere where he can compete, get playing time, and return to Manchester.'

Having observed the academy teams closer than most in recent seasons, Leon hasn't shown anywhere near enough to merit becoming a project player for Pochettino.

VERDICT: Send out on loan

MIDFIELDERS

Mason Mount (Midfielder, 27)

Mount left for United in the same summer Pochettino was hired by Chelsea, so their crossover was minimal.

How much say Pochettino had in that decision remains unclear, perhaps it was insignificant, but now they will finally work together.

Mount feels disposable, not least because he hasn't registered a single assist in the Premier League for United since joining in 2023 for £60million.

With so many options ahead of him in those inverted winger roles, and with Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans preferred as No 10s, Mount needs shifting.

VERDICT: Replace

Bruno Fernandes (Midfielder, 32)

Contract talks have stalled in recent weeks and months but an ambitious new manager could swing momentum back towards reigning Player of the Year Fernandes staying at Old Trafford.

The way Pochettino platformed Christian Eriksen and Dele Alli at Tottenham, as well as Cole Palmer at Chelsea, suggests Fernandes will get the role he needs to be at his very best.

Fernandes' mobility, and ability to run beyond his centre forward, is a strength, as is his vision to supply team-mates in open play and at set-pieces. If Fernandes plays well, so do United, generally. Pochettino favours inverted attackers, so Fernandes could even start off the left if his manager wanted to position Matheus Cunha or Tielemans more centrally.

'He's given me the freedom to play my stuff and I like it when he frees you because I feel I can express my stuff more,' Palmer said of Pochettino's coaching back in 2024.

'I'm loving it. Every day he's talking to you about different things, not just football things but life things as well. He's good at making you feel good and trying to get the best out of you.'

That's music to the ears of Fernandes.

VERDICT: Keep

Pochettino's free-flowing approach could be exactly what is needed to keep Bruno Fernandes

Andrey Santos (Midfielder, 22)

Pochettino knows all about Santos having worked with him at Chelsea when he was a teenager still finding his way.

The reports at that time, during a pre-season tour in North Carolina and Philadelphia, were that Santos' profile appealed to Pochettino, only for the club to go ahead and sanction loan moves to Nottingham Forest and then Strasbourg.

Santos is a summer arrival for £50m and will get more time to find his role in this United side.

He has enough talent to become a reliable deputy to Baleba as the deep-lying midfielder when everyone is fully fit.

VERDICT: Keep

Youri Tielemans (Midfielder, 29)

Tielemans is a high-IQ player that signed a five-year contract in the summer so, truthfully, won't be going anywhere.

That being said, Tielemans' running power isn't there and the demands of a Pochettino system, if he is still the same coach that bowed out at Chelsea, may make that secondary midfield role difficult.

It feels like Tielemans could be a specialist player that Pochettino uses in games where his side expect to dominate possession.

Tielemans' composure on the ball is superior to that of many of his team-mates and that's not a trait Pochettino will overlook quickly, even if he reportedly had reservations on a younger Tielemans when he was managing at Tottenham.

VERDICT: Keep

Carlos Baleba (Midfielder, 22)

A big winner. The £70m summer signing needs to be used in the correct way to realise his potential and Pochettino's track record should be music to Baleba's ears.

Pochettino has typically liked one of his central midfielders to drop deep in possession to create a back three – see Eric Dier at Tottenham – and Baleba should be comfortable fulfilling that role.

Moises Caicedo and Wanyama are two other success stories in the deeper No6 role that Baleba should now thrive in under Pochettino's watch, with his combativeness and tackling making him a natural fit.

'Tactically, he has taught me a lot,' Wanyama previously said of Pochettino.

'Before, I was just thinking, "I'll just sit here and defend". But if you're playing for him, it's not only defending. You have to attack also. You have to know the right time. I have learned so much from him.'

Now it's time for Baleba to study up and take his game to the next level.

VERDICT: Keep

Carlos Baleba has a had a slow start to life at United but a managerial change could unlock his potential

Manuel Ugarte (Midfielder, 25)

It transpired that Pochettino wanted to make Ugarte his first signing at Chelsea, only for United to get in ahead of them for the Uruguayan.

Ugarte was all set to leave United in the summer were it not for a serious injury at the World Cup that left him sidelined for months.

Pochettino liked the profile of player he saw when Ugarte was scouted at Sporting Lisbon but he looks a different, far less effective, player in England.

Minds appear to be made up upstairs when it comes to moving on from Ugarte.

VERDICT: Replace

Kobbie Mainoo (Midfielder, 21)

Where Baleba will need to drop deep, the other midfielder in Pochettino's system is the one who is expected to drive and bypass midfield blocks.

Pochettino will be acutely aware that Mainoo is extremely popular among United fans and while athleticism is often levelled against him as a weak point in his game, Pochettino will need to find a way of improving that while also nurturing his many talents.

Tottenham's Mousa Dembele was moulded by Pochettino from an attacking midfielder into a deep-lying controller, urged to dribble to break lines and open up the game.

Mainoo has many similar traits to others Pochettino has worked with, such as Weston McKennie with the US national team.

'They will get pushed in training more than the games they will be playing. It is all a mental thing,' former Southampton striker Rickie Lambert once said.

If Mainoo can come through the initial boot camp, he can flourish.

VERDICT: Keep

Kobbie Mainoo is one of United's top talents and will stay but has to improve his physicality

Jack Fletcher (Midfielder, 19)

A better player than people give him credit for but one that really needs to put a full season together at first-team level to see where he is at.

That won't be under Pochettino at United but United, if they really believe he can be part of their future, need to find Fletcher a loan move where he can feature in 35-40 games.

Clubs in League One would be all over him.

VERDICT: Send out on loan

Tyler Fletcher (Midfielder, 19)

The deep-lying midfielder that can drop in to form a back three is fundamental to how Pochettino wants to play and that's a style that would suit Tyler Fletcher, rather than the more attacking Jack.

Again, figures at United and up in Scotland, just want to see Fletcher get a run of games under his belt.

Kilmarnock wanted him in the summer, but United wanted to keep Fletcher in house.

If Pochettino and United really care about his career, he should be one of the first out the door on loan in January.

VERDICT: Send out on loan

Jim Thwaites (Midfielder, 19)

Senior academy figures are the most excited about Thwaites' potential, even if it would be unfair to expect him to make a big impact on the first team in the near future.

Technically his level is particularly high, a European pass-first, press-resistant game that will appeal to Pochettino and his coaches.

But physically there is a way to go, which should mean Thwaites is kept around as a project player.

VERDICT: Keep

Sekou Kone (Midfielder, 20)

Brought in as an Ineos project piece, after two mediocre loan spells in Switzerland with Lausanne, it's time to have Kone come back into the building and put him to work with a relentless coach like Pochettino.

Kone's twitchy game-style and desire to break through lines makes him something of a hybrid of players Pochettino has coached in the past.

Having watched him up close in the academy set-up before he went out on loan, and spoken to those who coached Kone then, it would be a big gamble for Pochettino to put his trust in him.

But Kone's ceiling feels sky high. It's time to see if he can go into the lab and come out as a Dembele-Wanyama hybrid.

VERDICT: Keep as project player

Cristian Orozco (Midfielder, 18)

Physically he has an advanced profile for his age but United have long preached that they want to take things slow as Orozco settles into life in England and gets a grip of the language.

He is neat and tidy on the ball and has shown an ability to zip passes through the lines but not enough to suggest an elevation to the first-team group.

Academy football doesn't develop players quickly enough so a carefully selected loan move, perhaps in a technical league like the Netherlands or Belgium, would be ideal.

VERDICT: Send on loan

ATTACKERS

Matheus Cunha (Attacker, 27)

He needs to look at how Pochettino used players like Lucas Moura and Eriksen in the past to see how he can take his game to the next level.

Cunha has a swagger about him that United like and while he was better suited to Ruben Amorim's system than he was Michael Carrick's, Pochettino's preference for narrow wide players, funnelling them into central areas while full backs create the width, means this managerial shift should play into his hands.

'Cunha is a maverick who does things that are hard to find in some players,' Amorim once said of the Brazilian.

'He plays with the ball, but he has an aura that can do something to the opponent's heads. And that is really important.'

VERDICT: Keep

Marcus Rashford (Attacker, 29)

It was recently suggested to Daily Mail Sport that a move for Rashford could be explored as early as January, with a desire to go back abroad.

A managerial change always puts things into flux and not least given that Pochettino said in 2022 that he'd 'always liked' Rashford, before adding: 'I think he's a great player. He just needs the confidence and for himself to believe, to put him at the top level. The quality is there for him.'

Pochettino is unlikely to have changed an opinion as solid as that one in the years that followed and so it will be curious to see if Rashford could become the athletic, pressing No9 in Benjamin Sesko's absence.

Rashford wants to feel the love and has shown what he can do when his confidence is high. It isn't right now but don't bet against Pochettino showing him that love.

VERDICT: Keep

Rashford has been linked with another move away but could become a pressing No 9

Joshua Zirkzee (Attacker, 25)

One of the more interesting profiles for Pochettino to consider.

On the face of it, Zirkzee lacks the intensity in the press and the mobility that Pochettino demands of his forwards.

Yet, Zirkzee can drop in, allowing the No10 to run in behind, which Pochettino values in a striker.

In the long term, expect Zirkzee to depart. In the short term, Pochettino may see him as a very specific tool to exploit certain opponents.

VERDICT: Replace

Amad Diallo (Attacker, 24)

Tenacious defensively after improving immeasurably out of possession under Amorim, that's a big plus for Amad in the eyes of Pochettino.

He's among the glut of hybrid 10-wingers that United seem to stockpile and, once Sesko returns, Amad will find himself locked in a battle with Shea Lacey and Bryan Mbeumo for regular starts.

Amad's energy should give him the edge from day one to be a natural fit for Pochettino's high press.

VERDICT: Keep

Shea Lacey (Attacker, 19)

Pochettino loves working with young players and Lacey is ready-made for that inverted winger style that the Argentine prefers, so he should be licking his lips at the prospect of more opportunities.

Lacey has played both off the right and as a No10 in academy teams and that stands him in good stead to operate in central areas, as well as isolate his full back one v one, which too many in this squad are not confident to do.

Lacey should be studying the development of Dele Alli under Pochettino and hoping he can bring his game on similarly.

VERDICT: Keep

Shea Lacey is (right) is a hugely promising youngster who will love working with Pochettino

Bryan Mbeumo (Attacker, 27)

Like Cunha, Mbeumo looked a more natural fit in Amorim's two-10s system and there are similarities that could put him back in those positions under Pochettino.

He's played a lot as a No 9 and may need to deputise there for the time being but the long-term dilemma for Pochettino will be the battle between Mbeumo, Amad and Lacey cutting in from the right.

It's one of the few areas of the pitch where there will be decent competition for places.

Mbeumo will need to find a position and master it or he may be caught in between roles.

VERDICT: Keep

Benjamin Sesko (Attacker, 23)

Injured until, most likely, the end of January and so it will take some time for Pochettino to get his teeth into Sesko's development.

The Slovenian feels very close to Pochettino's ideal No9 profile given his athleticism, physicality in the air, ability to press from the front and his instinctive finishing ability.

VERDICT: Keep

Benjamin Sesko could raise his level under a manager who routinely improves forwards

Tynan Thompson (Attacker, 18)

Academy sources feel the teenager, who arrived for an initial £4million, has been unfairly criticised so far as he tries to adapt to a new club since moving up from Tottenham.

Thompson has picked up in recent academy games but in terms of his profile he looks more comfortable as a touchline winger, minus the blistering pace we usually see in that position.

His best bet is to remain in the academy and look towards a season-long loan next season.

VERDICT: Stick with academy

Noah Ajayi (Attacker, 18)

One of the most intriguing academy prospects now that JJ Gabriel is closing in on a move to Real Madrid.

Ajayi looks physically capable of holding his own in first-team sessions and before a ball was kicked this term the development plan was to have him make a first-team debut before the season was out.

On-pitch failings may kick that can down the road but Ajayi is comfortable anywhere across the front line, has an acceleration that's invaluable and a technical level beyond his years.

Pochettino needs to take him under his wing to see what he can squeeze out of him before next summer.

VERDICT: Integrate into first-team training

Now have your say!

Sports.title: Axed British Cycling star under investigation for making 'racist and homophobic comments' makes low-key return - claiming victory over arch-rival in London
Sports.content:
Matthew Richardson will likely look back on 2026 as a year of missed opportunities after the under-investigation British Cycling star made a low-key return to action at the London 3 Day event on Friday.

Billed as the fastest cyclist on the planet after smashing the 200m flying lap world record last August, Richardson has missed out on competing at the Commonwealth Games and World Championships this year.

His absence from the first had been unfortunate, having suffered a broken shoulder in a keirin race in July. One that left him complaining months later that he had been yet to receive an apology from Japanese rival Gento Suzuki for causing the incident.

The second was also serious but for a different reason, with Richardson sent home by British Cycling on the eve of the World Championships after a formal complaint was made about his conduct.

Richardson, who switched to represent Britain from Australia in 2024, was reported by The Times to have made discriminatory remarks about people from minority backgrounds on a regular basis.

The complaint was reportedly sparked by him sending team-mates an offensive image referencing another GB rider.

Matthew Richardson, who is subject of an investigation into his conduct, made his return to competition at the London 3 Day event at the Lee Valley Velopark on Friday night

Richardson came out on top in his battle with Dutch star Harrie Lavreysen, left, who had won three gold medals at last month's World Championships after the British sprinter was sent home

Among the allegations are that Richardson appeared to use the n-word in six messages, as well as making offensive references to the Asian community and homophobic comments.

Richardson’s appearance at the London 3 Day event was his first since the investigation began, with the 27-year-old vowing last month to ‘co-operate fully’ and ‘with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected’.

The interest around Richardson’s return to action may have contributed to organisers informing Daily Mail Sport this week that they had reached capacity for media.

As a result, Daily Mail Sport opted to purchase a discounted ticket – reduced by 25 per cent from £72 to £55 – on Friday morning and take a seat in the velodrome’s less than half-full stands to watch the action unfold. Curiously seats in the media tribune opposite were sparsely attended.

Daily Mail Sport also approached organisers of the London 3 Day – an event not associated with British Cycling – about Richardson’s participation while the investigation remains ongoing.

The extent to which Richardson has missed out this year was highlighted by his showdown with Dutch rival 'Harrie Lavreysen', which had been billed by organisers as the 'Race of the Year'.

Five-time Olympic gold medallist Lavreysen had been among the biggest winners from the World Championships in Richardson’s absence last month, coming away from Shanghai with gold medals in the sprint, keirin and team sprint events.

As it happened Lavreysen was the one admitting to being rusty after Richardson won the first of their battles on the night, clocking 9.624 to win the 200m flying lap. Still some way short of his world record time of 8.857 set last August.

Richardson, who switched from Australia to represent Britain in 2024, has been billed as the fastest man on the planet but has missed two major competitions this year

Richardson is one half of British Cycling's golden couple alongside his girlfriend Emma Finucane

Richardson had been received with polite applause and cheers in his first competitive race in months and since he was placed under investigation. This was the Lee Valley Velopark not the nearby London Stadium after all.

The in-house announcer later declared that Richardson was 'Doing his talking on the track' after the 27-year-old came from a race down to beat the newly crowned world champion in a best-of-three sprint series.

The deciding win came after Richardson showed his track craft by diving down the track, catching Lavreysen by surprise and pulling clear for victory.

Richardson would go on to round off the evening by beating the Dutchman in a 500m time trial, making it 4-1 to the Brit on the night.

It was a reminder of Richardson's clear talent and potential to claim the biggest honours in British colours. The 27-year-old has been billed as one part of the GB's golden couple alongside his girlfriend Emma Finucane, who has three Olympic medals and a hat-trick of world titles to her name.

‘I felt really good out there to be back racing and putting the legs to good use,’ Richardson said during an on-track interview.

‘We are a close match up wherever we go and tonight was no different.'

Richardson will ultimately end this year with sprint and keirin European titles to his name, having beaten Lavreysen in both events back in February. But it was the Dutchman who cleaned up in his absence at the worlds.

Having been forced to watch from back home, the question as to whether Richardson can win major titles and perhaps add to his three Olympic medals at Los Angeles 2028 will likely now depend on how he emerges from the ongoing investigation.

Sports.title: The four problems Mauricio Pochettino needs to fix at Man United: From big names causing unrest in the dressing room to an issue which plagued Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick before him, these are the items top of his Old Trafford in-tray
Sports.content:
The four problems Mauricio Pochettino needs to fix at Man United: From big names causing unrest in the dressing room to an issue which plagued Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick before him, these are the items top of his Old Trafford in-tray

Mauricio Pochettino will see out his final two games as US national team boss with a double-header against Haiti before starting work at Manchester United on Wednesday.

The 54-year-old won’t have any time to waste with a daunting first game against United’s bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday followed by a European clash with Sporting Lisbon in Portugal three days later.

With United languishing in the Premier League relegation zone and 17th in the Champions League standings, it’s clear why Pochettino has been brought in to replace Michael Carrick on a two-and-a-half-year contract.

Daily Mail Sport looks at the most pressing matters in Pochettino’s in-tray at Carrington as the former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss and his backroom staff head for Manchester...

Mauricio Pochettino is the new manager of Manchester United - but the problems he has to fix are already piling up

Winning mentality

It sounds obvious, but winning games to get United out of the Premier League drop zone has to be the first priority.

Everything at a football club flows from the results on the pitch, and United’s humiliating decline this season has had ramifications throughout Old Trafford and Carrington.

The players are clearly low on confidence which has only exacerbated the team’s dismal performances and brought just one win in 10 Premier League games, against newly-promoted Ipswich – United’s worst start in 40 years.

Diogo Dalot is a prime example, after fans cheered his substitution in the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa last weekend, and the defender cut a crestfallen figure as he left Old Trafford to go on international duty with Portugal.

The Stretford End also turned on the players as the atmosphere turned toxic after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth at the end of last month, having vented their anger towards the club’s ownership – the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – as well as chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox at every opportunity.

That won’t go away anytime soon, but a winning team will at least take some of the sting out of the situation if appointing Pochettino can give United a ‘bounce’ and divert attention back onto the pitch.

United players are low on confidence, not least Diogo Dalot (left) whose substitution was cheered by his own fans against Aston Villa

The United team were also lambasted by the Stretford End after the 3-0 loss to Bournemouth last month

Survival of the fittest

Carrick enjoyed a good start, losing just two of his 17 games in charge in the second half of last season to earn a two-year contract, but United struggled under him this term due to a combination of poor recruitment, injuries and lack of fitness.

These are all issues that Pochettino must try to put right. There is little he can do about recruitment until the January transfer window opens and United have a chance to atone for their mistake in not signing cover at left back and centre forward last summer, which backfired spectacularly when both Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko picked up injuries.

He can, however, try to get more out of United’s £155million midfield signings Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again – Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, and a United squad that was good enough to finish third in the Premier League last season.

Injuries have been a major problem with the hamstring strain that will keep Baleba out of action for Pochettino’s first few weeks in charge just the latest setback.

As well as Shaw, Sesko, Baleba and long-term casualty Manuel Ugarte, United have also lost Amad Diallo, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Lisandro Martinez, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui for parts of this season.

Pochettino must get more out of United’s £155million midfield signing Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again

United have struggled to keep up with their opponents since the opening day - a lack of fitness has plagued every manager since Ole Gunnar Solskjaer

The good news for Pochettino is that Shaw and Rashford are hoping to be fit for Anfield, while Matthijs de Ligt is available again after a year out with back problems. However, Sesko’s absence until the new year leaves the new boss without his most natural source of goals.

Fitness is another matter and United have looked short of it since the opening-day defeat at Hull City amid concerns that the coaching levels dropped off under Carrick and were too relaxed.

They covered 120.8 kilometres against Villa – the most in a league game under Carrick – and Pochettino will demand that and a whole lot more as he increases the work-rate among his new squad.

It’s a problem that has hindered a succession of United bosses going back to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and the Argentine must find a way to drill a better work ethic into United.

Get Bruno back to his best

The problems at United this season have inevitably led to unrest in the dressing room, with the biggest issue centred around captain Bruno Fernandes.

News that Fernandes has rejected United’s latest contract offer has come as no surprise given his dramatic change in fortunes from last season, and Pochettino must find a way to get arguably United’s best player back in form and onside.

Having set a new Premier League record for assists and picked up a string of player of the year awards last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off a cliff as he struggled with an injury sustained at the World Cup, and he suffered the rare indignity of being benched for the loss to Bournemouth.

Never one to hide his mood very well, the 32-year-old criticised Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat by Como in what was a major blow to his head coach.

Never one to hide his mood very well, Bruno Fernandes has been disgruntled of late and rejected United's offer of a new contract

Lisandro Martinez looks to be headed for the exit door - although the arrival of his fellow Argentine Pochettino may help things

While the United hierarchy will try to persuade Fernandes to sign a new deal in keeping with their reduced wage structure and the fact he will turn 33 next year, Pochettino has to find a way of relighting the fire in his skipper.

Whether the club will make as much effort to keep Lisandro Martinez as he comes towards the end of his contract remains to be seen after another member of United’s leadership team took aim at Wilcox’s recruitment after the defeat by Atletico Madrid. It is said to have caused an angry clash between Martinez and summer signing Tielemans on the way back from Spain.

Martinez looks to be heading for the Old Trafford exit, but it will be interesting to see if the arrival of his compatriot Pochettino – a combative Argentine centre back in much the same mould as a player – has an impact on that.

Plug the leaky defence

As a former defender, Pochettino won’t need telling that leaking 15 goals in the last five games simply isn’t good enough. United have now let in 30 in all competitions this season, the most of any club in Europe’s top five leagues apart from Lens.

They have been appalling at the back, conceding in the opening seconds to Atletico, Como and Villa. Had they been able to hold out and prevent late equalisers against Everton and Tottenham, the additional four points would have them 12th in the table rather than in the relegation zone.

A revolving door of makeshift left backs in the absence of Shaw and Dorgu, De Ligt’s belated comeback and Martinez’s needless red card at Chelsea haven’t helped.

Goalkeeper Senne Lammens, so composed last season, looks considerably more shaky behind a leaky and ever-changing back-four, and had arguably his worst game against Villa last weekend.

Pochettino couldn’t ask for a tougher first test than going to Anfield, and knows that United will have to start by being solid at the back.

Sports.title: Antoine Dupont has a genuine case to be considered the greatest Test player of all time - as France's famous win over South Africa shows England what best in class looks like: ALEX BYWATER
Sports.content:
The clock was inching towards midnight local time as the great man collapsed to his haunches, exhausted by the exertions of yet another totemic performance.

‘Toto’, as they know him here, had nothing left to give. His job was done. Around him, Antoine Dupont’s French team-mates – led by the Tigger-like Louis Bielle-Biarrey – jumped for joy, barely able to believe what they had done. GALA’s Freed From Desire was the soundtrack to France’s latest rugby party.

Just seconds before, it was a combination of the great Dupont and Bielle-Biarrey that had won the game, sealing one of the most famous victories in France’s history. How fitting. What a night. What a privilege to see this truly miraculous game unfold live. By downing double world champions South Africa without a mammoth 25 injured players, France and their iconic captain Dupont made a big statement.

A thrilling 21-19 success saw them enact sweet revenge on the Springboks for their 2023 World Cup quarter-final loss. At the same time, it was also far more than that. It was confirmation of France’s genuine hopes for the 2027 tournament, that these are the best two teams in the world – regardless of what the rankings say – and that Dupont’s case to be the greatest Test player of all time must now be considered as genuine. It was also confirmation to England of what best in class looks like and the ground they still have to make up on it.

‘It was really important to us to win this game for so many reasons,’ said Dupont. ‘When we heard the whistle, it was a huge thing to share this with a stadium who helped us during the entire game. It was an amazing atmosphere. We were able to celebrate with the last kick. We were proud to represent the French nation with a remarkable mindset. We made some mistakes, but we counteracted them with unbelievable energy. That’s why we won.’

No one does beautiful chaos quite like the French. And this was it on steroids. When Bielle-Biarrey smashed hulking Springbok centre Jesse Kriel, it was Dupont who pounced on the loose ball. Maxime Lucu kicked the ball dead to start the celebrations. Dupont and Lucu – les deux petits généraux – masterminded this success. The former wore No10 with his team decimated in that position, but played in his usual scrum-half role. Lucu did the opposite as France proved all their doubters wrong. No Thomas Ramos. No Thibaud Flament. No Romain Ntamack. No Matthieu Jalibert. No Emmanuel Meafou. The list goes on and on. No problem!

Maxime Lucu and Antoine Dupont celebrate after France earned a 21-19 win over South Africa

Dupont’s case to be the greatest Test player of all time must now be considered as genuine

The French star is alongside the likes of legendary figures such as Jonah Lomu, Dan Carter, Jonny Wilkinson and Sir Gareth Edwards and he continues to raise the bar of rugby excellence

France coach Fabien Galthie had said pre-match victory would have been ‘unimaginable’ given his list of absentees. His fringe players made that dream a reality.

‘When the players are wearing the blue jersey, they just believe. It is powerful. It gives them something that helps them go over their limits,’ said Galthie. ‘Of course, I heard comments saying we were going to get trashed. I want to live the day. The future is now. I want to savour the victory. It’s huge, but it’s not the end. It’s part of the continuation of our ambition.’

Dupont is now alongside the likes of legendary figures such as Jonah Lomu, Dan Carter, Jonny Wilkinson and Sir Gareth Edwards. He continues to raise the bar of rugby excellence. Here, he kicked off both feet with aplomb. He tackled. He did the dirty work. He led from the front. Hell, he probably even swept the changing room floor on the way out too.

‘He was a nine. He was a 10. He was also a six at times!’ Galthie said of Dupont. France were second best at the scrum throughout against a South African team that changed their whole starting front row just before kick-off and then again in only the 35th minute. They also suffered three yellow cards. It made their success all the more remarkable.

‘Since the start of the season, he's been at his best,’ try machine Bielle-Biarrey said of Dupont. ‘He feels good in the game plan. When he plays like that, in attack, in defence, in game management, it's a real pleasure.’ If England are to win the next World Cup, they will likely have to beat one of these two sides and right now, that feels a stiff – if not totally insurmountable – task.

France’s strength in depth is enviable. South Africa were missing Cheslin Kolbe, but him aside this was the game’s dominant force at full strength. And they were still beaten.

‘It feels good to shut people up,’ said France hooker Peato Mauvaka. ‘It’s bloody annoying when people predict our defeat before a match.’

France’s backs-to-the-wall display sent a capacity Stade de France crowd wild with delight. Their defence and physicality were on point and when Dupont snatched possession cat-like at the death and Lucu ended the game, the place exploded. On nights like this, it is Paris that is the best place in the world to watch international rugby.

‘For me, Dupont is the GOAT (greatest of all time),’ said France wing Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, who opened the scoring. ‘I’m absolutely not afraid to say it. Once again we saw a great Antoine. He’s so important for our team. We’re lucky to play with a player like him.’

France proved their doubters wrong with victory and showed their strength in depth, while demonstrating to England of what best in class looks like and the gap they must make up

France were devastated not to win their home World Cup three years ago. Their win here also meant England will likely have to beat New Zealand to top the northern Nations Championship pool and make the final.

‘Dupont is a player that’s so instinctive,’ said beaten South Africa boss Rassie Erasmus. ‘We didn’t know if he was going to play 10 or 9. That made it difficult. We weren’t just outplayed, we were outsmarted. I think we’ve killed our dreams for the Nations Championship with this result. It’s s*** losing.’

South Africa also suffered a 20-minute red card and a yellow. Andrea Piardi’s refereeing was far from perfect, but it only served to add to the relentless anarchy. Piardi warned France twice on the hour mark for poor discipline both at the set-piece and in general play, but didn’t hand out a card or penalty try. Les Bleus were fortunate to escape there, but they made the most of it. Erasmus aimed a sly dig at Piardi by saying he was ‘just human’, though his grievances in that area were just. The better overall team won, however.

Chapeau, France. And chapeau, Dupont.

Sports.title: English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man
Sports.content:
A teenage English boxer has said they have been left 'broken' after being denied the chance to compete at the World Championships due to officials failing to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.

George Francis, 18, had been due to represent England at the Under-19 World Championships in Budva, Montenegro last month.

Francis was withdrawn from competition on the eve of the event after an administration error by England Boxing, with the governing body having failed to arrange the necessary sex verification test.

'They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically,' Francis told the BBC.

'The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.

'Somehow I wasn't on the system.

George Francis, 18, missed out on competing at the Under-19 World Championships after England Boxing failed to arrange a necessary sex verification test. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

'It was the worst news I've ever had in my life.

'I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated.

'I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there.'

Francis's situation, first reported by The Times, followed the mandatory introduction of sex verification tests by the sport's governing body World Boxing.

World Boxing announced the move last year, with genetic sex testing initially introduced for female competitors aged 18 and above. The governing body stated the move was due to a 'duty of care to deliver safety and competitiveness fairness'.

It followed controversy at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where boxers Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting won gold.

Khelif and Lin had been disqualified from the previous year's World Championships, with boxing's former governing body – the International Boxing Association – claiming the pair had failed sex eligibility tests.

Earlier this year, Lin was cleared to compete in women's events following a review of her sex eligibility.

World Boxing's mandatory tests were extended to include male boxers earlier this year.

Francis had been required to undergo a test due to turning 18 four days before travelling to the World Championships.

Francis, a multiple national champion, had been required to undergo a mandatory test after turning 18 days before the World Championships. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

World Boxing introduced sex testing last year amid the controversy surrounding Algerian boxer Imane Khelif's participation at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games

The multiple national and GB champion has claimed he is considering turning professional following the mix-up.

England Boxing reportedly contacted Francis's father to apologise for the 'administrative oversight', with the governing body stressing it will 'strengthen processes' to avoid a repeat incident.

'We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible,' an England Boxing statement read.

'George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.

'England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence.'

World Boxing's policy requires boxers to undergo a once-in-a-lifetime PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test to determine their sex and their eligibility to compete in either the male or female category.

The PCR test is a laboratory technique used to detect specific genetic material, in this case the SRY gene, which reveals the presence of the Y chromosome that is an indicator of male biological sex.

A dozen boxers, representing five nations, were last year blocked from competing at the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

Under World Boxing rules, national federations are responsible for testing and will be required to confirm the sex of their athletes when entering them into World Boxing competitions
