World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
World.content:
Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.

Share US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO on social media

US negotiators have floated the idea that Ukraine should cede parts of eastern Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after the latest rounds ⁠of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi and Ireland.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from ⁠Donbas?” he said. “That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda.”

Zelenskyy said the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine the US asked about were areas Russia does not control. The Ukrainian president said he refused to cede territory.

“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

Putin has long said that Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy did say that if Ukraine received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, military and reconstruction funds, and a recovery plan from the US and other partners, he would put the question about ceding parts of Donbas to a national referendum.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said.



He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognising occupied territories as Russian. Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country’s constitution.

“If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in NATO right now anyway.”

Despite the diplomatic push to end the conflict, Russia and Ukraine reported numerous overnight attacks. Russian officials reported on Friday that about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets, while Ukraine reported attacks on a hospital and the port of Odesa.

At the summit in Ireland over recent days, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers – non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland – as well as EU officials. They would hold talks ‌with ‌US and Ukrainian officials, but not with Russia.

World.title: Italy fines Meta $880m over photo privacy
World.content:
Regulator said Meta’s ‘lack of cooperation’ and the large number of people affected contributed to size of the fine.

Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.

The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.

The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.

This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.

Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.

The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.

Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.

The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.

The amount is roughly 0.47 percent of Meta’s global turnover.

The proceedings did not address the possible use of content to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies.

Meta has not yet publicly commented on the matter, and it has the right to appeal the regulator’s decision.

World.title: EU calls for immediate humanitarian access to Gaza
World.content:
The EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies” after the group was blocked access into Gaza.

The European Union has urged Israel to reopen all Gaza border crossings and grant “immediate, unimpeded access” for aid groups to provide humanitarian relief in the territory following devastating flooding in Gaza this week.

Civilian infrastructure and medical facilities in Gaza “must be protected,” said an EU statement released on Saturday by the office of Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and the Vice-President of the European Commission.

The EU call came as an Israeli drone attack killed two more Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday.

The drone struck them as they walked down a street in Jabaliya on the northern edge of Gaza City, according to Mohamed Abu Selmiya, director of Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, where the casualties were taken. The American field hospital said several other people were wounded but did not provide a number.

The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas “militants” in the area.

An Israeli air attack on Thursday at the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon, and left dozens wounded.

“The EU underlines the need to respect international law, including international humanitarian law, at all times,” the 27-nation bloc said on Saturday. “This includes the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as medical personnel and facilities. The recent airstrike on the Nasser Hospital is deeply alarming,” it added.

Heavy rains

Damage from Israeli attacks on Gaza’s infrastructure has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials and the UN said this week. Gaza’s media office reported that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.



Heavy rain has directly affected at least 106,000 people in Gaza in recent days, according to the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged and latrines overflowing into camps.

In response, the EU said that “Israel must enable the work of the UN and its agencies, and humanitarian organisations including NGOs, and comply with all its obligations under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law.”

The EU reaffirmed “its commitment to the two-state solution” and called for “the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza” as it called for “sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale” to ease the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

World.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 to hit new space distance record of one light-day
World.content:
The probe was launched in 1977 but it continues to relay space-related data back to a team of NASA scientists daily.

Share NASA’s Voyager 1 to hit new space distance record of one light-day on social media

NASA has announced that its Voyager 1 probe will soon become humanity’s first object to travel one light-day from Earth.

On Wednesday, the robotic space probe will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977, a distance equal to one light-day, or how far light can travel in 24 hours.

The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission, and is currently travelling at roughly 36,000 miles per hour (58km/h) in interstellar space, the vast gap between stars.

NASA expects it to take 18,000 years to travel a full light-year, and double that before it nears another star.

Plutonium-powered Voyager 1 was launched shortly before another probe, Voyager 2. Both continue to relay data back to Earth daily, including readings on the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as on the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays.

Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.

Both are kept active by a skeleton team of NASA engineers who send commands roughly once a week, and more if the probe gets into trouble.

In October, the team briefly lost communication with Voyager 1, and they have not yet figured out why.

Voyager 1 project manager Suzanne Dodd described Voyager 1 as “a national treasure” and told The Associated Press news agency that the two probes’ activities are akin to that of weather satellites.

The probe’s cultural impact has been significant. The famous “Pale Blue Dot” photo of Earth was taken by Voyager 1 in 1990.



“All of us — everyone on Earth — have been touched by these missions,” the Planetary Society’s Bill Nye said in a statement.

World.title: Canada’s Stelco to recall 175 workers after government pressure
World.content:
Steelmaker promises back pay for workers whose layoffs its US owner blamed on tariffs, weak demand and imports.

Canadian steelmaker Stelco says it will recall all 175 workers laid off at its plant in Hamilton and pay them retroactively, following a weeks-long standoff that pitted workers and the Canadian government against its owner in the United States.

The announcement on Friday came shortly after Canada’s Industry Minister Melanie Joly said she would seek a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Stelco unless she heard from management by the end of the day.

The company said in a statement on Friday that it had reached agreements with enough customers to restart its finishing operations and that workers would be recalled on December 1. They would receive back pay for the standard wages they would have earned while laid off.

The president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, Ron Wells, welcomed the announcement and credited pressure from workers, the union and the government.

At a news conference, he called the layoffs “illegal” and “immoral” which should never have happened.

Alongside him was Joly, who said the outcome sent a message to investors that Canada was “a country of the rule of law and that the law applies to everyone, notwithstanding the size of your wallet.”

“This fight was absolutely worth it,” she said.

Cleveland-Cliffs, which bought Stelco in 2024, announced in late September that up to 500 workers would be laid off at Stelco’s plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario, citing weak demand and difficult market conditions for cold-rolled and coated steel products used to make everything from cars to appliances.



It blamed US President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, which made it more expensive in the US, as well as competition from cheaper foreign steel, which it argued was eating into domestic demand for Canadian steel.

Ottawa said the layoffs violated binding commitments the company made when it bought Stelco, including keeping the same number of Canadian unionised employees through 2029.

The government and the union also argued that Cleveland-Cliffs’ CEO Lourenco Goncalves violated a commitment to advocate for policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US when he publicly supported Trump’s tariffs on steel, including Canada’s.

Goncalves’ open support for the tariffs raised questions, given that he also blamed them for Stelco’s financial troubles.

In its statement, Cleveland-Cliffs said its customers had committed to supporting its operations in Hamilton “despite the lack of response from the federal government to address the shortfalls in their tariff response program.”

It didn’t provide details on the agreements it had reached with customers or explain what had changed to make restarting operations viable.

Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Why US Democrats are expected to keep Schumer and Jeffries in power
World.content:
The prospect of keeping the Congressional leaders in power is exposing long-running tensions in the party.

Share Why US Democrats are expected to keep Schumer and Jeffries in power on social media

Over a week after Democrats rode a historic wave of support to retake the United States Congress, divisions within the party seem to be threatening to undermine its newfound political momentum.

Despite growing calls for a change in Congressional leadership, Democrats Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries appear likely to remain at the helm of their respective US Senate and House caucuses.

After amassing the most Democratic power in Washington since 2009, the two New Yorkers are seeking to retain their leadership positions as their party prepares to take control of both chambers in January.

Schumer, the US Senate’s 75-year-old minority leader, is vying to lead Democrats’ new majority in the chamber, a post he previously held during Joe Biden’s presidency. On the other side of the US Capitol, the 56-year-old Jeffries, as the current minority leader in the US House, is seeking the top role of speaker, placing him second in the line of succession for the US presidency.

But the prospect of keeping Schumer and Jeffries in charge has frustrated some Democrats, exposing long-running tensions between Democratic lawmakers who want to maintain continuity and those who believe their midterm victories offer an opportunity to fundamentally reshape the party’s priorities.

Here’s why Schumer and Jeffries could prevail:

An election victory buys political goodwill

Perhaps the biggest reason the top two Democrats in the US Congress will hold onto their posts: the party’s massive electoral gains.

Schumer’s supporters argue he helped Democrats secure at least eight Republican-held Senate seats, including victories in traditionally conservative states. The party is poised to hold as many as 56 seats in the next Congress, giving it a substantial majority not seen since former President Barack Obama’s first term in office.



“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract”, Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego, with Schumer by his side, told reporters on Tuesday. “And this has been a really good election cycle for us”.

Schumer also played a central role in recruiting candidates who could compete in states where Democrats have struggled in recent elections, including former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown and former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper.

Adam Jentleson, a longtime US Senate aide and author of, Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power, argued Schumer’s electoral success makes it difficult for critics to mount a successful challenge.

“It’s hard to argue with somebody who just oversaw the biggest election the Democrats have had since Watergate,” Jentleson said during an interview with public radio station WBUR earlier this month.

“The only people who matter are the members of the Democratic caucus,” Jentleson said, explaining that lawmakers who had recently benefitted from the midterm results would have little incentive to remove the person who helped deliver those victories.

Schumer’s allies have made a similar argument. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who oversees the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, credited Schumer’s candidate recruitment and fundraising efforts for helping the party reclaim the US Senate.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership,” she said.

Schumer himself has expressed confidence that he has enough support to retain the position.

In an interview with The Washington Sun on Wednesday, he said he had secured more than enough backing from his colleagues.

“I am going to be elected leader, OK, and we’re united on the issues,” Schumer told the Sun. “We’re united.”

Schumer faces a challenge

Not every Democrat believes last week’s victories are enough to anoint Schumer as the party’s leader in the Senate in the next Congress.

Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday he would mount a challenge for the role after factions of the Democratic base, particularly progressives, have called for new leadership.

The Maryland Democrat attracted attention at the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term after he travelled to El Salvador to meet with his constituent, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who had been deported to the country despite a judge’s ruling barring his removal.



That, according to a senior Senate Democratic aide who spoke with Al Jazeera, exemplified “the fight Schumer just doesn’t have”.

“This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said during a Thursday appearance on MSNOW, adding that US voters sent a message to “reject the status quo and to reject business as usual”.

Another Senate aide, who would only speak on condition of anonymity to talk freely about an internal matter, suggested Van Hollen’s bid may be more about extracting concessions from Schumer, like a promise to serve as a short-term “bridge” to a new generation of Democratic leadership.

An analysis by Al Jazeera showed that 12 Democratic senators have publicly committed to backing Schumer in next month’s leadership election. At least 10 senators, including independent Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, have said they will not. However, only half of those opposed to Schumer’s leadership have backed Van Hollen’s challenge.

In an interview with The Nation published on Wednesday, the Vermont independent senator acknowledged knowing Schumer for decades and even liking him personally. But he argued that personal relationships should not determine who leads the party.

“In this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is,” Sanders said.

He added that Schumer was not in tune with Democratic voters on the issues, arguing the party needed a new and more ambitious direction.

Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin has also questioned Schumer’s leadership, calling for a concrete plan outlining how Democrats intend to use their newly won congressional power.

Slotkin went further on Tuesday, suggesting to reporters at the US Capitol that senators withhold a quorum — the minimum number of lawmakers required to conduct official business — if Schumer runs unopposed, until he presents a plan that gives members a meaningful voice in setting the party’s priorities.

Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock has also declined to commit to supporting Schumer, telling CNN on Tuesday that Democrats are at an “inflection point” and any senator who believes they should lead deserves an opportunity to make their case.

Still, there is a difference between public dissatisfaction and the votes needed to remove a leader. Senate Democrats select their leader through a private ballot, requiring only a simple majority of the caucus.

Tre Easton, vice president for public policy at the Searchlight Institute and a former deputy chief of staff for Democratic Senator John Fetterman, has also questioned the timing of the push against Schumer, arguing calls for new leadership would have carried more weight following the Democrats’ losses in 2024 rather than immediately after their electoral successes in 2026.



“The job of the leader in each legislative chamber here in the U.S. isn’t to articulate a vision for the party”, Easton said in a social media post. “It’s to keep each respective caucus together and count votes. Dassit”.

Jeffries faces a different kind of challenge

The outlook is considerably clearer for Jeffries, who is seeking to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on January 3.

Unlike Schumer, Jeffries does not face a prominent challenger for his leadership position, despite criticism from some progressives over his approach to Trump and his longstanding support for Israel.

His backing from moderate Democrats has been particularly visible.

The New Democrat Coalition, a group of Democratic centrists representing 142 current and newly elected lawmakers, issued a statement on Tuesday endorsing his bid for speaker.

“Hakeem Jeffries is the right person at the right time to lead our party”, the group said. “He’s smart, strategic, and action-oriented, with strong relationships across the Democratic caucus”.

The coalition added that it “can’t wait to vote for Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the House on January 3, 2027”.

But support from the party’s moderate wing has not eliminated dissatisfaction among progressives.

Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she is withholding her support for Jeffries unless he commits to advancing Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a government-funded universal healthcare system.

Jayapal has also acknowledged that the lack of an alternative candidate complicates the leadership debate.

“You can’t beat somebody with nobody,” the Washington state Democrat told Talking Points Memo, adding that the emergence of a challenger would change the calculations of lawmakers considering whether to support Jeffries.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, meanwhile, was asked by CNN whether she supported Jeffries.

“The race is unopposed. Yeah,” she responded, suggesting that the absence of a challenger was an important factor in the debate.

The tensions in the US House have also been illustrated by the case of Don Leonard, an incoming Democratic congressman from Ohio who said he will withhold his support for Jeffries unless the party commits to specific policy changes.

Leonard, who has called for an end to US support for Israel and the war in Iran, alleged in a video posted to social media that senior House Democrats threatened to make his life a “living hell” in Washington and undermine his chances of re-election in 2028 if he continued attaching conditions to his support for Jeffries.

He has not identified the lawmakers involved, and the allegations have not been independently verified. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar told reporters on Tuesday he did not know which senior Democrats Leonard was referring to.

Jeffries, who has denied reports that US House Democrats have been receiving calls to oppose his bid for the speakership, spoke to reporters on Thursday about frustrations within the party over his leadership.

“We take nothing for granted, because all of us in the House of Representatives are on a two-year employment contract”, Jeffries said. “And we have to continue to make our case both with respect to our track record up until this point, as well as, perhaps even more importantly, our vision for the future”.



The pressure will come after the leadership votes

The leadership contests are scheduled for November 18 and 19 for House Democrats and at an unannounced date in December for Senate Democrats.

If elected, both Schumer and Jeffries will likely continue to face competing demands from progressives seeking more aggressive action against Trump and from moderates representing districts and states where a more centrist approach may be politically important.

They will also have to contend with the practical limitations of governing. Even with control of both chambers, Democrats will not have the 60 Senate votes generally required to overcome a filibuster, meaning they will need Republican support for much of their legislation.

For now, however, the party’s electoral gains have given Schumer and Jeffries an argument for continuity.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote in an X post on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

World.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
World.content:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

World.title: ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets
World.content:
Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London.

In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life.

Since the U.S.-Israeli war began, Iran and its proxies — who sometimes act on their own — have stepped up such attacks, particularly in Britain, which has allowed the United States to use its military bases to strike Iranian forces. By hitting American allies, Iran aims to sow fear and try to weaken their support for the U.S. and Israeli military deployments, experts said.

“What we are seeing right now is the application of a playbook Iran has refined over decades,” said Adrian Shtuni, an associate fellow with the International Center for Counter-Terrorism. In addition to the criminal attacks, he also cited Iran’s efforts to build proxy militant networks outside Iran and enhance its abilities to carry out cyberattacks.

World.title: Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
World.content:
Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.

Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.

Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.

World.title: Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity
World.content:
Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.

Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.

“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”

Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.

World.title: South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
World.content:
The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.

With Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.

The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.

World.title: Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
World.content:
Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics.

The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force.

In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies.

Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself.

World.title: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
World.content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who is trying to form the next Israeli government, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fueling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab citizens, in some of the strongest public criticism of his rival’s attacks on the community.

The comments were made days after Mr. Netanyahu delivered a divisive speech to the opening session of Parliament, or the Knesset, in which he referred to Arab lawmakers as “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel.” Diplomats and analysts condemned the remarks as a brazen display of hatred and incitement against Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the overall population, and voted in massive numbers in inconclusive elections last month.

“Since the beginning of the election campaign, they have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimization, fueled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Mr. Eisenkot said in a statement on social media.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” he said, adding that it was wrong to malign an entire community.

World.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
World.content:
There was nothing of the sort in Biakato, despite the surging cases. In 2013, four Doctors Without Borders workers were abducted in an A.D.F. raid on a village in North Kivu Province. One escaped after 13 months; the other three have never been found.

The World Health Organization, which is leading the effort to get help to Biakato, has its own painful history in the town. During the last outbreak in this area, in 2019, armed men attacked its guesthouse in Biakato, killing three Ebola responders. Officials blamed the violence on the Mai-Mai, a term for local militias.

That leaves health officials walking a tightrope. Proceed too slowly, and Biakato could become a deep reservoir of Ebola, spreading infection across the region. Move too quickly, and they risk an attack, like a killing or a kidnapping of aid workers, that could collapse the entire effort.

Mistrust among local residents is also a problem. After decades of war, and numerous failed military operations, faith in the government has collapsed, officials said. The same Congolese soldiers who are supposed to protect the community also prey on it, seeking bribes or profiting from gold. When Ebola came along, locals saw the disease as yet another plot to suppress them.

“They don’t trust outsiders,” said Julien Harneis, the United Nations Ebola coordinator in Congo. “Experience has taught them not to.”

As infections began to rise in September, a W.H.O. team returned to Biakato to see how they might help. The omens were ominous, at first. The health workers woke one morning to find a headless sheep dumped outside their hotel — a sign they were not welcome, said Dr. Steve Ahuka, the head of Congo’s Ebola response.

But within weeks, Ebola had become so overwhelming that Biakato’s distrustful leaders were pleading for help.

On Oct. 12, Dr. Ahuka and Catherine Smallwood, a senior W.H.O. official, returned to Biakato to a very different reception. Local leaders formed a circle around Ms. Smallwood and, after apologizing for the 2019 killings, implored her to send help.

“They asked me to put the past in the past,” she recalled. “It was an extremely touching moment.”

World.title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
World.content:
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.

The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.

Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.

World.title: What we know about the ground stop and what to do if you're affected
World.content:
In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.

As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.

But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws.

Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly.

It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.

In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers.

However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights.

Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.

This includes:

a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)

a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)

free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day

transport to and from that accommodation

If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.

The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.

World.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
World.content:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The Ukrainian president's comments come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.

Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Russia has now raised the stakes further. It has revived 2021 demands for Nato to halt any expansion in Russia's vicinity and to roll back military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe that became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

The US and other Western nations dismissed these demands then - and Moscow invaded Ukraine a few months later.

However, questions of European security were on the agenda of the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Russia has insisted it will not agree to cease fighting until a final peace deal is in place that would include territorial settlements as well as security arrangements.

World.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
World.content:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.

The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment.

Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

World.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
World.content:
Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.

The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.

Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.

The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.

It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.

The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.

Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.

This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.

The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
World.content:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.

World.title: Second catch attempt for SpaceX Starship rocket
World.content:
SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday.

This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time on Friday.

The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned.

A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.

World.title: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
World.content:
Nearly $20m (Â£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor OrbÃ¡n, authorities have said.

MiklÃ³s SesztÃ¡k, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Hungary's new Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar unseated OrbÃ¡n in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.

On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".

Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into SesztÃ¡k, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.

The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, â¬2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.

The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the OrbÃ¡n rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".

Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many OrbÃ¡n-era policies since entering office.

Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged OrbÃ¡n, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".

World.title: Why ‘MKO’ documentary took 13 years, cost over $1million — Ose Oyamendan
World.content:
More than three decades after the annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election plunged Nigeria into a pro-democracy struggle, filmmaker Ose Oyamendan revisited the life and political legacy of the late Moshood Abiola in a new documentary, “MKO.”

Mr Oyamendan premiered the documentary on 1 October at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts in Iganmu, Lagos, as part of activities marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary.

President Bola Tinubu, Senate President Godswill Akpabio, Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu and the President’s Chief of Staff, Femi Gbajabiamila, and others attended the event.

The documentary entered cinemas nationwide on 2 October, taking viewers through Mr Abiola’s life, political ambitions and legacy while revisiting the military government’s controversial decision to annul the 1993 election.

In this exclusive interview with PREMIUM TIMES, Mr Oyamendan discusses the motivation behind the documentary, his decision to feature Mr Abiola’s eldest son, Kola Abiola, and the accounts of prominent figures who featured in the documentary.

Excerpt:

PT: What inspired you to make this documentary, and why did you choose the documentary format rather than a biopic featuring an actor portraying MKO Abiola?

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Oyamendan: I think the first reason we had to do it, or why I wanted to do it, was to fill a gap in our history. There is a huge gap, and many people, especially young people, know very little about our history. As a result, many misconceptions exist in public life. So, it was very important to tell this story and get it right.

I did not train as a documentary filmmaker. I went to film school to study filmmaking, and documentaries are one aspect of it. But when you tell a story like this, you have to rely on facts. I wanted to tell the story with evidence so we wouldn’t be interpreting events, but simply telling the story as it happened.

That is why making it a documentary was important. When you make a biopic, you often end up editorialising. I did not want that. We may do that later, but for now, it is important to put this story into the public consciousness exactly as it happened.

PT: Are you saying that if you had made it a film with actors playing the roles, some of the facts might have been distorted?

Oyamendan: When you make a biopic, you need some artistic licence to interpret how a person looks and talks. You rearrange history. This film is about more than MKO Abiola; it is about the crisis in Nigeria, and Abiola is our entry point into that story. That became the film’s focus. When you want to make a biopic about him, how do you begin? You have to take an angle, and we chose the political crisis angle. All of this is based on facts.

PT: How long did it take?

Oyamendan: We shot our first lens in November 2013. So, it took 13 years to get to this premiere, but we’ve done it. We could have shown it in the last four or five months.

PT: Why did you wait this long to tell this story?

Oyamendan: When we jumped into it, I thought it was a great opportunity to start because some of the people involved were getting old, while others were passing away. It took us that long to get started because I wanted to involve everybody, including the Abiola family. It was important to me to get Kola Abiola involved because, apart from being Abiola’s eldest child, he was actively involved in the campaign.

Once I got him on board, we started. We started in a rush and ran out of money. We didn’t secure much funding, and much of the challenge involved raising money to finish the project and getting key figures to speak towards the end.

PT: Did the documentary take a different direction from what you initially planned as you uncovered more of the story?

Oyamendan: It’s funny. My friend Azaria just sent me a treatment I shared with him about 17 years ago, in 2009, when I was only beginning to think about the project. It was about the same thing I set out to do, but the journey was different, what we discovered was different, and I learned as I went along.

It was very interesting because most of the key characters didn’t know the whole story. None of them knew everything. They all wanted to ask, “Well, did you find out?” I kept telling them, “You’ll see the movie.” There were a lot of surprises.

PT: I know you partnered with Nile; what informed your decision to take the film to cinemas?

Oyamendan: I mean, this is how films work. We wanted as many people as possible to see it. For me, as a cinephile, the usual process is to release a film in cinemas first and then make it available on streaming platforms. Streaming comes later because some people think, ‘Oh, we should start with streaming.’

I don’t think streaming platforms are paying a lot of money for African films at the moment, anyway. It’s important to follow the process step by step. That’s why we’ve taken this approach, and hopefully, the film will end up on a streaming platform at some point.

PT: How much did it cost to make the documentary, and did you receive any funding?

Oyamendan: The movie cost over a million dollars to make. We secured some private funding, but a lot of it came through gap financing. So, we owe a lot of money. It’s our film, but we don’t own it outright. We have to pay that money back, and we’re hoping we can raise the funds.

PT: Before MKO, what other projects had you worked on?

Oyamendan: I’ve worked on commercials, producing films and directing a lot of series. However, this is the first major project I’ve done in Nigeria. I mean, I made a short documentary about President Buhari and worked on several other projects, but this is the first big one. This is probably the first major documentary to be shown in a Nigerian cinema.

I’ve worked on TV series and some major web series. I also worked on Big Brother; they called it Obama at one point. However, the first major film I worked on was in the Middle East. It’s called As What I Remember? or Other Voices? I’m not sure which title it goes by, and I think it’s on Amazon. We filmed it in Israel and Palestine. It told the story of friends in Gaza who were friends with people in southern Israel, which is at the heart of the conflict and war. We filmed in both Gaza and Israel. That was my first really big project and probably the one that announced my arrival in the industry.

I don’t know; perhaps there have been one or two others. But this isn’t just a documentary like the ones you’ve seen excerpts from. It’s more like the story of our lives, and that makes it different. In many countries around the world, documentaries have had a transformative impact when shown in cinemas. I hope this one does well because, if it does, it will show others that they can do the same and give them the confidence to try.

PT: What role did you play in it?

Oyamendan: I was both the director and the producer.

World.title: INTERVIEW: Why many Nigerian marriages fail – Therapist Shamseddin Giwa
World.content:
In this exclusive interview with PREMIUM TIMES, marriage therapist Shamseddin Giwa discusses the factors contributing to marital breakdown, the societal pressures that keep some women in unhappy unions, and why women should consider leaving toxic relationships.

Excerpt:

PT: What hurts more in a marriage: infidelity or the lies and manipulation surrounding it?

Giwa: The actual infidelity hurts more because it doesn’t just begin with the affair; it begins with the intention behind it. There was a thought, a desire, then a deliberate action that followed, and it is this sequence, confirming a breach in loyalty, that hurts. The lies make it worse, but even without the lies, the infidelity on its own will still sting.

The lies don’t exactly stand alone; they form a part of the complete package of disloyalty. will factor into how much it will sting: who the infidelity is happening with, how long it has been going on, and the circumstances surrounding it. Complexity without wisdom and decency should not be enough reason for marriage. Has society become too obsessed with physical attraction at the expense of character?

Giwa: Unfortunately, this has been the trend for a while now; surface-level features have become much more important than deeper-level substance.

There aren’t enough people presenting themselves as worthy examples to the younger generation, and as such there’s a question mark over the essence of marriage to them. Many grew up hearing only the negative side of marriage and will argue it isn’t worth the stress, so they opt for something that can immediately offer the reward of fame and glamour.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Physical looks and beauty are important; attraction is key, but to sustain a marriage you’d need more. Social excitement has settled; the reality hits home on how much work needs to be done to make the marriage a success. That’s the point many realise: the beauty they went for needs so much more. Again, I’m saying beauty improves your chances of success with physical attraction, but it shouldn’t be the only thing to look for.

That said, if there aren’t many success stories of marriages out there, what incentive does that give society’s deeper values? Aren’t people and mentors helping to teach the coming generation about the importance of character, honour, loyalty and much more? How will they acquire this knowledge? We are a social media generation, but we are not maximising it to help reshape the narrative around marriage. I receive hundreds of messages daily on marriages, and most of them are negative.

This isn’t because there aren’t more success stories; it’s because people experiencing them choose to stay silent, believing it helps protect their homes. At some point, we need to step up and see this situation beyond our own units, from a broader societal perspective. That point, by the way, is now. Beauty without wisdom and decency is not enough for marriage, but what does that matter to people who want to snap pictures for weddings, push hashtags, get visibility, and be done with it?

PT: Are we witnessing a collapse of traditional marriage values, or are people finally becoming honest about unhappy unions?

Giwa: There’s an evolution in what marriage means, and there’s a huge decline in the popularity or practice of marriage using so-called traditional values. The socioeconomic angle is a huge influence. In the past, being a husband centred around financial provision and welfare, while being a wife was mostly about keeping the home. Today, the reality is very different.

Women have grown in aspiration and no longer want just to be confined to household chores and tending to children. This may not conform to traditional values, but it has numerous advantages, especially if balanced so the home front doesn’t suffer. How many young men today, given the economic state, can single-handedly provide for the homes and marriages of their choice?

This has shifted the mindset, with a more team-oriented approach taking hold. Instead of waiting several years in uncertainty, it is easier to find a woman to build with. For a woman to be financially present in the home, she needs a proper source of income, which takes us back to the earlier point about ambition. You’d find that having a means of livelihood certainly makes a woman stronger even from the marital perspective (again, if balanced right).

This throws up another issue, though. If the woman has to support herself financially, she needs to earn. She needs to work to earn, and work takes time, meaning she’d have less time to dedicate to the home. Unfortunately, many young men today want this support but aren’t ready to compromise by being more available themselves to help on the home front. The above is only about finances and welfare; every other area of marriage is evolving too. Men are being asked for emotionally.

Quality time is more of a priority now; you cannot just claim to have provided the funds and then become a spectator, as was common in the past. Now, you need to build an emotional connection that involves higher-quality intimacy, and Cohen, people speak about values changing; it is true, but it is not as negative as they make it out to be. Unhappy marriages have always existed in sizable numbers; the only difference is that the women from previous generations weren’t as vocal.

They were told to manage and focus on their children, almost as if having a happy marriage didn’t include emotional satisfaction. We saw many of those women grow into older women who neglected their aged husbands and went around to spend time with their children as nannies to grandchildren; the same children they were told to focus on when society should have helpedaage; the achievement achievement achievement achievement achievement achievement men should have been helped to become better and face the emotional needs of the wives. Today, more of those women are speaking up, and that’s why it seems like there are more unhappy marriages.

PT: What conversations about marriage make society uncomfortable but desperately need to happen?

Giwa: Any conversation around religion and tribe tends to be very sensitive and emotionally charged. This is even more important in marriage. One of the important things for a marriage to be successful is aligned values. A man must be on a life journey the woman can key into. The same goes for a woman; her journey must be one the man can and is willing to be a part of. We call coming together for continued growth and happiness a marriage.

Now, when it comes to value sets, nothing divides us like religion. Yes, it’s a live-and-let-live world, but there’s a huge difference between being good friends or neighbours and being married. In marriage, you are supposed to be aligned. If you believe salvation exists on a path, you should have a spouse who’d not just believe in that but be able to help you grow in it. This is unlikely to happen if your partner believes your path will lead to damnation. When children come, they inherit this disunity and often float around without proper grounding, or drift toward whichever parent they like better.

For me, worship of our creator is the primary purpose, and marriage should key into that. As such, it should be reflected in one’s choice of a partner; otherwise, there’d need to be a compromise of that worship (the one thing you should never have to compromise). Of course, people will point to prominent members of society who practice it, but just because a few popular people do something doesn’t make it the standard.

The complexity that comes with it also makes it a direction one should actively avoid, but speaking this truth in our community means being labelled. When these cases come to me, on the verge of a breakup, I often wonder why they weren’t told how complex it was going to be.

PT: If you could change three things about how Africans prepare young people for marriage, what would they be?

Giwa: The first will be in upbringing. The focus has mostly been on the girl child. While it is compulsory to raise the girl child right, it is also to raise the boy child right if we are to have a balanced society. In the end, girls’ education gets the focus, and boys are left untrained to choose from as husbands. Next is how much focus is placed on professional premarital counselling. Many people have been going through marriages for generations, making mistakes and gathering experiences in the process.

For a continuously growing society, it is key to leverage that knowledge to improve your chances of marriage. You cannot know it all, but knowing what’s possible and how to handle such possibilities upfront will definitely help people create stronger marriages. The third is our society’s value system. Truth be told, when you hear how some people talk about marriage and what they believe it should be, it feels abusive.

A wife cannot express herself freely; a man engages in infidelity and gets pardoned or even applauded, while it’s taboo for women, domestic violence, emotional abuse, neglect, lack of care, and so much more. If, as a society, we can create more loving narratives of marriages built around inclusiveness, transparency, honesty, loyalty, kindness and mutual growth, we’d be better for it.

PT: You often challenge men to take accountability in marriages. In your view, why do many men still struggle with emotional responsibility despite claiming to love their wives?

Giwa: You cannot give what you don’t have. A man raised to believe that marriage means he’s a ‘leader’ and, as such, can do whatever he pleases without question will often become a husband who lacks accountability. Our society doesn’t challenge men in this area. If you take society’s position on welfare and financing the home, there is no ambiguity: it’s clearly the man’s responsibility.
