Unfortunately, it is not the same when it comes to emotional responsibility. So a man goes into marriage believing all he needs to do is provide money, and that’s it; job done. He conditions his mind to meet this task and does so after a lot of hard work. At that point, because that’s all he planned for, there’s nothing left in the tank to be there emotionally except when he has a sexual urge. What consequences exist for the neglect? Nothing.

Our society tells the wife to manage what he provides. When we were defining responsibility in marriage, we, as a people, did not include the emotional aspect for men, and we appear to continue to make it acceptable. The irony is that this is contributing to cases of extramarital affairs by wives. A woman is human, too; she has emotional needs. Women in previous generations were told to ignore theirs and focus on children; we know how that played out.

The women today are either embracing their vulnerabilities in this capacity and engaging in extramarital affairs or remaining in marriages like that, broken and depressed. We need to do better in this regard.

PT: Some critics argue that social media has made women “too independent” and men “too defensive.” Do you agree, or is social media simply exposing problems that always existed?

Giwa: Social media, in this regard, merely acts as a resource tool and a convergence point, enabling expressions like never before. Whatever social media appears to be showing already existed. If a woman is speaking up more because she has found a space that makes her feel safe enough to express herself, it is because those feelings already exist. Social media didn’t create the feeling.

A man doing well as a husband and leader has nothing to get defensive over. Long before social media, salons, marketplaces, and radio call-in shows existed where people shared their feelings, found social connection, and discussed issues. Yes, social media does a significantly better job at this, but in the end, it all goes back to individual conduct within our spaces. A happy wife, treated well in her marriage, will have beautiful things to share. A man who is a good husband has nothing to worry about.

PT: You’ve said some men use pregnancy as a condition for commitment. Why do you think many women still fall into emotionally exploitative relationships despite seeing the red flags?

Giwa: We live in a society where marriage, as a woman, raises your status in people’s eyes. They see it as achieving something massive, and in some ways, it is. This increases the pressure to achieve it, especially when parents and family members keep piling on, urging you to bring somebody home. When friends run into you after a bit of time, the question they want to ask is whether you are married. Beyond that, low self-esteem can also make people accept poor standards as the norm.

A man asking you to get pregnant is directly telling you he wants to have the ability to sleep with you as he pleases until you get pregnant, if you get pregnant. He is not hiding his intentions; he is telling you directly how he rates you. Only if you get pregnant will he consider marrying you. That man, at best, will marry you as a vessel for bearing children or, at worst, will sleep with you until he is tired and moves on. You’d think this should be easy to refuse, but when social pressure and family taunts become too much, the man’s offer starts to feel like the easier option.

We talk about red flags, but how can a woman look out for red flags if she doesn’t even know what they are? The situation is so bad in some cases that the women are already conditioned to believe that if a man doesn’t desire them in this manner, then they are doing something wrong.

PT: Many people stay in unhappy marriages because of religion, children or public image. How do you help people separate endurance from self-destruction?

Giwa: As mentioned earlier, religion always sparks emotions, so the moment you begin to talk to people about what they can do better, they look at you as if you are asking them to betray their religion. There are so many exploitative interpretations that have been given to different scriptures across different religions, some twisted and the rest misunderstood. Take, for example, the concept of “for better or worse”, often used to keep people tied in many toxic marriages today. It goes further, even to keep people unable to marry if they somehow can break free from the marriage.

Our creator did not design marriage to be toxic, so when it is, the condition of staying together forever does not apply. Take the scenario of a woman who is married to a man who always beats her up physically. We all understand clearly that this woman should not be in that marriage, but somehow she is told to stay in it because of certain religious positions. Imagine this woman finding another woman who is ready to care for her and be kind to her in marriage, and she’s told that she cannot be married to that man because she was married to the previous man who was beating her.

Can anyone say that sounds right or is even fair? Yet, it still plays out in different areas because of religion. Marriage can be beautiful and good; don’t let anyone tell you otherwise. But if you have tried everything possible to make it better without success, then you know it’s time to leave. Pray for your marriage, have serious discussions about growth with your spouse, improve yourself, spice things up, create quality time, seek professional mediation and help. However, if you still find yourself on the negative side of life as a direct or indirect consequence of that marriage, I always tell people to draw the line there.

Don’t stay for the children; leave for the children! You do not want to raise broken individuals who would then go on to be spouses to other people someday, causing them heartbreaks and hurt. Perseverance is key, and patience is important, but if you have given all that’s listed above without any sign of improvement, leave that marriage before it breaks you.

PT: Do you think the African society romanticises suffering in marriage?

Giwa: Yes, I do, especially for women.

A good wife is the one who can manage lack and poverty while making the most of it. She is seen as the one who can keep quiet even when she is being wronged. She is the one who should never express herself, or it becomes disrespectful. She is the one who ignores the infidelity of her husband and focuses on her children. She is expected to be a glorified maid to her husband’s family before considering her own.

A popular cleric once said publicly, and it was reported across different media outlets, that the children of a woman who washes her husband’s clothes with a washing machine (and not by hand) will not be successful. If a so-called cleric is making such a statement publicly, imagine how much damage it does to his followers. But it’s not just him; many others, silently or vocally, share a similar mindset.

PT: What uncomfortable truths do men and women need to hear about marriage that society rarely tells them?

Giwa: There is always an option out there! Many people get married and fall into complacency, believing that a spouse is somehow stranded and cannot go anywhere. A spouse may stay, but it is never out of a lack of options. There is always a man or woman out there willing to replace you in whatever capacity. The false ideology of scarcity of men makes many women believe this, but in truth, there are more men than women in the world. There’d be many reading this and feeling the need to argue, but take five minutes to run the research.

Don’t just ask Google; check the numbers from the Bureau of Public Statistics. If you are not satisfied with that, check other reputable organisations like the United Nations, World Health Organisation (WHO), and even the World Bank. You’ll find the shocking truth that there are more men in the world than women. If this is the case, then you see how self-deceptive it can be for a man to convince himself that there are more women in the world and, as such, he can behave as he likes without consequences.

Also, you will change. Your spouse will change. It is easy to complain about physical changes, especially weight, but that’s normal. As you age, wrinkles will form, weight will fluctuate, erections will eventually weaken, the scrotum will sag, and so will the breasts. While it is important to be deliberate about fitness and wellness, accepting the normal ageing process helps condition expectations, especially for spouses. You should not be several years married and expect your spouse to have the body, energy, or performance level they had when you first got married.

Men engage in extramarital affairs; women do too. It is not one-sided. Don’t get so comfortable thinking your spouse cannot do it that you begin to neglect or maltreat them.

PT: From your experience, what are the leading causes of marital issues and divorce in Nigeria?

Giwa: At the top of the list are upbringing and values. Many young people today are going into marriage not even understanding what marriage means. They don’t understand the level of commitment required, and that’s what leads to many of the other issues that come up.

Take infidelity, for example, which is the most common case; the average man involved in it doesn’t even consider it an issue. To him, it’s a normal thing for men. Some would also hide behind seeking more wives, often with the statement “men are polygamous in nature”, when in truth, they only want to have multiple affairs.

While temptation is normal, your values and your ability to maintain boundaries keep you doing right by your spouse in marriage. Money is also a big issue today. This includes not meeting expected responsibilities, the distance created by seeking a livelihood in separate locations, and the general discomfort of lack and poverty. A family that is financially comfortable has one less area to worry about; arguments are less charged, frustrations are better addressed, and solutions are generally easier to find.

In law, dynamics play a big role in today’s society too. Women who were told, as wives, to ignore the misbehaviours of their husbands have now grown into mothers-in-law who use their children as a coping mechanism. These women have a very dominant presence in their children’s homes, resulting in tension and eventually conflict with their children’s spouses. The children are often caught between their mother and spouse, unsure how to take sides or resolve the issues.

The imbalance in how we address issues is also not helping. If we spend more time teaching and showing men how to be better husbands, instead of always making it about the woman who is expected to cook better meals, pray for him, wear sexy lingerie, and focus on children, we’ll resolve more issues before the marriage reaches the point of dissolution.

World.title: Podcast host to sue MTN, other telcos over alleged disappearance of 150GB data
World.content:
Kel Armstrong Amobi, host of the KaaTruths Podcast, said he vowed to take MTN Nigeria and other telecommunications operators to court over an alleged disappearance of more than 150GB of his mobile data.

Mr Amobi, popularly known as KAA, disclosed this in a post on X on Saturday, accusing MTN of failing to provide a satisfactory explanation of the incident, despite holding two telephone conversations with the company’s customer service representatives.

Mr Amobi said he and other parties will meet MTN and other telecommunications operators at the Federal High Court in Abuja on 18 November over the mysterious data disappearance.

According to him, about three weeks ago, he complained to MTN that more than 150GB vanished from his line, including the depletion of 20GB from his data balance within eight minutes, even though his mobile data was switched off at the time.

“Within minutes of making that post, @MTNNG replied publicly. They said they had investigated and that I actually used the data. They said this without even knowing which number was affected,” Mr Amobi stated.

The podcast host said MTN subsequently contacted him privately through X and requested to have a telephone conversation with him.

“On the call, a customer service agent apologised when I asked why they had lied publicly about an investigation that never happened. Then we got to the real issue. She admitted she had no answers. She said she would send the case to their technical team and call me back, he stated.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Amobi said the representative later called back with the outcome of the investigation, claiming that he had used 30GB on Google services and another 19GB on YouTube on the day in question.

Mr Amobi, however, disputed the claim, particularly the assertion that he consumed the 19GB on YouTube while attending a meeting at Transcorp Hilton Abuja.

The customer care officer could not give a convincing response to what happened to the remaining data, he noted.

“But let’s take it even further, according to my phone records. The iPhone 17 Pro Max eSIM has a 5,088 mAh battery capacity, and at 95 per cent battery health, it would take about 25-30 per cent to stream a 4K Video on YouTube for three hours. Still, on that day, my battery usage records showed that YouTube used only 2% of Battery and spent about 20 minutes of screen time,” he remarked.

He also claimed that his iPhone’s records showed total YouTube data consumption of 23.8GB over the 10 months he had used the device, making MTN’s insistence that he used 19GB on YouTube in one day questionable.

According to him, MTN’s explanation did not account for the remaining data or establish how the alleged consumption occurred while his mobile data was switched off.

The podcast host said he would not blame the customer service representative, describing her as an employee carrying out her duties, but insisted that the company’s management should account for its public claims and the unresolved complaint.

“My last words to her were: tell your people not to bother sending you again. Bring the explanation and the results of your so-called investigation to court. We meet MTN and the other telcos at the Federal High Court, Abuja, on the 18th of this month,” he said.

As of the time of filing this report, Mr Amobi has not responded to PREMIUM TIMES with the details of the legal steps he plans to take or other circumstances surrounding his experience with the mobile network operator. MTN is also yet to respond to this newspaper’s request for comment.

Similar encounters

Mr Amobi’s post triggered similar reactions from other social media users with similar past experiences with Nigerian telecommunicationsservice providers.

Akinrinlola Olamide, a software engineer, said she has had comparable incidents repeatedly, alleging that MTN’s data usage meter is no longer functioning on the telco’s app.

“This is ridiculous; it has been happening to mine too, and they keep doing it because I’m not talking; their data usage meter is no longer working on their app,” Mr Olamide said.

Also sharing his experience, an X user, Big Sam @_samueld_, expressed his displeasure with the disappearance of his 1.28 terabyte data subscriptions, adding that he reached out to the telco for a remedy to the situation but got no response.

“I wish I could go to court too. My 1.28TB data disappeared overnight! I have sent a detailed email to MTN and tagged necessary regulatory bodies; nothing has been done. More than a month has passed,” he said.

The complaints persist despite regulatory measures introduced by the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) to shield telecommunications subscribers from unexplained data depletion, billing errors, and poor network services.

In January 2021, the NCC announced that it had instituted a forensic audit to investigate complaints of unexplained data depletion and wrongful deductions from subscribers’ accounts, with the possibility of compensating affected consumers.

ALSO READ: MTN partners Omoni Oboli to unveil seven Christmas films on YouTube

However, complaints persisted, prompting the regulator in May 2024 to direct mobile network operators to audit their billing systems, following renewed reports of unexplained data depletion.

In July 2024, the commission also introduced the Nigerian Communications (Quality of Service) Regulations, which established minimum service-quality standards for telecommunications operators. It provided for the measurement, reporting and monitoring of network performance.

When complaints about rapid data depletion and inaccurate billing persisted, the NCC, in August 2025, directed telecommunications operators to engage independent audit firms to scrutinise their billing systems.

The regulator has also introduced additional consumer-protection measures, including a refund framework for failed airtime and data transactions in January 2026 and a compensation framework for subscribers affected by poor network services in March 2026.

That notwithstanding, complaints of unexplained data depletion remain commonplace, raising questions about the efficacy of existing regulatory measures and the transparency of operators’ billing systems.

The extent to which subscribers can accurately verify their data consumption also remains uncertain.

World.title: Concerns mount as APC failed to present party’s flags to candidates at Ondo rally
World.content:
The failure of the All Progressives Congress (APC) to present its National and State Assembly candidates at Wednesday’s presidential campaign rally for President Bola Tinubu in Akure, the Ondo State capital, has heightened concerns about deepening divisions within the party in the state.

The omission has triggered speculation about the level of cohesion within the Ondo APC, particularly against the backdrop of lingering disagreements arising from the party’s primaries and the emergence of the Rainbow Coalition.

The development was particularly noticeable as the APC had presented its candidates to voters in other states, including Rivers, Ebonyi, Cross River and Ekiti, where candidates for governorship, National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly elections were publicly recognised.

In Akure, however, the flag presentation ceremony, widely regarded as a symbolic endorsement and formal introduction of candidates as the party’s standard-bearers, was conspicuously absent.

Although the rally attracted a large crowd, with candidates and their supporters adequately represented, none of the party’s 12 National Assembly candidates or 26 Ondo State House of Assembly candidates was publicly presented or handed the party’s flag.

The rally was colourful, featuring campaign banners, branded outfits, drums and enthusiastic supporters. However, there were moments of tension when a group of supporters reportedly became agitated with the musician performing at the event over what they perceived as his failure to acknowledge their candidates while recognising prominent party chieftains.

A party chieftain in Odigbo Local Government Area, Ademokun Folorunsho, expressed concern over the omission, noting that the candidates had attended the rally with their supporters but were not given the recognition accorded to their counterparts in other states.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He also drew attention to the invitation extended to D.I. Kekemeke to offer the Christian opening prayer, noting that despite his presence, he was not introduced as the APC candidate for Ondo South Senatorial District.

“Another detail worth mentioning was the invitation of Hon. D.I. Kekemeke to offer the Christian opening prayer. However, he was not introduced as the APC candidate for the Ondo South Senatorial District,” he observed.

According to Mr Folorunsho, the development raises questions about the political direction of the APC in Ondo State, particularly regarding its National Assembly contests.

He recalled that the reported absence of some candidates from the inauguration of the Ondo State Presidential Campaign Council at The Dome, Akure, had earlier generated concerns about the extent of cooperation among party members.

While cautioning against drawing definitive conclusions from the rally, Mr Folorunsho argued that the failure to present the candidates could suggest that the National Assembly contests remained politically unsettled.

“While it may be premature to draw a definitive conclusion from the ceremony alone, one possible interpretation is that the National Assembly contests in Ondo State remain open, with no public endorsement or presentation of any candidate as the party’s preferred candidate at the rally. And this presents hope for the Rainbow Coalition in Ondo State,” he said.

“For now, the absence of flag presentation has left room for speculation. The rally has not communicated a clear political direction. It has been established that the NASS contest is open to everyone.

“Only President Tinubu will get one million votes, but the remaining candidates must contest on their personality and credibility in Ondo State.”

The concerns over the party’s internal divisions were also reflected in the speeches of prominent APC leaders at the rally.

The Senate Leader, Opeyemi Bamidele, appealed to party leaders in Ondo State to set aside their political differences, particularly those arising from the party’s primaries, and work together to secure the votes needed for President Tinubu’s re-election.

Similarly, the Secretary of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Governor Hope Uzodimma of Imo State, expressed concern about the divisions within the Ondo APC, warning that the party’s ability to deliver its promised one million votes for the president could be undermined if its members failed to unite.

A former governorship aspirant and APC chieftain, Olusola Oke, however, expressed confidence that party members in the state would overcome their differences and rally behind President Tinubu.

The speeches at the rally suggested a willingness among party leaders to close ranks for the purpose of securing victory for the president, although questions remain about whether the apparent unity will extend to the National and State Assembly contests.

Reacting to the concerns, the Ondo State Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Idowu Ajanaku, said the responsibility of determining the order of activities at the rally rested with the Presidential Campaign Council and not the state chapter of the APC.

He said he was unaware that candidates had been presented or handed party flags at the event, explaining that the rally was primarily organised to advance the president’s campaign.

“I can assure you that the APC leaders in the state will be united in the canvassing of votes for the President,” he said.

Mr Ajanaku, however, acknowledged that the influence of the Rainbow Coalition could affect the party’s fortunes in some State Assembly constituencies, conceding that some seats might be won by candidates of other political parties.

The APC Director of Publicity in Ondo State, Steve Otaloro, also dismissed suggestions that the omission was targeted at any candidate or group within the party.

According to him, the rally was specifically organised to flag off President Tinubu’s campaign, while the tight schedule of national party leaders made it impossible to accommodate the presentation of other candidates.

“We had no time for the presentation of candidates because the national leaders were to leave for Abuja that same day,” Mr Otaloro said.

He assured that the opportunity would be provided at the zonal campaign flag-off, where Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa would make efforts to present the party’s candidates to the electorate.

Mr Otaloro attributed the suspicions surrounding the omission to existing divisions within the party, alleging that some individuals were attempting to challenge the leadership of the APC in the state and its relationship with the state government.

With the presidential campaign now underway, the challenge before the Ondo APC appears to extend beyond mobilising voters for Tinubu. The party must also address lingering grievances among its members and establish a common political direction ahead of the National and State Assembly elections.

Whether the promised unity will translate into collective support for all APC candidates or remain limited to the presidential contest is a question that the party’s subsequent campaign activities may answer.

World.title: Nigeria risks repeating oil-era failures in minerals sector, expert warns
World.content:
Nigeria risks reproducing the economic and environmental failures of its oil industry in the development of its solid minerals sector unless it strengthens regulation, improves resource management and ensures host communities benefit from extraction, an expert has warned.

Tengi George-Ikoli, Nigeria Country Manager at the Natural Resource Governance Institute (NRGI), said the country had failed to translate nearly seven decades of commercial oil production into broad-based economic development.

“We have not,” Mrs George-Ikoli said when asked whether Nigeria had benefited from its petroleum resources.

She spoke in an interview with PREMIUM TIMES on the sidelines of the ongoing COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye.

She said although oil and gas had remained important sources of government revenue and foreign exchange, successive governments had failed to use the proceeds to build other productive sectors, create sufficient jobs and improve conditions in oil-producing communities.

The scale of the country’s dependence is reflected in its extractive sector’s contribution to public finances and trade.

Nigeria’s 2023 Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) report showed that extractive industries accounted for 54.4 per cent of government revenue and 82.52 per cent of exports.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Yet, Mrs George-Ikoli said, communities where extraction takes place continue to contend with poverty, unemployment and environmental damage.

She warned that Nigeria could repeat these failures as it seeks to attract investment into minerals increasingly important to global energy and industrial supply chains.

‘Mining needs stronger foundations’

Nigeria’s solid minerals sector remains small compared with its petroleum industry.

The 2023 Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative Solid Minerals Industry Audit Report put its contribution to gross domestic product at N1.76 trillion, or 0.75 per cent.

The report also recorded mineral exports of 4.32 million metric tonnes, valued at N117.29 billion, while royalties amounted to about N9.01 billion.

Mrs George-Ikoli said the country should not assume that mineral wealth would automatically deliver economic diversification or replace oil revenues.

In an August 2026 report co-authored by her, NRGI similarly cautioned that mining projects could take years to develop and might generate less public revenue and employment than governments expect.

She said Nigeria needed to strengthen the institutions governing the sector before expanding investment, pointing to the Nigerian Minerals and Mining Act of 2007 as a framework that requires reform.

“We need to strengthen our governance structures. It took us how many years to reform that in the oil and gas sector with the Petroleum Industry Act,” she said.

She identified effective regulation, transparent licensing, a sound fiscal regime and reliable geological information as priorities.

According to her, Nigeria must establish what minerals it has, where they are located and whether they exist in commercially viable quantities before negotiating with investors.

“We need to provide data. We need to really map out where our resources are, what it is that we have, in what level of commercial quantities as well, what sort of value, so that as we continue to have increasing investments or interest in us, we will be able to negotiate better for Nigeria,” she said.

She also stressed that communities must have a meaningful role in decisions about extraction and a fair share of its benefits, warning against reproducing the weaknesses she sees in the host community development trust arrangements under the Petroleum Industry Act.

Beyond extracting raw minerals

Mrs George-Ikoli said Nigeria should pursue mineral processing and value addition where commercially viable, rather than insist on processing every mineral locally regardless of available resources or capacity.

She advocated cooperation among African countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia, Ghana and Uganda, to develop regional processing and manufacturing industries.

She said Nigeria’s market size and industrial potential could position it as a regional processing hub, while collaboration with other mineral-producing countries could strengthen Africa’s bargaining power in global supply chains.

“We are feeding global supply chains, but we’re not really benefiting as much as we could individually,” she said.

She argued that countries working together could retain more economic value from their resources and create technical jobs beyond raw mineral extraction.

Gas expansion also raises concerns

Beyond mining, Mrs George-Ikoli questioned whether Nigeria’s ambitious gas expansion plans adequately reflect production constraints and changes in international energy markets.

The country’s Decade of Gas initiative seeks to expand production and develop a gas-powered economy by 2030. However, an NRGI report published in September 2026, co-authored by Mrs George-Ikoli, found that Nigeria was unlikely to achieve its target of adding 4.6 billion cubic feet per day of gas production by 2030.

Even under the report’s most expansive scenario, additional production would reach about 1.3 billion cubic feet per day.

Mrs George-Ikoli said Nigeria also needed to consider how much of its future gas supply would meet domestic needs, including electricity and industrial development, rather than be directed towards exports.

She warned that investments in long-term oil and gas projects could become less commercially attractive as global energy markets and regulations change.

She called for greater investment in renewable energy and other productive sectors, alongside plans to support workers and communities affected by the energy transition.

She said these priorities should feature in Nigeria’s national development plans and future climate commitments, as well as ongoing negotiations on the Just Transition Work Programme under the United Nations climate process.

World.title: Awujale Succession: Why govt can’t abdicate its statutory responsibility, By Soji Adeyemi
World.content:
The controversy surrounding the succession to the revered Awujale throne of Ijebuland has reached a point where the distinction between legitimate customary authority and the statutory responsibilities of government must be clearly understood. What should ordinarily be a structured process governed by tradition, established chieftaincy procedures and the laws of Ogun State is increasingly being complicated by misinformation, political insinuations and attempts to portray legitimate government oversight as interference.

At the heart of the controversy is a fundamental question: Should the Ogun State Government abandon its statutory responsibilities simply because the succession involves a traditional institution?

The answer is unequivocally no.

The Awujale stool is not an ordinary traditional institution. It is one of the most distinguished and historically significant traditional thrones in Yorubaland. Its integrity, prestige and continuity are matters of considerable public interest. Consequently, the process of selecting its next occupant must be conducted with the highest standards of transparency, fairness, procedural discipline and fidelity to the law.

The Ogun State Government is not the kingmaker. It has no authority to impose its preferred candidate on Ijebuland, nor should it attempt to substitute its judgment for the legitimate functions of the ruling house and kingmakers. However, this does not mean that government must become a passive observer when questions arise about the legality, regularity and credibility of the succession process.

The Ogun State Obas and Chiefs Law, 2021, together with the applicable Chieftaincy Declaration, provides the statutory framework for the appointment and recognition of traditional rulers. These provisions are not decorative legal instruments. They establish the boundaries within which customary authority must operate and define the responsibilities of government in ensuring compliance.

It is therefore fundamentally erroneous to suggest that government has no business with the process once a ruling house begins the nomination exercise.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The ruling house has its customary responsibilities. The kingmakers have their legally recognised functions. Government, on its part, has regulatory and administrative responsibilities under the law, including the exercise of applicable approval and review powers. These roles are distinct but interconnected. Respecting customary authority does not require government to abandon the law, just as exercising statutory oversight does not confer on government the power to select a monarch.

This distinction is particularly important in the present circumstances. The late Oba Sikiru Kayode Adetona occupied the Awujale throne for an extraordinary 65 years, transforming the institution into a symbol of authority, stability and cultural pride. His reign elevated the profile of Ijebuland nationally and internationally. The process of selecting his successor must therefore reflect the dignity of the institution he left behind.

It would be a grave disservice to that legacy if the succession became defined by procedural controversies, competing claims, financial inducements or political manoeuvring.

Government has indicated that its interventions have been informed by petitions, procedural concerns and considerations relating to peace and security. These are not matters that a responsible administration should ignore. Where credible questions arise about the conduct of a chieftaincy process, the appropriate response is to examine them within the provisions of the law, rather than allow unresolved disputes to undermine the legitimacy of the eventual outcome.

Indeed, permitting a process clouded by unresolved procedural questions to proceed unchecked could create a more complicated situation in the future, potentially exposing the emergence of the next Awujale to prolonged litigation and avoidable institutional instability.

There is also the equally important question of protecting the sanctity of the throne from commercialisation. The selection of an Awujale must never become an exercise in financial competition, where the ability to deploy money, political connections or personal influence becomes more decisive than the provisions of customary law.

The throne is an institution of history, heritage and collective identity. It must not be reduced to an instrument of personal ambition or financial advantage. The applicable customary procedures and statutory provisions must remain the ultimate determinants of the process.

Those who disagree with the government’s interpretation of its statutory responsibilities are entitled to challenge its actions through appropriate judicial channels. Indeed, the Fusengbuwa Ruling House has instituted legal proceedings challenging aspects of the government’s intervention. That is a legitimate constitutional avenue, and the courts remain the appropriate authority to determine contested questions of law.

What should be discouraged, however, is the growing tendency to substitute anonymous publications, social media campaigns and unsubstantiated allegations for established legal processes.

At the same time, government must recognise that the legitimacy of its intervention depends on the manner in which it exercises its powers. Every action must be transparent, impartial, properly documented and firmly anchored in the law. No aspirant should receive preferential treatment, and no ruling house or kingmaker should be deprived of rights guaranteed under the applicable customary and statutory framework.

The objective must not be to secure an outcome favourable to any individual or interest, but to guarantee a process that commands the confidence of Ijebuland and withstands judicial scrutiny.

Governor Dapo Abiodun has publicly assured the people of Ijebuland that a new Awujale will emerge before 29 May 2027. This commitment should be pursued with the seriousness and urgency it deserves. However, speed must not come at the expense of due process. A credible succession is far more important than a hurried conclusion that could generate fresh disputes.

Ultimately, the Awujale throne belongs to Ijebuland and its people. It is not the personal possession of any aspirant, ruling-house official, kingmaker or political interest. Its preservation is a collective responsibility that transcends individual ambitions and temporary political disagreements.

The responsibility of government is not to choose who wears the crown. It is to ensure that whoever eventually occupies the throne emerges through a process consistent with the law, established custom and the overriding interest of peace and stability in Ijebuland.

Those who genuinely desire the preservation of the Awujale institution should be more concerned about the credibility of the succession process than about manufacturing controversies around government’s involvement.

Government must not usurp customary authority. But neither must it surrender its statutory responsibility in the name of avoiding controversy. Protecting the integrity of the Awujale throne requires both respect for tradition and fidelity to the law.

*Soji Adeyemi is a member of the Ijebu Focus Group, Ijebu-Ode

World.title: Tinubu flags off construction of $3.5bn Bakassi Deep Seaport
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu on Friday flagged off the construction of the $3.5 billion Bakassi Deep Seaport in Cross River State, reviving a project that had suffered years of delays and which the federal government says will expand Nigeria’s maritime capacity.

The groundbreaking ceremony took place in Bakassi, with Vice-President Kashim Shettima representing Mr Tinubu. The president described the project as a strategic investment that could diversify the economy and position Nigeria as a major hub for maritime trade.

The project is expected to include a deep seaport with a 20-metre draft and a 260-kilometre superhighway to evacuate cargo to other parts of the country, Stanley Nkwocha, a senior special assistant to the president in the office of the vice president, said in a statement on Friday.

Mr Tinubu said the port would reduce the concentration of Nigeria’s foreign trade through Lagos and create opportunities for other coastal states.

“There is a rumour I hear in some corners. That the West, Lagos, or Abuja never wanted a port to work anywhere outside Lagos. If that were true, would I be standing here today with a shovel in my hand?” he said.

He added: “Lagos is our elder brother in trade. No country eats with one hand. No country carries all its load on one shoulder. That shoulder will break.”

According to the president, more than 80 per cent of Nigeria’s foreign trade currently passes through Lagos, a situation he said could cause congestion, delayed shipments and higher prices.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“This project is not against Lagos. It is for Nigeria. When Lagos is free, Nigeria breathes. When Calabar works, Nigeria walks on two legs,” he said.

Mr Tinubu said the port was first conceived during the colonial era and re-engineered in 2014, with its Environmental and Social Impact Assessment completed in March 2015. He said the project later stalled before Cross River Governor Bassey Otu revived efforts to secure its implementation.

The president said the state secured $3.5 billion in financing from the African Export-Import Bank and formalised a public-private partnership arrangement in February 2025.

“Today, the Federal Government is standing fully behind it. This is beyond a Cross River dream. It is a Nigerian project,” he said.

Mr Tinubu said Nigeria’s blue economy could generate $44 billion annually if the country captured cargo traffic currently moving through neighbouring countries. He urged residents to support the project and protect it from political interference.

Otu recounts hurdles

Speaking at the ceremony, Mr Otu said the project had faced political, environmental and legal obstacles before the Tinubu administration supported its revival.

“When this project was conceived by the immediate past administration in the state some years ago, its implementation was encumbered by political, environmental, and legal bottlenecks. Arising from this hurdle, our hope of realising the project was dimmed until President Tinubu took over the mantle of leadership of Nigeria,” the governor said.

He said the president approved additional marine corridors, including the Bakassi port, as well as the expansion and upgrade of existing seaports.

According to Mr Otu, the initiative would give coastal states a greater role in the national economy by diversifying economic activities and strengthening their revenue base.

Mr Otu said his administration completed technical and regulatory processes before securing final approval for the Bakassi project.

“We carried out an environmental impact assessment, conducted and obtained a report of the hydrographic, geotechnical, and geophysical surveys. We also secured a federal executive council approval for the project with a $2.27 billion initial funding,” he said.

He said the project would be executed through a public-private partnership and stimulate investment in logistics, trade, fishing, shipping, tourism and shipbuilding.

The governor also said the state was preparing local workers for the construction and operation phases.

“While we cannot rule out the need for foreign technical expertise in the construction of the seaport, we are conscious of the need to complement the same with our indigenous manpower,” he said.

He added that selected Cross River residents were undergoing specialised skills training, with the aim of transferring the knowledge to more people in the state.

Economic prospects

The Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority, Abubakar Dantsoho, said the port could strengthen trade links between Nigeria and landlocked countries, including Chad, Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

The African Export-Import Bank also backed the project. Its president, George Elombi, represented by the bank’s Executive Vice-President for Intra-African Trade and Export Development, Kanayo Awani, said the investment could expand port capacity and facilitate trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area.

Mr Tinubu said the port would accommodate large vessels that cannot currently access some Nigerian ports, while the planned highway would connect cargo to markets across the country.

At the African Sub-Sovereign Governments Network Investment Conference in Calabar on Friday, Mr Shettima urged state governments to identify their competitive advantages, prepare bankable projects and attract private capital.

He said development depends on implementation at the subnational level, where infrastructure connects producers to markets and businesses create jobs.

World.title: Diphtheria: MSF warns of treatment shortages as Nigeria records over 1,100 deaths
World.content:
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned that shortages of a lifesaving medicine are forcing medical teams to ration treatment for diphtheria patients in northern Nigeria, where more than 28,000 confirmed infections and 1,100 deaths have been reported this year.

The warning comes as figures attributed to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) show that the outbreak continues to spread, particularly among children who are unvaccinated or have not received all their recommended vaccine doses.

In a statement issued on Friday, MSF said supplies of diphtheria antitoxin (DAT), which neutralises the toxin responsible for potentially fatal complications, were dangerously low.

The organisation called on federal and state authorities, donors and international partners to urgently secure additional medicines and vaccines, ensure their timely clearance at ports and improve distribution to affected communities.

Treatment shortage threatens patients

MSF’s Medical Coordinator in Nigeria, David Kizito, warned that the shortage could compromise the treatment of severely ill patients.

“Our stocks are dangerously low, and we risk being unable to treat children and save lives as the outbreak continues,” he said.

Diphtheria is a vaccine-preventable bacterial infection that can cause fever, sore throat and a thick membrane in the throat, sometimes obstructing breathing. Severe infections can damage the heart, nerves and kidneys.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), diphtheria antitoxin neutralises toxins circulating in the bloodstream, while antibiotics help eliminate the bacteria and reduce transmission.

Early administration of antitoxin is particularly important because it cannot reverse damage once the toxin has entered body cells.

MSF said limited global production and inconsistent availability had left treatment facilities struggling to obtain adequate supplies.

However, the organisation did not specify which facilities had exhausted their stocks, how many patients had been unable to obtain treatment or whether any deaths were directly attributable to the shortages.

Nigeria records 1,126 deaths

The warning comes amid a prolonged outbreak that began in late 2022.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that a situation report issued on 11 November by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and the Nigerian Red Cross Society, citing NCDC data, indicates that Nigeria recorded 37,529 suspected diphtheria cases, 28,151 confirmed infections and 1,126 deaths in 2026 as of 7 November.

The report said the outbreak had affected 26 states and the Federal Capital Territory, covering 361 local government areas.

Kano accounted for 12,008 confirmed cases, approximately 43 per cent of the national total.

The figures are substantially higher than those in MSF’s latest statement, which relied on NCDC statistics from 9 August, when 406 deaths had been reported for 2026.

The difference reflects reporting from separate periods and may include subsequent updates to surveillance records.

Katsina: 70 severe cases in 18 days

In Katsina State, MSF reported managing 86 diphtheria cases between 26 October and 12 November, including 70 classified as severe and 16 as non-severe.

Severe infections accounted for approximately 81 per cent of the patients managed by its teams during the period, although the figures do not represent the severity of all diphtheria infections recorded across the state.

MSF said its teams also reached 1,315 contacts through surveillance and contact-tracing activities. Of these, 1,301 received vaccinations, while 1,311 were given preventive antibiotics.

The organisation did not provide the locations of the cases or a breakdown of recoveries and deaths.

The development follows earlier concerns about the capacity of health facilities to manage the outbreak.

On 31 August, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Federal Teaching Hospital (FTH), Katsina, was struggling with an influx of suspected and confirmed diphtheria patients, leaving its children’s ward under considerable pressure.

The hospital attributed the overcrowding partly to referrals from other facilities across the state.

In response, the federal government announced an emergency multi-agency task force to strengthen surveillance, immunisation and access to treatment in Katsina and Kano.

The intervention included plans to supply additional antitoxin, antibiotics, medical personnel and protective equipment to FTH Katsina.

Authorities also announced plans to establish treatment annexes across Katsina’s three senatorial districts — Katsina, Daura and Funtua — to reduce pressure on the referral hospital.

MSF’s latest statement did not indicate whether those facilities had become operational or how much additional antitoxin had been delivered since the intervention was announced.

Zamfara vaccine shortage

In neighbouring Zamfara State, MSF said its supported facilities in Gusau recorded more than 671 diphtheria admissions over approximately one month beginning on 6 October.

Most patients were children, while four out of every five had not been vaccinated.

The organisation also reported a substantial shortfall in vaccine supplies for an emergency immunisation campaign.

Of the 90,000 doses required, only 25,000 had been supplied, representing approximately 28 per cent of the stated requirement.

MSF said it was working with government health authorities to secure the outstanding doses and expand vaccination activities.

The shortfall highlights the continuing difficulties facing efforts to protect children against the disease.

In October, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Executive Director of the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), Muyi Aina, said about 93 per cent of children affected by recent diphtheria outbreaks had not received their full recommended vaccine doses.

Mr Aina said some had never been vaccinated, while others had received fewer than the three recommended doses. He identified misinformation and vaccine hesitancy among the challenges affecting immunisation uptake.

MSF’s response

Despite the challenges, MSF said its teams had treated more than 9,000 diphtheria patients through facility-based and community interventions since the beginning of its 2026 response.

In Kano, the organisation supported vaccination campaigns in April and June, administering more than 835,000 doses to children in partnership with the state Ministry of Health.

It also supported two vaccination rounds in Sokoto between February and April, reaching 49,018 children under 15.

The organisation said it was supporting treatment, surveillance, infection prevention and vaccination efforts in several northern states, alongside government health authorities.

MSF called for increased global production of diphtheria antitoxin and sustained investment in routine childhood immunisation to prevent further outbreaks.

The latest warning also draws renewed attention to the emergency measures announced by the federal government in August, particularly the delivery of antitoxin supplies and the proposed expansion of treatment facilities in Katsina.

The extent to which those interventions have improved access to treatment remains to be established.

World.title: 2027 UTME: JAMB moves to block wrong subject combinations, introduce pre-registration app
World.content:
Professor Segun Aina

…to deploy tougher biometric checks, allow candidates report faulty questions, rate CBT centres

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, JAMB, is set to introduce sweeping technology-driven reforms ahead of the 2027 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination, UTME, including a pre-registration mobile application, stricter biometric verification and a system that will automatically block candidates from selecting wrong subject combinations.

The reforms, which are aimed at reducing registration difficulties, preventing examination malpractice and strengthening the credibility of the admission process, will also give candidates access to vital admission information before making their course and institution choices.

JAMB Registrar, Professor Segun Aina, disclosed the plans on Saturday in Abuja, saying the proposed pre-registration application would enable prospective candidates to complete key registration procedures from the comfort of their homes before visiting accredited centres for final registration.

Aina spoke after a five-kilometre fitness walk organised for the board’s staff as part of activities to prepare for the 2027 UTME.

He explained that the application would allow candidates to retrieve their personal information from the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), fill in their biodata, and select preferred subjects, courses, and institutions ahead of the actual registration.

According to him, the application would also provide candidates with advance academic guidance, including information on the previous year’s entry marks for their preferred courses.

The initiative, he said, would help candidates make more realistic academic choices based on their abilities and available admission requirements, rather than making uninformed selections that could jeopardise their chances of securing admission.

“There are a lot of innovations that are coming up. Now we are rolling out what we are calling a pre-registration application.

“It’s a mobile application that allows you, from the comfort of your own home, to get your details from NIMC, register with your biodata, select your subjects, your courses and your institution.

“During that process, we will be giving some advanced advisory that we didn’t use to give before. For instance, when you are trying to select a course, you will see an idea of what the entry marks for that course were in the previous year,” he said.

The registrar said the application would significantly reduce the time candidates spend at registration centres, particularly during the capture of their biometric information.

Beyond making registration easier, Aina said JAMB was also working on a system that would make it technically impossible for candidates to submit applications containing incorrect subject combinations for their chosen courses.

He noted that candidates had, in previous examinations, made subject selections that were incompatible with their preferred courses, sometimes creating avoidable difficulties in their admission pursuits.

“We are going to make that technically impossible, which means you cannot progress with your application if the subject combination is wrong. And a lot of other innovations are coming,” he said.

On examination security, the JAMB boss said the board would strengthen biometric verification at examination centres to prevent impersonation, malpractice and other irregularities.

He explained that although the board had introduced some concessions to reduce the difficulties candidates encounter when correcting their biodata, such flexibility would be matched with stricter identity checks during the examination.

“We have given up some ground and made some concessions to reduce trauma for the candidates in terms of being able to change their biodata and things like that.

“And in exchange for that, we will be applying enhanced checks at the point of the examination to make sure that we protect the integrity of the system,” Aina stated.

In another innovation, candidates sitting for the 2027 UTME will have the opportunity to report examination questions they consider faulty through a dedicated button on the computer-based test platform.

Aina said the feature would enable candidates to flag potentially defective examination questions in real time, allowing the board to investigate such complaints and determine whether the questions were properly framed.

He, however, cautioned against the assumption that difficult questions were necessarily faulty, stressing that the proposed reporting mechanism would help JAMB obtain evidence-based feedback for assessing the quality of its examination items.

The board is also planning to introduce a post-examination rating system that will allow candidates to assess the quality of services provided by their respective Computer-Based Test (CBT) centres.

According to the registrar, the feedback mechanism is intended to strengthen accountability among private sector partners operating the centres while helping JAMB maintain high operational standards.

He acknowledged the contributions of CBT centre operators to the examination process since the board adopted computer-based testing more than a decade ago, but stressed that continued partnership would go hand in hand with strict monitoring.

The proposed rating system, he said, would give candidates a direct channel to evaluate their examination experience and provide the board with information needed to identify centres that fall short of expectations.

Aina said the innovations were part of broader efforts to improve candidates’ experience, eliminate avoidable registration errors, strengthen examination security and sustain public confidence in the nation’s tertiary education admission system.

World.title: Atiku tackles FG as bakers lose 40% membership
World.content:
Atiku Abubakar

By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja

Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar has blamed President Bola Tinubu’s economic policies for the loss of nearly 40 per cent of the membership of the Premium Breadmakers Association of Nigeria in two years, warning that soaring energy costs and high interest rates are driving local businesses out of operation.

The development, he said, underscores the growing strain on businesses, with bakeries shutting down, workers losing their jobs and households paying more for bread, one of Nigeria’s everyday staples.

Atiku, who was in Bauchi on Saturday to promote his affordable life campaign and sympathise with Nigerians grappling with the effects of government policies, spoke in a statement signed by his Director of Strategic Communication, ADC Presidential Campaign Council, and Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu.

“From farmers to manufacturers and now bakers, the verdict on Tinubu’s economic reforms cannot be clearer: they have been a monumental failure,” he said.

The former vice president identified rising energy costs and expensive credit as major constraints on bakery operations, noting that energy alone accounts for about half of production costs.

He cited the case of a bakery operator whose monthly diesel bill reportedly increased from N9 million to N19 million, while small-scale bakeries require between N40 million and N50 million to switch to alternative energy sources.

He added that businesses seeking loans face interest rates of up to 34 per cent, further limiting their ability to sustain production and invest in more efficient operations.

Atiku said the pressure extends beyond the baking industry, citing rising cooking gas prices, which he said had reached N1,800 per kilogramme in Abuja and N1,650 in parts of Lagos and Ogun states.

He also cited a 31.8 per cent increase in depot prices within one month, from N1,100 to N1,450 per kilogramme.

Turning to the Federal Government’s borrowing, Atiku questioned the accumulation of domestic and foreign loans amid the reported closure of local businesses, alleging that Nigerians were yet to see tangible benefits from the debt.

“The irony is that while the economy is falling under Bola Tinubu’s watch, his government has accumulated local and foreign loans in astronomical figures. If local businesses are dying while the government continues to borrow, Nigerians are entitled to ask where these loans are going. One is forced to conclude that they are feeding the corruption in Tinubu’s government,” he said.

He called for a shift in economic priorities towards strengthening domestic production across sectors, rather than concentrating exclusively on crude oil refining.

“The major policy plank of my administration will be to improve local production in every sphere of the economy, not just crude oil refining.

“To farmers, manufacturers, bakers and everyone involved in local production: the Atiku Economic Recovery Plan understands your pains, and your concerns are captured in my policy objectives,” he added.

Atiku urged the Federal Government to urgently address rising energy costs and the lack of affordable financing, warning that continued pressure on productive businesses could further undermine employment, local manufacturing and household purchasing power.

World.title: Spain will host 2030 World Cup final, federation president insists
World.content:
The 2030 World Cup final will be in Spain, Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) head Rafael Louzan reiterated on Saturday, adding that he is not considering “withdrawing” should he be wrong.

Spain is organising the next World Cup with Portugal and Morocco. The decision on the venue for the final will be made in 2028, Louzan said.

Spain favours Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu Stadium for the final. Portugal does not have a suitable stadium but Morocco has suggested the 115,000-capacity Hassan II Stadium being built in Benslimane near Casablanca.

“There is no other plan than for the final to be held in Spain,” said Louzan at a conference at the RFEF’s Ciudad del Futbol on the outskirts of Madrid.

“I am not currently considering the possibility of withdrawing from Spain, as the prospect of Spain not hosting the final is not on the table,” he said.

Louzan was responding to Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the right-wing People’s Party.

In a television interview on November 5, Feijoo said that were he to become prime minister in the general election on November 29, he would advocate withdrawing Spain’s bid to host the World Cup should Morocco be awarded the final.

Luzon said the question was entirely hypothetical.

“That notion simply doesn’t exist,” he said, adding that under FIFA’s tradition of rotating the World Cup the staging of the final “belongs to the European continent”.

A delegation of FIFA technical experts spent last week visiting Spanish stadiums that are hoping to host matches during the tournament, Louzan said.

World.title: 2027: I’ll restore fuel subsidy, tackle insecurity if elected — Atiku vows
World.content:
By Christopher Ameh, Bauchi & Ayobami Okerinde

Former Vice-President and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) Atiku Abubakar has promised to restore fuel subsidy and tackle insecurity if elected president.

Atiku made the pledge on Saturday during the ADC presidential campaign rally in Bauchi State, where he urged residents to vote for candidates of the party across all elective positions.

“I have already promised all Nigerians that I will restore petroleum subsidy. Not only that, I will also restore subsidy in electricity,” he said.

Atiku also pledged to address insecurity in the Northeast and other parts of the country, while promising to expand petroleum exploration in the Kolmani area to generate additional revenue.

He called on Nigerians to support the ADC, urging voters in Bauchi to elect the party’s candidates from the presidency to the councillorship positions.

The former vice-president thanked the people of the state for their previous support, saying Bauchi had consistently given him substantial votes in past elections.

He urged residents to turn out in large numbers during the 2027 polls and ensure their votes were protected and counted.

“I want you to make sure you come out in your thousands. You vote for ADC. You defend the vote. You ensure that the votes are counted, and results are transmitted before you leave the polling booth,” Atiku said.

President Bola Tinubu announced the removal of petrol subsidy on May 29, 2023, during his inauguration, declaring that “the fuel subsidy is gone”. He said the funds would instead be redirected to infrastructure, education, healthcare and job creation.

Atiku has repeatedly promised to restore petrol subsidy if elected in 2027. In August, he reiterated the pledge, questioning how the savings from its removal had been spent.

The former vice president was accompanied by his running mate and former Minister of Transportation, Rotimi Amaechi, ADC National Chairman, Senator David Mark, and other party leaders, said his administration would prioritise policies aimed at alleviating the economic hardship confronting Nigerians.

Also associated with the Bauchi campaign delegation was the party’s governorship candidate in the state, Senator Halliru Dauda Jika, alongside other ADC chieftains and political stakeholders.

World.title: Kwankwaso’s daughter seeks divorce from Kano gov, offers to refund dowry
World.content:
File image for illustration.

By Hadiza Yusuf

The second wife of Kano State Governor, Abba Kabir Yusuf, Zainab Musa Kwankwaso, has filed for divorce at an Upper Area Court in Gudu, Abuja, offering to refund the dowry paid by the governor.

Zainab, a daughter of former Kano State Governor Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, is seeking to dissolve the marriage through Khul’i, an Islamic procedure that allows a woman to seek divorce by returning her dowry or offering compensation.

According to court documents, the court has summoned Governor Yusuf to appear on November 17, 2026, to respond to the suit.

In her claim, Zainab cited a breakdown of the marriage, alleging a persistent lack of love, care, affection and emotional connection.

She also told the court that efforts to reconcile them had failed and expressed willingness to refund the dowry paid on their wedding day.

Zainab married Yusuf on July 29, 2006, and their marriage produced six children.

Her divorce suit comes weeks after she reportedly left the Kano Government House for her father’s residence before travelling to Abuja.

World.title: Microsoft announces service ‘restored,’ global outage over
World.content:
This illustration photograph shows the Microsoft Outlook logo (L) displayed on a smartphone with the backdrop of Microsoft logo on a screen, in New Delhi on November 13, 2026. Microsoft said on November 12 that efforts to repair a major outage of Outlook were not going as expected and the firm was seeking alternative solutions as users around the world were left without its crucial services. (Photo by MANAN VATSYAYANA / AFP)

Tech giant Microsoft said Saturday it has “restored service” to customers, effectively drawing a close to a massive outage that caused chaos and disrupted public services and business around the world.

“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the US-based company said in an X post.

Microsoft had already reported a “broad recovery” for Outlook email and other services the day before, stating the major disruption was due to a technical issue and “not related to cyber or AI/agents.”

The outage swept the globe on Thursday, taking the company’s products offline in at least 74 countries and territories across the Americas, Europe, Asia and Africa, according to the monitoring site Downdetector.

Microsoft had attributed the disruption to “elevated load” on its infrastructure.

It said the stoppage affected its Outlook email service, as well as Microsoft’s Teams communication platform and the company’s Copilot AI assistant.

World.title: 2027: We won’t allow religion to divide us, Makinde declares
World.content:
…seeks Muslim community’s support for Adekanmbi

By Adeola Badru

Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), ‘Seyi Makinde, has declared that his administration will not allow religious differences to divide the people of the state, insisting that they share a common ancestry and must remain united irrespective of their faith.

Makinde, who made the declaration on Saturday, also appealed to Muslim leaders across the state to use their influence to promote unity, peace and political stability ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The governor spoke at the opening of a three-day conference for Imams, Alfas/Ulama, political office holders and traditional rulers, tagged Rabitah 2026, organised by the League of Imams and Alfas in Yoruba Land (Rabitah tul Aimma wal Hulammai fii Biladi Yoruba) at the Jogor Event Centre, Ibadan.

The conference, with the theme, “The Responsibilities of Politicians and Electorate During and After Electoral Process,“ brought together prominent Islamic clerics, scholars, traditional rulers and political stakeholders from across the South-West.

Makinde noted that discussions surrounding the choice of the next governor of the state had intensified ahead of the elections, urging political and religious stakeholders not to allow such developments to create divisions along religious lines.

“We won’t allow religion to divide us. Let us pray for our state and country because this is the period leading to the next election, when a new set of leaders will emerge.“

“There is a lot of discussion going on right now about the choice of who will become the next governor.“

“What matters most is that we must stay united. The progress of Oyo State is what is important to us, and I believe God will answer our prayers. For us in Oyo State, religion is not an issue.“

“We have all religions in our various families, and we have always coexisted peacefully,” he said.

Makinde further illustrated the historical and familial connections between Muslims and Christians in Oyo State, disclosing that his own family background reflected the religious diversity he was advocating.

He said: “I, standing before you, am Oluseyi Makinde.

“Makinde was my grandfather on my father’s side. My father’s name is Olatunbosun, and my grandfather, Makinde, lived and died as a Muslim. Those who are familiar with Oyo know this history.“

“If I were to convene an extended family meeting this evening, about 65 per cent of those who would attend would be Muslims.“

“I want to appeal to us that we must not allow ourselves to be divided along religious lines because we share the same ancestry and the same blood flows through our veins.”

The governor urged participants at the conference to use the gathering to pray for the continued peace and development of the state, stressing that religious differences should not undermine the bonds that unite the people.

“Therefore, as this conference progresses, let us pray and work towards sustaining our unity. We must continue to recognise that we are one, irrespective of our religious differences,” he added.

He also cautioned Muslim clerics against allowing individuals to exploit religious sentiments to create confusion and division during the forthcoming electoral process.

Makinde urged them to deploy their influence towards promoting peaceful participation, tolerance and responsible political engagement, rather than allowing religious identity to become a tool for political manipulation.

In support of the conference, the governor announced a donation of N50 million to the organisers, describing the gathering as an important platform for religious engagement and collective prayers for the state and the country.

He also called on Muslim clerics and traditional religious leaders to play a constructive role in the 2027 electoral process, noting that they would have a significant opportunity to engage voters before they make their choices at the polls.

According to him, political office-seekers and candidates would inevitably approach religious leaders and worship centres to solicit prayers and support as the elections draw closer.

“As the Lord has designed the democratic process, the 2027 elections are approaching. Irrespective of what happens during the political process, you, as religious leaders, will have the final opportunity to interact with the electorate before they cast their votes.“

“Politicians and political candidates will visit your various mosques to seek prayers and support ahead of the elections.“

“I therefore urge you to use that opportunity to appeal to the people to support us and, more importantly, to pray for Nigeria,” Makinde said.

Meanwhile, the League of Imams and Alfas in Yoruba Land declared that it will neither endorse nor declare support for any politician or political party ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The Chairman of the League’s Board of Trustees, Sheikh Muhammad Habibullah Adam Abdullahi El-Ilory, said the organisation could not announce any preferred candidate or political platform ahead of the forthcoming elections.

He stressed that Islamic clerics were not politicians and that their responsibility was not to campaign for political office-seekers or parties but to pray for the emergence of credible leaders.

“We are religious leaders; we are not politicians, but we are the fathers of politicians. We will not declare support for any political party or politicians.“

“We, the League of Imams and Alfas in Yorubaland, cannot declare support or announce our support for any politician or political party. We can only pray to God for Him to give us credible leaders,” he said.

The League’s President, Sheikh Jamiu Kewulere, also maintained that religious leaders should concentrate on their spiritual responsibilities rather than become involved in partisan political activities.

According to him, Imams and Islamic clerics were expected to guide the people, promote moral values and preach Islam in accordance with its principles.

“We are not politicians. An Imam is not supposed to be involved in politics. Our focus should be to guide people and preach the religion of Islam in line with Islamic principles,” he said.

Similarly, the Grand Mufti of Yoruba Land, Sheikh AbdulRasaq AbdulAzeez Ishola, explained that the conference was convened to strengthen unity, understanding and cooperation among Muslims across Yorubaland before, during and after the 2027 general elections.

He said the gathering was also designed to encourage religious leaders, political office holders and traditional institutions to appreciate their responsibilities in sustaining peace and democratic stability.

The conference was attended by the APM governorship candidate in Oyo State, Abimbola Adekanmbi; his running mate, Mr Open Salawu; and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, Alhaji Hazeem Gbolarumi.

Also present were the League’s President, Sheikh Jamiu Kewulere; Chief Imam of Ibadanland, Sheikh Abdulganiy Abubakar; Alfa Agba of Ibadanland, Sheikh Abdulbari Adetunji; Grand Mufti of Yoruba Land, Sheikh AbdulRasaq AbdulAzeez Ishola; Secretary-General of the League, Sheikh Mustapha Oseni Adewale Hamzat; Chairman, Oyo State Pilgrim Welfare Board (Muslim Wing), Sheikh Hashim Atere; and Professor Kamil Olosho.

Others included the Aare Musulumi of Yorubaland, Alhaji Daud Akinola; the Soun of Ogbomosoland, Oba Afolabi Olaoye; the Onigbeti of Igbeti, Oba Bashir Abioye; and the Iyalode Adini of Yorubaland, Alhaja Sedeekat Aderibigbe, alongside other prominent Islamic clerics, scholars and Muslim faithful from Oyo, Osun, Ogun, Ekiti, Lagos and Ondo states.

The opening ceremony also featured lectures delivered by two university professors, Professor Amidu Sanni and Professor Adam Surajudeen, who addressed participants on issues relating to the responsibilities of political leaders and the electorate during and after elections.

The conference is expected to provide a platform for discussions on the role of religious institutions, political office holders, traditional rulers and citizens in ensuring peaceful elections, responsible leadership and national development.

World.title: ‘It’s unfortunate’ – Melaye reacts to Galadima’s claim on Justice Lifu’s illness
World.content:
Dino Melaye has described as unfortunate elder statesman Buba Galadima’s comments linking him to discussions surrounding the health of Federal High Court judge, Justice Peter Lifu.

Melaye said he never made any comment about Lifu’s health, noting “I was extremely shocked to hear that Alhaji Buba Galadima mentioned that I made comments on Justice Lifu’s health.

“It is most unfortunate because I never made any comment on Justice Lifu’s health.

“Old age must be catching up with Buba Galadima. Now I know you can’t cure old age, you can only manage it,” he wrote on his X (Twitter) page.

Galadima had criticised members of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, over their reported reaction to Lifu’s health.

In an interview on African Independent Television, AIT, on Wednesday, Galadima mentioned Melaye while referring to information that the ADC had obtained a certified true copy of the judgment delivered against the party.

Galadima, a chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, said: “You know there was a judgment against ADC, isn’t it? Yes. And I’ve just heard you read something that Dino Melaye said.

“They’ve got a true certified copy of the judgment, and I know some ADC people are jumping up and down that the judge (Peter Lifu) who gave a ruling against them has fallen ill and is supposed to be taken to hospital in Europe.

“I just found out that maybe there aren’t intelligent people in the ADC. They didn’t know that if that is true, it is deliberate to deny them appeal. Because if the judge goes to London or Europe or anywhere outside the country, the records of proceedings from his judgment cannot be signed by any judge.

“So no appeal could be had until he’s back. They didn’t know that they are playing on their intelligence, and that’s why Nigerian politicians are lazy. They don’t think,”

Vanguard News

World.title: Ondo APC Dismisses Division Claims, Rules Out Political Violence
World.content:
Fidelis David in Akure

The Ondo State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) yesterday dismissed claims of internal divisions within its ranks, declaring that its reconciliation efforts are yielding results as it mobilises support to secure at least one million votes for President Bola Tinubu in the January 16, 2027 presidential election.

The party also expressed confidence that its growing unity would translate into electoral victories for Tinubu and other APC candidates, insisting that no member or interest group had been excluded from its ongoing reconciliation and mobilisation efforts.

Speaking at a press conference at the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) Press Centre in Akure, the state chairman, Mr. Babatunde Kolawole, dismissed reports of rivalry among party leaders, maintaining that members remained part of the same political family.

He argued that there was no reason for political rivalry, particularly as Ondo State would not conduct a governorship election in 2027 and Tinubu had already emerged as the party’s sole presidential candidate.

“Therefore, there is no rivalry. There is no cause for alarm. I can assure you we are on top of it and everything will be okay,” Kolawole said.

The chairman appreciated Tinubu, the APC National Chairman, Senate Leader, Senator Michael Opeyemi Bamidele, and other party leaders for their support and contributions to strengthening the party.

Also speaking, the Director General of the APC Presidential Campaign in Ondo State, Victor Olabimtan, said the reconciliation committee constituted after the party congress had reached out to party organs, interest groups and individuals within and outside the state.

He disclosed that the committee had visited Abuja to engage some party leaders and extended its consultations to Lagos and other parts of the country, adding that the participation of previously estranged leaders, including Wale Akinterinwa and Princess Oladunni Odu, at the recent presidential campaign rally in Ondo State demonstrated the progress made.

Olabimtan said he had personally reached out to some aggrieved members, while Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa had made the unification of all tendencies within the party a major priority.
