World.title: Travelers stranded, flights canceled after ground stop. Here's what we know
World.content:
Airspace across the United States slowly began returning to normal on Saturday after a rare national ground stop canceled thousands of flights and stranded travelers.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference Saturday, "We are back at full operations."

He thanked the pilots, airline staff, air traffic controllers and the FAA for their professionalism during the ground stop.

"They safely landed all of our aircraft," he said, also thanking the passengers for their patience during the significant disruption.

"Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly," Duffy said earlier in a social media post on Saturday.

"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."

More than 4,100 flights were canceled Saturday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, while around 3,200 others were delayed.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, arrives for a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

How did the FAA ground stop happen?

The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. EST Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air.

"The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.

It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. EST Friday.

This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country.

Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said.

Duffy said Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. The router that was being switched then started flooding other routers, overloading the system. There were 1,000 attempts to log on every four to five seconds, he said.

Visitors watch an airplane as it prepares to land at Washington Dulles International Airport after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted nationwide ground stops in Chantilly, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Cliff Owen/ AP Photo

The transportation secretary said the FAA is working to determine if the issue was human error or if a faulty router was installed. Duffy said that many contractors "take our money and provide really poor service." He also said that L3Harris, a technology and defense company, owned the system.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said updating the wires was a routine maintenance issue that the agency had been working on for years. About 70% of the system has been transferred from copper wires to fiber. After the router began flooding the system for 45 minutes, the FAA could not determine the cause of the instability. The instability then spread to 17 facilities, he said.

"Out of an abundance of caution," the FAA decided to issue a ground stop, Bedford said. He said he stands behind that call.

Bedford said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious or anything AI-related.

Senior government sources told CBS News on Friday that the issue was isolated to specific hardware: Cisco 600 series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Duffy said in a post that the FAA is working to modernize "this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down payment secured by President Trump, but that isn't ENOUGH." The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $50 billion late Friday.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Friday briefing there were no indications the ground stop was the result of a cyberattack. Duffy said Saturday he doesn't believe it was a cyberattack, but that it was an FAA system that didn't "meet the moment."

Can Americans still travel safely?

Several U.S. officials said it is completely safe for Americans to fly.

"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said. He added on Saturday that the U.S. has the "busiest" and "safest" airspace in the world.

The FAA administrator said on Saturday there were 50,000 flights scheduled for Friday and by the time the ground stop happened, 30,000 flights had been completed. Due to the ground stop, about 12,000 flights were not able to be completed — around 3,000 of those were private flights, while the rest were commercial, Bedford said.

Bedford said there will possibly be 5,000 flight cancellations on Saturday, but airlines should be fully back on schedule by the end of the day Sunday.

Delays remain possible at major airports nationwide, including those in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

An American Airlines flight takes off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

Duffy said travelers should check with their airlines before heading to the airport. Delta said on Saturday it would offer customers flexible rebooking options. The airline said it was continuing to restore operations after a four-hour ground stop.

"Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft, " Delta said.

American Airlines said on Saturday the airline has taken a number of steps toward recovery, but travelers should continue to monitor the situation as operations return to normal.

"While we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations."

World.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide
World.content:
The United States has lost its measles elimination status, researchers with knowledge of the decision confirmed to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. The agency is set to hold a news conference on Tuesday.

A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continue to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. New York and Wisconsin have each reported one death.

Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that the disease's spread can be sustained, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."

Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."

How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?

A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.

Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshhold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.

Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."

Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.

Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.

By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.

That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.

Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.

Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 did not get vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.

While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.

Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.

Some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated for measles, so they rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading. Awan said that these groups of people will bear "the brunt of the consequences" of increased measles spread.

"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.

World.title: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
World.content:
FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images North America

Friday's nationwide ground stop was declared after an error occurred while a contractor was updating an old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication line, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

L3Harris, a long time contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration, was doing routine maintenance in at least one of FAA's remote locations changing copper wire to fiber, he said. Duffy said the routers in these facilities were manufactured in 2001. These updates have been happening in American institutions for decades, Duffy said.

"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital," Duffy said. "Just maybe the FAA is the last one to be doing this work because the investments haven't been made, but this is not complicated."

Sponsor Message

L3Harris did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.

Duffy said the FAA is still investigating the exact error that started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system.

"It's pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location. So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?"

Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, who joined Duffy at the briefing said there was no evidence of anything nefarious happening or AI-related issues.

Thousands of passengers miss flights

Tens of thousands of passengers across the U.S. are still stranded Saturday after a rare ground stop halted all flights.

The chaos is expected to linger for days.

The aviation system is back online and slowly returning to normal Saturday morning, but delays and cancellations will continue after yesterday's nationwide ground stop, Duffy said in the press briefing Saturday.

"Based on everything that we're hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they'll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday," Bedford said.

Duffy told reporters Friday night: "I think we're going to be back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving."

Sponsor Message

For about four hours on Friday, thousands of flights at U.S. airports were grounded in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

Nearly 25,000 flights were delayed, and over 9,000 were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking site. The disruption seeped into Saturday morning with more than 4,000 cancellations recorded. That's 14% of flights departing the U.S., according to data from Cirium, which tracks aviation analytics.

Duffy said Friday that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed "old switches, old routers" for the failures. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.

Flight boards at airports across the country Saturday morning continued to be riddled with red cancelled marks. At Tampa International Airport in Florida, people in the main terminal area before security curled up in chairs to grab a wink of sleep.

On Friday night, a flight board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in D.C. showed dozens of flights delayed into the early morning hours or cancelled.

Passengers Erin and Jake Britt spent half the day at the airport in D.C. on Friday. Their plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. boarded at 3 p.m. By 5:30 p.m., they were getting off the plane — but they were still in D.C.

"Overall, our plane was definitely annoyed, but reasonable," Erin Britt said, as the couple left the airport at 8pm. "People being upset and asking like, 'Well, how are you not prepared for this?' And it was like, 'Well, no one was prepared.'"

She said neither the pilot nor flight attendants had any more information than passengers."They seem just as in the dark," she said.

Sponsor Message

The pair decided to cancel their weekend trip, but the night didn't end there. They spent over nine hours overnight waiting on the JetBlue customer service call line to be reimbursed. "I was setting alarms in 20 minute intervals in case I fell asleep," Erin Britt said.

For people who had events or plans over the weekend – the delay added an extra layer of stress. Joe Romano and Maddie Cabana had a cruise leaving Orlando, Fla. Saturday afternoon.

"It was a big eye roll. I mean, I travel a lot for work already, so I'm constantly dealing with flight delays," Romano said. "When this happened, I was just like, 'Of course, it always happens to me.'"

"Just rather inconvenient and frustrating," Cabana added, as the pair contemplated checking their bags or going home. "Hopefully, everything will be fine. It'll all work out. It always does."

And it did – eventually. After their JetBlue flight was ultimately cancelled, they quickly booked another one on Southwest Airlines and made it early Saturday morning.

toggle caption i Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images

Others, like Suze DiPietro decided flying wasn't worth it anymore. Her husband drove about four hours down from Ocean City, New Jersey to pick her up in D.C. Luckily, they had friends in the area where they spent the night.

"My husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me," DiPietro said.

Other alternatives included people switching to Amtrak trains as they struggled to get to their destination. Although, even Amtrak's system had a brief outage Friday night.

This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

Sponsor Message

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.

World.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
World.content:
Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president

toggle caption i Esteban Felix/AP

SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

Sponsor Message

But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.

Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.

But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.

Sponsor Message

In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.

toggle caption i Esteban Felix/AP

This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.

On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.

It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.

"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.

Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.

To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

World.title: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries
World.content:
Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries

toggle caption i Lindsey Wasson/AP

A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly.

Loading...

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Sponsor Message

Opponents of Alaska's elections say the current system is confusing and can be manipulated.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

Democrats denied recruiting the independent Sullivan, who made the top-four general election ballot and has defended his candidacy.

However, proponents of Alaska's system have said that the state's ranked choice voting system could blunt the effects of any confusion. Voters had the ability to rank both Dan Sullivans and not rank Democrat Mary Peltola, for example.

Massachusetts voters this year decided not to switch to a top-two nonpartisan primary system. And during the last election cycle, in 2024, several states considered measures that would create a nonpartisan system similar to Alaska's. Voters rejected all of those ballot measures.

World.title: Perspective: A new kind of White House press secretary
World.content:
Perspective: A new kind of White House press secretary

toggle caption i Alex Brandon/AP

There has been no White House press secretary for almost a month. But have you really noticed?

Katie Zacharia held the position for 5 days in the middle of October, but her lone briefing was … brief and not well-reviewed.

After several secretary-less weeks, President Trump declared in an online post that he would ask Dana White, the head of the UFC, to take the job, calling him "a violent Fighter and Warrior." Reporters imagined how the CEO of a martial arts league might answer a sharp question with a swift kick to their journalistic chops. "What's the President's plan to bring down inflation?" Then, Bang! Thwap! Ooof!

Sponsor Message

The president later clarified that he, "was only kidding," about Dana White. He added wistfully, "You wouldn't mess around with him so much."

Even as the number of White House press briefings has declined during the second Trump administration, the president himself has had almost 500 "interactions" with the press: in interviews and press conferences, or impromptu Q&As at a ceremony, aboard Air Force One or while walking to the new White House helipad.

And, really, what is the need for a press secretary when a chief executive can announce whatever they want directly to millions of people on social media at any hour? President Trump posts dozens of times a day on his Truth Social platform, without those pesky reporters around to interrupt his message with fact-checking, contrary opinions or context.

I'd like to float another idea. Why not make the next White Press secretary an AI chat bot? That's how so many corporations now respond to customer complaints and inquiries.

They could call the new White House spokesperson Ben. As in Ben Franklin. Who doesn't like Ben Franklin?

When reporters call or log in to Robo-Ben and ask, "What is the president's response to President Putin's latest statement?" Ben might mellifluously reply, "I'm glad you asked that. I understand your interest." And nothing else. If White House reporters snap back, "But Ben, you're not answering the question!" Robo-Ben might respond, soothingly, "I understand your frustration. Thank you for your patience. Please stay on the line for our Media Satisfaction Survey."

World.title: As Democrats win big, thirst traps of male candidates take social media by storm
World.content:
As Democrats win big, thirst traps of male candidates take social media by storm

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

If you're on social media, there's a good chance you've seen the videos: people getting hot and bothered about the young men Democrats just elected.

"I'm looking at you, Rob Sand. I'm looking at you, Jon Ossoff. I'm looking at you, El-Sayed," said fitness coach Jesse Barton, reacting to the midterm results. "I am looking, I am not the only one, and I'm very happy about what I see."

There are debates over candidates' relative levels of hotness. There are a lot of AI-generated images. And there are many, many montages of the politicians set to sexy pop music.

Sponsor Message

One of the most viral pieces of content was a parody Tiger Beat magazine cover featuring Democratic men … which Manoushka Guerrier, an LA-based chef and content-creator, took one step further.

"I created the entire Tiger Beat style personality quiz, complete with the different boy band personas," she said. The quiz gives people matches including "the Babyface" (Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico) and "the Heartthrob" (Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel).

Guerrier pays a lot of attention to politics, and she emphasizes that these guys' looks are just a bonus.

"They're young and they're ballsy and they're smart, and they're not just smart; they're brilliant," she says.

The tidal wave of attention on these young men creates a striking contrast to the first Trump midterm, in 2018. That election — after the Women's March, Me Too and the long list of assault and misconduct allegations against President Trump — yielded a record-setting wave of Democratic women. It all suggests that the thirsty social media posts aren't just a cheeky trend; they also say a lot about how Democrats have responded to the Trump era.

A response to Trump

Two main forces are behind the wave of attention on these men according to Christina Wolbrecht, a political science professor at Notre Dame University.

"I think it's a function of our kind of society-wide debate about masculinity," she said. "And I also think it's about age."

Sponsor Message

The age side is straightforward — just ahead of the midterms, a majority of likely voters said they favored candidates with new ideas over those with experience in the job, according to a NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll.

The masculinity side, meanwhile, is in response to MAGA and its elevation of a very specific type of manhood, Wolbrecht said.

"For 10-plus years, Donald Trump has presented one very distinct version of masculinity," she said. "It's very much power over [others]. It's very much power through wealth and status."

Manliness took center stage on the Democratic side this election. Candidates leaned into it, with people like Rutinel and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed posting weightlifting videos. El Sayed at one point did a video spoofing Love Island.

Voters noticed, posting admiring videos well before the election. Meanwhile, the media noticed and amplified this narrative, with profiles and think pieces throughout the midterm cycle, and reporting on Democrats' "rugged" and "authentic" candidates.

'That's a girly thing to be, is a Democrat'

Amplifying young, "manly" men may have boosted the party in this election. That's because Democrats had a problem after Kamala Harris lost the presidency in 2024, according to Democratic strategist Monica Venske.

"The feeling within the straight male demographic, if you will, [was] that it just wasn't cool to be a Democrat," she said. "It wasn't sexy to be a Democrat. It's not manly to be a Democrat. That's a girly thing to be, is a Democrat."

That's why she started the Instagram account Boyfriends We Deserve, where she highlights attractive Democrats — mostly men, but a few women as well.

Venske explains she is careful in how she posts about women's looks — unlike when she talks about men, like Montana's incoming Democratic congressman.

toggle caption i Tailyr Irvine for NPR

"Like when I call Sam Forstag hot, it will most likely never, ever hurt him," she said. "But I can call someone like Keisha Lance Bottoms hot and that could hurt her every time."

Sponsor Message

She said she instead will call the women "baddies" or focus on their hair, as opposed to highlighting their bodies or overall looks.

To Venske, the Boyfriends We Deserve posts are part of making it clear that the Democratic party is a big tent that includes young men.

"I'm like, 'Look at all these manly guys who are Democrats,'" she said. "Sam Forstag is an example I usually give. He was like a smokejumper in Montana. And in his announcement video for Congress, he's fixing up a truck. If a guy who is jumping out of planes to put out fires and fixing up trucks can be a Democrat, you can be a Democrat, I promise."

…But Democratic women won, too

All of that said, plenty of Democratic women ran and won this year, including several historic firsts: Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms, for example, will be the first Black woman governor. New Mexico's Deb Haaland will be the first Native American woman governor. Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan will be the nation's first Native American woman senator.

That highlights a big difference between this midterm and 2018's wave of women.

Since that election, Democrats have seen Joe Biden defeat Trump, and then watched a second woman lose the presidency to Trump. And while Democrats most certainly do still elect women — far more than Republicans — the masculinity of their male candidates received outsized attention this year.

It's possible, then, that the attention on Democratic men isn't simply lighthearted, but is part of Democrats' continual conversation about electability.

"I hear it from all sorts of people with all sorts of engagement that 2016 and 2024 proved that it took old-guy, aviator sunglasses Joe Biden to defeat Trump," Wolbrecht said, "and we need more of that and not more Kamala Harrises or Hillary Clintons."

"I think that's a mistake," she added quickly. "I think it's a misunderstanding of what happened in '16 and in '24. But the meaning we put on elections has consequences and it really shapes what parties do strategically going forward."

Sponsor Message

Democrats have struggled to win over men in recent elections. For example, Harris won 43 percent of men overall in 2024. This year, the party won 50 percent of the men's vote.

Guerrier disagrees that the attention on candidates' looks is about electability, but she thinks that for a lot of voters, this election was about changing the Democratic Party's story.

"It was just like these guys came out of nowhere, and it was just so refreshing that, wow, we can get out of this darkness and into something that is hopeful," she said.

World.title: Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?
World.content:
Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/Getty Images

Democrats are not in the majority yet, but the first post-election test of their ability to get things done was a failure.

The House was unable to advance an impeachment effort of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats were no-shows for the vote. Based on the math in this vote: If those 11 had been there and if no more Republicans showed up, the attempt would have gone forward.

Now, for those who want to see Hegseth impeached, it's fair to ask why only one Republican was in favor of it, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who led the effort, especially after an election that saw GOP wipeouts in no small measure because of the Iran war? The GOP still controls the floor, so a Democratic speaker would have been able to leave the vote open longer for the 11 to be able to cast their votes.

Sponsor Message

But it's also fair to ask if this would have happened under Nancy Pelosi's watch? (Ironically, she was one of the 11 who didn't vote for advancing Hegseth's impeachment because she had flown back to San Francisco for a veterans' event.) Or if this kind of effort is what people want in the first place.

First, on the Pelosi point: The former House speaker and retiring congresswoman was known for the discipline she kept in her caucus. She knew where the votes were, who was voting how and why – and, most importantly, did not move forward with efforts that didn't have the votes.

Hakeem Jeffries, the heir apparent Democratic leader, is going to have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. His leadership and agenda priorities are going to be scrutinized and compared to Pelosi – and this wasn't a great start to this new era.

Second, on whether impeachments are what people want to see: it depends on which people. Certainly, the Democratic base — and some beyond that — wants accountability for the Trump administration.

Voters more broadly also said corruption was a top issue in the campaign. But walking the line between reasonable accountability and oversight versus impeachments is a potential tight rope.

Sponsor Message

Democrats will have to balance the mandate they were given to bring down prices (sound familiar?) and end the war with the accountability of the Trump administration that many in the Democratic base feverishly wants and expects.

What do voters want?

A Reuters/Ipsos poll taken after the election, found that 8-in-10 people think Democrats' focus in the first 100 days should be on the cost of living, three-quarters said lowering health care costs, 7 in 10 said lowering gas prices, while 6 in 10 said ending the Iran war and eliminating President Trump's tariffs.

What about investigations and impeachment? Only 40% said investigating the Trump administration should be a priority in those early days. But 71% of Democrats do want this to be a first 100 days focus. Only 36% of independents said the same.

Almost two-thirds said they are concerned that Democrats will spend too much time on investigations, which included, by the way, half of Democrats.

When it comes specifically to pursuing impeachment of Trump, only 33% said they think it would be good for the country. On the other hand, 63% of Democrats do. Only 30% of independents said it would be good for the country.

More than half also said they think Democrats should at least make efforts to work with the Trump administration. That, however, only included 40% of Democrats.

So this is going to be tricky to navigate for Democratic leadership, but a major part of a speaker's job is messaging, particularly when that speaker's party does not control the White House.

So what will Democrats focus on when they're in charge?

People are going to be watching the new Democratic majority for what it focuses on, and even with the Hegseth effort, it was clear that many conservatives were thrilled with not only how it went but that Democrats were fueling Massie's effort.

It arguably backfired and strengthened Hegseth's position within the administration. The White House and Republicans rallied around him. Even if some Republicans on Capitol Hill might have misgivings with Hegseth for one reason or another, and they and Vice President Vance think the war in Iran was the main reason for the midterm losses, opposing Democrats is far more unifying.

Sponsor Message

Politics is often (some would say too often) a team sport, and no group is more conditioned to put the T-shirt on and run the playbook than the red team.

It certainly gave Republicans more of a chance to go on offense than talking about health care, the cost of living or the war and gas prices.

Democratic leadership is certainly aware of the line it has to walk, but Jeffries is going to have to make some decisions. Asked on PBS NewsHour this week if Democrats would be impeaching more Trump officials, he said, "We will cross that bridge when we get to it."

But a House speaker is the one who builds the legislative bridges. He or she controls the agenda.

Jeffries, of course, also noted, as he has elsewhere, that affordability is a priority.

"We're committed to driving down the high cost of living in every area," he said. "That's housing, that's health care, that's groceries, that's gas, that's caregiving – to making this country affordable again for everyone."

Democrats will be tested

Democrats have been given a huge opportunity with majorities in both the House and Senate — but the balance of priorities, timing, messaging and discipline are all going to be major tests.

The stakes couldn't be higher. Arguably, what Democrats focus on will lay the foundation for views of the party's competence heading into the 2028 presidential election, and they don't want to squander the advantages they have.

The Ipsos poll showed that Democrats have big leads on which party has a better plan, policy or approach for health care (42%-23%), the cost of living (40%-25%) and the economy (37%-30%).

But they have to be careful. A lot of people are not convinced that Democrats are focused on the issues that are important to them. Only 47% in the Ipsos poll said that, including only 40% of independents.

Sponsor Message

Only 44% said they're confident that Democrats are putting the best interests of the American people above their own personal interests.

So while Democrats have the wind at their backs, the jury is still out on whether people are confident in their leadership.

World.title: A new policy could help solve the U.S. organ shortage. Critics say it's unethical
World.content:
A new policy could help solve the U.S. organ shortage. Critics say it's unethical

toggle caption i Olga Pankova/Getty Images

The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.

The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known as NRP. It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.

"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.

Sponsor Message

NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says. More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.

Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates the Dead Donor Rule, which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.

"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross, a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."

The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.

"We have seen signs of life in NRP when the brain has been reperfused," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee and was the first to report such cases to HRSA. "It's extremely disturbing."

Sponsor Message

Those cases prompted HRSA to instruct the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN), which runs the organ system, to investigate and develop a response. On Nov. 6, the OPTN board of directors approved the first phase of the first uniform national guidelines for how to perform NRP.

The new guidelines, which will go into effect Dec. 6, call for surgeons to do more than just clamp the blood vessels to the brain. They should also cut holes in them, according to the new policy.

"Clamping the blood vessels should stop blood flowing to the brain," says Lynch. "Cutting or venting above the level of the clamping is a second safeguard to make sure that if the clamping is insufficient that it immediately drains out of the head and is not supplying warm oxygenated blood to the brain."

The new policy also includes other protections, including recommending against giving donors drugs that would paralyze them and mask any movements.

But critics say the new safeguards are insufficient. Most surgeons already both clamp and vent blood vessels to the brain, for example, they say.

"I honestly don't believe they have created a policy that creates much or any more protection than these donors already had," says Morgan, who also disagrees with the decision to implement the first phase of the new guidelines on an emergency basis before the public had a chance to weigh in.

Critics also say the new policy doesn't begin to address the bigger concerns that NRP donors are not technically dead when surgeons remove their organs. They worry the adoption of the policy could speed the use of NRP before the troubling questions have been fully aired.

"I really think the policy is the cart before the horse," says Dr. Matthew DeCamp, a University of Colorado bioethicist. "The fundamental issues around NRP still remain unresolved."

Sponsor Message

Lynch, however, argues the new guidelines will protect donors and that NRP is ethical.

"This is an important first step to make sure NRP care is available but that the safety of the family's loved one is always at the forefront," Lynch says. "This is life-saving care that will extend the supply and improve the quality of organs that patients can get in transplant. And if it is done properly, it is safe."

World.title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican
World.content:
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican

toggle caption i Eric Stone/Alaska Public Media

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in state history.

Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.

Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign.

He's said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.

Sponsor Message

Alaskans have had enough of zero-sum partisan politics, he said in an interview just before voting at a precinct in Anchorage on Election Day.

"I strongly believe people just want things to work, and want people to work together," Kreiss-Tomkins said.

Loading...

The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes, including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. Winning requires getting a majority of the votes.

Voters were also facing a question on the ballot about whether to scrap that unique, ranked-choice system. That proposal failed, according to another AP race call, keeping the system in place.

With Kreiss-Tomkins' win and others in the midterms, Democrats will hold 30 governors' offices across the country, up from 24 now.

Kreiss-Tomkins will take office in a state where voters have loudly complained that things aren't working as they should.

Rising costs and relatively flat state funding have forced schools to close and class sizes to rise. Already-high costs for food, fuel and housing have risen sharply, and a looming shortage of easily accessible natural gas near the state's population centers is threatening to push prices higher. And Alaskans have been migrating out of the state for more than a decade.

Sponsor Message

The Republicans in the race were Trump-backed business owner Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor.

Kreiss-Tomkins is set to take office at noon Dec. 7.

Eric Stone covers state government for Alaska Public Media.

World.content:

World.title: They called her 'Mommy': Vulnerable senior dies after 2 strangers take over her life
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dorelia Licorish didn't know where she was. Her confusion came after she was asked a simple question by a Toronto judge presiding over a video court hearing last May.

"Are you in Guyana right now?"

Licorish, an 86-year-old Toronto resident who was in the South American country at the time, turned to the two men with her.

"I'm supposed to say yes?"

"Yes," one of them responded.

A provincial agency had gone to court to get legal guardianship over Licorish, arguing she was mentally incapable and the men were taking advantage of her financially.

Back in Canada, members of her family had been searching for Licorish. They called police after they hadn't been able to reach her for weeks and her house looked abandoned.

Less than six months after that call, Licorish died in hospital from an infected bedsore so deep her pelvic bone was exposed. The two men with her in Guyana are living in her Toronto home. Police have laid no charges.

Licorish’s nieces, Susanne Perch, left, and Andrea Phillips-Beckles, right, are seeking answers from police about what happened to their aunt. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

An investigation by CBC's the fifth estate into Licorish's death reveals that even when government agencies and law enforcement are alerted to a case of suspected elder abuse, they can fail to protect the most vulnerable seniors.

Licorish's family believe she was neglected by the men who had moved in as tenants before declaring themselves her caregivers.

"I would like to get justice for her because [the police] didn't take anything seriously at all," said Andrea Phillips-Beckles, Licorish's niece.

Watch the full documentary, "They called her 'Mommy,'" from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

Mistreatment of older adults is on the rise, experts say, as Canada becomes a " super-aged" country this year, with one in five people aged 65 or older.

While rates of elder abuse are not tracked nationally, a 2022 study by University of Toronto researchers found one in 10 Canadians over age 65 experiences some form of elder abuse — physical, financial or sexual — every year, and racialized and cognitively impaired older adults are at higher risk.

"Dorelia's story is one that's being played out in so many places, among so many individuals each and every day in our country, and this issue is only growing bigger," said Dr. Samir Sinha, geriatrician and clinician scientist a t Sinai Health System and University Health Network in Toronto.

"What's preventing this from happening to you?"

An undated photo of Licorish. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

Beloved auntie

Licorish immigrated to Canada from Barbados in the early 1960s. She was sharp-witted and fiercely independent, her family and friends said. She did not have any children of her own, but after her sister died, raised Phillips-Beckles.

"She was one vibrant, vibrant woman," Phillips-Beckles said.

Licorish worked as a nurse at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen Street West in Toronto for decades before retiring.

Christiana Egi, Licorish's former nursing colleague and close friend of 35 years, told the fifth estate she noticed Licorish was displaying memory problems as early as 2018.

WATCH | Remembering an independent woman: Remembering a much-loved family member | Duration closed caption 2:02 Dorelia Licorish is remembered by her friends and family as a fiercely independent woman who loved fashion, travelling and gardening.

In early 2024, Licorish told Egi that a married couple, Daniel Gopie and Elton John Rambarrat, had moved into her basement and were helping her around the house.

"I was like, 'I hope this is for real, that something doesn't happen.'"

The first red flags for Licorish's family came in June 2024. Licorish's landline had been disconnected and a second cousin received word the new tenants had said the house was now in their name.

The cousin showed up at Licorish's home in Toronto with police, but Licorish got angry and asked them to leave.

Daniel Gopie, left, Licorish and Elton John Rambarrat in an undated photo. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

A month later, she gave Rambarrat and Gopie powers of attorney over her property and personal care — giving them control of her finances and health should she be deemed incapable. Then she signed a will leaving all her assets to them, including her million-dollar Toronto home.

When Phillips-Beckles went to the home in August 2024, she says Licorish didn't immediately recognize her and the men never left her aunt's side. One of the men told her Licorish's will is "bulletproof."

"He started calling her 'Mommy,' and then she said, 'These are my sons from God.' I said, 'No, they're sons from the devil,'" Phillips-Beckles said.

Legal documents in question

In September 2024, Ontario's Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee (OPGT) began looking into the relationship between Licorish and her tenants after receiving a tip from a real estate lawyer.

The OPGT is a provincial agency tasked with safeguarding the interests of mentally incapable Ontarians.

The lawyer told the agency he had been asked to add Rambarrat and Gopie to the title of Licorish's property. He refused after Licorish could not recall the men's names.

In a 120-page affidavit filed in Ontario Court of Justice, the OPGT detailed what allegedly happened after Rambarrat and Gopie moved in. The men said they had met Licorish at her church and she allowed them to live in the basement rent-free in exchange for helping her with shopping and chores.

They began going with Licorish to appointments with her longtime family doctor, court records show. The doctor told the OPGT that after an appointment in September 2024, she asked Licorish about the men and the powers of attorney document they had shown her, Licorish was "very surprised" and didn't remember signing it.

An undated photo of Gopie, left, Licorish and Rambarrat. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Her family doctor wrote she had "concerns with Ms. Licorish's memory" and had booked a mini-mental status exam. However, Rambarrat cancelled the appointment. In medical notes from August 2025, doctors wrote Licorish had a history of dementia but it is unclear when it was first diagnosed.

In an interview with the fifth estate, the men said Licorish did not have dementia and was capable of granting them powers of attorney and creating a will that named them sole beneficiaries.

"The lawyer did the will. She did think it was fine and we didn't see it as a problem; it's something [Licorish] wanted to do," Rambarrat said.

The lawyer, Veena Pohani, told OPGT that while the three had "an unconventional relationship," she did not see signs of abuse and Licorish appeared happy.

Pohani declined to be interviewed for this story, citing client-solicitor privilege.

Rambarrat says lawyer Veena Pohani created the powers of attorney documents and will for Licorish. (veenapohani.com)

While a dementia diagnosis does not necessarily mean someone is incapable, lawyers have a duty to ensure clients have the mental capacity to understand the legal decisions they are making and that they are not being pressured by outside forces, according to the Ontario Law Society.

Pohani told the OPGT Licorish was capable of making these decisions, although no information is included about how she determined that.

Allegations of financial abuse

Banking records submitted in court show a dramatic change in Licorish's spending around the time the men entered her life. Thousands of dollars in ATM cash withdrawals and near-weekly alcohol purchases quickly depleted her modest pension and drove her account into overdraft.

Rambarrat and Gopie were added to Licorish's accounts in early October 2024. They cashed out some of her investments and withdrew money from her line of credit a few weeks before they took Licorish to their home country of Guyana for the first time.

Undated photos of Licorish with Gopie and Rambarrat in Guyana. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Bank staff wrote to OPGT that Licorish told them she "trusts them fully" and the transactions were completed with her consent.

However, about six weeks later, Licorish told OPGT investigators that she was not aware of withdrawals in the thousands.

Rambarrat and Gopie deny using Licorish's money for their own purposes and say they used it for home repairs.

However, when asked by OPGT investigators, they could not provide a receipt.

Family tries to intervene

Over 18 months, Licorish's family members made multiple calls to Toronto police, voicing concerns about the men's relationship with their elderly relative.

Body camera recordings and records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act show police treated multiple reports as "family disputes."

The fifth estate also learned police went to Licorish's house in March 2024, the same month the men allegedly moved in, and noticed she had cognitive issues.

Court records also reveal Gopie, who became Licorish's main caregiver, pleaded guilty to two assault charges in 2013 and 2018, unrelated to Licorish. Yet, police took no action to intervene.

Retired Durham police detective Martin Franssen, who specialized in suspected cases of elder abuse and reviewed the OPGT court file, says Licorish's case is "textbook."

He says Gopie's criminal history and Licorish's vulnerable mental state should have alerted officers to look into the situation more.

"This is the future of Canada — based on the changing age demographics — and we have to change our ways."

OPGT goes to court, Licorish goes to Guyana

In October 2024, the OPGT filed a notice in court to remove Rambarrat and Gopie as Licorish's powers of attorney for property and for the agency to take over her financial affairs.

However, seven months passed before OPGT submitted evidence.

By then, the men had taken Licorish to Guyana for a second time. All three attended a virtual court hearing to assign Licorish a lawyer who would be tasked with discerning her wishes.

In the audio recording of the hearing, obtained by the fifth estate, the OPGT's lawyer said the agency went to court "hastily" and did more investigative work after speaking to Pohani.

The lot in New Amsterdam, Guyana, where sources say Rambarrat and Gopie intend to build a house. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

The men told the judge they were in Guyana because they are building a house. They said they brought Licorish with them because they were her caregivers and it wasn't safe for her to be left alone.

The men spoke for Licorish until the judge asked if there was anything she wanted to say.

"I don't want them to leave me," she replied weakly.

Franssen says it is common in predatory relationships involving older adults for the perpetrator to quickly make the victim feel dependent upon them, making it less likely that they will report the abuse.

"If cognition comes into play … they may not even realize it's being done, but they will believe, in a lot of cases I've seen and dealt with, that they have that reliance on that individual."

The fifth estate spoke to several residents who saw and interacted with Licorish while she was in Guyana. Fearing retaliation, CBC News agreed not to identify them.

Multiple sources questioned how well Licorish was being cared for because Gopie would drink heavily, sometimes becoming intoxicated with Licorish. They said the three of them stayed in a dilapidated home where several other people connected to Rambarrat also lived.

Sources say the men and Licorish stayed at this house for weeks alongside several other members of Rambarrat’s family. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

During the trip, Licorish grew too weak to leave the house independently and would be left alone for hours, several sources said.

The men deny this, saying she was on vacation and well-cared for. They say she only visited the rundown home during the day and slept elsewhere.

The fifth estate has learned that when Licorish returned to Canada in July 2025, the lawyer assigned to her at the court hearing was unable to obtain instructions, though there was no explanation as to why.

"We have a system that, as designed, can't act quickly enough," Sinha said. "We don't have the luxury of time in these cases."

Licorish's final months

Upon returning from Guyana, Licorish's mental and physical health had declined, Licorish's friends and family said. She became bedridden after a brief hospitalization in August for a swollen knee and began receiving visits from personal support workers and nurses.

Partial records from the province's home-care agency, Ontario Health atHome, obtained by the fifth estate show Licorish had a pressure injury on her tailbone on Oct. 5, 2025. Nursing notes say the men were not "willing and able" to care for the wound.

The Victorian Order of Nurses, a non-profit nursing agency, was authorized to send someone to tend to the bedsore every three days.

A nurse reported to Ontario Health atHome Rambarrat had assisted him with turning Licorish because she would not allow the male nurse to touch her and he advised Rambarrat to turn Licorish frequently.

That same nurse said on Nov. 5 he requested a specialist to come to look at the wound because it was getting bigger and deeper. However, it's unclear if that occurred.

Licorish was unresponsive when she arrived at Scarborough General Hospital on Nov. 7, 2025. (Submitted by Susanne Perch)

On Nov. 7, 2025, Licorish was rushed to Scarborough General Hospital after a nurse found her unresponsive, medical records show.

She had gone into septic shock, a reaction to an infected Stage 4 bedsore, the most severe rating, that was oozing brown liquid and had a foul smell. Doctors also noted "profound dehydration" and high blood sugar levels.

When asked why he or Gopie did not take Licorish to the hospital sooner, Rambarrat said they deferred to the health-care professionals caring for Licorish.

Both S.R.T.-Med-Staff, the agency sending PSWs to care for Licorish daily, and the Victorian Order of Nurses did not respond to detailed questions, citing privacy laws.

The men, as Licorish's attorneys for personal care, had a legal duty of care to her, retired police detective Franssen said.

"Why didn't you pick up [and call] 911? Why did you need a health-care professional to walk in that day and turn to you and say, 'I suggest you call 911?'"

Licorish died on Nov. 21, 2025, 10 days after the men agreed for her to be moved to palliative care.

Sinha says her death was preventable.

"If she arrived at the hospital sooner, she may still be alive."

Because of her passing, the OPGT's case in court was dismissed.

Police close the case

Licorish's family only found out she was in hospital after a cousin driving by her house saw an ambulance out front. When they became aware of Licorish's condition, they called Toronto police again. This time, they alleged the men neglected Licorish and begged police to investigate.

In May, six months after Licorish's death, Toronto police detectives informed the family they had closed the case.

Toronto police declined interview requests, saying in a statement they conducted a thorough review of the circumstances surrounding Licorish's care, finances and death.

"The investigation included the examination of extensive medical, home care and other records, consultation with multiple parties involved in her care.... Following that investigation, no evidence was identified to support the laying of criminal charges," a media spokesperson wrote.

Multiple members of Licorish's extended family called Toronto Police Service's 43 Division about Rambarrat and Gopie's relationship with their elderly aunt. They accuse the police of not taking their concerns seriously. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Family members are in the process of contesting Licorish's will, arguing she wasn't mentally capable at the time of signing.

Rambarrat and Gopie say Licorish's family did not care for her and they are entitled to her house.

"I'm obligated to get something," Gopie said in an interview. "Does nobody come and clean her piss? Clean her shit? Do anything for her?"

Phillips-Beckles has a binder of files and contacts she's been collecting as she tries to piece together what happened to her aunt.

"I can't wrap my head around it at all, that she's gone and how she went," she said. "She shouldn't have gone that way."

World.title: Premier says Manitoba nearing limits of what it can do on affordability, so he's going after big corporations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says the provincial government is reaching the limits of what it can do to ease the cost of living without sacrificing the revenue needed to fund public services, and that corporate giants need to do their part.

Kinew said he wants to raise this conversation with Manitoba NDP members at the party's annual convention, underway this weekend at the RBC Convention Centre in Winnipeg.

"We've listened very closely to the cost of living being a top concern, and we've taken action," he told reporters Friday afternoon about his first three years in office.

"But for us to go further, I think we have to have a serious conversation about: should we be taking revenue away from health care and education to help with the cost of living? Or should we go look at these big companies around the country and continent that are making record profits while you can't even get by?"

During the NDP's first term, it removed the provincial gas tax for a year and then brought back the levy but at a lower rate of 12.5 cents per litre, instead of the previous 14 cents.

Kinew's party also froze electricity rates and the price of milk for a year. It has also removed the provincial sales tax on the remaining grocery items that were still subject to the tax.

Each of those measures helped people save money but also reduced the province's revenues, Kinew said.

If the province continues down this path, "it's going to affect the nurse salary and the police officer salary and the teacher salary," he said.

Kinew introduces NDP MLAs and candidates for the upcoming election during the Manitoba party's convention Friday. (Rudy Gauer/CBC)

"Right now there's this huge, huge profit happening on the corporate side, with energy companies and with grocery companies. Shouldn't we start to look there for the future steps to try and save you money?"

The premier didn't outline how he would pressure the corporate giants.

It's not the first time he's taken aim at their influence over consumers.

In 2023, Kinew warned grocery retailers that if they didn't pass along savings from the provincial gas tax holiday, his government would act. While inflation went down during this time period, it doesn't appear grocery prices declined in any measurable way.

In later years, his government proceeded to outlaw property restrictions that keep new grocery stores from opening near existing stores, and it has banned grocers from offering some customers different prices than others.

Kinew pointed to the price of gas as an example of corporations gouging the public.

Prices spiked this year because the war in Iran disrupted global oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

"But our oil here, our gasoline doesn't come through the Strait of Hormuz, it comes from Alberta," Kinew said.

"These big energy companies are charging the market price, right? And that's just pure profit."

NDP is election-ready: Kinew

He also told reporters the NDP is ready for next year's election, highlighting the $3.5-million war chest it has built up. That's the highest amount Kinew is aware of.

The NDP also has 38 of 57 candidates nominated for the election, a party official said.

Kinew introduced all of the NDP MLAs and candidates who were at Friday's convention, commenting on their accomplishments or sharing a personal story about them.

Kinew eats rotisserie chicken at a March 2025 news conference promoting his government's plan to remove the provincial sales tax from all food in grocery stores. He argued Friday that grocery stores can do more to lower the public's cost of living. (Steve Lambert/The Canadian Press)

He said increasing the size of his majority — his party has 34 seats — is a personal goal. He's looking to make gains in rural areas of the province, telling the convention, as one example, that Lac du Bonnet used to vote NDP routinely when Ed Schreyer was premier in the 1970s, and it will vote NDP again.

"I think it would make our government better if we get the voices of southwestern Manitoba, the Interlake, southeastern Manitoba, other regions to sit around the government table with us and bring that perspective on the issues like health care, on issues like affordability," Kinew said.

The next election is scheduled for Oct. 5, 2027, but could be called earlier.

Kinew offered no indication when Manitobans would head to the polls. He called 2027 an "election year" and said he’s looking forward to releasing a budget in the spring.

He said balancing the budget next year is that "one big piece that we promised you" in the 2023 election campaign, "and we've got to deliver on that before we come back to ask for another mandate."

The province's deficit for the 2025-26 fiscal year is $832 million — about half of what the government forecasted last December.

Kinew also said he has no regrets about his government's decision to abandon the time change ritual. The adoption of permanent daylight time is resulting in later sunrises during the next few months, leading to complaints around kids walking to school in the dark and businesses that said their computer systems didn't adapt to the new times.

There was a "huge consensus" to end twice-yearly clock changes, Kinew said, "and what I would say to people … is this change requires an adjustment, and we're going through the adjustment now."

The NDP's convention continues Saturday with a speech from federal party leader Avi Lewis and a sold-out gala dinner, with 800 tickets purchased.

World.title: 4 decades ago, Robert Munsch attended Moira Green's birthday. Her story became a children's classic
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On Moira Green’s 10th birthday, she put on a giant paper bag and a homemade crown and headed down to Hay River’s public library, where a surprising number of residents from the remote Northwest Territories town were waiting.

There were 200 pizzas and 200 little cakes. She ran into a dragon, Prince Ronald and other valiant attempts by her Grade 5 classmates to bring the beloved characters from Robert Munsch’s earliest works to life.

Technically, Green could have come dressed as herself: the inspiration behind Moira’s Birthday.

“After we did our little performances and stuff, they got Robert Munsch on the line,” Green said in a recent interview. “I don't know how they did it back in the day, but everyone in the library could hear him. And then, he read the story [to] all of us."

It was November 1987.

Six months earlier, Toronto-based Annick Press had published Moira’s Birthday. And exactly four years previous, the Guelph, Ont., children’s author had visited the Northwest Territories for the first time, leaving behind a trail of memories for many in the community of roughly 3,500 people living there at the time, and, as Green recalls, whenever anyone new turned up, her parents insisted they come for supper.

Green, shown wearing the Paper Bag Princess costume, is seen here at her 10th birthday party in Hay River, N.W.T., in November 1987. She and other kids performed skits based on Munsch's books. (Submitted by Moira Green)

That small-town friendliness was how Munsch, known for billeting with families during his tours, came to stay with Bruce and Marilyn Green and their five children, all of whom would make an appearance in the first of three books he would dream up during the trip.

Those connections Munsch forged with kids, living in big cities and tiny hamlets, became the fabric of the nearly 100 books he has written in his career. In an interview with CBC News last year , his “last hurrah,” the author revealed that another 50 books will likely be published after his death.

As first reported in the New York Times in September 2025, Munsch has been approved for medical assistance in dying (MAID), when he chooses. He has been living with Parkinson’s disease and dementia.

Munsch and his wife, Ann, who have been married for more than five decades, are shown here at their home in November 2025. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

“Nobody lives forever," he told CBC in December. “But I will at least have a couple of years, as many years as I’ve already had [after I’m gone], and that will be nice," he said, of his hope to publish a book per year after his death.

The breadth of his travels helped him capture what it was like to be a kid in a country as vast as Canada.

Even in a place as remote as Hay River.

Moira’s 6th birthday

On the morning of her sixth birthday party in November 1983, Green and her siblings went to see Munsch perform at the library. He captivated his audience, she said, despite having just flown in hours before from Yellowknife.

Her party had already been planned for that afternoon before news of Munsch’s visit came out.

Green, left, shown in her Grade 1 photo, which helped artist Michael Martchenko illustrate the book, shown right. (Submitted by Moira Green/Annick Press)

It was not quite as raucous as the story suggests — a handful of friends, not the whole school, showed up. And during a quiet moment, her dad walked over.

“He said ‘You should ask Mr. Munsch if he could tell you a story.’ And I was like, ‘Mmmm, I'm not going to do that. I'm way too shy.’”

But a friend did it for her, she said. The author recalls that he couldn’t refuse.

“Sometimes when a kid asks me to make up a story, I get this strange feeling that something is going to happen,” Munsch wrote of the experience . “I look out at a group of kids and get this firm conviction that I can tell a new story about a particular kid.

“Usually, it’s not true, but I do always try a new story when I get the feeling.”

Green was just as surprised, as she had assumed he would retell a previous story.

“But he came over … sat down and then he just sort of started telling — making up — the story on the spot: Moira’s Birthday.

Anyone who has heard Munsch perform knows how he revs up a crowd, along with his own volume, asking questions and weaving the answers into his words.

“Lots of interactions, stopping to talk about the local bakery and, you know, other things from around town and kind of integrate that into the story."

The Green family's home, shown here in the 1980s, in Hay River, N.W.T. It became part of the iconic story. (Submitted by Moira Green)

Even before he finished, Munsch said, he knew he had a winner.

He added Green to his “Story Kids file" and asked if he could stay in touch, both recalled. Illustrator Michael Martchenko followed up, looking for pictures of the family, their green house and even the dog.

“We heard later that he had continued to tell that story,” Green said, “kind of fine-tuning it and shaping it as he does by telling it to the kids and gauging their reaction."

When Munsch sent her an early draft, Green saw the story had evolved.

In the first rendition, she had received money in all of her presents. And she said she used the money to either pay for the massive order of pizza and cake — or paid her guests to help clean up.
