World.title: Blocked Estuary May Explain Playa Langosta Fish Die-Off
World.content:
Sand blocking an estuary’s connection to the ocean, combined with reduced freshwater flow during a period of little rain, may explain the mass fish deaths at Playa Langosta, according to National University (UNA) biologist Teresita Ulate. Ulate said the interruption of water exchange between the mangrove and the sea could have reduced the oxygen available to aquatic animals. Her assessment offers a possible explanation, but the cause has not been confirmed.

The deaths occurred at the San Francisco Estuary in Playa Langosta. The Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) opened an investigation after images showed dead fish, rays and other animals along the shoreline and in the water, including two bull sharks found dead in the estuary.

The ministry said the analysis, led by the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), would examine the blocked outlet, water quality and possible effects of El Niño, including warmer Pacific waters and changing coastal conditions. Authorities cautioned that assigning a cause before a technical evaluation would be premature.

Ulate explained that reduced rainfall meant less freshwater was reaching the mangrove while accumulated sand restricted its connection to the sea. She said El Niño had contributed to that drop in rainfall, part of the dry conditions now straining water supplies across Guanacaste, and that the episode could have been anticipated given the lower rain forecast.

Decomposing organic matter can add pressure because bacteria consume oxygen as they break it down, leaving less available for fish. Ulate said water testing she carried out in the San Francisco mangrove in June had already found low oxygen levels, which she described as a warning sign for the ecosystem. She added that daily monitoring would be needed to produce precise data.

The animals were reported dead on Nov. 4. Local lifeguards urged people not to collect or eat them because they were decomposing, and asked residents to stay away from the estuary, warning that the loss of fish could draw crocodiles closer to shore. The environment ministry also asked residents not to alter the estuary’s mouth without authorization.

Eduardo Vargas, director of the Tamarindo Integral Development Association, said strong seasonal tides had carried sand from other stretches of coast and sealed the opening. He said residents initially tried to clear it with shovels before bringing in heavy machinery, that the work had the necessary permits and that subsequent heavy rain helped widen the opening.

Vargas described the reopening as a stopgap rather than a fix, saying a lasting solution would require managing the mangrove from the surrounding watershed. Restoring that connection does not establish what killed the animals. Ulate cautioned that human activity could not yet be ruled out as a contributing factor and that SINAC’s analysis would be needed to better understand the episode.

World.title: US Ground Stop Canceled 15 Costa Rica Flights. Here’s What to Expect Today
World.content:
The nationwide US ground stop that froze flights on Friday afternoon is over, but if you are flying between Costa Rica and the United States this weekend, you may still feel it. Fifteen flights were canceled on Friday at Costa Rica’s two main international airports, 10 at Juan Santamaría International Airport and five at Guanacaste Airport in Liberia, and US airlines were still canceling thousands of flights early Saturday as planes and crews worked their way back into position.

Aeris, which runs the airport outside San José, said 23 flights there were affected on Friday, 12 departures and 11 arrivals. Six departures and four arrivals were canceled. The other 13 flights were moved to overnight and early Saturday morning slots.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the order at about 8 p.m. Eastern time on Friday, or 7 p.m. in Costa Rica, after more than four hours. That made it the second-longest nationwide ground stop on record, behind the shutdown that followed the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. When it began, it was only the third nationwide US ground stop ever.

Aeris said operations will return to normal gradually, depending on each airline’s schedule. Guanacaste Airport in Liberia canceled five departures on Friday, flights to Dallas, Toronto and Ottawa carrying 473 passengers, who were left waiting for new itineraries. Airport officials there had said on Friday afternoon that 23 flights were scheduled for Saturday.

The knock-on effects are what matter today. The flight-tracking service FlightAware counted more than 9,100 cancellations and more than 24,500 delays in the United States on Friday, and more than 3,000 additional cancellations by early Saturday. Many US airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same jet straight back, so a canceled flight in Miami, Houston or Atlanta can mean a canceled departure here.

Check your flight in your airline’s app before you leave for the airport. App and text alerts usually update before departure boards do. Copa Airlines said the US disruption could cause delays and cancellations on its flights to and from the United States and asked passengers to confirm their status on its website or app. United and JetBlue both said they would cancel most of their remaining Friday night flights, a fresh strain for JetBlue’s Costa Rica routes.

If your flight was canceled, look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. These let you change dates without a fee, which is often faster than waiting in a rebooking line. If you decide not to travel at all, US rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines do not have to cover hotels or meals in that case, so keep your receipts if your travel insurance covers delays.

If you are connecting through a US hub, rebook through the airline that sold you the ticket rather than each carrier separately. And if you are heading north, remember that every passenger flying to the United States must now sign a new form, which can slow check-in on a day when lines are already long.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications problem had affected all of the country’s Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the facilities that guide planes between airports, and blamed aging equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a hostile attack. Duffy said he had asked Congress on Thursday for $30.1 billion to modernize the air traffic control system.

The disruption was the second to hit air travel at Juan Santamaría airport in less than a month, after a power failure affected its control tower in October. Costa Rica relies on US gateways for much of its air traffic, and the busy high season is just weeks away, so even a few hours of trouble in US airspace can strand travelers here for a day or more.

World.title: Dollar Falls to a Record Low of 446 Colones in Costa Rica
World.content:
The U.S. dollar closed at its weakest level on record against the Costa Rican colón on Friday, falling to a weighted average of 446.10 colones on the country’s wholesale foreign-exchange market. The Monex close came in 0.72 colones below Thursday’s average of 446.82 and beat the previous low of 446.80, set on Sept. 17, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) trading data. On Thursday, the rate had sat just 0.02 colones above that record.

Friday marked the eighth consecutive session of decline, a slide that began on Nov. 4, when the average stood at 452.01 colones. Trades ranged between 445.80 and 446.30 colones per dollar, with $49.3 million changing hands in 228 operations. The BCCR’s reference rate for Friday stood at 442.74 colones for buying dollars and 448.37 for selling. The currency had already fallen to around 448 colones earlier this week.

The dollar has now lost 50.97 colones, or 10.3%, since the first trading session of 2026 on Jan. 2, when it opened the year at 497.07. After the September low, it recovered to 460.45 on Oct. 1, then fell 3.1% in a little over six weeks. Measured against its peak of 696.76 colones on June 21, 2022, the dollar has lost 36% of its value in Costa Rica.

In practical terms, every $1,000 converted at the Monex average now yields about 446,100 colones, roughly 51,000 fewer than at the start of the year. Bank and exchange-house rates sit on either side of the wholesale average, but they have moved in the same direction. The shift cuts both ways. Households and businesses that earn in dollars and pay their bills in colones receive less local currency for each dollar, while anyone who needs dollars, whether to pay a dollar-denominated loan or to import goods, needs fewer colones to buy them.

For people living on income from abroad, the squeeze comes as lawmakers weigh a bill that would tax residents’ foreign income at 15%. Dollar debt is a significant part of the picture. Data from the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (Sugef) through August show that 62% of foreign-currency loans in the financial system go to borrowers exposed to exchange-rate risk, meaning their income is not in dollars.

A strong colón lowers those payments for now. Sugef has warned, however, that if the exchange rate rises, the ability of a significant share of those borrowers to pay could be affected. Foreign-currency lending has also been growing faster than lending in colones. Sugef figures for September show dollar loans grew 6%, compared with 2.7% for colón loans.

The Central Bank has been buying dollars as the rate falls. Through Nov. 12, it had purchased $94.9 million this month in stabilization operations, bringing its 2026 total to $1.36 billion.

On Thursday alone, the BCCR bought $13.7 million for stabilization and another $11 million to cover the currency needs of the non-bank public sector. Stabilization purchases are meant to smooth sharp swings in the rate rather than to defend a specific level. Costa Rica has operated under a managed float since February 2015. Monex began operating in November 2006, which makes Friday’s close the lowest in the platform’s two-decade history.

Trading has been heavy in recent weeks. On Oct. 27, Monex recorded $153.4 million in transactions, the largest volume since its creation. Monex trading resumes on Monday, Nov. 16, when the market will show whether the slide extends to a ninth session.

World.title: Costa Rica Flights Caught in Only the Third Nationwide US Ground Stop Ever
World.content:
If you’re flying between the United States and Costa Rica this afternoon or tonight, expect delays and possible cancellations. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) stopped every departing flight across the United States on Friday, citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.”

The order took effect shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern time, just before 3 p.m. in Costa Rica. It stays in place until further notice. Any flight scheduled to leave a U.S. airport for San José or Liberia is grounded for now. That includes flights from the Florida hubs that carry much of Costa Rica’s U.S. traffic, such as Miami, Fort Lauderdale and Orlando, as well as other major gateways.

Planes already in the air are being allowed to continue to their destinations. Flights from Costa Rica to the United States are less clear. The FAA said inbound international flights will be handled case by case. Even if your flight is cleared, it may still be late. Many U.S. airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same aircraft back, so a jet stuck on the ground in Miami or Houston means a late or canceled departure here.

The FAA hasn’t officially said what caused the stop. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue is affecting all of the country’s Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle planes flying between airports. Outages on radio frequencies used by controllers had been reported in parts of the country before the order was issued.

There’s no confirmed time for flights to restart. Some flight-tracking services listed 5 p.m. Eastern time, or 4 p.m. in Costa Rica, as the first point the order would be reviewed, but it could be extended. Delays will likely last well past the end of the stop, because planes and crews will be out of position. In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop of about 90 minutes, triggered by the failure of a computer system that sends safety notices to pilots, led to more than 11,000 delays and cancellations.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. The January 2023 one was the most recent. Before that, the only other was ordered after the September 11, 2001, attacks. Check your flight with your airline before you head to the airport. Airline apps and text alerts usually update before airport departure boards do.

Look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. During large disruptions, airlines often let you change your flight without a fee, which can be easier than waiting for a rebooking. If your flight is canceled and you decide not to travel, U.S. rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines aren’t required to pay for hotels or meals when the disruption isn’t their fault, so keep your receipts if you have travel insurance that covers delays.

If you’re connecting through a U.S. hub, you may miss your connection even after flights restart. Rebook through the airline that issued your ticket rather than each carrier separately. Updates on local flights are posted on the official social media channels of Juan Santamaría International Airport and Guanacaste Airport.

This is a developing story and will be updated as the FAA and airlines release more information.

World.title: Banks and Businesses in Costa Rica Must Accept Digital ID Starting January
World.content:
Starting January 1, 2027, banks, government agencies, businesses and other institutions in Costa Rica will be required to accept the Costa Rican Digital Identity (IDC), the smartphone version of the national ID card, for any transaction or procedure that requires identification. The Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) said the digital credential carries the same legal validity as the traditional plastic ID card. From that date, institutions will no longer be able to turn it away simply because it is presented on a phone.

The digital ID has been available since September 9, 2025, but until now institutions could decide whether to accept it. According to the TSE, 107,243 people had requested one as of November 1, 2026. The change could make everyday procedures simpler, from banking to administrative paperwork and any service that requires proof of identity. It does not replace the physical card, which will continue to be issued and accepted throughout the country.

Unlike the physical ID, which is free for most applicants, the digital version costs 2,600 colones (about $5.80) and is valid for four years. Senior citizens are exempt from the fee. The service is available only to Costa Rican citizens. Applicants need a valid physical ID card, a smartphone with an active phone line running iOS or Android, and no identity document waiting to be collected at the TSE.

People applying for their first Costa Rican ID must get the physical card before they can request the digital version. Applications are handled online through the TSE website at tse.go.cr/idc. Applicants enter their ID number, complete an identity verification step, provide a valid email address and pay with a Visa or Mastercard credit or debit card.

Once the application is approved, the credential is activated through the official IDC-Ciudadano app, available on Apple’s App Store and Google Play. It is protected by a personal PIN and facial recognition, which the TSE checks against the biometric data collected during the holder’s most recent physical ID procedure.

Citizens can still obtain or renew their physical IDs free of charge at the TSE’s headquarters in San José or at any of its 32 regional offices. A fee applies only when a person exceeds the annual limit on duplicate replacements. The January requirement applies to the institutions that must accept the credential, not to citizens. Getting a digital ID remains optional, and anyone who prefers the plastic card can keep using it.

World.title: Heavy Storms Could Drop Nearly 3 Inches of Rain on Costa Rica Today
World.content:
The rest of this Friday afternoon could bring short, heavy downpours and thunderstorms to the Central Valley, the northern zone and the Caribbean. If you still have to get somewhere today, plan your trip around them. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects intense storms lasting one to three hours, with 20 to 40 millimeters (0.8 to 1.6 inches) of rain in most affected areas. In the Central Valley, the Caribbean and the northern zone, totals could reach 70 millimeters (2.8 inches).

That much rain in a short window can overwhelm city drains and push creeks over their banks, especially in the Central Valley. If you live or park near a stream or on a street that floods, move your car early and don’t drive through standing water. Wind is the other risk. Isolated gusts could reach 80 kilometers per hour (50 mph), strong enough to bring down branches and power lines. When a storm hits, get indoors and keep away from trees and fallen cables.

The mountains and the eastern and northeastern parts of the Central Valley have the highest chance of storms. Rain could also spread to the northern lowlands and the northern Caribbean. On the Pacific side, expect storms in the mountains of the Central and South Pacific. The Nicoya Peninsula and the southeast of the North Pacific should see less activity.

The storms come in bursts rather than as an all-day rain. If one hits while you’re on the road or about to drive home, it is usually safer to wait it out than to push through it. The reason for the change is the trade winds. They usually keep the Pacific side dry at this time of year, and earlier this week they were bringing strong gusts across the country. Now they have weakened, which lets sea breezes and westerly winds carry moist Pacific air inland. Warm temperatures then build storm clouds over the mountains by afternoon.

This back-and-forth is typical of the transition from the rainy season to the dry season, which has already begun in Guanacaste and the Central Valley. Unsettled weather continues into Saturday, with more chances of afternoon rain. From Tuesday, the IMN expects rising pressure over the Caribbean Sea to strengthen the trade winds again.

If you’re driving between the Central Valley and the Caribbean coast, keep an eye on Route 32. Heavy rain in the mountains is what brings rock and mud down onto the highway through Braulio Carrillo National Park, which has closed repeatedly this year. If Route 32 closes, the usual alternatives are Route 10 through Turrialba and Route 126 through Vara Blanca. Both are narrower and slower, so leave extra time.

Check the IMN’s website and social media for updated warnings before you head out this afternoon or on Saturday.

World.title: Salvadoran Troops Turn Haiti National Stadium Into Base After Retaking It From Gangs
World.content:
El Salvador will turn Haiti’s national soccer stadium into a forward base for its troops after Salvadoran and Haitian forces retook the Sylvio Cator stadium in Port-au-Prince from armed gangs on Thursday, President Nayib Bukele announced. The joint operation took place in the early hours yesterday and involved the Haitian National Police, the Armed Forces of Haiti, a government-contracted security unit known as the Task Force, and Salvadoran special forces, according to Bukele and Haitian police. Bukele said it was carried out under a bilateral agreement between the two governments.

The Haitian National Police said in a statement that its officers had taken full control of the stadium and its surroundings before handing security of the complex to the Salvadoran armed forces. More than 20 armored vehicles and trucks carrying Salvadoran military personnel were stationed inside the stadium after the operation, according to local media reports.

Bukele said troops found several human skulls inside the facility. Authorities have not announced any identification of the remains or said whether they will be examined. The Salvadoran president said his forces would use the stadium as a base to advance deeper into territory held by gangs, and that the allied forces now hold the advantage on the ground.

In a message addressed directly to gang members, he told them to leave the area before the next phase of operations begins and warned that those who stay to fight Salvadoran and Haitian forces will face the consequences. He did not give a start date. The stadium, home ground of Haiti’s national soccer team, had been held by gangs since early 2024. Its loss forced Haiti to play every one of its home qualifiers for the 2026 World Cup outside the country.

The recovery is the latest step in a rapidly expanding Salvadoran military presence in Haiti. El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 troops since October 18, when gangs ambushed an armored vehicle carrying four Salvadoran Air Force aviation technicians in Croix-des-Bouquets, northeast of Port-au-Prince. The Salvadoran military said the vehicle was struck by gunfire and explosives and caught fire, and that the four men got out before going missing.

The technicians were serving with the Gang Suppression Force, a multinational mission authorized by the United Nations Security Council to support Haitian police against armed groups that control large parts of the capital and other areas. Salvadoran officials have described them as non-combat personnel whose main job was carrying out medical evacuations.

The Salvadoran government maintains that the four are alive, but their whereabouts remained unknown as of now. Bukele has previously offered to withdraw all Salvadoran forces from Haiti if the technicians are released unharmed. The Gang Suppression Force has distanced itself from the actions of the Salvadoran troops sent in after the ambush, which operate under the separate bilateral arrangement with the Haitian government. Bukele has said the contingent is focused on confronting the gangs responsible for the October attack and related violence.

The stadium operation came two days after Bukele said Salvadoran troops had destroyed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang, an operation for which Haiti’s prime minister publicly praised the Salvadoran leader. Gang violence in Haiti has forced nearly 1.5 million people from their homes, and the international force sent to help contain it has so far deployed only a fraction of the 5,550 personnel the Security Council authorized.

World.title: Shakira Returns to Costa Rica in 2027 After More Than 15 Years
World.content:
Shakira’s world tour has added Costa Rica to its 2027 Latin American leg. It’s the strongest sign yet that the Colombian superstar will perform at the National Stadium in La Sabana on Sunday, January 31. It would be her first concert in the country since April 2011. The tour’s official accounts posted a graphic this week listing six countries for the new leg: Brazil, Venezuela, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Puerto Rico and Panama. The post gave no dates or venues for any of the stops.

The January 31 date comes from the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Commerce (MEIC). In October it authorized a presale plan for the show. The authorization lists an 8 p.m. start at the National Stadium and lets the production company, Two Shows Ltda., sell 53,114 tickets through eticket.cr.

Ticket prices and the on-sale date have not been announced. The ministry requires a presale authorization before any large event goes on sale, to protect buyers, but it doesn’t mean tickets are available. Wait for an official announcement and buy only through the authorized seller.

There is a reason for caution. In September 2024, the ministry approved a presale of 51,446 tickets for a Shakira concert at the same stadium on March 27, 2025. That show never happened bug the difference this time is that the tour itself has named Costa Rica as a stop.

The show is part of the Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, named after her 2024 album, her first studio record in seven years. The tour opened in Rio de Janeiro in February 2025. Her production team says the tour has grossed more than $534 million and sold over four million tickets worldwide. Shakira recently closed a 13-show residency in Madrid that drew more than 700,000 people.

She has played Costa Rica twice before. She brought her Pies Descalzos tour to the Palacio de los Deportes in Heredia in 1995. She then performed at the National Stadium on April 3, 2011, shortly after the stadium opened. A full stadium on the last Sunday of January would also land in the middle of high season, when flights and hotels around San José are already busy.

Prices, seating sections and the sale date are expected once the producers make a formal announcement.

World.title: Mopan Technical High School wins Gold at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Mexico
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School wins Gold at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School has made history after securing first-place Gold award at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Monterrey, Mexico.

The school’s delegation proudly represented Belize as the only participating school from the country, earning top honours in the Social Sciences category for its project titled “Supporting Multilingual Learners!”

The achievement marks the first time Mopan Technical High School has secured a first-place award at an international competition.

Students Karoly and Jasiely were recognized for their dedication, creativity and hard work in developing the project, which earned them international recognition and brought home the gold medal for Belize.

The school also credited the achievement to the guidance of their coach, Marcelo Torres, and mentors Casiana Sagastume and Karen Figueroa.

Appreciation was also extended to the school’s administration, staff, wider school community and sponsors whose support helped make the international participation possible.

Mopan Technical High School celebrated the victory as more than just a medal, highlighting the importance of investing in young people and creating opportunities for students to showcase their talents internationally.

Mopan Tech says that the achievement is a proud moment for Benque Viejo del Carmen and Belize, as its students made their mark on the international stage.

World.title: Belize’s Maya-led Climate adaptation project highlighted at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
Belize’s Maya-led Climate adaptation project highlighted at COP31 in Türkiye

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Indigenous leadership took centre stage on November 11 during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) and Belize’s Julian Cho Society hosted a side event at the CARICOM Pavilion titled “Project Q’anil: A Maya-Led Pathway to Green Climate Fund Adaptation Finance,” highlighting the importance of placing Indigenous communities at the centre of climate adaptation efforts.

The discussion explored Maya principles, including “Aj ral Ch’och” (people of the land), “Loq’la Tzuul Taq’a,” which recognizes the sacred relationship between the land, forests, animals and the spirit world, and “Komonil,” which emphasizes mutual support, collective work and commitment.

The Julian Cho Society works to advance Indigenous rights and environmental conservation in southern Belize. The event highlighted how traditional knowledge, community leadership and partnerships can help Indigenous communities access climate financing and develop solutions that reflect their needs and priorities.

Elishah St. Luce, Social Inclusion and Gender Specialist at the CCCCC, emphasized the importance of ensuring that Maya communities lead efforts shaping their future. “It is our responsibility to take the future the Maya people have dreamt and place that in a project ensuring that the Maya-led aspect dominates,” she stated.

COP31 is being held from November 9 to 20, 2026, bringing together world leaders, governments, Indigenous representatives and climate advocates to advance global climate action.

World.title: Belize brings Kulcha to International stage in Mexico
World.content:
Belize brings Kulcha to International stage in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: The Mopan Technical High School delegation brought a taste of Belizean culture to the international stage during ExpoCiencias 2026 in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico.

Beyond showcasing scientific knowledge and innovation, the international science fair also provided an opportunity for participating countries to celebrate their cultural identities, traditions and talents.

During a cultural presentation, Belize was represented through a dance celebrating Creole culture, accompanied by music from Belizean cultural icon Leela Vernon. The performance highlighted Belize’s rich cultural heritage and gave international audiences an opportunity to experience a piece of the country’s music and traditions.

Among those participating were students Karoly and Jasiely, alongside Mopan Technical High School Principal Katie Jones, who also made a special appearance in the cultural presentation. The delegation proudly showcased their talents and represented Belize with enthusiasm and national pride.

Mopan Tech noted that experiences such as ExpoCiencias go beyond classroom learning by encouraging cultural exchange, building friendships and allowing students to discover different perspectives.

From sharing scientific innovations to celebrating Belizean culture, the Mopan delegation continues to represent the country in Monterrey, Mexico.

World.title: Caribbean youth leaders highlight Climate Solutions at COP31
World.content:
Caribbean youth leaders highlight Climate Solutions at COP31

By Zoila Palma: Young climate leaders from across the Caribbean shared their efforts to address climate challenges in their respective countries during a side event at COP31 titled “From Advocacy to Action: Caribbean Youth Driving Climate Solutions.”

The discussion was hosted by Island Innovation at the CARICOM Pavilion, highlighting the growing role of young people in advancing climate action across the region.

The panel explored how regional collaboration can create opportunities for knowledge-sharing and expanding successful climate initiatives.

Participants also discussed challenges facing youth-led projects, including limited resources, differences in national circumstances and the need for more flexible and accessible financing to transform innovative ideas into sustainable, long-term solutions.

A key message from the discussion was the importance of meaningfully including young people in climate decision-making, not only as advocates but also as active partners in developing and implementing solutions.

Panelists emphasized that Caribbean youth have the ideas and capacity to drive change but need greater access to resources, partnerships and platforms to ensure their initiatives have a lasting impact.

World.title: Institute for Social and Cultural Research brings Belize’s cultural heritage to students at Itz’at STEAM Academy
World.content:
Institute for Social and Cultural Research brings Belize’s cultural heritage to students at Itz’at STEAM Academy

By Zoila Palma: The Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) participated in Cultural Day at Itz’at STEAM Academy in Belize City on November 13, 2026, engaging students in an interactive exploration of Belize’s history, culture and living heritage.

Through an outreach booth, students learned about the Belize Food Heritage Project, ongoing digitalization initiatives and how technology can help preserve and promote cultural traditions.

A highlight of the activity was an immersive 360-degree virtual experience featuring cultural celebrations and performances, including Krismos Bram, Sambai and the Traditional Maya Deer Dance.

ISCR-NICH expressed appreciation to the students, teachers and visitors who engaged with its team, reaffirming its commitment to safeguarding Belize’s diverse cultural heritage through innovative approaches to education and outreach.

World.title: International News: Colombia and Venezuela agree to coordinate border security after 2 kidnappings
World.content:
International News: Colombia and Venezuela agree to coordinate border security after 2 kidnappings

By Zoila Palma: The governments of Colombia and Venezuela have expressed their willingness to coordinate security efforts to combat transnational crime following two recent kidnappings along their 2,219-kilometre shared border. Colombia is seeking Venezuela’s assistance in locating the victims, amid concerns that they may have been taken across the border.

One of the victims is Nancy Gómez, the wife of the mayor of Uribia, in Colombia’s northern La Guajira department. She was kidnapped on November 11, and Colombian authorities suspect her captors may have taken her into Venezuela to evade law enforcement.

Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella ordered the deployment of military personnel to assist in the search, while the ELN armed group is suspected of involvement.

The second case involves Colombian Army Sub-Lieutenant María Camila Pantoja Hernández, who was kidnapped on November 4 in Saravena, in the border department of Arauca. The ELN is suspected of responsibility for her abduction, Reuters report.

Colombia’s Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora said the government had also sought assistance from the United States to help secure Venezuela’s cooperation in locating the officer.

Venezuela’s government has expressed its willingness to coordinate with Colombian authorities on security matters, including information-sharing and efforts to combat criminal organizations.

World.title: Infrastructural works continue in Punta Gorda, Toledo East Area Rep says
World.content:
Infrastructural works continue in Punta Gorda, Toledo East Area Rep says

By Zoila Palma: Infrastructure works are underway along Front Street in Punta Gorda, Toledo, as part of ongoing efforts to improve road conditions in the municipality.

Toledo East Area Representative Osmond Martinez announced that the project covers the section from the junction of Church Street to Victoria Street.

Martinez noted that Front Street was the first established street in Punta Gorda and said the project will result in the entire length of the historic roadway being concreted for the first time.

The works form part of Martinez’s goal to have every street in Punta Gorda concreted by 2035. He said the initiative is aimed at improving infrastructure and the quality of life for residents.

Martinez thanked the Ministry of Rural Transformation, the Punta Gorda Town Council, Prime Minister and Cabinet for their support in advancing infrastructure projects in the municipality.

World.title: Ministry of Health urges early screening for World Diabetes Day 2026
World.content:
Ministry of Health urges early screening for World Diabetes Day 2026

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness is commemorating World Diabetes Day on November 14, 2026, under the theme “Early Action on Diabetes,” encouraging Belizeans to get screened and take proactive steps to protect their health.

The ministry is highlighting the importance of early detection, prevention and proper management of the chronic disease.

Data from the United Nations indicate that an estimated 422 million adults worldwide were living with diabetes in 2014, compared to 108 million in 1980.

Diabetes occurs when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or when the body cannot effectively use the insulin it produces, resulting in elevated blood glucose levels. The three main types include Type 1, Type 2 and gestational diabetes, which develops during pregnancy.

Diabetes is a major cause of blindness, kidney failure, heart attacks, strokes and lower limb amputations. However, Type 2 diabetes can be prevented or delayed through healthy eating, regular physical activity and avoiding tobacco use. Regular screening, medication and proper treatment can also help people manage the disease and prevent or delay complications.

World Diabetes Day is observed annually on November 14 following a 2007 United Nations General Assembly resolution recognizing the need to strengthen global efforts to improve diabetes prevention, treatment and healthcare education.

World.title: EU reiterates ‘grave concern’ over Gaza humanitarian crisis as winter approaches
World.content:
Kallas also called on Israel to comply with international law and allow the United Nations and humanitarian organizations unimpeded access and to reopen all border crossings into Gaza. | Nicolas Tucat/ AFP via Getty Images

The bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to allow more humanitarian aid into Gaza as weather worsens living conditions.

Europe’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to protect civilians in Gaza as severe flooding batters the enclave, saying an airstrike on the Nasser Hospital on Thursday was “deeply alarming.”

“The severe flooding and winter conditions that have struck Gaza are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering,” Kallas said in a statement Saturday.

Kallas also called on Israel to comply with international law and allow the United Nations and humanitarian organizations unimpeded access and to reopen all border crossings into Gaza.

World.title: Italy hits Meta with €805m fine over privacy law violation
World.content:
The investigation, launched in 2025, established that access to a user's camera roll is requested with a single permission for the entire app, which the authority said covers multiple features with different needs. The authorization request was preceded by a generic warning that didn't allow users to understand that they were authorizing picture and video suggestions, the authority said.

"If granted in full, this type of permission allows the app to read the device's entire photo archive, usually permanently, without the user or the authorities being able to verify which information is actually being used,” the statement reads.

The authority also said it "rejected the objection of lack of jurisdiction raised by the company in favor of the Irish authority, because the ePrivacy regulation does not provide for the 'one-stop-shop' mechanism."

Meta has 60 days to get consent separately and specifically for the feature, clearly explain what it does and how it can be disabled, the authority said. It also must be disabled by default, including for those who have already authorized it.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. It has the right to appeal the decision.

World.title: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
World.content:
The money — more than 5 billion forints, €2.6 million and €1.2 million — was found across locations in Budapest, Pest, Békés and Nógrád counties, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, an anti-corruption body, said in a statement.

“This officially marks the end for the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” Magyar posted on Facebook, originally in Hungarian, in reference to Orbán’s government.

It took 12 Treasury staff eight hours to tally the cash using 5 counting machines, Finance Minister Kármán András said.

The announcement comes after Hungarian authorities detained Aron Orbán, the former prime minister’s brother, as part of an investigation into people smuggling. The former prime minister said on social media that the move, announced by Magyar on Monday, was part of a “political witch-hunt” to get him.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted wryly to the latest announcement, referring to the arrest of Orbán’s brother and the cash discovery on X.

“Dear Victor, I’ve always been an admirer of your creativity, but now I must say I’m impressed as never before,” he wrote.

World.title: US suggested Ukraine could give up Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Giving up Donbas has long been part of the proposals put forward by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, including the 28-part plan for a peace agreement proposed by the White House in 2025. Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously demanded that Ukraine abandon its efforts to join NATO and accept strict limits on the size of its military.

“I have said repeatedly: Ukraine is not retreating and is not giving up its land to terrorists,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

The White House and U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Zelenskyy said he was discussing a “comprehensive security package” with partners that would include specific guarantees from NATO and the EU, a strong Ukrainian army with adequate troops, weapons and financial support for a set period and a recovery plan with clear funding attached.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own,” Zelenskyy said. "Of course, this would be without any recognition of the occupied territories as Russian," he added.

“But we need specifics, and we don't have them yet. All of this is still under discussion,” the president said.

Veronika Melkozerova contributed to this report.

World.title: Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks
World.content:
Russia proposed withdrawing its nuclear weapons from Belarus and refraining from stationing intermediate-range missiles there in exchange, Bild reported.

But it remains unclear which proposals Russian President Vladimir Putin would support after discussions between intermediaries, according to the report.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a new security framework for Europe for after the war raised by the Americans “can be dangerous."

“Russia certainly cannot make decisions on behalf of all the societies that are members of NATO,” he told reporters on Friday.

Zelenskyy’s comments were not in direct response to the demands reported by Bild, but came after a meeting between Zelenskyy and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Thursday in Dublin.

“Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe. This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

World.title: EU deal on Ukraine talks overshadows AI-focused summit in Dublin
World.content:
Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency and hosted the informal gathering, had billed the meeting as a rare chance for a high-level discussion on how to develop artificial intelligence in accordance with European values.

But the question of how to secure peace in Ukraine — and who should negotiate on Europe’s behalf — quickly dominated discussions, as leaders sparred over the format of future peace negotiations and warned about the risks of a potential deal brokered between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Indeed, a meeting next week between the U.S. and Russian leaders has set Europe on edge, prompting warnings about a possible Yalta-type agreement in which superpowers would decide on European security questions over the heads of countries directly concerned, reminiscent of talks toward the end of World War II that divided Europe up between the four allied powers.

UAE’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al-Nahyan, members of the Ukrainian and Russian delegations hold talks mediated by U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Jared Kushner in Abu Dhabi on November 10, 2026. | Pool photo by Altaf Qadri/AFP via Getty Images

“That is why I want to make our message to the U.S. very clear: Please, no surprises!” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said regarding the Trump-Putin meeting, scheduled to take place during an APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19. “Continue to play on Team Europe and on the same team as Ukraine. And let’s work together for genuine peace in Ukraine.”

The question of who should represent Europe in future discussions about Ukraine and the post-conflict security order was added to the summit’s agenda at the last minute, following a request from Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Earlier in the day, Merz had voiced preference for a narrower group made up of officials from Berlin, Paris and London, while Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, argued that she was best placed to lead discussions.

World.title: Why Europe failed to find a superhero to take on Putin
World.content:
The push to identify one representative to speak for Europe was understandable. The appeal of having a single, respected leader taking the reins is largely based on a desire to project European strength and unity — as well as an interest in making negotiations with Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine efficient and effective.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself said this week he wanted Europe to identify within days who will take its place in the talks, and suggested he’d prefer it was one person (he even indicated that he had a preference, though would not reveal a name).



He didn’t get his way. Instead, leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, decided that the “E5” made up four big EU countries ― Germany, France, Poland and Italy ― and the U.K., plus officials from the European Commission and Council, would take the work forward as a team.

Technical discussions

The search for a top representative to fill Europe’s seat at the negotiating table at the next round of peace talks had become a political obsession in Brussels that missed at least two big points.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy takes part in a press conference at Government Buildings in Dublin on November 11, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images

The first is that the leadership level is not currently where the negotiations are at. Talks this week in Abu Dhabi were technical discussions between senior officials. The big political players like Putin and Zelenskyy were not there, never mind Trump. Russia sent a Kremlin aide to lead its team and Ukraine tasked its intelligence chief with making its case.

If these officials make progress toward a deal, leaders will no doubt want to get involved. Ultimately, it will be leaders who sign any peace agreements that follow — and there’s no limit on the number of EU presidents or prime ministers who could join such a meeting as signatories or guarantors of the final deal.

The next thing that needs to happen, according to both Ukraine and the U.S. envoys mediating the talks, is for Europe to join the discussion with Russia — at this technical level.

World.title: Le Pen offers to meet Zelenskyy in Brussels
World.content:
Marine Le Pen delivers a speech during a visit of the "Salon Made in France" at Parc des Expositions of Porte de Versailles, in Paris on November 13, 2026. | Geoffroy van der Hasselt/ AFP via Getty Images

The Ukrainian leader wants to persuade the far-right leader to continue supporting Ukraine if she becomes president of France.

PARIS — Far-right leader Marine Le Pen said she would be prepared to hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels, in the wake of her promises to stop French financial aid to Ukraine.

Speaking on the sidelines of a trade fair in Paris, Le Pen said a meeting in Brussels would be “justified” because “the topic of Ukraine financing is rattling Europe.”

“The German chancellor is starting to threaten people, it’s starting to be an issue in Europe and it would be interesting to discuss this,” she said in a reference to Friedrich Merz’s threats to cut EU funds for countries who refuse to support Ukraine financially.

World.title: Canada and the Philippines conclude talks on free trade deal, Mark Carney says
World.content:
Canada has concluded talks with the Philippines on a free trade deal, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on Saturday, as Ottawa continues to look to reduce its reliance on the US following a breakdown in relations with Washington.

 

"One year ago, Canada and the Philippines launched talks on a new free trade agreement," Carney wrote in a post on social media. "Today, we’ve already concluded the negotiations."

"We’re diversifying our trade partnerships to build a stronger, more resilient Canadian economy," Carney, who is in Manila to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit, added.

Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the summit, Carney said his government would work quickly to finalise the deal and that it would come into force in 2027. It is expected to take around six months for the agreement to be signed, he added.

"This is good news for Canadians in the agriculture sector, in the aerospace sector, even in AI, and our businesses working across forest products, mining, energy, services and beyond," he told reporters.

Ottawa is also hoping to secure a broader trade deal with the 11-member ASEAN group as a whole. Negotiations on such an arrangement have been "substantially completed," per Carney.

The prime minister said Saturday's announcements were "part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities for our businesses, more choice for Canadians, better jobs for our workers and reducing our relative reliance on the United States."

Canada has been seeking to double non-US exports by 2035 and has been aligning itself more closely with Europe as part of its push to reduce its reliance on the US, prompted by repeated clashes with US President Donald Trump over trade.

Trump is due to arrive in Manila early next week, before heading on to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. Carney is scheduled to next head to Cambodia before also arriving in China.

World.title: Qatar and Turkey sign defence agreement for “unified position” facing external attacks
World.content:
Turkey and Qatar signed a landmark mutual defence agreement on Friday, strengthening their strategic and security partnership for deterrence amid a rapidly changing security landscape of the Gulf and the Middle East.

 

Turkish president President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met in Istanbul on Friday to co-chair the Supreme Strategic Committee between Qatar and Turkey, concluding a wide range of bilateral agreements.

The two leaders adopted the mutual defence agreement "aimed at bolstering collective defence and achieving regional security and stability, as well as adopting a unified position in the face of any external armed attack targeting either or both parties", according to a joint statement released by the two countries.

"The two parties agreed to hold consultations on threats to their security... and to strengthen cooperation through joint military exercises, collaboration in the field of defence industries, and the exchange of personnel training," the statement said.

Both countries said that their agreement underlines their shared vision of a more secure and stable regional order, with Erdogan’s office stating that it will “add a new dimension to the brotherly ties between the two countries."

"President Erdogan stated that ​we would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the ​Gulf region and establish a basis for dialogue and achieve peace," according to a Turkish presidency statement on X, and that the agreement will expand defence industry cooperation between the two countries.

Turkey and Qatar would continue working together "to prevent a renewed outbreak of war in the Gulf region and to promote dialogue and peace", Erdogan said.

The leaders discussed Israel's attacks on Gaza and the humanitarian situation in the Palestinian territory, efforts towards normalisation in Syria and the latest developments in Libya, the statement added.

Qatar and Turkey also signed multiple agreements on trade and energy cooperation as well as diplomacy, education and culture.

A new map of regional defensive alliances is taking shape

The new partnership comes at a time of rapid regional defence realignments triggered by the Iran war as Turkey, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Indonesia have been shaping a new map of defence alliances in the region in a matter of a few months.

The Gulf nations have been clear that the United States' regional security umbrella continues to be central to their security architecture, but with Washington signalling its own global realignment, the Gulf countries are now widening their defence strategies, in the context of the ongoing "no war, no peace" reality.

In August, Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement,” a regional defence pact under which the three countries would come to each other's aid if one of them came under attack.

Ratified by the Turkish parliament last week, the pact links NATO member Turkey, which has the alliance's second-largest military, with Pakistan, the Muslim world's only nuclear-armed state, and Saudi Arabia, the Gulf's leading power.

Turkey has said the agreement is not aimed at any other country and remains open to other states, including Egypt.

Also in August, Pakistan and Kuwait signed a joint defence and military cooperation agreement.

In October, Qatar, Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia signed the “Badr” multilateral memorandum of understanding on defence industry cooperation.

World.title: Armed and ready to quack: German military launches rubber ducks with assault rifles
World.content:
Anyone who likes a bit of military company in the bath might soon find just what they are looking for at the Bundeswehr. Germany's armed forces have launched their own online shop, and one of its most eye-catching products is, of all things, a camouflage-clad rubber duck armed with a miniature assault rifle.

 

What might initially sound like a joke is, in fact, part of a new marketing strategy. Through the shop, the Bundeswehr aims to reshape its public image, raise its profile and, above all, appeal to younger audiences. Alongside the unusual rubber duck, the range also features other branded merchandise and clothing.

Bundeswehr duck makes a splash

The duck is attracting particular attention. The small rubber toy, dressed in military gear, has quickly become a bestseller and was temporarily sold out shortly after the shop launched.

The Bundeswehr's camouflage rubber duck, armed with a miniature assault rifle, has attracted plenty of attention. Bundeswehr

Demand for the new online shop has exceeded expectations, reportedly causing technical issues soon after launch. Clearly, military-themed marketing can make quite a splash, even when it ends up in the bath.

Bundeswehr seeks to boost its public image

Behind the unusual merchandise is a serious objective: the Bundeswehr wants to raise its public profile and build its brand beyond barracks, trade fairs and recruitment campaigns.

Recruitment is a key priority as the armed forces seek to expand their ranks. The merchandise is designed to make the Bundeswehr more visible in everyday life and strengthen its connection with the public.

Criticism of military marketing

Not everyone is convinced by the new strategy. Critics warn that merchandise and light-hearted promotional items risk trivialising the realities of military service. The marketing of weapons and military equipment as lifestyle products has drawn particular criticism.

The strategy has also drawn criticism from politicians. Representatives of the Left Party warn that such marketing risks making the military an increasingly normal part of everyday life.

From the parade ground to the bathtub

Whether the rubber duck will actually help attract new recruits remains to be seen. But as a promotional tool, it has already completed its first mission: generating attention, sparking conversation and, apparently, selling out in record time.

And who knows what might come next? Perhaps a lifebuoy in Bundeswehr camouflage for emergencies in the bubble bath, or a mini drone to keep an eye on rising foam levels.

A camp bed for exhausted bath ducks could also be on the cards. After all, the troops need to be prepared for every mission – even in the bubble bath.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV continues trip through South America as health authorities keep watch
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV is holding a mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba in northern Peru on Saturday as he continues his tour of South America, drawing huge crowds as people seek to catch a glimpse of the 71-year-old pontiff.

 

After travelling by helicopter from Chiclayo air base to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, Leo flies back for a prayer meeting with the Catholic community at the shrine of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo in the evening.

The pope returned to his beloved former hometown of Chiclayo on Friday.

The Chicago-born pontiff, who previously worked as a missionary and then bishop in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship, presided over an open-air mass for around 500,000 people in the city.

"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said. "Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming."

But the huge crowds turning out to see the pope have prompted heightened fears among health authorities in Latin America, which has seen a surge in measles cases this year.

From January to the end of October, 57,666 confirmed cases were recorded in 17 countries and territories in the Americas, almost five times more than in the same period the previous year. At least 81 deaths have been reported.

Ahead of Leo's visit, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) considered the public health risk of measles "very high" in the context of the expected religious mass gatherings.

The concern is mainly linked to low vaccination rates in some countries, particularly Argentina and Peru.

"We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized," Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO, said. "It’s a very complex situation."

Worshippers attend a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV in Pampas de Pimentel, near Chiclayo, Peru, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Measles

Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease caused by a virus. It can lead to severe complications and is potentially fatal.

The disease infects the respiratory tract and then spreads throughout the body. It can cause symptoms including a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and a rash.

An effective and relatively cheap vaccine is available.

According to the World Health Organisation, "children should receive two doses of the vaccine to ensure they are immune."

"The first dose is usually given at nine months of age in countries where measles is common and 12–15 months in other countries. A second dose should be given later in childhood, usually at 15–18 months," the agency says.

To stop the disease from spreading in a community and to protect infants and others who are unable to get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated.

According to WHO data for 2025, only Uruguay had reached this threshold. In Peru, coverage stood at 90% for the first dose and 82% for the second. In Argentina, the figures fell to 84% and 55% respectively.

Peru has recorded almost 3,000 cases in 2026, the fourth highest number in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.

In the five cities included in the Pope's itinerary - Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa - 170 infections have been detected so far this year.

In the run-up to the visit, Peruvian authorities stepped up vaccination campaigns, focusing especially on areas with higher transmission rates.

Initiatives have also included bringing forward vaccination for children between six and eleven months of age and campaigns targeting people up to 29 years old. By the end of September, 1.2 million doses had been administered since the push began in April, while more than two million additional doses were available.

Faithful attend Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV at the Basilica of Our Lady of Lujan in Lujan, Argentina, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The situation is also tricky in Argentina, where at the end of October, authorities issued a warning about the health risks linked to the Pope's visit. Up to four million people were expected in Buenos Aires province.

Experts are also worried about government cuts to health spending, which have scaled back the structures responsible for planning, funding and monitoring immunisation campaigns.

For its part, Uruguay has launched a period of enhanced epidemiological surveillance across the nation, which will continue until 29 November, weeks after the pope's departure.

Authorities have also intensified appeals to the public to complete their vaccination courses. The aim is to detect any new infections quickly and limit the spread of the virus after the large gatherings.

World.title: Hungary seizes millions in cash found buried in forests amid corruption investigation
World.content:
Hungarian authorities said they seized more than €17.5 million in cash buried in forests and hidden in other places across the country this week.

 

On 12 and 13 November, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) carried out coordinated searches at multiple locations across Hungary, including in Budapest and the counties of Pest, Békés and Nógrád, as part of a criminal investigation involving Miklós Seszták, a former minister of national development.

During the searches, investigators uncovered large amounts of cash hidden in a variety of spots: buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings and warehouses, stashed inside residential properties and stored in a high-value safe in a remote location.

Over the course of the two-day operation, investigators recovered a total of 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100. On Friday, NVVH staff paid the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury.

According to the investigation, there is reason to suspect that between 2015 and 2018, Seszták and the CEO of Hungarian National Asset Management (MNV) received more than 11 billion forints in illicit payments from representatives of companies contracted by Volánbusz, a national bus operator.

The NVVH previously announced that an earlier search carried out in October at the Kisvárda home of Seszták had uncovered safes of a type more commonly used by financial service providers and pawnshops.

On 30 September, the Buda Central District Court ordered the detention of Seszták at the request of the NVVH.

In late October, the court announced that Seszták's detention had been extended until 30 January. It cited the seriousness of the case and the risk that he might flee or go into hiding.

World.title: US floats Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership: Zelenskyy
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington had proposed the idea of Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership as efforts to bring an end to the war continue.

 

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday in comments embargoed until Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

Zelenskyy added that Ukraine was discussing "specific security guarantees" from NATO and the European Union and that he would ask Ukrainians if they accepted the terms should Western nations confirm.

"I have no right to make that decision on my own," he said.

It comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow earlier this week.

During their meeting, Putin signalled that Russia would not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country.

The US envoys later met with Zelenskyy in Ireland on Thursday to discuss ongoing diplomatic efforts, with the trio announcing that, moving forward, Europe would have a "voice" in peace negotiations.

"This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia," Kushner wrote in a post on X.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova appeared to dampen hopes of such an agreement on Friday, saying that as far as her department was aware, "the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."

In further comments shared by the ministry on Friday morning, presidential aide Yuri Ushakov added: "For our part, the position of the Europeans has been comprehensively outlined."

"They are striving by every means possible to join the negotiations, but, as our President has said, they must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war," he said.

World.title: Turkey talks green at COP31 while cracking down on activists
World.content:
As the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya co-hosts the COP31 climate conference with Australia, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is using the global spotlight to promote his country’s climate ambitions. But his green image is being challenged at home by environmentalists, who say they face an intensifying government crackdown.

Advertising

The summit opened with a cinematic video highlighting the growing threat of global warming. “When did you decide to look at nature as if it’s not your nature?” a narrator asked during the opening presentation.

Addressing world leaders, Erdogan stressed Turkey’s determination to tackle climate change and presented Antalya’s ancient, multicultural history as fitting for its role as host.

Three-quarters of world's displaced people 'on frontlines of climate crisis'

“At the centre of our civilisations lies respect for nature,” he said. “The earth is a sacred trust that must be protected and guarded. We are a nation that considers even harming an ant a violation of rights, and that embraces the principle of planting the last sapling in your hand even if you know the apocalypse will come tomorrow.”

A different reality

The COP31 summit gives Erdogan a prominent international stage, but human rights campaigners warn of a very different reality outside the conference halls.

Last month, the US-based Human Rights Watch raised the alarm over a widening campaign against Turkey’s environmental movement. The report’s author, Deniz Bayram, said activists face a growing wave of arrests, fines and intimidation.

“People told us that when they protested, they faced police violence and abusive tactics by security officers, as well as legal harassment through unfair criminal investigations with no criminal evidence,” Bayram said.

She said the authorities had also put pressure on demonstrators through their families. In the eastern Black Sea region, security officers contacted the adult sons of women protesters who lived in other cities and told them to stop their mothers attending further rallies, according to Bayram.

“Women told us that they are not really afraid of facing such violence from the authorities, but they are having a hard time with these family matters with their own relatives,” she said. “So these abusive tactics create a chilling effect, preventing people from attending further demonstrations.”

Tear gas and court cases

Police intervention at environmental protests has become routine across Turkey, where local demonstrations have surged since the government relaxed restrictions on gold and coal mining.

Suheyla Dogan, a retired civil engineer who has become a leading voice in protests against gold mines, has repeatedly rallied villagers against mining projects. She said the personal cost of activism was rising sharply.

“If we take any direct action, we are punished; they open court cases against us,” said Dogan, who faces four separate legal cases. “At the demonstrations, we have faced a lot of tear gas, water cannon, beatings and so on.”

Ahead of a planned demonstration in Antalya during the climate summit, Dogan said, several organisers were detained by police and released a day later. She believes the move was intended to deter people from turning up, even though the rally had not been banned.

African push to triple climate adaptation finance left off Cop31 agenda

Legal experts warn that a climate of fear is deepening as pre-trial detention becomes standard practice, leaving activists in jail for weeks before their cases are heard, often only to be released later. The government maintains that the right to protest remains protected, but environmental lawyer Ismail Hakki Atal said lawyers defending activists were increasingly being targeted too.

Atal represented villagers fighting to protect the Akbelen Forest near the south-western town of Milas, where he alleges that the government-backed conglomerate Limak breached Turkey’s Olive Law by cutting down olive trees and dumping rubble on olive groves.

“Because I exposed this in a live news broadcast, police detained me twice within five days, even though I was acting as the villagers’ lawyer,” Atal said. “The ruling AKP has effectively established a judiciary in Turkey capable of having anyone it wishes arrested. The judicial system currently hangs over us like the Sword of Damocles and is used as a stick when necessary.”

Retirees on the front line

Dogan acknowledged that the mounting pressure was beginning to sap the movement’s strength, particularly among younger people.

“People are now more afraid to join us. Villagers are more afraid because if they protest and are taken to prison, they stay there for a long time,” she said. “When we call people on to the streets, they ask: ‘How are you going to protect us if something happens to us?’ Young people who have jobs and children are especially afraid.”

World set to breach 1.5C warming limit as UN warns time is running out

With fewer people of working age willing to risk their jobs and their freedom, the burden of frontline protest is increasingly falling on retirees such as Dogan.

“I am retired, I have my pension, and I don’t have a job to lose,” she said. “Maybe retired people are now more willing to be on the streets than young working people. I see it as my duty; I have to do it.”

For now, Turkish environmentalists say they refuse to be silenced. They have vowed to make their voices heard on the sidelines of COP31, as an older generation steps forward to keep the movement alive.

World.title: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
World.content:
The UN climate chief warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.

The United Nations' top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to "avoid tactical delays" that would prevent a deal to stop global warming.

Delegates from more than 200 nations are gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya with the core goal of preventing the planet from warming by 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit).

Downtown, thousands of civil society and environmental activists from around the world protested against the consequences of climate change.

COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the UN climate chief say?

Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said getting an agreement is "tough but vital work."

"There ​is no collective success without compromise from every party," he added.

"As we head into the second week, ​I urge ‌parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."

Unlike previous UN climate summits, expectations for COP31 are muted Image: Murad Sezer/REUTERS

Climate protest draws activists from around the world

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of protesters marched through Antalya on Saturday for climate protection and human rights, according to the organizers.

Many were dismayed at the lack of progress and how the climate crisis is taking a back seat.

"The pursuit of profit at all costs continues to set the [global] agenda [and] govern the trajectory of our world, so there is a need to push back," environmental activist Zaki Mamdoo from South Africa told DW.

Luisa Nebauer, the main organizer of Germany's Fridays for Future movement, lamented that Chancellor Friedrich Merz was absent from the conference, along with several other European leaders.

"We won't have a chance to solve any of the crises as long as our planet is destabilizing by the hour," Nebauer told DW. "We must show up!"

Turkish authorities permitted the rally to go ahead, in a country that often bans large public gatherings.

Alongside the march, a parallel "People's Climate Summit" involving hundreds of domestic and international civil society groups takes place in Antalya this weekend.

As Turkey hosts COP31 its beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate crisis pushed down agenda

With inflation, wars, deindustrialization and debt being seen as bigger immediate threats, many governments are watering down their commitments to the clean energy transition, along with the billions required to help developing nations to adapt.

The United ⁠States has snubbed the talks ​for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.

Delegates also face pressure from large fossil-fuel-producing nations to avoid setting stricter targets for a faster phase-out of oil and gas.

The COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, runs until November 19 Image: Ozan Kose/AFP

Climate advocates in Antalya are growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of commitment and delaying tactics preventing an ambitious deal.

COP31 is seeking to unlock finance and investment, reduce the use of so-called super-pollutants and methane and ensure food security.

Turkey seeks electrification deal

Host Turkey is, meanwhile, pushing a plan to expand global electrification. Yet, some environmental groups are disappointed the proposal doesn't push increased electricity use from renewable sources.

A UN report last month warned that, within a few years, the world is set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming threshold, set in Paris in 2015.

Prioritize 'People over polluters,' read one banner on Saturday's protest Image: Umit Bektas/REUTERS

This is the figure most scientists believe should stop the worst effects of climate change.

A first draft of a deal text is expected to emerge next week, according to Australia's ​COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.

World.title: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
World.content:
At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

Germany's public broadcasters under fire from far-right AfD To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

Call for more international coverage

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

Why press freedom matters to everyone, not just journalists To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

Belief in the power of dialogue

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.
