World.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.content:
The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.

The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, Nov. 6, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Carmelle bags first-ever Eurovision Asia crown
World.content:
FILIPINA WINNER. Carmelle is the first-ever winner of Eurovision Asia.

With her high-energy performance of 'Sobra-Sobra,' Filipina singer Carmelle Collado tops the jury and fan votes to win the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia

MANILA, Philippines – Carmelle Collado of the Philippines emerged as the first-ever winner of Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

The Bicolana singer received 211 points — topping both the jury and fan votes — to win over artists from 10 other countries on Saturday, November 14, in Bangkok Thailand.

Carmelle performed the high-energy, dance-pop track “Sobra-Sobra,” which was composed by Nica del Rosario and Mat Olavides.

Play Video

The Filipina teen received a jury vote of 93 points, and then received 118 points from the fan vote to emerge as the overall winner.

Carmelle beat Thailand’s representatives Mang and Daou, who sang “Aroma.” The duo received 170 points to finish in second place.

Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, performing “EM TIÊN,” rounded out the top three with 164 points.

Carmelle, a 19-year-old Tawag ng Tanghalan singing champion, was chosen to be the Philippines’ representative during the country’s selection night on August 30.

This is the first-ever Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest. The annual singing competition was first organized in 1956 by the European Broadcasting Union.

Notably, in 2025, Filipino-Austrian singer JJ won Eurovision with the song “Wasted Love.”

Eleven countries competed in the inaugural Eurovision Asia: Bangladesh, Nepal, Cambodia, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam, South Korea, Laos, Bhutan, and Mongolia. – Rappler.com

World.title: From micro to massive, ASEAN’s entrepreneurs face regulatory hurdles
World.content:
BIG BUSINESS. Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala speaks during a panel at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on November 14, 2026.

‘It's incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,’ former CIMB chairman Nazir Razak says, criticizing ASEAN’s slow progress toward economic integration

MANILA, Philippines – A food vendor at a weekend bazaar might have little in common with a conglomerate investing across Southeast Asia, yet both can find themselves grappling with regulations that make growing their business harder than it should be.

For Go Negosyo founder Joey Concepcion, governments should give microentrepreneurs some wiggle room, particularly when they are just starting out.

Speaking on the sidelines of the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on Saturday, November 14, Concepcion recalled how he began his own entrepreneurial journey.

“When I started as an entrepreneur, I didn’t apply for any permit,” he said, also pointing out that many successful food vendors at bazaars sometimes sell products without certificates of product registration.

Play Video

Concepcion knows a thing or two about building a business. He heads RFM Corporation, which is behind the Selecta ice cream Filipinos love, while his family’s other business, Concepcion Industrial, makes the Condura refrigerators that keep it cold. Through Go Negosyo, he has also spent years helping fledgling entrepreneurs get their businesses off the ground.

“If I were the government, I’d just let it go for now and allow them to continue. And eventually, they will gradually follow the rules,” he said. “It cannot be too strict in the process though.”

Beyond permits, Concepcion said small entrepreneurs also struggle with financing and developing better products. This is where mentorship becomes important, particularly in helping businesses become viable enough to qualify for bank loans.

Larger businesses also have a stake in their success. After all, Concepcion noted, sari-sari stores are important outlets for products sold by major manufacturers.

“Because if they close shop, then our sales obviously will also go down,” he said.

Different barriers for bigger businesses

The difficulty of navigating regulations does not disappear as businesses grow; it only changes. Across ASEAN, even its most successful businessmen still grapple with differing national standards, investment approvals, and employment requirements.

Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala said these differences complicate efforts to expand across the region, despite the complementary strengths of Southeast Asian economies.

“There’s still a lot that needs to be done,” he said during a separate panel. “How we would like as a company to be able to move within these different countries in a much easier way, but the standards that we have, the approval standards, the way to get your investment filed, it’s different in each of these countries.”

Play Video

Malaysian banker Nazir Razak, former CIMB Group chairman, had stronger words for ASEAN’s slow progress toward economic integration.

“It’s incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,” he said.

Nazir recalled how CIMB expanded across Southeast Asia in anticipation of the ASEAN Economic Community, launched in 2015 to great fanfare and with the ambition of establishing a single market and production base.

“I felt we were all dressed up with nowhere to go,” he said.

ASEAN has nevertheless continued attracting investment. Foreign direct investment rose 10% to a record $246 billion in 2025, according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2026. Investment originating within the regional bloc also grew 34% to $40 billion, accounting for 16% of total inflows.

Still, Nazir feels that ASEAN has plenty more unlocked economic potential, but its leadership structure could be holding it back. He criticized how much of the authority rests with the chair, which changes every year, rather than the secretary-general, who serves a five-year term. He argued that the arrangement needed reform to help the bloc move faster.

“So you imagine a company where all power is with the chairman, but the chairman changes every year. That would be completely dysfunctional,” he said.

The Philippines is set to hand over ASEAN’s rotating chairmanship to Singapore for 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: Thousands of students protest vs Pax Silica, Trump’s arrival in Manila
World.content:
PROTEST. Students of the Polytechnic University in Sta. Mesa, Manila stage a walkout on November 13, 2026, to protest the Pax Silica initiative and the arrival of US President Donald Trump for the 49th ASEAN Summit.

More groups are expected to stage protests across the country in the coming days, coinciding with the ASEAN Summit

MANILA, Philippines – Thousands of students from different parts of the Philippines staged protests on Friday, November 13, against the US-led Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump’s expected arrival in the country for the ASEAN Summit.

Filipinos have raised concerns about the initiative’s potential environmental impact and the possible displacement of indigenous peoples and farming communities.

In Manila, students from the University of Santo Tomas (UST), Asia’s oldest Catholic university, walked out of their classrooms to join the protest.

“Pax Silica is reported to generate hundreds of thousands of indirect and induced jobs. However, projections are not promises and promises are not guarantees, especially when dealing with a global power like the United States,” the UST Central Student Council Executive Board said.

“It is not enough to ask what development Pax Silica can offer; we must also ask who stands to benefit from it, and more importantly, who will bear its costs,” it added.

At De La Salle University, at least 1,500 students also walked out of their classrooms to protest against the initiative.

STUDENT PROTEST. Students from De La Salle University’s Manila Campus walk out of their classes on November 13, 2026, in protest of Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s visit for the upcoming ASEAN Summit. Photo by Zara Pineda/Rappler

Students from different campuses of the University of the Philippines, Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Miriam College, and Ateneo de Manila University also joined the demonstrations.

RALLY. University of the Philippines Manila students stage a snake rally at the College of Arts and Sciences in accordance with the UP system-wide walkout on November 13, 2026. Photo by Axel Cainglet/Rappler

In Benguet, around 9,000 students from various schools, including UP Baguio, Saint Louis University, and the University of the Cordilleras took to the streets to express their opposition to Pax Silica.

Play Video

Students from Central Luzon State University also staged a protest on Thursday, November 12.

The signing of the Pax Silica agreement had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.

However, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified that the Philippines would not sign the agreement during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters on Tuesday, November 10.

Amid the protests, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the public to reconsider holding demonstrations during the summit.

“’Kung ano man ang panawagan ito ay sana hindi dinadaan sa pagprotesta although ito ay kanilang karapatan. Pero sa panahon ngayon mas magandang nagkakaroon ng mas masinsinang paguusapan kung ano man ang concerns ng mga estudyante,” Castro said during a press briefing on Saturday, November 14.

(Whatever their demands may be, I hope these are not pursued through protests, although I recognize that this is their right. In these times, however, it would be better to have more in-depth discussions about whatever concerns the students may have.)

Different groups are also expected to stage protests in different parts of the country in succeeding days, coinciding with the ASEAN Summit. – Rappler.com

World.title: 5 Philippine creative cities team up to make UNESCO badge count
World.content:
UNITED. National Artist Kidlat Tahimik raises his arms during the ceremonial lighting of the fire at the opening of the 9th IBAGIW Baguio Creative Festival in November 2026. Behind him are representatives of Philippine UNESCO Creative Cities, who gathered in Baguio to strengthen cooperation in arts, culture, creative industries, and community development.

Baguio, Cebu, Iloilo, Dumaguete, and Quezon City hope to turn global recognition into real support for local artists, educators, and communities

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Being recognized by UNESCO is one thing. Making that recognition work for artists, cultural workers, educators, and ordinary communities is another.

This was the challenge confronting representatives of the Philippines’ UNESCO Creative and Learning Cities who gathered in Baguio from November 5 to 8, and agreed to strengthen cooperation beyond the international distinctions their cities have earned.

The gathering, organized by the UNESCO National Commission of the Philippines (UNACOM) and the Baguio City government, brought together the country’s five UNESCO Creative Cities: Baguio for Crafts and Folk Art, Cebu for Design, Iloilo for Gastronomy, Quezon City for Film, and Dumaguete for Literature.

Representatives of the UNESCO Learning Cities of Balanga, Baguio, Legazpi, and Quezon City also participated, linking creative industries with education, lifelong learning, and community development.

Held alongside the ninth IBAGIW Baguio Creative Festival, the convergence was part of UNACOM’s 75th anniversary activities.

At the center of the gathering was a Pledge of Cooperation among the five Creative Cities, witnessed and supported by Learning City representatives.

The pledge commits the cities to sharing resources and expertise, pursuing joint initiatives, and promoting their creative communities nationally and internationally. It also seeks to expand opportunities for women, including access to creative spaces, leadership positions, and industry resources.

The agreement builds on the Philippine Creative Industries Development Act, which provides a national framework for supporting creative enterprises and cultural workers.

Baguio Mayor Benjamin Magalong, whose city became the country’s first UNESCO Creative City in 2017, said international recognition should be measured by the opportunities it creates.

“Bilang kauna-unahang lungsod sa Pilipinas na napabilang sa UNESCO Creative Cities Network noong 2017, naniniwala tayo na ang pagkilala ay hindi lamang isang karangalan,” Magalong said.

“Mas mahalaga ang mga oportunidad na nalilikha nito para sa ating mga artists, artisans, cultural workers, educators, at mga komunidad na patuloy na nagpapanatili ng ating kultura at pagkakakilanlan.”

(As the first city in the Philippines to be included in the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2017, we believe that this recognition is not merely an honor. More important are the opportunities it creates for our artists, artisans, cultural workers, educators, and the communities that continue to preserve our culture and identity.)

The meeting also examined how cooperation could address challenges that individual cities face in sustaining their creative industries, from access to markets and training to the preservation of traditional knowledge.

Creative Baguio City Council co-convenor Marie Venus Tan stressed the importance of connecting creativity with learning and preserving Filipino cultural identity.

Paolo Mercado, president of the Creative Economy Council of the Philippines, argued that creative education must extend beyond the arts.

“Creative thinking is not just artistic thinking; it is also scientific thinking because it is innovation,” Mercado said.

The discussions took a more community-focused turn on November 6, when UNACOM and Baguio City held a consultation on expanding learning opportunities for women and girls.

Participants examined the contributions of indigenous women and traditional knowledge holders to cultural preservation, while identifying barriers to education, resources, leadership, and decision-making.

On November 7, Creative City representatives also agreed to approach the Department of Trade and Industry through the Philippine Creative Industry Development Council to seek support for their continued participation in international UNESCO activities and networks.

They discussed possible joint projects, partnerships between cities, and exchanges that could benefit artists, artisans, and creative enterprises.

The delegates’ visit to Baguio offered examples of how these ideas could work beyond conference rooms.

They toured creative spaces and community enterprises, including the BenCab Museum, Asin Road woodcarving establishments, Ili-likha, Pilak, Mandëko Kito, and other venues participating in IBAGIW.

Learning City representatives also visited Vivita Philippines, a learning space where young people develop ideas through hands-on experimentation, design, and creative problem-solving.

The visits brought attention to the practical challenges of sustaining traditional crafts, creating livelihoods, and passing cultural knowledge to younger generations.

National Artist Kidlat Tahimik, speaking during the festival’s opening ceremonies, cautioned against measuring development solely through economic indicators.

“Now, we always equate progress with the quantifiables. Nakakalimutan na natin ang (We forget the) soul of the city,” he said, referring to the knowledge inherited from ancestors and elders that cannot easily be measured but remains important to the future.

UNACOM deputy executive director Lindsay Barrientos commended Baguio for translating its UNESCO designation into local programs but called for stronger systems of cooperation among cities.

The next test for the newly strengthened network will be turning its commitments into actual projects, with participating cities expected to pursue partnerships, seek institutional support, and expand opportunities for their creative communities.

The IBAGIW Baguio Creative Festival continues throughout November with exhibitions, performances, artisan fairs, workshops, and other cultural activities across the city. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lula: Philippine state visit start of ‘new age of relations’ with Brazil
World.content:
BILATERAL MEETING. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (L) and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (R), pose for pictures before a bilateral meeting at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City, Metro Manila, Philippines 14 November 2026. The Brazilian leader is on a state visit happening alongside the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Meetings in Manila.

'A new age not just trade-wise but also a new age in politics as we have very common ideas and thoughts in relation to the need for reforming the UN, in advocating for multilateralism,' says Brazilian President Lula

MANILA, Philippines – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said on Saturday, November 14, that his state visit to the Philippines is expected to usher in a “new age of relations” between the two countries who are marking their 80th year of diplomatic ties this year.

Lula, the first Brazilian president to go on a state visit to the Philippines, said this at the start of his expanded bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit, which the Philippines chairs.

“This visit to the Philippines, may it be the start of a new age of relations between Brazil and the Philippines. But a new age not just trade-wise but also a new age in politics as we have very common ideas and thoughts in relation to the need for reforming the UN, in advocating for multilateralism, in the recovery of the WTO, and strengthening UN institutions also at the same time,” he said.

Play Video

“We are also very much interested in reforming the UN Security Council for us to give United Nations the necessary credibility once more of an institution that may work to ensure peace in the world,” Lula added.

Marcos, in his statement, cited Lula’s visit as a “high point” of the 80th year of Philippines-Brazil ties.

The Philippine leader noted that the two countries share many commonalities. “In the international arena, we stand shoulder to shoulder in advocating for an international order grounded on dialogue, cooperation and international law,” Marcos added.

At the state luncheon in honor of Lula, Marcos called his visit a “watershed moment” for their countries.

“I hope to enhance our cooperation in regional and multilateral fronts such as the United Nations and in ASEAN,” Marcos said.

Play Video

Lula is joining the plenary session of the ASEAN Summit on Sunday, November 15, as guest of the chair. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos creates National Artificial Intelligence Council
World.content:
TURNOVER. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. leads the turnover of laptops under the DepEd Computerization Program at Dagupan City National High School in Pangasinan on November 9, 2026.

Alongside the creation of the National Artificial Intelligence Council, Marcos' executive order also adopts the country's governance framework for AI policy formation and development

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed an executive order adopting a national artificial intelligence governance framework alongside creating the National Artificial Intelligence Council to oversee and guide implementation of AI tech in the country.

EO 131 was signed on Thursday, November 12, and adopts the AI Governance Framework for the Philippines as the country’s “national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development, capacity-building, and other governance measures necessary to support and strengthen” the Philippine AI ecosystem.

The NAIC, meanwhile, was set up to serve as the inter-agency body responsible for the coordination, facilitation, and monitoring of Al Governance Framework implementations, alongside other related initiatives.

NAIC will be chaired by an executive secretary, while the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) secretary will act as vice chair.

Alongside the chairperson of the Commission on Higher Education and the director general of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, members of NAIC include the secretaries of the following institutions:

Department of Science and Technology

Department of Information and Communications Technology

Department of Trade and Industry

Department of Finance

Department of Education

Department of Labor and Employment

Department of Budget and Management

Further, a representative from the private sector will be appointed by the President for the three-year term with one reappointment.

AI governance framework

The AI Governance Framework of the Philippines comprises four interconnected elements: ethics and principles, standards and assurance, a risk-based policy toolkit, and enabling resources.

As per the framework, AI development, deployment, and use must be human-centric, transparent, explainable, secure, safe, pursue fairness and equity, have accountability and integrity measures, and allow for sustainable development.

The framework calls for appropriate technical standards, testing and evaluation, a conformity assessment, interoperability, and other assurance mechanisms to be set up to “support the responsible, safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of Al.”

Meanwhile, under the risk-based policy toolkit section, the framework noted that Al governance measures should be “proportionate to the nature, context, and level of risk, and may include general and sector-specific guidelines, Al impact assessments, regulatory sandboxes, review of existing laws and regulations, and coordinated complaint and grievance mechanisms.” It added that regulators that currently work in this sector should continue exercising their respective mandates under applicable laws.

Lastly, the framework noted that the government shall “strengthen institutions, data research and development, capabilities, infrastructure, and demand generation to support responsible Al development, deployment, and use.”

Monitoring and review

A number of technical working groups will be set up to facilitate implementation of the framework, with concerned government agencies to be required to submit and regularly update the required information quarterly.

The NAIC, through DEPDev, will lead overall monitoring and reporting efforts on the implementation of the Al Governance Framework and will be required to report on the status and progress of AI Governance Framework implementation within 30 days from the end of each quarter, alongside any other reports requested by the President.

The NAIC shall review the Al Governance Framework at least once every two years — earlier if needed based on any significant technological, regulatory, or market developments — and will recommend amendments or other measures as necessary to the President.

This executive order takes effect immediately upon its publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation.

A copy of the executive order can be downloaded here. – Rappler.com

World.title: BINI Mikha back to work after driving controversy
World.content:
BINI MIKHA. Mikha and the rest of the P-pop girl group BINI are set to perform in Taiwan.

BINI is currently in Taiwan for its 'Signals' world tour

MANILA, Philippines – After getting her license suspended by the Land Transportation Office (LTO), BINI’s Mikha Lim is back to work.

Lim in currently Taiwan for the P-pop girl group’s “Signals” world tour. They arrived in the country on Friday, November 13, and were welcomed by their fans, BLOOMs, at the airport.

Since then, BINI has completed several activities around Taipei, first meeting with Filipinos at the Golden Brother Dormitory, and then hosting a welcome lunch and media conference, followed by another fan meeting at the Meteor Garden Dormitory.

The 23-year-old P-pop idol had earlier been the subject of controversy after a clip of her using her phone while driving went viral. The video was a part of her livestream from November 9.

Internet users had been quick to express alarm regarding the issue, urging the LTO to take swift action against the BINI member.

On November 11, she had then voluntarily appeared before the office of LTO assistant secretary Markus Lacanilao after a show cause order was issued against her, ABS-CBN News reported.

The same report stated that Lim had originally been scheduled to appear at the LTO on November 20, but chose to come earlier to “show good faith,” and then surrendered her driver’s license.

Lim was being asked to appear before the LTO for possible violations under the Anti-Distracted Driving Act, which prohibits the use of electronic mobile devices while on the road.

The LTO had then issued a preventive suspension on her license for 90 days.

Lim had issued her own apology on X on the evening of November 11, further confirming that she had reported to the LTO to face the penalties of her violation.

“There is absolutely no excuse for using my phone while behind the wheel. It was careless and irresponsible. I take full accountability for what happened,” she wrote.

“This has been a big lesson for me to be much more mindful, disciplined, and responsible moving forward. Road safety rules exist to protect everyone, and something we need to take seriously.”

The Taiwan stop of BINI’s 2026 “Signals” world tour will happen on Sunday, November 15, at the New Taipei City Exhibition Hall. – Rappler.com

World.title: Bohol-Panglao airport wins sustainability award in Singapore
World.content:
The Bohol-Panglao International Airport, one of the three airports operated by Aboitiz InfraCapital, has received top honors at the 2026 Travel Daily Media (TDM) Travel Trade Excellence Awards – Asia for its environmental sustainability initiatives. — Leo Udtohan

TAGBILARAN CITY, Bohol — The Bohol-Panglao International Airport (BPIA) has been recognized for its environmental initiatives after winning the Sustainability Initiative of the Year – Philippines award at the 2026 Travel Daily Media (TDM) Travel Trade Excellence Awards – Asia.

The award was presented on Nov. 10 at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre in Singapore, recognizing the airport’s efforts to promote sustainable operations through its ECO-Airport Project.

READ: Panglao Island among most visited island destinations in C. Visayas

Article continues after this 

The project comprises seven initiatives covering solar power, water conservation, the use of electric ground equipment, plastic reduction and a partnership with the Bohol Island UNESCO Global Geopark.

The recognition places BPIA among three airports operated by Aboitiz InfraCapital (AIC) Airports that received top honors in this year’s awards.

Mactan-Cebu International Airport (MCIA) won Airport Experience of the Year – Philippines, while Laguindingan International Airport (LIA) in Misamis Oriental received the Health and Safety Initiative of the Year – Philippines award.

AIC Airports chief executive officer Athanasios Titonis said the recognition reflected the company’s commitment to developing world-class airport infrastructure while promoting sustainability, regional economic growth and passenger safety.

The awards recognize the airport operator’s efforts across three key areas: passenger experience, environmental responsibility and safety.

Article continues after this 

For Bohol, the recognition highlights the role of the province’s international gateway in advancing environmentally responsible tourism and airport operations.

BPIA ranks as the ninth-busiest airport in the Philippines, handling approximately 2.22 million passengers annually, driven by strong post-pandemic tourism growth and its transition to AIC management.

Article continues after this 

The BPIA serves as a major gateway for domestic and international visitors traveling to Bohol, a popular destination known for its natural attractions, marine biodiversity and United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) Global Geopark status.

AIC said the latest recognition adds to the growing list of awards received by AIC-operated airports, including MCIA’s Airport of the Year in Asia title at the 2025 TDM Travel Trade Excellence Awards.

World.title: Group renews call for safer roads on remembrance day of crash victims
World.content:
Traffic jams and road accidents stem from many reasons including driver discipline — GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines – As the country commemorates the National Day of Remembrance for Road Crash Victims, Survivors, and Their Families on Sunday, a transport advocacy group has urged lawmakers to invest more in road safety programs to prevent further deaths on Philippine roads.

The Move As One Coalition cited the deaths of 90-year-old Erlinda Santos Tagle and 11-year-old Dawn Rafael Linga, who were both hit by pickup trucks while crossing designated pedestrian lanes.

Tagle was volunteering outside a church in Pampanga when a pickup truck struck her last June. Meanwhile, Linga was crossing a pedestrian lane in Oriental Mindoro when a speeding pickup truck hit him last January.

Article continues after this 

READ: 11-year-old road crash victim laid to rest as LTO probes driver

Observed every third Sunday of November under Republic Act No. 11468, the National Day of Remembrance honors road crash victims, survivors, and their families.

The coalition said the deaths of Tagle and Linga underscored the need to make Philippine roads safer.

“Their deaths show how little progress has been made in making Philippine roads safer,” the group said.

It also cited Philippine Statistics Authority data showing that road crash fatalities increased by 65.34 percent, from 7,938 in 2011 to 13,125 in 2023.

Article continues after this 

The group urged the government to go beyond offering prayers and lighting candles for road crash victims, calling instead for greater investment in programs and infrastructure that protect people from road hazards.

READ: Motorists: Better road conditions to help prevent accidents

Article continues after this 

“The Coalition calls on the Senate and the Bicameral Conference Committee to fund investments to make roads safer for people, not promote motor vehicle speed,” it said.

Road safety funding

Move As One Coalition raised concerns over the lack of funding for the Philippine Road Safety Action Plan (PRSAP), saying the Department of Transportation’s (DOTr) proposed ₱111.29-million allocation for the program was reduced to zero in both the National Expenditure Program and the House General Appropriations Bill.

According to the PRSAP 2023-2028, a review of the previous 2017-2022 plan found that underfunded organizations and the low priority given to road safety had hampered the implementation of its goals.

READ: House subpanel OKs P2.35-B DOTr budget boost for 2027 key programs

“Many challenges have hampered the full attainment of road safety goals.”

“The most striking realities were that organizations were underfunded, and road safety was not the top priority,” the coalition said, quoting the plan.

The previous plan also failed to meet its interim target of reducing the road death rate by at least 20 percent by 2022, the coalition noted.

The group likewise called for the restoration of the DOTr’s proposed P1.13-billion budget for active transport in the 2027 national budget, saying the House bill allocated only P33.9 million.

In comparison, road-widening projects received a total of P223.07 billion from 2020 to 2026, while the Active Transport Bike Share and Safe Pathways Program received P3.87 billion during the same period, according to the coalition.

The group said the government should prioritize infrastructure that protects pedestrians, including safer and raised pedestrian crossings, wider sidewalks, and traffic-calming measures.

It also urged lawmakers to reconsider spending on footbridges, arguing that at-grade crossings are more accessible to people of different ages and abilities.

“The Move As One Coalition urges lawmakers to pass a 2027 national budget that values human life over vehicle speed,” the coalition said.

World.title: Holiday gridlock looms as P150-M overhaul of Bukidnon bridge set
World.content:
BRIDGE RETROFITTING. Traffic personnel assist motorists along Atugan Bridge in Barangay La Fortuna, Impasugong, Bukidnon. PHOTO from DPWH Bukidnon 1st DEO

MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Motorists and cargo haulers traversing Sayre Highway, Mindanao’s primary inland artery, brace for massive holiday gridlock as major retrofitting work on the structurally compromised Atugan Bridge in Barangay La Fortuna, Impasugong, Bukidnon, is set to roll out in December—right at the height of the Christmas travel rush.

Shara Vinessa Garcia, spokesperson for the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Bukidnon 1st District Engineering Office, confirmed to the Inquirer on Friday, November 13, that the procurement process has officially commenced for the P150-million emergency rehabilitation project.

READ: Bukidnon bridge shows cracks; P150-M retrofitting works set

Article continues after this 

The urgent engineering intervention, to be spearheaded by District Engineer Maria David, comes after structural assessments uncovered alarming cracks along the 43-year-old 223.04-meter span, forcing authorities to declare the bridge unsafe for unrestricted public access.

Towering roughly 64.5 meters (212 feet) above a deep canyon floor, Atugan Bridge is among Mindanao’s highest bridges and serves as a critical economic and transportation lifeline along the Sayre Highway, directly linking Northern Mindanao to the Davao region.

Any severe bottleneck at the crossing threatens to disrupt both peak holiday passenger travel and the movement of agricultural goods across the island’s interior.

Garcia revealed that the P150-million allocation—drawn from savings under the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA) through the Department of Budget and Management (DBM)—was initially requested during the previous fiscal year and was only released this year.

Full project implementation, encompassing procurement, consultancy, and actual structural retrofitting, is scheduled to begin next month.

Article continues after this 

Travelers along the busy highway have already been enduring daily bottlenecks since October 13, when the DPWH abruptly enforced a strict one-lane, stop-and-go traffic scheme upon discovering the structural defects.

With construction activities expected to compound congestion next month, the DPWH is strongly urging light vehicles to divert to the Impasugong–Patulangan bypass road (old Sayre Highway) to avoid severe delays at the bridge approach. /jpv

World.title: BARMM government returns to 5-day workweek on Nov. 16
World.content:
BARMM official logo

COTABATO CITY — Starting Monday, Nov. 16, all government offices in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will drop the four-day compressed workweek and go back to the regular five-day schedule.

The change was agreed on during the first regular Cabinet meeting of the Bangsamoro Government on Nov. 6. The Office of the Chief Minister put it into effect through Memorandum Circular No. 0150, issued in Nov. 10.

The circular lifts and revokes Memorandum Circular No. 0049, Series of 2026, which had set up the four-day onsite work arrangement and compressed workweek. Any other issuances that conflict with the new circular are superseded or modified to match it.

Article continues after this 

READ: Opapru, MinDA vow support for BARMM peace, economic development

All ministries, offices and agencies will work Monday to Friday, from 8 a.m. to 12 noon and from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m., with a one-hour lunch break. That comes to eight working hours a day, or 40 hours a week, in line with Civil Service rules and regulations.

All heads of ministries, offices and agencies were told to make sure the circular is strictly followed and to take the steps needed for an orderly shift back to the regular schedule.

The Bangsamoro Parliament followed with its own order.

In Memorandum No. 1126-004, dated Nov. 10 and released on Nov. 11, Bangsamoro Parliament Speaker Amer Zaakaria A. Rakim directed the members of Parliament, the Office of the Secretary General and all organic offices of the regional legislature to go back to the five-day schedule on the same date.

Article continues after this 

The Speaker’s memo also formally lifts and ends the Parliament’s own compressed workweek, set up under Memorandum Circular No. 0326-073 on March 12, 2026.

The Office of the Secretary General, service directors and division chiefs were told to monitor attendance and make sure the order is strictly followed. INQ

World.title: 2 dead, 2 hurt in biogas explosion in Masbate
World.content:
Police investigators inspect the site of a biogas explosion outside LCC Market and Department Store along Tara Street in Barangay Pating, Masbate City, on Nov. 14. The blast killed two people and injured two others. (Photo courtesy of PRO 5)

LEGAZPI CITY — Two people were killed and two others were wounded in an explosion outside LCC Market and Department Store along Tara Street in Barangay Pating, Masbate City, on Saturday afternoon, Nov. 14.

Police Lt. Col. Maria Luisa Calubaquib, Bicol police spokesperson, said initial findings indicated that the incident was caused by a pressurized biogas explosion, based on coordination with the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) and the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO).

However, these initial findings remain subject to confirmation pending laboratory examination of soil samples and swab specimens collected from the scene by the Police Forensic Unit (PFU), as well as further investigation.

Article continues after this 

READ: 1 cop hurt in Masbate bomb blast

The Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Team also conducted initial sniffing operations, during which no explosive components were detected at the scene.

Investigators are also identifying and interviewing witnesses, securing available CCTV footage from nearby establishments, and examining physical evidence to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

PRO 5 Regional Director Brig. Brig. Gen. Randy Glenn Silvio assured the public that authorities are pursuing all necessary investigative measures to determine the exact cause of the explosion.

He also urged the public to remain calm, refrain from spreading unverified information, and report any relevant information, photographs, or video recordings to the nearest police station or the Masbate City Police Station. INQ

World.title: PPA logs over 10,500 passengers amid Asean long weekend
World.content:
Philippine Ports Authority | INQUIRER.net

MANILA, Philippines — More than 10,500 passengers were recorded to have passed through Batangas port on Saturday, Nov. 14, amid the long weekend due to the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit, the Philippine Ports Authority (PPA) reported.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. previously declared Nov. 16 to 18, as special (non-working) days in the National Capital Region to make way for the regional high-stakes gathering, which will take place in Pasay City.

READ: PNP boosts security ahead of Asean Summit, holiday travel rush

Article continues after this 

The PPA monitored at least 10,593 passengers at Batangas port around 12 p.m.

The figure is 13 percent higher than the over 9,000 passengers recorded in the previous days, it added.

Meanwhile, at Calapan port, the total number of inbound and outbound passengers reached 3,350.

Baseport Lucena also reported nearly 2,000 passengers, while the terminal management office Balanacan in Marinduque also logged at least 1,685 passengers, according to the PPA.

“Maaga po tayo nakapaghanda lalo’t namonitor natin yung mga pasahero nitong Undas, kaya’t tinitiyak natin na maayos ang operasyon sa ating mga pantalan at handa ang ating mga tauhan na magbigay ng kinakailangang tulong upang maging ligtas, maginhawa, at maayos ang paglalakbay ng bawat pasahero,” PPA General Manager Jay Santiago said in a statement.

(“We were able to prepare early, especially since we monitored passenger movement during the Undas period; we are therefore ensuring that operations at our ports are running smoothly, and our personnel are ready to provide the necessary assistance to ensure that every passenger’s journey is safe, comfortable, and orderly.”) /mr

World.title: Protesters burn Trump effigy ahead of his Asean Summit arrival
World.content:
US President Donald Trump meets with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC. (Photo by ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS / AFP)

MANILA, Philippines — Protesters burned an effigy of US President Donald Trump on Saturday ahead of his expected arrival in the country for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit to show their opposition for the US-led Pax Silica initiative.

The protest took place at the University of the Philippines (UP)-Diliman in Quezon City, which was joined by students, environmental groups, farmers and members of the Aeta community.

Earlier, around 200 members of the Aeta community from Central Luzon arrived in UP Diliman as part of a “kampuhan” (camp out) that will also serve as the “staging center” of the groups’ “Trump Out campaign.”

Article continues after this 

The groups began their protest by marching along the Academic Oval from Vinzons Hall to Quezon Hall, where they gathered behind the Oblation statue that was draped with banners that bear the words “Trump Out.”

READ: Trump’s ‘late arrival’ won’t affect Asean Summit sked–DFA

The protesters were opposing Trump’s arrival because of the proposed Pax Silica initiative led by the United States. They claimed that the initiative would displace indigenous communities and farmers from Central Luzon while also destroying the environment.

“Our future must not be built on stolen land and destroyed livelihoods. Students must stand with communities—not with an imperialist agenda that puts corporate profit above people’s rights,” said Gio Biglaen of the UP University Student Council in a statement after the protest.

As part of the protest, Aeta community members shot flaming arrows at Trump’s effigy, dubbed as “Trumplunderer.” It will be the first of at least four images of the US President that the groups will burn in anticipation of Trump’s arrival.

Article continues after this 

“Ancestral lands are not sacrifice zones for corporate expansion. Indigenous Peoples are not obstacles to development—we are defending our right to determine what development means for our communities,” said Jeoff Larua of the Cordillera Peoples Alliance.

According to the progressive group Bagong Alyansang Makabayan, another kampuhan will be set up at the Liwasang Bonifacio freedom park in Manila, to be joined by the Molbog Indigenous Peoples to show their opposition to the construction of an airbase in Balabac.

Article continues after this 

The 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits is being hosted by the Philippines from Nov. 15 to 17 at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City. It is expected to be capped with a meeting between Trump and leaders of the 11 Asean member states. /ms

World.title: Murder raps filed vs 3 suspects in slay of Basilan judge
World.content:
INQUIRER.net stock photo

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — Police have filed a murder complaint against three suspects linked to the fatal shooting of Regional Trial Court Presiding Judge Joseph Wee Sit in Zamboanga City on Thursday.

Lt. Col. Shellamie Chang, spokesperson of the Police Regional Office 9 (PRO 9), said the criminal complaint was lodged before the Zamboanga City Prosecutor’s Office at around 12:36 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 14.

READ: PNP intensifies manhunt for Basilan judge’s killers

Article continues after this 

The respondents include one identified suspect, believed to be the gunman, and two still unidentified ones who allegedly served as the motorcycle driver and the driver of a getaway support vehicle.

Chang said the filing followed sustained case build-up by the Special Investigation Task Group (SITG) “Wee Sit,” backed by judicial affidavits alongside documentary and forensic evidence gathered by investigators.

Brig. Gen. Elmer Ragay, PRO 9 regional director, said the filing demonstrates the police force’s commitment to pursuing justice through diligent, evidence-based investigation and close coordination among concerned units. INQ

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Myanmar Junta Seeks Record Military Budget as Millions Struggle With Poverty
World.content:
The Myanmar regime plans to increase the military budget to a record high for the 2026-27 fiscal year, even as approximately one-third of the country’s population lives in poverty.

Since 2021, the regime has been waging war against several established ethnic armed organizations as well as newly emerged resistance forces, including the People’s Defense Force, across the country, spending a large portion of its budget on military expenses.

Last Thursday, the regime’s rubber-stamp Union Parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw), where the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and its allies hold a majority of seats, debated a supplementary budget allocation bill.

The proposed allocation would bring total defense spending to 10.53 trillion kyats (US$5.01 billion), combining the initial 2026-27 fiscal year estimate of 7.95 trillion kyats with a supplementary grant of 2.58 trillion kyats.

Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Mideast Crisis Fuels Oil Conflict in Myanmar’s Heartland
World.content:
Myanmar’s small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry that is becoming increasingly lucrative amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

“As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us,” said Htun Aung, a worker on an oil well in Myanmar’s arid heartlands.

“But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder,” said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.

Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

But the central region of Magwe hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.

The area is dubbed “Anyar Dubai,” associating the Anyar or central dry zone landscape with the oil boom emirate, despite the pitiable US$50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.

With prices at Myanmar’s petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground “black gold” is a coveted prize.

“We just want to live in peace,” said Htun Aung. “But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other—they keep attacking each other.”

“We’ve had to flee three, four, five times already,” he added. “We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again.”

Digging in

Pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magwe’s Myaing Township since 2023.

They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy River in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.

Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025’s total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the 2021 putsch.

Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.

Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of meters down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.

Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill, one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.

Some wells yield dribbles while others gush, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel.

“Anyar Dubai” has been “going viral” for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when regime-held areas are rationing petrol.

He touted recent offensives fending off military advances but admitted being battered by counter-attacks.

“We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us,” said the 35-year-old.

Myanmar’s military could not be reached for comment.

In September, the military claimed a month-long military operation captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighboring Pakokku Township.

Black market

Scores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic armed groups are fighting the military.

As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill their war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.

Oil projects are not generally contested.
