World.title: Tajikistan’s per capita gas consumption falls to 19 cubic metres in 2025 - Eni
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Tajikistan’s per capita natural gas consumption amounted to 19 cubic metres in 2025, down from 25 cubic metres in 2024, according to Italian energy company Eni’s World Energy Review 2026.

Eni’s figures show that per capita natural gas consumption in Tajikistan stood at 24 cubic metres in 2019, before declining to 23 cubic metres in 2020 and recovering to 24 cubic metres in 2021. The indicator then fell to 19 cubic metres in 2022, rose to 21 cubic metres in 2023 and reached 25 cubic metres in 2024, before falling back to 19 cubic metres in 2025. Eni did not provide a figure for 2015.

For comparison, the regional indicator for Russia and Central Asia stood at 2,615 cubic metres in 2025, down from 2,658 cubic metres in 2024. It amounted to 2,199 cubic metres in 2015 and 2,310 cubic metres in 2019, dipped slightly to 2,308 cubic metres in 2020 and peaked at 2,677 cubic metres in 2021. It then declined to 2,550 cubic metres in 2022 and 2,535 cubic metres in 2023.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan’s population reached 10.8 million in 2025, compared with 10.6 million in 2024, according to Eni. The company reported year-on-year growth of 1.8% and a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 2.2% over 2015–2025.

The country’s population increased from 8.6 million in 2015 to 9.5 million in 2019, then to 9.7 million in 2020 and 10 million in 2021. It rose further to 10.2 million in 2022, 10.4 million in 2023 and 10.6 million in 2024, before reaching 10.8 million in 2025.

World.title: Date set for Xi Jinping, Putin and Trump meeting
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States — Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump — will take place on November 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, Russian Presidential Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov said.

World.title: Citibank to redeem $3 billion in notes due 2027 on November 19
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Citibank, N.A. will redeem a total of $3 billion in notes due 2027 on November 19, 2026, according to a company announcement.

The redemption will cover $2.2 billion in 4.876% fixed-to-floating-rate notes (ISIN: US17325FBL13) and $800 million in floating-rate notes (ISIN: US17325FBM95).

The notes will be redeemed at par, plus accrued and unpaid interest up to, but excluding, the redemption date.

Citibank said the redemptions are in line with its liability management strategy and reflect its efforts to improve the efficiency of its funding and capital structure.

The bank added that it would continue to consider opportunities to redeem or repurchase securities, taking into account factors such as their economic value, regulatory changes, potential effects on net interest margins and borrowing costs, the remaining maturity of its debt portfolio, capital implications and overall market conditions.

Interest on the notes will cease to accrue from the redemption date. Citibank, N.A. will act as the paying agent.

Citibank, N.A. is the primary U.S. banking subsidiary of Citigroup Inc., one of the largest global financial services companies. Founded in 1812 as the City Bank of New York, Citibank ranks among the top banks in the United States by assets, with approximately $2 trillion in total assets. Headquartered in New York, it provides a broad range of consumer, commercial, and institutional banking services and operates as part of Citigroup’s global network spanning more than 180 countries and jurisdictions.

World.title: Shohin Airlines announces plans for flights to four Tajik cities
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Tajik Shohin Airlines has announced its readiness to launch regular domestic flights from Dushanbe to four cities across the country: Khorugh, Khujand, Bokhtar and Kulob, according to a company statement on November 14, 2026.

The planned routes are Dushanbe–Khorugh–Dushanbe, Dushanbe–Khujand–Dushanbe, Dushanbe–Bokhtar–Dushanbe and Dushanbe–Kulob–Dushanbe. The airline intends to use its modern L410 NG turboprop aircraft, which can accommodate up to 19 passengers, to serve the new destinations.

Shohin Airlines said flights would be operated subject to weather and meteorological conditions.

The company noted that the development of domestic air services would help reduce travel times between cities and make journeys more convenient for regional residents, business travellers and tourists. The new routes are also intended to strengthen transport links between Dushanbe and regional centres and create additional opportunities for domestic tourism.

An important step in the expansion of Shohin Airlines’ operations was the addition of an L410 NG plane named Badakhshon to its fleet. Presented in Dushanbe on October 2, 2026, the turboprop was manufactured by Czech company LET Aircraft Industries, which specialises in the development and production of aviation equipment, and is designed for regional transportation and short-haul routes.

Shohin Airlines CEO Zafar Ahmadzoda said that developing domestic air services was an important part of the company’s efforts to strengthen connections between Tajikistan’s regions. He added that the new routes were intended to make travel between cities easier and faster, reduce the time required for business trips, and give tourists and regional residents more opportunities to travel. He described the routes as "air bridges" that would connect cities, people and opportunities.

The airline also noted that the initiative was particularly significant in the year marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence, reflecting its commitment to developing transport infrastructure and strengthening links between regions. Shohin Airlines said it would continue working to expand domestic air services, improve transport accessibility in the regions and develop a modern system of regional air transportation in Tajikistan.

World.title: Cargo ships are being sunk here and some say it's all part of Russia's plan
World.content:
Just after 1am on October 13, Commander Ivan Ivanov and his crew received a mayday call.

A Malta-flagged ship, the Chelsea 3, was in distress and sinking in the Black Sea, 40 kilometres from the Bulgarian port of Varna.

The vessel had been hit by a drone that had blown an enormous hole in its side, and it was taking on water.

Within minutes, Commander Ivanov's crew were heading out to sea to try and reach it.

"The weather was extremely bad. The sea was stormy, with a very strong wind, and the visibility was very low," Commander Ivanov told the ABC.

A Russian shaddow fleet vessel is struk with a drone in the Black Sea last year. (Supplied: Ukrainian Armed Forces)

The Black Sea has become a deadly theatre of battle as merchant ships carrying things like grain, chemicals and oil are increasingly caught in the crossfire of Russia's war in Ukraine.

Both countries have ports on the Black Sea and have been hitting ships going to and from each other's docks since Moscow's full-scale invasion began.

But in the last few months, the attacks have taken on a whole new dimension, and sailors have become collateral damage.

At least 38 have been killed since June, making the Black Sea the deadliest waterway in the world, even surpassing the Strait of Hormuz.

Commander Ivan Ivanov says the drones are making his job more difficult. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

When the crew arrived, the Chelsea 3 was already listing to the left hard and the choppy seas made it too dangerous to deploy a lifeboat.

The sailors had to jump from their sinking ship to the border patrol vessel to save themselves.

The ABC has gained rare access to embed with Bulgaria's border police, which act as the country's coast guard, undertaking search and rescue missions at sea.

Commander Ivanov has worked on the sea for 20 years, but the Chelsea 3 was the first sinking cargo ship in distress he had dealt with.

Just as his crew returned to port having saved all on board, he received a second mayday call. Another cargo ship, the HS Dignity, was sinking after also being hit by multiple drones.

But the worsening weather conditions would prove too dangerous. While five of the HS Dignity's crew were rescued after abandoning ship in a life boat, 11 remain missing.

Bulgaria's border police have noticed a spike in distress calls from cargo ships. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

Commander Bozhidar Penev, who has spent more than a decade on the water with Bulgaria's border police, was also on call that night.

"Definitely, the last few weeks have been tough for us," he told the ABC.

"We have increased surveillance even further. We are always on high alert; we have multiple systems on board our ships to aid us in both daytime and night."

He said drones had made his job more dangerous.

Bozhidar Penev and his colleagues have been trying to keep Bulgarian waters safe. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

"I am afraid of this [drones]; the possibility is always there. But if I am afraid or not, this is my job and when there is a task, I have to do it," he said.

The HS Dignity, flagged Guinea-Bissau, had been travelling from Algeria to Romania. Among those missing is Mohammed Mreish's 20-year-old cousin, Amjad.

"I feel they are alive, that's my real feeling. I have a big hope," he told the ABC last month.

He said Amjad's mother was distressed and would not have closure until her son was found.

Amjad was one of the sailors on the HS Dignity, and is still missing. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

Mohammed travelled from his home in Germany to Varna and spoke to some of the rescued sailors to find out more information about what happened.

"They woke up at the middle of the night ... and found the ship full of water, so they decided to run to the deck again to launch the lifeboat," he told the ABC.

He said they saw what they thought were two vessels coming towards them at speed and believed it was a rescue mission. They were actually sea drones.

Amjad was one of 14 Syrians among the crew. The country has been in turmoil and economically unstable as it rebuilds itself after former long-time dictator Bashar al-Assad was removed in 2024.

"They need money to live. They need money to survive. The situation in Syria is really not that good," Mohammed said.

"There's no work, no jobs, no money ... and the young people, they need to start their life. They need to work somewhere. And the only way is the sea."

Mohammed Mreish is searching for information on his cousin, Amjad, in Bulgaria. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

'An attack is an attack'

Cargo ships traversing the Black Sea are forced to run the gauntlet of attacks by drones and missiles as Russia and Ukraine battle for control over the vital shipping corridor.

More than 500 ships have been hit within the waterway during the past year.

The number of sailors killed has risen fast because the nature of the strikes has changed from simply trying to disable ships to targeting their hulls and bridges in an attempt to sink them, a tactic known as "double tap".

Damage can be seen on the cargo ship Chelsea 3 after it was struck by a drone in the Black Sea. (Supplied)

The attacks are also now edging closer to Ukraine's neighbours and that means closer to territory falling under the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

Tomas Alexa from global maritime security agency Ambrey said he expected the attacks to continue.

"The Russians are testing the response, the unity of the Eastern flank," he said.

"They are monitoring and looking very closely what is the reaction of NATO, but also of the European Union to these attacks.

"In a way, we assess that it is likely that third attacks will take place in Romanian-Bulgarian waters simply because the glass was broken."

The Black Sea is a critical trade route, for multiple countries, including Ukraine. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

Romania and Bulgaria, which hug the western border of the Black Sea, are members of NATO alongside Turkey, which controls the access of ships through the Bosphorus Strait to the rest of the world.

During October, nine cargo ships were hit with drones within the exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania.

One was even inside the territorial waters of Romania.

The reason ships are travelling closer to shore now is the simple fact that wartime insurance premiums have skyrocketed. Sailing close to the shore comes with fewer risks.

The attacks are being seen as a major escalation and a test of NATO's collective security agreement, in which an attack on one member state is considered an attack on all.

The alliance, which aims to deter conflict, was formed after World War II between the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and many European nations.

Former Bulgarian defence minister Todor Tagarev says Russia is trying to test NATO's resolve. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

Bulgaria's former defence minister Todor Tagarev, who was in office when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said the Kremlin's primary goal is to crush Kyiv's economy by cutting off sea trade.

However, it was also trying to test NATO's resolve, to see how far countries in the bloc will go to protect each other.

"One of the centres of gravity for Ukraine in this war is the European support to Ukraine," Mr Togarev said.

"When the Russians demonstrate how dangerous this is becoming for European countries, for European societies, then they hope that the support to the Ukrainian war effort will be diminished."

Despite being a member of NATO and the European Union, Bulgaria has historical ties with Russia that Mr Tagarev said was holding back a stronger response.

"They are really afraid to refer to Russia as an aggressor. And they do not want to have this as the basis for planning a response," Mr Tagarev said.

Bulgarian border guard vessels ready for their next mission in the Black Sea. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

NATO's Article 5 (in which member states are obliged to come to each other's aid) has only been triggered once previously, after the September 11 attacks in New York.

Professor Kevin Rowlands from the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) spent three decades in the British Navy and retired as a captain.

He said it was easier from a political standpoint to go to war for America in 2001 than what it would be against Russia.

"Some of the NATO allies are more closely aligned to Russia than others. Some would be pushing for this kind of declaration, others would be holding back, so it becomes very political," he said.

Beyond calling out Russia's actions, Europe is grappling with how to deter the attacks and often resorts to labelling it "hybrid" or "shadow" warfare.

"An attack is an attack. If two countries are at war, let's call it for what it is, it's a war," Professor Rowlands said.

NATO has sent reinforcements to the Black Sea including more patrol planes, radar systems and intelligence officers.

But with the frontline in Ukraine practically at a standstill, analysts believe Moscow is likely to continue hitting ships that fuel Kyiv's economy.

World.title: Can these true crime sleuths solve Australia's most infamous cold cases?
World.content:
At a seaside festival in regional South Australia, true crime obsession meets the grief of families whose loved ones are presumed murdered.

Max Marten is speaking from a wheelchair beside a wooden stage in Victor Harbor's splendid art deco theatre. "We are dealing in a subject that affects every single person in this room," the podcast producer says. I look around me; the theatre is two-thirds full of mostly white, middle-aged women. "You have family and friends that may not be here anymore because of what happened," Max says.

What happened is usually murder, although many of the cases being discussed at "Crime Scene Victor Harbor" — billed as Australia's first true crime festival — have never been solved. Now, buffered from the wind in a seaside town an hour's drive from Adelaide, the audience is being asked to help. "Through conversation things get solved and people get listened to," Max says, before handing the microphone to Bryan Littlely, the brains behind the festival.

Bryan, a cowboy boot-wearing former journalist, farmer and now true crime podcast host, once saw an episode of CSI: Crime Scene Investigation about a murder at a true crime convention. In the episode, called "Merchants of Menace", a murder takes place at a convention selling "murderabilia": items that were used in crimes, once belonged to killers, or artworks they produced in prison. There have been attempts to outlaw murderabilia in the US, where opponents say it trivialises or glorifies hideous crimes and further traumatises victims' families. It exists at the grisly fringe of true crime obsession.

The Victa, Victor Harbor's art deco theatre lit up during the true crime festival. ( )

For Bryan, the episode seeded the idea of a true crime convention that he revisited after he began presenting his true crime podcast "Sleepers" in front of live audiences. "Making yourself available to answer questions and have the statements and the evidence challenged by the public who are ever hungry for true crime [is popular]," he tells me. "It just so happens that people want to pay to see that." Why not host a true crime festival in his hometown, he thought, and bring together writers, podcasters and citizen sleuths to discuss the crimes they've wrestled into stories?

As for why we're seeing a true crime renaissance, Bryan points to social media. "There's experts everywhere … anyone can be an investigator," including victims' families he told an Adelaide radio station ahead of the festival. "The families are speaking and there's less oversight by police, there's individual and independent investigations going on … not everyone wants to be spoken to by a police officer, and police are resource poor, they can't be looking at these cases." He promises the radio host that at Crime Scene Victor Harbor there'll be "revelations on some major cases".

Before arriving at the festival, I checked into a desolate caravan park on the edge of town. Leaving my phone on the bed, I took a shower in the cramped bathroom of a prefab cabin. When I pulled the handle of the sliding door to leave the bathroom it wouldn't budge. I tried again, willing my fingers into the space between the door and the frame, but nothing happened. I wasn't panicking — yet — but I started to wonder how long it would be before someone realised I was stuck.

I wedged open a small window. It wasn't big enough to climb out, but through a fist-sized opening I saw a single campervan and tent in an otherwise empty campground. Eventually, a woman wearing an over-sized t-shirt and pigtails tied with rainbow scrunchies appeared. I shouted, "hello, hello!", and she approached the window. She asked if the cabin door was locked. I wasn't sure. Then I could hear her inside the cabin. "There's frayed carpet under the door catching it," she said before pulling the carpet out and opening the door.

I was free. In a rush of relief, I walked out of the bathroom, smiling. Then I realised I was standing beside a bed wearing nothing but a towel face-to-face with a stranger. "Lucky it was me," the woman said before leaving. I took that to mean lucky I wasn't a man.

One theory that tries to account for true crime's popularity is that for women, the overwhelming consumers of the podcasts, TV shows and books that have proliferated over the past decade or so, it imparts useful life lessons. A sorry guide on how to escape killers and abusers and avoid becoming a victim.

But this alone doesn't explain the rise of amateur sleuths or victims' families telling their own true crime stories. We live in an age of super sleuths like "mushroom murderer" Erin Patterson — who belonged to an online community researching the crimes of Keli Lane, convicted of murdering her newborn daughter in 2010 before her own case descended into true crime mania. I've come to Victor Harbor curious to figure out what's fuelling this phenomenon.

Victor Harbor, on the south coast of the Florian Peninsula, in South Australia. ( )

From audience to sleuth

On Friday night Victor Harbor's main street is deserted. A warm glow seeps from a sandstone pub opposite the theatre. Inside, Sharon Ferguson and Nanette Simpson are talking intently at the festival's "hub", their heads bowed together to combat the noise in the room. The two retirees have known each other for 50 years and have bumped into each other at the event.

When I ask why they're here, they place newspaper clippings and scribbled notes on the table. Sharon has an article about Hazel Pope and Joyce Eastwood who were last seen in 1970 outside the meatworks where they worked. According to Crime Stoppers SA, they unloaded two suitcases, were picked up by a male taxi driver and never heard from again. Sharon says she knew one of the women.

She also says she used to work with a man believed to have been involved in Adelaide's horrific "family" serial killings. Since Sharon realised her connection a few years back, she's been writing down names and memories as they arise — some day one might prove useful to someone.

Sharon Ferguson and Nanette Simpson have become avid true crime consumers since retiring. ( )

True crime has existed as a literary genre since the mid-1800s, but over the last 15 years it's become more participatory and immersive, as criminology professor Michael Arntfield writes: "Amateur sleuths, advocates, pundits and activists proliferate with each new feature. Podcasts beget further podcasts." Fanatics are dedicating their own time and resources trying to solve cold cases. Sometimes they make breakthroughs, sometimes fingers are pointed too hastily at innocent people. And like most things on the internet, true crime isn't immune to conspiracy theories.

The next morning, I pass a group of older women dressed in Lycra discussing the fate of the Adelaide Crows' coach as they shuffle along the foreshore. It occurs to me that football, that great unifier, shares something with true crime obsession. Both tap into a desire for community and conversation through endlessly analysed strategy. And perhaps like football, true crime affords us a universe where the heroes and villains are easy to identify. As English writer Kate Summerscale argues, true crime "can relieve our anxiety by locating badness in a single person, rather than in our society or ourselves".

At the first Crime Scene Victor Harbor event on the Saturday, Meni Caroutas is talking about the murder of Peter Falconio and the attempted kidnapping of Joanne Lees. Meni, host of the "hit podcast" The Missing Australia and an ex-TV reporter and police officer, tells the crowd that the evidence that saw Bradley John Murdoch convicted of murder is overwhelming. But, he says, there are people who believe Murdoch is innocent.

Footage of Bradley John Murdoch, taken in the final weeks of his life, showed him refusing to share any information about the final resting place of Peter Falconio. ( )

The "Peter Falconio what really happened" Facebook page, dedicated to canvassing alternate theories on the case, has 18,000 members. As I write, the most recent post says: "Let's look at the people who were in Barrow Creek and what connection do they have with motorcycle gangs." Every time Meni mentions the conspiracy theories that surround the Falconio case, one woman in the crowd nods vigorously. There's research that suggests a link between morbid curiosity and conspiracy theories. A heightened interest in learning about threats, say through binging true crime, can lead people to conspiracy theories, the study's authors argue.

Beside me, a woman with a bright face wearing a white beanie is rapidly writing notes that seem unrelated to the talk. Then she texts someone: "This may be a good spot to look." I wonder if she trying to solve a crime in real time. Later, I'll speak with her and discover a community of trauma survivors who are organising searches, supporting families of the recently disappeared, and honing their investigative skills to help research crimes privately or for true crime productions.

South Australia's "family" murders remain unsolved. So far, only one man, Bevan Spencer von Einem, has ever been convicted of any of the abductions. ( )

The 'family' murders

Debi Marshall is small but formidable. The long-time investigative crime journalist is speaking to a large audience about the "family" murders, which she calls Australia's Epstein case. She says numerous sexual assaults of boys snatched from Adelaide's streets led up to the murders of five young men between 1979 and 1983. She reads out more details about the suspected paedophile ring behind the abductions and killings — four of which remain unsolved. The woman next to me lets out a heavy sigh and crosses her arms.

Some of the victims' family members are sitting in the front row watching Debi speak. Their faces are ragged and they're running out of time to see justice done. Along with Debi, they're currently campaigning for decades-old suppression orders on the names of people who were either police witnesses, informants or suspects to be lifted.

Debi says the "family" murders are the most depraved of the many cases she's worked on — and she wrote a book on which the Snowtown film is based. As Debi talks about the mutilation of these young men's bodies, I look out the window, a stand of Norfolk Island pines is motionless. Nothing is happening outside to distract, not even a breeze.

Bevin Von Einem, who died in prison in 2025, was serving a life sentence for the murder of Richard Kelvin and police had linked him to the "family", whom detectives suspect were also responsible for the four other murders. ( )

She tells the audience that investigating such crimes has taken a toll on her. Later she tells me she used to be too afraid to let her teenage daughter walk to school. And her work visited her in nightmares. "My specialty, for want of a different way of putting it, is serial killers," she says. "So, when you're chasing serial killers, you need to be careful they don't start chasing you. But they do start chasing you in your dreams. And sometimes they catch you, which is awful."

Debi raises this toll when people on social media accuse her of "doing this for the money". She has little time for those who she says peddle in true crime on social media for attention and revenue: "It's like the Salem witch hunts, this hysterical mob, each ramping the other up higher and higher into putting out this nonsense about what's happened in their opinion and then calling it fact … when the work involved in separating fact from rumour is so intense and time consuming."

Investigative journalist Debi Marshall has researched a number of serial killings in Australia, and has spent years working on Adelaide's "family" murders. ( )

After Debi's presentation I get talking with the woman next to me. Deb Phali says she grew up in Western Sydney near where Anita Cobby was brutally killed in 1982. Deb remembers "driving past the area with my family and seeing all the cops everywhere" and she wonders if that sparked her interest in true crime. She says the fascination is really a desire to figure out human behaviour: "It's about trying to understand what makes people do this. You just hope that maybe you can listen to something and find some answers to help people. Not that I've got any."

Deb's ex-husband also had a relative who went missing in 1982 and she says it's given her a particular interest in missing person's cases. Of 10-year-old Bradford's disappearance, she says it destroyed his family and that the case wasn't investigated properly by police. He was a Koori and had been in foster care, "so they didn't give a rats", she says.

I wonder out loud how everyone in the crowd can stomach sitting through story after story of violence and tragedy. "Talking about it brings some support and some light to the darkness of it all," Deb says. "To know that people do care and are out there trying to do the right thing and you've got investigative people out there trying to help people, that's the positive I take out of it."

Deb Phali (right) says she's taken an interest in true crime since a murder took place near where she grew up in western Sydney. ( )

The Lady Vanishes

When Sally Leydon is asked to say something about her mother Marion Barter on stage at the festival, she smacks her lips together creating a loud pop. Sally says her mother used to kiss her on her ears, so that a kiss would be something heard as well as felt. For a moment, Marion, who hasn't been heard from since 1997, comes into focus. In 2024, a NSW Coroner said Marion was dead, but that she could not make a finding about where or how she died.

Sally's mother Marion Barter before she disappeared in 1997. ( )

The inquest into Marion's disappearance was announced the year after Sally launched The Lady Vanishes, a podcast which has captivated millions of listeners. Created with Seven News, Sally says it was unusual at the time for a family member to be involved in the production. "Me being involved and speaking on the podcast and working in real time with the journalists made the difference in how people connected with the podcast," Sally tells me later. "Journalists can't bring that lived experience." But it complicated her relationship with the police working on her mother's case. "If you speak your truth, police might not help you and not want to work with you, it's a fine line," she says.

Sally says her podcast isn't entertainment. But having millions of people download it is comforting, she says, and gives her hope. And it has helped. Armchair sleuths who listened to the podcast helped identify the man of interest in her mother's case. It's also given Sally a platform from which to advocate for the families of missing people, and she's started The Green Seat Project to raise awareness about missing persons cases and the trauma their families experience. "I can't change what's happened to me, or my mum or the impact it had on my brother [who died by suicide after their mother's disappearance], but I can certainly talk about it to make a change to make it better for the next family," Sally says.

Sally Leydon presenting at Crime Scene Victor Harbor. ( )

The crowd applauds Sally Leydon at Crime Scene Victor Harbor festival. ( )

At the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into Unsolved Murders and Long-Term Missing Persons Cases, Sally called for police to have greater sensitivity when they talk to and work with families of missing persons or murder victims. She also pushed for reforms around death in absentia and death certificate processes, the establishment of a voluntary disappearance register and improvements to how NSW Police process unidentified human remains.

On stage Sally is relaxed and commanding. It's easy to see why she's drawn so many people to her mother's case. I'd count her as one of the growing number of women who as Caroline Fraser writes in the New York Review of Books is changing true crime from a "soiled brand" and "dismantling the age-old Master Detective myths—that women are responsible for what's done to them, that policing necessarily makes us safer, that cops are good at catching killers".

It's dark when the crowd leaves the theatre and steps onto Victor Harbor's main street. Festival organisers have drawn chalk outlines of bodies on the footpath to stage a fake crime scene. After hours spent discussing the missing and the murdered the gimmick feels off. As any true crime obsessive would tell you, police don't actually do this because it risks contaminating the crime scene. The imaginary body seems to speak to the uncomfortable intersection of crime, entertainment and narrative that true crime still can't resolve.

A fake crime scene on Victor Harbor's main street. ( )

'Never get in front of the plough'

The presence at the festival speakers like Sally talking alongside traditional journalists is a reminder that legacy media is no longer the gatekeeper, says Adam Shand, a former newspaper reporter turned podcaster and author. And this has complicated things for police, he argues. "You had the odd journalist who would break ranks," he says. "But largely speaking, across Australia, crime journalists have been police journalists, and they've had to rely upon access to coppers … now people can access the audience, can access the subjects and they can do their own investigations, and they can become their own publishers most importantly."

Adam says a cop once told him to "never get in front of the plough". But that's now common practice and has become the domain of legacy media podcasts too. "We saw this with The Teacher's Pet," Adam says. "Hedley Thomas and Damian Loone and others stepping in front of the plough constantly and showing people that the police had not done their job and therefore that drove the investigation and I think it led to the charging without the body."

Hedley's success in solving a crime might also be an outlier. Of the seemingly infinite number of true crime podcasts or TV shows, how many lead to convictions in unsolved cases? All of the weekend's presenters speak with certainty — or is it hubris? Two of them tell me confidently who is responsible for the disappearance of the Beaumont children from an Adelaide beach in 1966, and they offer up different names.

Often referred to as "The Beumont Children", nine-year-old Jane, seven-year-old Arnna and four-year-old Grant disappeared from Glenelg on Australia Day in 1966. ( )

I leave Adam in the bar, as some women with armfuls of newly purchased books approach and ask to have their photo taken with him. I walk back to the caravan park along a dark footpath occasionally illuminated by the headlights of a passing car. I'm used to travelling alone. I'm not scared of the dark. But after the day's talks I feel jumpy.

Psychologists often offer another theory, called "benign masochism", about why so many of us consume true crime. As Arntfield explains, although true crime involves consuming content that provokes fear or anxiety, audiences remain safe. "The theory proposes that intense emotional experiences trigger a secondary, opposing emotional response. Dread, tension and even revulsion can give way to relief; anxiety to reassurance," he writes. Repeated exposure can lead to more prolonged highs, and he argues this is likely why true crime is prevalent on platforms built for binging, like streaming services.

Back in the cabin I lie in bed worrying that my car — the only one in the carpark — is in a space with a number corresponding to the cabin. Anyone watching from the shadows will know mine is the only occupied cabin. The true crime weekend seems to be having the opposite effect on me.

'Considerable suspicion'

When 33-year-old Nadine Haag’s body was found in her Sydney apartment in 2009, police quickly concluded that she had died by suicide. But her family never believed Nadie had taken her own life. Four years later, after mounting their own investigation, they succeeded in having the finding overturned by a NSW coroner, who said, as The Sydney Morning Herald reported, that “the actions of Ms Haag's former partner ‘raised considerable suspicion’ that her death was the result of a homicide”.

Tasia and Chantal Haag have spent the past 17 years trying to understand what happened to their sister Nadine. ( )

After Nadine’s death, her sister Tasia wanted to learn as much as she could to understand Nadine’s case. She signed up for courses in crime scene staging, forensics and DNA, blood pattern analysis, crime scene photography – anything she thought might help. She also received a diploma in crime and justice. Seventeen years later, Tasia and her twin sister Chantal say they are still hoping to “see justice and the truth get out there”.

This search has led the sisters to the festival, and to supporting other families of missing or allegedly murdered people. Tasia belongs to an embryonic organisation called the Centre for Missing Persons, which is aiming to become the national voice for people in the missing persons space. The sisters also help families navigate police investigations, administrative and legal processes like obtaining death certificates, and they put their boots on to deliver flyers about missing people and help with bushland searches. They’re also calling for police to listen to victims’ families. “The family has so many answers, they have so much information, sometimes police take some of the information in … but quite often they don’t,” Chantal says.

For Tasia and Chantal, the true crime festival is a chance to connect with people with similar experiences. It's "reassurance" that they're not alone, Chantal says. "That you’re not going crazy, that what’s happened is not just in your head.”

Blood in the barrels, maybe

Afterwards, I follow Tasia and her family into a dark room at a hilltop golf club for the final event of the weekend. Bryan Littlely, the festival founder, is presenting a slideshow of some of the cases he’s investigating in his “Sleepers” podcast. Bryan, who left the Adelaide Advertiser in 2015, tells me he started Sleepers because he “had information that had never made it to print”. He’s now firmly “in front of the plough” and his relationship with police is rocky.

Earlier this year, Bryan told his followers he was sent a video showing what appeared to be human remains in regional south Australia. “The circumstances of this discovery place it firmly on my list to investigate in the hope of bringing answers to a family missing their loved one,” he wrote online. South Australian Police later told Seven News the skeletal remains were legally purchased medical teaching aids and warned against speculation as it “can unnecessarily distress and re-traumatise victims of crime, their families and loved ones, who may see inaccurate information circulated before the facts are established”.

Bryan tells me he’s unperturbed: “I'll continue to do the work that I'm doing and unless I'm doing something that's illegal, which I don't do, then I'd expect that [police] let me go about my business.”

Bryan Littlely doing a podcast recording on Victor Harbor's main street. ( )

Victor Harbor's main street. ( )

It’s not the first warning Bryan has received. In February, police warned against creating “false hope” in missing persons cases after they tested bone fragments found in a search Bryan organised and concluded the bones weren’t human. Bryan was looking for the remains of Joanne Ratcliffe and Kirste Gordon, who were abducted from Adelaide Oval during a football match in 1973.

Bryan, who co-founded missing persons advocacy foundation Leave a Light On with Joanne’s sister Suzie Ratcliffe, talks about the case in his presentation. At one point, he points to a photo of an alleged paedophile he believes was involved. “Who is he?” Bryan asks. People in the audience shout out the man’s name. Then he begins to speak about the barrels that he believes could contain their remains.

A barrel which is now in South Australian Police custody for testing in relation to the disappearance of Joanne Ratcliffe and Kirste Gordon. ( )

Sharing the weight of a case with a victim's family is a heavy responsibility. Sometimes Bryan becomes emotional when he talks about cold cases. But today he’s clear-headed as he explains how he’s had the barrels independently analysed, after police discounted them more than a decade ago. He tells the crowd they’ve found blood in the barrels. Suzie Ratcliffe is watching from the back of the room, expressionless.

It’s the end of a long weekend and the details of cold cases are blurring into each other. I wonder how much longer we can collectively stare into the abyss. But this doesn’t feel like everything critics mount at true crime. Maybe that’s because it’s not occurring online. It feels like community coming together to help victims and their families.

A few weeks after the true crime festival, South Australian police will accept Bryan’s offer to take possession of the barrels for analysis. Police are yet to provide an update.

World.title: US floated NATO membership for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
US negotiators raised the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, the president said.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" he said.

"That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Mr Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia's full-blown invasion in 2022.

Mr Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory.

Mr Zelenskyy and Ireland leader Micheal Martin (right) attend the summit in Dublin. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

But he also said that if it received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.

'This war must be ended first'

Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Mr Zelenskyy dismissed Russia's call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.

"We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war," he said.

"This war must be ended first."

Mr Zelenskyy also dismissed Mr Putin's suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, saying it reflected Moscow's inability to take the city by force.

Mr Putin wants Uranians to leave Kostiantynivka, Mr Zelenskyy says. (Reuters)

Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.

"Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way," he said.

Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Mr Zelenskyy said.

Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.

Large prisoner exchange agreed

The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough.

The sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Mr Zelenskyy said.

The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.

US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Mr Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskyy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.

"Putin personally does not support a ceasefire," he said.

Mr Zelenskyy met Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow.

He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.

In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine's largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe's team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU officials.

Reuters

World.title: 'We're still standing': King Charles jokes with Elton John in birthday clip
World.content:
Britain's King Charles has joked that he and Sir Elton John were "still standing" in a clip recorded for the singer's radio show which was aired on the monarch's 78th birthday.

King Charles had joined Sir John for a special edition of the singer's Elton John's Rocket Hour on Apple Music to celebrate 50 years of The King's Trust and musicians who have supported his youth charity.

During the episode, which was first broadcast on Saturday to coincide with the king's birthday, the pair discussed benefit concerts held in support of the Trust.

This included a Rock Gala held at Wembley Arena in 1986 where Sir Elton performed his 1980s hit, I'm Still Standing.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience," King Charles said.

" And certainly 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing. "

Sir John, who turns 80 in March, replied, "I'm still sitting now, though", prompting laughs from the king.

"With occasional bits dropping off here and there," King Charles said.

"I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

Both men have suffered well-documented health problems in recent years, with the king still undergoing treatment for cancer and Sir Elton suffering problems with his eyesight.

King Charles and Sir Elton John at the Royal Variety Performance in 2024. (Reuters: Toby Melville/Pool/File Photo)

When he was the heir, King Charles founded the Prince's Trust in 1976 using his Royal Navy severance pay to help disadvantaged young people prepare for work, find jobs or start businesses.

It was renamed the King's Trust after Charles became king in 2022.

The charity says it has supported more than one million young people since its launch.

Rocket Man turns 50 Rocket Man came at a vital time in Elton John's then-burgeoning career, saving him from being written off as a one-hit wonder.

"Music has always been at the heart of The Prince's, and now The King's Trust," King Charles said, adding that the program offered a chance to showcase performers who had supported the charity and newer artists it had helped launch.

The pair recalled benefit concerts stretching from Wembley Arena's rock galas in the 1980s to shows in Hyde Park and at the Royal Albert Hall.

Among them is British rock band Muse, which received a grant to buy sound equipment when it performed under its former name Rocket Baby Dolls.

The group later held a sold-out Royal Albert Hall concert in aid of the Trust in 2018, Buckingham Palace said in a statement.

"If you champion a young artist and show you believe in them, it makes all the difference," Sir Elton said.

" Young people are our future. "

Sir Elton received the Order of the Companions of Honour from Charles, then Prince of Wales, at Windsor Castle in 2021 for services to music and charity.

One of the best-selling artists of all time, with hits including "Goodbye Yellow Brick Road", "Rocket Man" and "Your Song", Sir Elton was knighted by Queen Elizabeth in 1998.

Rocket Hour is a weekly show that has aired globally on Apple Music 1 since 2015.

Reuters

World.title: Heat hammer Hurricanes to hand WBBL champions sixth straight loss
World.content:
Brisbane have continued their stunning WBBL rejuvenation in spectacular style, annihilating hapless Hobart by 10 wickets with a staggering 86 balls to spare.

After skittling the Hurricanes for just 86 in 17.5 overs at Bellerive Oval on Saturday, the Heat wasted no time securing themselves a fourth win in six matches, taking just 5.4 overs to race to 0-88 in reply.

Grace Harris (52 not out off 22 balls) and Charli Knott (34no off 12) looked like they were batting on a different deck to Hobart's confounded batters, who struggled to hit the ball off the square.

The 'Canes hit just six boundaries. Harris and Knott, in contrast, combined for 12 fours and four sixes.

Brisbane's 62-run powerplay set a new competition record.

Their intent was obvious as they crushed 17, 18, 20, seven and 13 off the five completed overs, Harris teeing off from the outset, before Knott applied the finishing touches, raising victory with back-to-back fours.

After going winless for 706 days, the Heat have now notched four victories in the past 10 days to consolidate third position on the ladder.

Meanwhile, reigning champions Hobart have crashed to a 0-6 record.

When captain Nicola Carey was castled by Lily Bassingthwaighte, the Hurricanes were staring down the barrel at 3-11 inside their own powerplay.

That soon became a perilous 6-42.

No 9 Lauren Smith top-scored with 20 before being bowled by Knott, ending Hobart's disappointing innings.

Bassingthwaighte (3-25) was the early destroyer, while Sianna Ginger (2-8), Lucy Hamilton (2-15) and Sarah Glenn (2-16) shared the spoils.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Vescio stars in milestone game as Blues and Swans reach preliminary finals
World.content:
Carlton has claimed a thrilling five-point semifinal win over Hawthorn, with 100-gamer Darcy Vescio starring as the Blues set up an AFLW preliminary final against Melbourne.

Hawthorn started fast at Princes Park, but the Blues fought back, with Vescio slotting the match winner to deliver a 6.7 (43) to 6.2 (38) win in front of 4,701 fans.

Hawthorn star Aine McDonagh could have kicked the winner with two minutes left but missed everything from close range.

Earlier, Sydney pulled off an upset, defeating Geelong by three points in the other semifinal to progress to a final-four clash with North Melbourne.

Hawthorn was without Eliza West for the pivotal final moments after the star on-baller suffered a left knee injury.

West was clearly best on ground and had 25 disposals, 10 tackles, 14 contested possessions and three clearances in the first half alone, before finishing with 31 touches.

Defender Jenna Richardson was important while Jac Dupuy kicked two goals and had an entertaining duel with Carlton's Harriet Cordner (six marks, 11 intercepts).

Carlton skipper Abbie McKay lifted and had 29 disposals and nine clearances.

The Hawks dominated the early exchanges, at one point leading clearances 10-1, kicking three goals to race to a game-high 19-point lead in the first term.

Carlton stopped the rot when Tara Bohanna cut the quarter-time margin to 11.

Lila Keck sparked Carlton before Lily Goss made the most of a contentious 50-metre penalty against Casey Sherriff to cut the half-time deficit to four.

Then, in the third quarter, Vescio won a free kick and kicked truly to put Carlton in front for the first time.

Mackenzie Eardley restored Hawthorn's lead before Vescio forced the ball forward and Sophie McKay spun on a dime in the square, beating three Hawks to put the Blues back in front.

Eardley struck again to make for a thrilling finish, but Vescio took a strong contested mark then snatched victory with her second goal of the game.

Concern for Cats ruck as Swans reach maiden preliminary final

Piper Dunlop collapsed after what looked like a glancing blow in a head knock with Tanya Kennedy. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

Earlier, there were concerning scenes as Geelong ruck Piper Dunlop was stretchered from the field on a motorised cart in the Cats' shock loss to Sydney.

Dunlop went down after a head clash with Sydney's Tanya Kennedy during the third quarter at Kardinia Park.

She initially returned to her feet before becoming unsteady and falling on the edge of the centre circle, caught by Sydney's Lexi Hamilton before trainers sprinted onto the ground to attend to her.

The game was stopped for nine minutes as medical staff gathered on the field, Dunlop eventually leaving the field on the motorised cart.

Geelong has since said Dunlop was taken to hospital for "further precautionary assessment".

Forward Chloe Molloy was the star for the Swans, kicking three goals and taking a key late mark to see her side through to its first-ever AFLW preliminary final.

The 8.2 (50) to 7.5 (47) victory means Sydney will face two-time defending premiers North Melbourne next weekend.

Geelong, meanwhile, bows out of the finals series in straight sets after just one loss in the regular season.

The Swans led by 16 points early in the final quarter, but goals to Chloe Scheer and Jacqueline Perry cut the deficit to four points minutes later.

Scheer proceeded to hit the post, with her behind proving the final score of the game.

Geelong experienced a torrid afternoon on the injury front.

In addition to Dunlop's concerning head knock, the Cats lost Amy McDonald to a hamstring injury in the shadows of half-time, Rachel Kearns was absent for most of the second half, and star midfielder Georgie Prespakis spent time off the field after a heavy collision.

All three of Molloy's goals came in the first half, including one spectacular effort in which she gathered and snapped from an acute angle on the right.

Young key forward Maddie Quinn (22 disposals, one goal) was also impressive for the Swans, while Scheer finished with three majors for Geelong.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Father Christmas greeted by estimated 335,000 at Adelaide pageant
World.content:
More than 300,000 people are estimated to have lined the streets for this year's Adelaide Christmas Pageant, the 94th edition of the annual yuletide parade.

Pageant-goers arrived in the city early, along with hundreds of performers who gathered near South Terrace and King William Road, ahead of the much-loved parade.

Young faces lined the CBD streets to watch the floats pass by, ahead of the arrival of Father Christmas. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Five new floats were added to this year's line-up, including The Magic Hat and A Bumper Christmas.

"Seeing all the floats go past, they love it," one parent said while sitting with his family.

" It makes it all kind of worth it, getting up super early. "

Hundreds of performers took part in the event. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Organisers believe about 335,000 people turned out for the event, which culminated with the much-anticipated arrival of Father Christmas.

Beneath grey skies, a slight shadow was cast on proceedings by the collapse of David Jones, whose Adelaide store has hosted the children's Christmas attraction, the Magic Cave, for almost three decades, although it will continue operating for the time being.

But, overwhelmingly, there were beaming smiles along the event's route.

Five new floats were added to this year's line-up. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Renowned children's entertainer Emma Watkins, better known by her stage name Emma Memma, said she was thrilled to be back after making her debut last year.

"The buzz is real, the festive spirit is out," she said.

This year Watkins was part of the float The Sounds and Signs of Christmas, a reference to her push to help make entertainment more accessible for deaf and and hearing children alike.

Emma Memma says she is thrilled to be back for the Christmas Pageant. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

"Today is the first time that my co-performer Elvin Lam is actually joining me in the pageant," she said.

"It's his first Christmas pageant ever, and Elvin is profoundly deaf, and he will be signing throughout the whole parade."

A delight for all generations

Kunal Dhingra and his family were among those who rose early to secure good spots.

"I can see a lot of people are here from different backgrounds. All the kids are really happy," he said while holding his slightly tired infant daughter.

"We're here from 6am, she woke up pretty early."

Kunal Dhingra and his family were among the early risers. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

A cross-section of the community was present at the time-honoured parade, with young pageant-goer Miabelle saying she relished "spending time with my cousins" and seeing the floats.

"There's one big teddy bear I'm looking forward to," she said.

Another attendee, a local grandmother, said her connection to the event went back decades.

"My dad used to drive trucks, and I remember when we were kids we used to get on the back of his truck and watching the pageant on King William Street," she said.

"Now I get to enjoy it with my grandchildren.

"I just love it. I think I'd come without the kids, if I had to."

The event brings Christmas magic to the streets of Adelaide. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The Magic Cave, currently held in David Jones at the Adelaide Central Plaza, has been part of the city's Christmas landscape since the 1890s. David Jones took over in 1998 when its original host John Martin's closed down.

While the Magic Cave welcomed Father Christmas this year, questions have emerged about what lies ahead for the attraction.

Last week, David Jones went into voluntary administration, with 19 of its 38 stores slated for closure across Australia and New Zealand.

Organisers estimate more than 300,000 people attended. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In SA, stores in Westfield Marion and Westfield West Lakes will shut down by the end of the year.

But the store in Rundle Mall will remain open, and locals are keen to keep the Magic Cave as part of Adelaide's Christmas festivities.

"It's an Adelaide icon, bringing my now baby like when I was a kid, and now letting her do it," local woman Erin said.

"We need David Jones … we need the Magic Cave, the kids love it, it's one thing they look forward to."

World.title: Australia's newest fast-bowling sensation tipped for big things from a young age
World.content:
While Mahli Beardman's record-setting demolition of England may have stunned the visitors, those who watched his development as a junior say it's no surprise.

On a day when fresh hostilities in the Sandpaper scandal dominated the headlines, the West Australian fast bowler's 6/24 skittled the visitors and gave Australian cricket a much-needed bit of good news.

But for West Pilbara Cricket Association secretary Christy Reed, Beardman's talent was always obvious.

Beardman (right) receives a representative cap while playing junior cricket in WA's Pilbara. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

While hailing from Cowaramup in WA's South West, the 21-year-old played his initial junior and representative cricket for Dampier in WA's Pilbara.

Initially spotted by scouts at a talent clinic in Karratha in 2017 as a 12-year-old, Beardman progressed quickly through the junior representative ranks, eventually landing at WA Premier Cricket Club Melville when he moved to Perth.

Ms Reed said he made an impression early.

"He was a tiny little kid, but his bowling was absolutely natural talent," she said.

Beardman (left) was identified early as a talented young bowler. (Supplied: Andrew Hayes)

"So fast for his size, and he absolutely loved his cricket.

" He would even go down to the senior team, Dampier Taverners, training and bully them in the nets. "

She hoped Beardman's success would show other talented junior cricketers across the Pilbara what could be achieved.

"For years it was really hard for kids to have a pathway through to that upper level, but I imagine this would get more kids interested in the sport," Ms Reed said.

"I couldn't be happier for him, his family and for Cricket Australia."

WA Cricket country area manager Andrew Hayes was working in the Pilbara around the same time Beardman and fellow Dampier quick Josh Vernon were making their way through the system.

"To take six wickets against our old foe on debut is an incredible achievement, and we couldn't be prouder," he said.

Mahli Beardman (back row, second from right) representing the West Pilbara at Junior Country Week. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

Hometown pride

The pride was echoed in Cowaramup, who are keen to embrace Beardman as a favourite son despite competing claims from nearby Dunsborough and Margaret River.

Loading...

Cowaramup Cricket Club stalwart and secretary Bob Biddulph coached a six-year-old Beardman before his family moved north.

"Unfortunately, he was only there for one year … but it was the start of his cricket journey, so we're very proud of him," he said.

"We're claiming it down at Cowaramup that's for sure; I think everyone associated with the cricket club is very proud of that."

Mahli Beardman walks off Perth Stadium after taking 6/24 on debut for Australia in ODI cricket. (ABC News: Sam Tomlin)

Mr Biddulph echoed the importance of seeing regional cricketers performing well at international level.

"It just goes to show that it doesn't matter where you are; if you start off and you enjoy the game and stick at it and keep practising, the sky is the limit," he said.

"We've got quite a few junior teams this year, so for them to actually see one of their own making it on the big stage is quite exciting."

Game two of the three-match ODI series is at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

World.title: I’m worried our super could get hacked. Is my money safer in the bank?
World.content:
November 15, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Hi Paul. There have been recent reports of the possibility of AI hacking into vast areas of the internet, including financial areas. Bitcoin and others have already suffered. How safe is my superannuation money? Would it be safer in a bank? Or under the bed? Yes, the recent bitcoin heist certainly made for some interesting reporting. Fortunately, our superannuation and banking systems bear no resemblance. Being vigilant for scams and hacks is wise, but there’s no need to be overly worried. We all need to be on the lookout for online scams and the like, but I think I’m on pretty safe ground when I say that taking your money out of super and putting it under the bed would be unwise. Cybersecurity is not my area of expertise. But I take comfort from the fact that Australia’s financial systems are extremely well regulated, with teams of experts at the various connections in the money pipes making sure our financial records are safe. Consumer protections here are also extremely high, so if something goes wrong, you have recourse.



As an aside, there is more money in our superannuation system than there are deposits in our banks, so the proposition that your money is somehow safer in the bank is, in this context at least, highly questionable. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’ve been renting my house for two years. Will I have to pay tax when I sell? Noel Whittaker Money columnist I am 39 years old on a salary of $125,000 per year and salary sacrifice an additional $200 per pay into my super, which is sitting at about $270,000. I also lease out an apartment which has around $285,000 left on the mortgage, at around a 6 per cent interest rate. I’ve been making extra fortnightly payments of $1000 to pay it down quickly, so expect it’ll be paid off in seven or so years. Would it be better to continue this strategy and then increase my contributions to super once my apartment is paid off – or increase my salary sacrificing to super now and take longer to pay off my apartment? My goal is to have a decent nest egg, so I can retire a little earlier than the standard age. The interest on this mortgage will be tax-deductible given the property is income producing (I’m making the assumption it is receiving the grandfathered provisions), and so there is a solution here whereby the after-tax cost of the borrowing is below the expected alternate returns (after tax). This being the case, it could be argued that you should slow down on the loan repayment, and focus your savings elsewhere.



My inclination, however, would be to continue with your current approach for two reasons. One, we are currently in a rising interest rate cycle and that will likely mean your interest expense will increase, raising the burden associated with carrying this property. Paying down this debt reduces your exposure to rising interest rates, which contributes to you being able to retain this property through the cycle. Secondly, you’ve advised that your primary goal is to be able to retire earlier than the standard. Money that you place in superannuation is inaccessible until you are at least 60 years of age. Given that you need access to money earlier, it makes sense to ensure that you hold wealth elsewhere. This investment property could produce income for you during that early retirement period. I’d be interested to know the cash flow position of the property. If the property was producing positive cash-flow, after allowing for all expenses, you could perhaps direct some savings to a non-super investment portfolio to improve your diversification, and have greater options with regards early retirement. Paul Benson is a certified financial planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. Questions to: paul@financialautonomy.com.au

World.title: We want to know if a recession is coming. It’s the wrong question
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingBudgeting Opinion We want to know if a recession is coming. It’s the wrong question Victoria Devine Money columnist November 15, 2026 — 5:01am

November 15, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This week, someone asked me a question on my podcast that has stuck with me. Should Australians be preparing for a recession? I can understand why they’re asking. Interest rates have been rising, inflation is proving stubborn and the economic headlines haven’t been reassuring. It feels like every other week there’s another economist warning us about what might be around the corner. Prices are going up and up, and so are interest rates. Louie Douvis I follow these conversations closely. It’s my job, after all. But I sometimes wonder whether we’re so focused on predicting what the economy will do next that we’re overlooking something much closer to home. After years working as a financial adviser and now in mortgage broking, my understanding of what it means to be wealthy has changed quite a bit. Early in my career, I probably would have measured wealth in the traditional sense.



How much someone earned, what their home was worth, how much they’d accumulated in investments. All perfectly reasonable measures, and ones that still matter. But having spent years looking at people’s finances behind closed doors, I’ve realised those numbers can tell you surprisingly little about how financially secure someone actually is. Some of the most eye-opening clients I worked with were households earning $600,000, sometimes upwards of $1 million a year. On paper, they were doing extraordinarily well. They owned beautiful homes, drove expensive cars and had the sorts of careers most people would consider incredibly successful. The older I get, the less impressed I am by the outward signs of financial success. I’m far more interested in whether someone has choices. Yet when we sat down and went through their finances, the reality was sometimes quite different. These clients’ mortgages were enormous, their spending had grown alongside their incomes and there was little room for anything to go wrong. Some had accumulated substantial assets but had surprisingly little put aside for retirement. Others were so dependent on maintaining their current incomes that even a relatively short interruption could have forced some very difficult decisions. I’ve met people who could afford almost anything, except the freedom to stop working.



I don’t share that to criticise them. It’s remarkably easy for your lifestyle to expand as your income increases, particularly when the people around you are doing the same thing. And a large mortgage isn’t necessarily a problem if you have the income and financial buffers to support it. What struck me was how different their financial reality could be from the picture everyone else saw. I’ve thought about those clients a lot over the years, particularly when conversations about recessions start making headlines. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock on November 3, after the bank raised interest rates for a fifth time this year. Dominic Lorrimer There are genuine reasons to be paying attention to the economy right now. This month, the Reserve Bank increased the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, while annual inflation reached 3.9 per cent in the September quarter. Unemployment averaged 4.6 per cent over the same period, and the RBA now expects it to climb to 5.1 per cent by the end of 2028. That’s hardly an economic outlook anyone would describe as particularly comfortable.



But Australia’s economy is still growing, with GDP increasing 2.1 per cent over the year to June, and the RBA’s central forecasts point to slower growth rather than an outright recession. Even economists working with sophisticated forecasting models can’t tell us with certainty what happens next. Editor's pick Opinion

Household debt Six months ago, Australians were optimistic. Now, we’re cutting back on toothpaste Victoria Devine Money columnist The difficulty is that a recession isn’t experienced equally. Some people will barely notice it. Others may lose their jobs, see their businesses struggle or find themselves needing to access savings much sooner than expected. And some Australians will experience serious financial hardship even if the economy never officially enters a recession. If you’re earning a comfortable income, it’s tempting to assume you’re financially secure. You can afford your mortgage, your bills are paid and your investments are ticking along. There might not be any obvious reason to question whether the life you’ve built is sustainable until something changes. I also think we need to be careful about how we talk about preparing for difficult economic conditions. There’s no shortage of financial advice telling people to build emergency funds, reduce debt and spend less. Those are sensible suggestions, but they’re considerably easier to follow when you have money left over at the end of each week.



For someone already struggling with rent, groceries and electricity bills, being told to save six months of expenses can feel almost insulting. Financial security isn’t just about making good decisions. Income, opportunity, family circumstances and plain old luck have an enormous influence on the options available to us. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide For those of us who do have some financial flexibility, there’s a responsibility to be more deliberate about what we do with it. That doesn’t mean living frugally for the sake of it or feeling guilty about enjoying the money you’ve worked hard to earn. I’m certainly not suggesting we should all stop going on holidays or buying things we love. It means recognising the difference between being able to afford something today and being able to sustain it if your circumstances change. It’s something I think about differently now, both professionally and personally. The older I get, the less impressed I am by the outward signs of financial success. I’m far more interested in whether someone has choices.



Whether they could take time away from work if they needed to, whether an unexpected expense would derail their plans, or whether they’re building towards a retirement that doesn’t depend on everything going perfectly. Editor's pick Opinion

Christmas The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor And that brings me back to the question I was asked this week. Should Australians be preparing for a recession? I think it’s worth understanding the risks, but I wouldn’t encourage anyone to make dramatic financial decisions based on predictions about when the next downturn might arrive. Trying to time the economy is difficult enough for economists, let alone the rest of us. I’d much rather see people take an honest look at how their finances would hold up if life became a little less predictable. That might mean building some savings, reviewing financial commitments or simply having a clearer understanding of where their money goes. What that looks like will be different for every household.



I don’t know whether Australia is heading towards a recession. But I do know that financial security has very little to do with impressing the people around you. These days, my definition of wealth is having enough peace of mind to know that if something unexpected happens, you have the freedom to work out what comes next without everything you’ve built falling apart. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. World.title: Alex gave me $1000 cash after I met him on Facebook Marketplace. An hour later he asked me if he’d paid me
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsShopping Opinion Alex gave me $1000 cash after I met him on Facebook Marketplace. An hour later he asked me if he’d paid me Roby D'Ottavi Writer November 15, 2026 — 5:00am

November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A few weeks ago, I signed a contract for a job in Adelaide, and my time in Melbourne is coming to a close. The city of churches is a wonderful place for the religious, and a so-so place for people in their late 20s. That said, it’s where my new employer is, so it’s time to clean out my apartment. Some of my favourite things are from random people on Facebook Marketplace. Their junk became vital to me. You can – and will – find anything here. Want a three-seater bench from the old Jetstar terminal? Marketplace. A full-size model of a battle droid from The Phantom Menace? Marketplace. Some creepy porcelain doll that is 100 per cent cursed? Marketplace. What was junk to you, can be turned into cash. But first you need to deal with a random person online. Tanya Lake Marketplace can satisfy any type of person with any type of demand. There’s no performance. Just a weird chair that a nonna is selling, and an arts student who wants it. It is also filled with some of the most fascinating people you will ever meet.



Recently, I tried to sell some memory cards for a camera I no longer own. I listed the items for $1, mentioning in the description that interested buyers should “make me an offer”. I do this because if there’s one thing people on Marketplace love more than a deal, it’s a haggle. Five minutes later after the listing went live, a man messaged me asking if the memory cards were “free”. I told him, “Nah, make me an offer. Do you have an offer?” He responded, “No, I don’t need them.” But he would have needed them if they were free? I sold some old camera lenses to a bloke called Alex. We agreed on a fee of $1000. Alex gave me the cash, and left with a pep in his step – I feel as if this purchase made his week. I was fascinated by the amount of trust Alex had in me. He brought $1000 in cash. I could have been a murderer. I’m not. Just in case you were curious. Related Article Opinion

Jobs I strutted to my interview at the bottle shop. It turned out to be a humiliation ritual Roby D'Ottavi Writer An hour later, Alex asked if he’d given me the money. I stared at his message for a few minutes, holding the cash in my other hand. A worse person would have said, “No, can you transfer the money?” I, on the other hand, told him he had. Alex responded five minutes later, “Oh, good. I forgot.” These situations arose only because someone actually messaged me. On countless situations I have had to message people four or five times before they even gave me a response, which is usually something like “Sorry, sold :(”



I once complained about these people to a friend, who told me people still message her about obsolete listings. Good, innocent buyers enquire about a bookshelf she left on the kerb in February. I asked why she didn’t just delete the listings, and she said, “I know I should, but it’s such an effort.” Has she never been on the cruel receiving end of this? I had imagined these non-repliers as poor salespeople. I’m literally begging to take their junk, cash in hand. In what world does that make sense? It turns out they’re just good folks who lose track of time. Marketplace is one of the last remaining networks where people are not performing or playing a role. Instagram tells us to post the most luxurious parts of our lives. LinkedIn says we must always be networking. Twitter/X exists for opinions, whether we believe them or not. On Marketplace, something as cataclysmic as a divorce is summarised as “Wood dining table. $100. Need gone ASAP.” We spend a stupid amount of time building stories in our heads. If you go onto Marketplace right now, you’ll see hundreds of wedding dresses in every conceivable size. You won’t see the marriage. A wedding dress is never just a wedding dress. Marketplace doesn’t care. That dining table that a happy family ate dinner at every night is now going to some share house in Northcote where one-night stands will drink crap coffee at 9am.



My sentimentality comes from the fact that in the next few months, I am going to have to sell many things that occupy my home. A couch I watched movies with exes on. A Seinfeld mug. The desk I bought with my first payment from The Age. Whoever buys these things won’t understand any of that. They’ll see a desk that was once $500, listed for a fifth of that because I can’t be bothered disassembling it. Related Article Opinion

Online shopping It seemed like a fuss-free Marketplace sale. Then the buyer showed up Shona Hendley Writer Marketplace is a network for people to rid themselves of things and start again. However, the second a stranger shows up in their rented GoGet van and takes that desk, dining table or wedding dress, it’s no longer junk. It’s someone’s new favourite piece. Someone might write the next great Australian novel at that desk. Or they might spill mi goreng on it. Whatever they do with the desk, they will not think of me. I am leaving a city I loved, and random people are arriving, one by one, to dismantle any evidence I lived there. Roby D’Ottavi is a writer and director based in Melbourne. World.title: At a ‘rustic luxury’ island resort in Canada, even the wildlife show is first class
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life At a ‘rustic luxury’ island resort in Canada, even the wildlife show is first class Stuart Hitchings November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
