This story is part of the November 15 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

We’re not long in our seats, and our guide, from British Columbia’s Homalco First Nations people, is explaining how crucial salmon are to the local ecosystem when one of our party exclaims: “Oh, look, a bear.” And, sure enough, it is. A full-grown male grizzly, sitting chest-deep in the river, eating a salmon. The minibus pulls over and we alight, phones front and centre, filming until the bear swims off downstream. We get back onto the bus, more slowly than we got off it, and our guide continues his chat. I miss his first name when he introduces himself and his colleague, Wilson. “But my ‘government name’ is Dude,” he tells us in his soft Canadian accent, smiling and gesturing to a name tag which, from my seat, I’d assumed said “Guide”. Sonora Resort is almost as spectacular as the nature that surrounds it. This bone-dry humour illuminates Dude and Wilson’s intimate knowledge of their country as they emphasise that the salmon spawning run (and subsequent carnival of salmony death) provides much of the nutrients that power the entire ecosystem; we’ve already watched bald eagles and a golden eagle tucking into the dead fish littering the river (and, to be frank, you can hardly miss the smell).



Later, as we’re crossing a bridge, Wilson suddenly pulls over. On the bank beneath are a mother bear and her two-year-old cub. It’s a fitting climax to an astonishing morning, and though we’d been told confidently by our hosts at Sonora Resort, located on its own island between Vancouver Island and the mainland, that we would see bears, it’s almost overwhelming to get so close to these magnificent animals. Sonora, accessible only by boat, seaplane or helicopter, is the epitome of rustic luxury. Part of the Relais & Chateaux group, it’s almost as spectacular as the nature that surrounds it. As well as stunning views, there are spacious rooms (all with binoculars, so you can watch the seals and sea lions from your room), a spa and gym, guided fishing, myriad hot tubs, minigolf and even archery. Not to mention the excellent Tyee dining room and bar, serving a mix of classic dishes and more innovative fare, all with an emphasis on fresh local ingredients. (There are also unlimited snacks scattered throughout the resort, ensuring no guest will ever go hungry.) The day after our close encounters with grizzlies, resort guide Robynne, who’s already demonstrated impressive boat-handling skills in the swirling tidal rapids on our way back from the bears, takes us at high speed around Sonora Island in a Zodiac boat as we search for a pod of orcas that have been spotted. After a teeth-chattering, high-speed ride we emerge from a bank of thick, low-hanging fog to find about 15, including a recently born calf, just a few hundred metres from the boat. The resort is located on its own island between Vancouver Island and the mainland. It’s this mix of luxurious amenities and unspoilt nature that makes Sonora special. While it can cater to almost every need, I love that you can walk five minutes in any direction from your room and find yourself in cool, lush forest, or on an otherwise deserted headland watching seals and sea lions hunting and playing. Not to mention the way nature comes right into the resort: as we’re eating dinner one evening, an adorable critter – it turns out to be a pine marten – pushes its nose against the windowpane, delighting everyone.



The gateway to all this natural splendour is Vancouver, and it’s well worth a few days of your time. My base in the city before heading to Sonora is the original Fairmont Hotel, in the centre of downtown (though some might prefer its newer, flashier harbourside sisters, Fairmont Waterfront and Fairmont Pacific Rim). Opened in 1939, the Fairmont is classic late-period art deco, with a copper roof, gargoyles and all the amenities you’d expect in a top hotel. I make a second home in its Notch8 restaurant, where I enjoy everything from moules frites at the bar to a full chef’s tasting menu. Related Article Sunday Life What three strangers taught a single mum on a trip to New Zealand The latter is just one of a string of memorable meals in Vancouver, including fantastic fresh sushi at Miku Waterfront, great bistro fare at industrial-chic Nightingale and, best of all, an extravagant tasting menu at the Michelin-starred Published on Main, one of the top restaurants along Vancouver’s “Michelin mile” – Main Street in Mount Pleasant. Here we’re served plate after delectable plate, all showcasing local ingredients, many of them foraged, accompanied by equally fine local wines. With all this culinary temptation, it’s lucky Vancouver is an excellent walking city; on my first day in town, anxious to stave off jet lag, I stroll to Canada Dock, then around the waterfront, and do half a lap of the enormous Stanley Park. And there are other distractions. While I’ve never truly been sold on the benefits of cold-water swimming, the prospect of sharing the water with seals and dolphins is enough for me to be talked into hopping aboard High Tide Sauna’s floating facility, where bouts of sweatiness are interrupted by plunges into Vancouver Harbour (even at the end of summer the water’s a crisp 14 degrees). Afterwards I feel so energised I take myself straight to the Fairmont’s Spa Solea for a hot-stone massage. Even in downtown Vancouver, as urban as it is, nature is never far away. An hour out of town is the Sea to Sky Gondola, where we enjoy mountain-top yoga followed by a gentle guided walk through Squamish Canyon, both led by ex-Sydneysider Nicki, of Wild Vedas. The mountain-top yoga has views to match the moves, and the canyon boasts beautiful mature trees, a spectacular waterfall and lots of cute furry animals – squirrels and chipmunks mostly – and a spectacular waterfall. But no grizzly bears. For that there’s always Sonora.



The writer was a guest of Destination Vancouver and Sonora Resort. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Crime writer Eve Thomson wants readers to know this sobering truth about court cases
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Crime writer Eve Thomson wants readers to know this sobering truth about court cases Mark Dapin November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 15 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

As a sometime crime novelist myself, I do my best to make sure the legal detail in my books is authentic, but authors who also work – or have worked – as lawyers have a bit of a jump on outsiders like me. That said, readers probably expect more of them: their courtroom scenes must be true to life, their legal arguments plausible, and the professional lives of their characters depicted within the bounds of reasonable possibility. Here, three women – two lawyers and a former one – share how their careers have influenced their writing. Eve Thomson, 47 Eve Thomson says some readers’ misapprehensions about the criminal justice system come from watching TV dramas. Ben Clough



“Obviously, when I read crime novels I get frustrated if the legal side of things isn’t right. The novels I love – including the non-crime ones – are those that you can see have been well-researched and you get that sense of truth. At the end of each chapter in my book, Smother, I include a scene from a cross-examination, or an examination, of a witness. You get each character’s and each witness’s perspective, and then the judge’s ruling at the end. It allows the reader to play along and pretend that they’re a juror, and decide whether the conduct of each person is deserving of punishment or not. I put a lot of work into trying to make those [scenes] correct and entertaining but it can be tricky to put forward a set of facts that hooks the reader but is also believable from a lawyer’s perspective. So they’re not going to be 100 per cent accurate. I suspect some misapprehensions have come about from American television series, with lawyers walking around the courtroom and banging on the table in front of the judge – that would never happen in Australia. And, probably, people think it’s a bit more exciting than it really is. Someone who’s watched American courtroom dramas – or even Australian courtroom dramas – might be horrified by the quagmire of procedural issues that happens before a case goes to trial.



It’s often the length of the process that takes its toll on individuals. It’s hard to explain to them why it’s taking so long to resolve what they see as a black-and-white matter. What I’ve tried to transfer into books is how humans immediately react in those moments when something’s happened, but how being ground down in a process can affect them, too. My novels are ‘crime adjacent’ in that often there’s no actual crime committed but they’re about a legal case. I’m interested in how, in civil law in particular, there’s a bit more grey and you can examine the moral choices people make and how the law decides who should be responsible versus who the reader thinks should be responsible. I do all the writing I can in the time I have available: it’s 20 minutes before the kids get up in the morning, it’s being the last person to go to bed at night. It’s not easy but it’s something I’ve always loved. I find it quite relaxing to sit down and do some creative writing, as opposed to writing that’s bound by what’s happening in my case and with my clients.” Joanna Jenkins, 62



Joanna Jenkins says she turned a career of meeting “sociopaths” into material for her books. Helen Henry - Rhubarb Photography “The first book I wrote was How to Kill a Client. I wanted to write about what it was actually like in a law firm. There are such vast amounts of money to be made; you’re sitting in meetings with people who are kind of … sociopathic. I was trying to work out what genre the book should be, then I thought, ‘I know: I’ll kill one of the f---ers!’ I think women probably have more subtle ways of killing people. There’s something very indirect about the way women wreak revenge. That book sparked many conversations. Other lawyers were obsessed with working out who was which character. But in some ways it’s more offensive than that: I was taking a number of people and popping them together into a Frankenstein figure. A lot of very creative people go into law just because they are told by their parents that they’ve got to have a job – and what they really want to do is write a novel or a musical. It gets beaten out of you as you become more grey and besuited. But if you’re really lucky you can break out and do the things you’ve always wanted to do.



Being a lawyer is very stressful. It can be interesting but sometimes it’s not. Writing is a very solitary thing. I do miss the ‘team sport’ associated with being a lawyer. But not enough to want to go back to it. Being a lawyer helps with the practical aspects of the craft of writing. It teaches attention to detail, you write a lot of words and become tolerant of withering criticism – because you get that from clients. So getting edited is a doddle, really! I never write courtroom scenes, mainly because courts are actually quite boring. My central character is a lawyer but she’s into working out what happened in a kind of resigned, obstinate and reluctant way, rather than pursuing it in a courtroom drama. I reckon lawyers on television could sometimes be sued for negligence – they always solve the case by accident, with someone walking in the night before the last day of trial.” Lisa Ellery, 51



Lisa Ellery: “Most people are not criminal masterminds. Most crime isn’t the serial-killing type.” “There are so many things that people don’t realise about crime. Psychopaths are very rare. Most people are not criminal masterminds. Most crime isn’t the serial-killing type. Many people who commit crimes are victims themselves. It wasn’t until I was in my 40s that it occurred to me I could try writing crime. A friend suggested that I read some West Australian crime authors. I read a couple of Alan Carter and Dave Warner books and I thought, gee! I hadn’t realised that West Australians wrote crime; I thought it was Americans! So I started writing a novel, Private Prosecution. I practised criminal law for seven years at the beginning of my career. All the stuff you expect to be the hard part of writing a crime novel – the legal procedure and the tricky terminology – was easy. I knew my knowledge wasn’t up-to-date; I had to look up the legislation a fair bit and I knew what I did and didn’t know. The legal training definitely helped me to structure a crime novel because you can’t have plot holes any more than you can have gaps in the evidence in a real situation.



Editor's pick Sunday Life Infertility can test even the strongest friendships. But it brought Yaelle and Lucy together In Hot Ground the protagonist was a police officer instead of a lawyer – that was not so easy. I had to really brush up on my knowledge of how police do their job. I had to actually ask for help from the police – they said, ‘You’re a defence lawyer and you’d like our help?’ But the Kalgoorlie detectives were really fantastic. There’s a huge appetite for reading about violence from people who are not exposed to it in real life. They’re fascinated by it. Someone described Private Prosecution as ‘cosy crime’, which is a fabulous euphemism for something that softens the impact of real-life violence. I want my writing to be authentic and realistic but I don’t want to portray violence for the sake of people enjoying that – I want them to be horrified and shocked by it. I like to avoid violence against women as well. Female killers are almost invariably victims. There is apparently an equal number of female and male psychopaths. But leaving those people aside, violence wouldn’t have become normalised for violent women if they hadn’t been victims in the first place.



In real life these things are really complex, but no one wants to read about that. When you write a crime novel, everything’s simplified.” Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: We can buy anything we want at the click of a button. But it is costing us more in other ways
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Opinion We can buy anything we want at the click of a button. But it is costing us more in other ways Jane Caro Novelist, author and commentator November 15, 2026 — 5:00am

November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 15 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

My grandfather ran a draper’s shop in Manchester in the UK before, during and after World War II. In those days, retailers had a relationship with those who purchased their wares, particularly if they were regular customers. The people behind the counter gave advice, to those looking to buy, about what would work best for their purposes, and so were often able to sell them a few other items that would make their task easier. The exchange between seller and buyer was not just monetary. It was social, mutually beneficial and human. At some point, retailers turned us from customers into consumers. Getty Images Shopkeeper and customer are both respectful terms, descriptions of roles in society that were important to keep the wheels of commerce turning. In those days, running a successful shop – my grandfather was about to expand his little draper’s empire into three until WWII intervened and put the dampeners on his plans; at the age of 39 he was called up to serve in the Eighth Army – relied on having a wide range of satisfied and regular customers. The customer, as they used to say in those days, was always right, and if you wanted them to return, you had to treat them courteously, no matter what. One of the most important members of any community used to be the bank manager. He is long gone and so are we. JANE CARO Many decades later I can still recall my marketing executive father’s enthusiasm for what he called “self-serve supermarkets” in the 1960s. He also waxed lyrical about things in the United States called hypermarkets. I think they are what became the Kmarts of today. It was right around then that the word “customer” began to be replaced by the word “consumer”, and I suppose that makes sense because supermarkets and hypermarkets were all about streamlining the process of shopping and making it more efficient. Supermarkets would be better, consumers were told, because they would enable retailers to lower prices by buying in bulk and reducing staff. No doubt they were better in many ways, especially at increasing retail profits, but they also began the dehumanisation of the marketplace.



When I think of a customer I think of a person – usually, but not always, a woman with a shopping basket and a list. We still have some shops that sell to customers: bespoke butcher’s, bookshops, expensive delis and patisseries. One of the most important members of any community used to be the bank manager. We accepted less-than-top-notch products from our bank for decades because the manager of our local branch was such a lovely and helpful person. He is long gone and so are we. The job of a customer is to give their custom to the retailers they choose. They make a conscious decision about what they want to buy and who they want to buy it from. When I think of a consumer I do not see a person. I see a worm-like creature with a gigantic open mouth being stuffed full of consumer goods that are being swallowed into a misshapen digestive tract that ends in an anus through which waste is endlessly excreted. The job of a consumer is to consume endlessly and voraciously. Consumers don’t make decisions, they just compulsively serve their own greed and that of the corporations pushing goods into their open maws. There are no individuals really involved in consumption; it is a group activity. It must be if anyone is going to make a profit. Related Article Opinion

David Jones collapse Want to know why DJs went bust? Walk through one of its stores at midday Melissa Singer Associate Editor, Sunday Life The indignity of being a consumer is one thing, and led to a huge fall in the level of service shoppers came to expect or receive, but things are so much worse today. I now find it difficult to think of those of us who buy things (and that’s everybody, I suppose) as much more than prey. We now find ourselves unable to contact any kind of human being if a purchase or transaction goes wrong. I recently bought a new Fitbit from an online retailer. I could not get it to pair with my phone. I even got my IT guy to try to help me get it working – no joy. The only contact I could get with the Australian-based retailer was via an AI chatbot. It gave me endless instructions, none of which helped. In the end, in disgust, I threw the Fitbit in the bin. Every product is a click away, thanks to Amazon, delivery services and streamers, and yet it’s exhausting and joyless. The amount of time it can take to find a TV program you want to watch via a streamer you pay for – passwords, verification numbers, confirmation emails, you name it – makes the whole process the opposite of relaxing. We are bombarded with ads, some selling us legitimate products but many attempting to scam us. I have stopped buying any clothes on the internet. When they arrive they never live up to the picture of the garment I saw online. We are there to be gouged, exploited, conned and ripped off.



I’ll pay a little extra to be treated as a customer. I can put up with being a consumer if there’s no other option, but if I even vaguely suspect I am being regarded as prey, I will take my custom elsewhere. World.title: The harsh brow is out. Here is an expert’s tips for keeping them balanced
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Hair trends come and go with the seasons, and the arrival of warmer weather means brows can also use a refresh. Brow queen Amy Jean Linnehan says there is a trend towards “softer, more natural brow tones in taupes, soft ash-browns and neutral brunettes, rather than overly dark, heavy brows”.

When filling in brows, use a powder to create fullness and definition; a fine-tipped pencil for mimicking individual hairs; and gel for hold and to create lift and the appearance of fuller brows. Getty Images

“Summer is the perfect time to reassess your brow colour and shape,” adds Linnehan, who recommends a Mist Brow Tattoo treatment, which she says “can make all the difference to framing up your face. With cosmetic tattooing, there is a preference for sheer washes of colour.”

Brows look best balanced with a subtle, rather than exaggerated, arch. According to Linnehan, the new brow is based around “a pixelated effect. The result should be so subtle that nobody can tell you’ve had your brows tattooed.”

For filling in sparse brows, Linnehan suggests using a powder to create fullness and definition; a fine-tipped pencil for mimicking individual hairs; and gel for hold and to create lift and the appearance of fuller brows.

World.title: I’m worried our super could get hacked. Is my money safer in the bank?
World.content:
November 15, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Hi Paul. There have been recent reports of the possibility of AI hacking into vast areas of the internet, including financial areas. Bitcoin and others have already suffered. How safe is my superannuation money? Would it be safer in a bank? Or under the bed? Yes, the recent bitcoin heist certainly made for some interesting reporting. Fortunately, our superannuation and banking systems bear no resemblance. Being vigilant for scams and hacks is wise, but there’s no need to be overly worried. We all need to be on the lookout for online scams and the like, but I think I’m on pretty safe ground when I say that taking your money out of super and putting it under the bed would be unwise. Cybersecurity is not my area of expertise. But I take comfort from the fact that Australia’s financial systems are extremely well regulated, with teams of experts at the various connections in the money pipes making sure our financial records are safe. Consumer protections here are also extremely high, so if something goes wrong, you have recourse.



As an aside, there is more money in our superannuation system than there are deposits in our banks, so the proposition that your money is somehow safer in the bank is, in this context at least, highly questionable. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’ve been renting my house for two years. Will I have to pay tax when I sell? Noel Whittaker Money columnist I am 39 years old on a salary of $125,000 per year and salary sacrifice an additional $200 per pay into my super, which is sitting at about $270,000. I also lease out an apartment which has around $285,000 left on the mortgage, at around a 6 per cent interest rate. I’ve been making extra fortnightly payments of $1000 to pay it down quickly, so expect it’ll be paid off in seven or so years. Would it be better to continue this strategy and then increase my contributions to super once my apartment is paid off – or increase my salary sacrificing to super now and take longer to pay off my apartment? My goal is to have a decent nest egg, so I can retire a little earlier than the standard age. The interest on this mortgage will be tax-deductible given the property is income producing (I’m making the assumption it is receiving the grandfathered provisions), and so there is a solution here whereby the after-tax cost of the borrowing is below the expected alternate returns (after tax). This being the case, it could be argued that you should slow down on the loan repayment, and focus your savings elsewhere.



My inclination, however, would be to continue with your current approach for two reasons. One, we are currently in a rising interest rate cycle and that will likely mean your interest expense will increase, raising the burden associated with carrying this property. Paying down this debt reduces your exposure to rising interest rates, which contributes to you being able to retain this property through the cycle. Secondly, you’ve advised that your primary goal is to be able to retire earlier than the standard. Money that you place in superannuation is inaccessible until you are at least 60 years of age. Given that you need access to money earlier, it makes sense to ensure that you hold wealth elsewhere. This investment property could produce income for you during that early retirement period. I’d be interested to know the cash flow position of the property. If the property was producing positive cash-flow, after allowing for all expenses, you could perhaps direct some savings to a non-super investment portfolio to improve your diversification, and have greater options with regards early retirement. Paul Benson is a certified financial planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. Questions to: paul@financialautonomy.com.au

World.title: We want to know if a recession is coming. It’s the wrong question
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingBudgeting Opinion We want to know if a recession is coming. It’s the wrong question Victoria Devine Money columnist November 15, 2026 — 5:01am

November 15, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This week, someone asked me a question on my podcast that has stuck with me. Should Australians be preparing for a recession? I can understand why they’re asking. Interest rates have been rising, inflation is proving stubborn and the economic headlines haven’t been reassuring. It feels like every other week there’s another economist warning us about what might be around the corner. Prices are going up and up, and so are interest rates. Louie Douvis I follow these conversations closely. It’s my job, after all. But I sometimes wonder whether we’re so focused on predicting what the economy will do next that we’re overlooking something much closer to home. After years working as a financial adviser and now in mortgage broking, my understanding of what it means to be wealthy has changed quite a bit. Early in my career, I probably would have measured wealth in the traditional sense.



How much someone earned, what their home was worth, how much they’d accumulated in investments. All perfectly reasonable measures, and ones that still matter. But having spent years looking at people’s finances behind closed doors, I’ve realised those numbers can tell you surprisingly little about how financially secure someone actually is. Some of the most eye-opening clients I worked with were households earning $600,000, sometimes upwards of $1 million a year. On paper, they were doing extraordinarily well. They owned beautiful homes, drove expensive cars and had the sorts of careers most people would consider incredibly successful. The older I get, the less impressed I am by the outward signs of financial success. I’m far more interested in whether someone has choices. Yet when we sat down and went through their finances, the reality was sometimes quite different. These clients’ mortgages were enormous, their spending had grown alongside their incomes and there was little room for anything to go wrong. Some had accumulated substantial assets but had surprisingly little put aside for retirement. Others were so dependent on maintaining their current incomes that even a relatively short interruption could have forced some very difficult decisions. I’ve met people who could afford almost anything, except the freedom to stop working.



I don’t share that to criticise them. It’s remarkably easy for your lifestyle to expand as your income increases, particularly when the people around you are doing the same thing. And a large mortgage isn’t necessarily a problem if you have the income and financial buffers to support it. What struck me was how different their financial reality could be from the picture everyone else saw. I’ve thought about those clients a lot over the years, particularly when conversations about recessions start making headlines. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock on November 3, after the bank raised interest rates for a fifth time this year. Dominic Lorrimer There are genuine reasons to be paying attention to the economy right now. This month, the Reserve Bank increased the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, while annual inflation reached 3.9 per cent in the September quarter. Unemployment averaged 4.6 per cent over the same period, and the RBA now expects it to climb to 5.1 per cent by the end of 2028. That’s hardly an economic outlook anyone would describe as particularly comfortable.



But Australia’s economy is still growing, with GDP increasing 2.1 per cent over the year to June, and the RBA’s central forecasts point to slower growth rather than an outright recession. Even economists working with sophisticated forecasting models can’t tell us with certainty what happens next. Editor's pick Opinion

Household debt Six months ago, Australians were optimistic. Now, we’re cutting back on toothpaste Victoria Devine Money columnist The difficulty is that a recession isn’t experienced equally. Some people will barely notice it. Others may lose their jobs, see their businesses struggle or find themselves needing to access savings much sooner than expected. And some Australians will experience serious financial hardship even if the economy never officially enters a recession. If you’re earning a comfortable income, it’s tempting to assume you’re financially secure. You can afford your mortgage, your bills are paid and your investments are ticking along. There might not be any obvious reason to question whether the life you’ve built is sustainable until something changes. I also think we need to be careful about how we talk about preparing for difficult economic conditions. There’s no shortage of financial advice telling people to build emergency funds, reduce debt and spend less. Those are sensible suggestions, but they’re considerably easier to follow when you have money left over at the end of each week.



For someone already struggling with rent, groceries and electricity bills, being told to save six months of expenses can feel almost insulting. Financial security isn’t just about making good decisions. Income, opportunity, family circumstances and plain old luck have an enormous influence on the options available to us. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide For those of us who do have some financial flexibility, there’s a responsibility to be more deliberate about what we do with it. That doesn’t mean living frugally for the sake of it or feeling guilty about enjoying the money you’ve worked hard to earn. I’m certainly not suggesting we should all stop going on holidays or buying things we love. It means recognising the difference between being able to afford something today and being able to sustain it if your circumstances change. It’s something I think about differently now, both professionally and personally. The older I get, the less impressed I am by the outward signs of financial success. I’m far more interested in whether someone has choices.



Whether they could take time away from work if they needed to, whether an unexpected expense would derail their plans, or whether they’re building towards a retirement that doesn’t depend on everything going perfectly. Editor's pick Opinion

Christmas The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor And that brings me back to the question I was asked this week. Should Australians be preparing for a recession? I think it’s worth understanding the risks, but I wouldn’t encourage anyone to make dramatic financial decisions based on predictions about when the next downturn might arrive. Trying to time the economy is difficult enough for economists, let alone the rest of us. I’d much rather see people take an honest look at how their finances would hold up if life became a little less predictable. That might mean building some savings, reviewing financial commitments or simply having a clearer understanding of where their money goes. What that looks like will be different for every household.



I don’t know whether Australia is heading towards a recession. But I do know that financial security has very little to do with impressing the people around you. These days, my definition of wealth is having enough peace of mind to know that if something unexpected happens, you have the freedom to work out what comes next without everything you’ve built falling apart. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. World.title: Alex gave me $1000 cash after I met him on Facebook Marketplace. An hour later he asked me if he’d paid me
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsShopping Opinion Alex gave me $1000 cash after I met him on Facebook Marketplace. An hour later he asked me if he’d paid me Roby D'Ottavi Writer November 15, 2026 — 5:00am

November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A few weeks ago, I signed a contract for a job in Adelaide, and my time in Melbourne is coming to a close. The city of churches is a wonderful place for the religious, and a so-so place for people in their late 20s. That said, it’s where my new employer is, so it’s time to clean out my apartment. Some of my favourite things are from random people on Facebook Marketplace. Their junk became vital to me. You can – and will – find anything here. Want a three-seater bench from the old Jetstar terminal? Marketplace. A full-size model of a battle droid from The Phantom Menace? Marketplace. Some creepy porcelain doll that is 100 per cent cursed? Marketplace. What was junk to you, can be turned into cash. But first you need to deal with a random person online. Tanya Lake Marketplace can satisfy any type of person with any type of demand. There’s no performance. Just a weird chair that a nonna is selling, and an arts student who wants it. It is also filled with some of the most fascinating people you will ever meet.



Recently, I tried to sell some memory cards for a camera I no longer own. I listed the items for $1, mentioning in the description that interested buyers should “make me an offer”. I do this because if there’s one thing people on Marketplace love more than a deal, it’s a haggle. Five minutes later after the listing went live, a man messaged me asking if the memory cards were “free”. I told him, “Nah, make me an offer. Do you have an offer?” He responded, “No, I don’t need them.” But he would have needed them if they were free? I sold some old camera lenses to a bloke called Alex. We agreed on a fee of $1000. Alex gave me the cash, and left with a pep in his step – I feel as if this purchase made his week. I was fascinated by the amount of trust Alex had in me. He brought $1000 in cash. I could have been a murderer. I’m not. Just in case you were curious. Related Article Opinion

Jobs I strutted to my interview at the bottle shop. It turned out to be a humiliation ritual Roby D'Ottavi Writer An hour later, Alex asked if he’d given me the money. I stared at his message for a few minutes, holding the cash in my other hand. A worse person would have said, “No, can you transfer the money?” I, on the other hand, told him he had. Alex responded five minutes later, “Oh, good. I forgot.” These situations arose only because someone actually messaged me. On countless situations I have had to message people four or five times before they even gave me a response, which is usually something like “Sorry, sold :(”



I once complained about these people to a friend, who told me people still message her about obsolete listings. Good, innocent buyers enquire about a bookshelf she left on the kerb in February. I asked why she didn’t just delete the listings, and she said, “I know I should, but it’s such an effort.” Has she never been on the cruel receiving end of this? I had imagined these non-repliers as poor salespeople. I’m literally begging to take their junk, cash in hand. In what world does that make sense? It turns out they’re just good folks who lose track of time. Marketplace is one of the last remaining networks where people are not performing or playing a role. Instagram tells us to post the most luxurious parts of our lives. LinkedIn says we must always be networking. Twitter/X exists for opinions, whether we believe them or not. On Marketplace, something as cataclysmic as a divorce is summarised as “Wood dining table. $100. Need gone ASAP.” We spend a stupid amount of time building stories in our heads. If you go onto Marketplace right now, you’ll see hundreds of wedding dresses in every conceivable size. You won’t see the marriage. A wedding dress is never just a wedding dress. Marketplace doesn’t care. That dining table that a happy family ate dinner at every night is now going to some share house in Northcote where one-night stands will drink crap coffee at 9am.



My sentimentality comes from the fact that in the next few months, I am going to have to sell many things that occupy my home. A couch I watched movies with exes on. A Seinfeld mug. The desk I bought with my first payment from The Age. Whoever buys these things won’t understand any of that. They’ll see a desk that was once $500, listed for a fifth of that because I can’t be bothered disassembling it. Related Article Opinion

Online shopping It seemed like a fuss-free Marketplace sale. Then the buyer showed up Shona Hendley Writer Marketplace is a network for people to rid themselves of things and start again. However, the second a stranger shows up in their rented GoGet van and takes that desk, dining table or wedding dress, it’s no longer junk. It’s someone’s new favourite piece. Someone might write the next great Australian novel at that desk. Or they might spill mi goreng on it. Whatever they do with the desk, they will not think of me. I am leaving a city I loved, and random people are arriving, one by one, to dismantle any evidence I lived there. Roby D’Ottavi is a writer and director based in Melbourne. World.title: At a ‘rustic luxury’ island resort in Canada, even the wildlife show is first class
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life At a ‘rustic luxury’ island resort in Canada, even the wildlife show is first class Stuart Hitchings November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. This story is part of the November 15 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

We’re not long in our seats, and our guide, from British Columbia’s Homalco First Nations people, is explaining how crucial salmon are to the local ecosystem when one of our party exclaims: “Oh, look, a bear.” And, sure enough, it is. A full-grown male grizzly, sitting chest-deep in the river, eating a salmon. The minibus pulls over and we alight, phones front and centre, filming until the bear swims off downstream. We get back onto the bus, more slowly than we got off it, and our guide continues his chat. I miss his first name when he introduces himself and his colleague, Wilson. “But my ‘government name’ is Dude,” he tells us in his soft Canadian accent, smiling and gesturing to a name tag which, from my seat, I’d assumed said “Guide”. Sonora Resort is almost as spectacular as the nature that surrounds it. This bone-dry humour illuminates Dude and Wilson’s intimate knowledge of their country as they emphasise that the salmon spawning run (and subsequent carnival of salmony death) provides much of the nutrients that power the entire ecosystem; we’ve already watched bald eagles and a golden eagle tucking into the dead fish littering the river (and, to be frank, you can hardly miss the smell).



Later, as we’re crossing a bridge, Wilson suddenly pulls over. On the bank beneath are a mother bear and her two-year-old cub. It’s a fitting climax to an astonishing morning, and though we’d been told confidently by our hosts at Sonora Resort, located on its own island between Vancouver Island and the mainland, that we would see bears, it’s almost overwhelming to get so close to these magnificent animals. Sonora, accessible only by boat, seaplane or helicopter, is the epitome of rustic luxury. Part of the Relais & Chateaux group, it’s almost as spectacular as the nature that surrounds it. As well as stunning views, there are spacious rooms (all with binoculars, so you can watch the seals and sea lions from your room), a spa and gym, guided fishing, myriad hot tubs, minigolf and even archery. Not to mention the excellent Tyee dining room and bar, serving a mix of classic dishes and more innovative fare, all with an emphasis on fresh local ingredients. (There are also unlimited snacks scattered throughout the resort, ensuring no guest will ever go hungry.) The day after our close encounters with grizzlies, resort guide Robynne, who’s already demonstrated impressive boat-handling skills in the swirling tidal rapids on our way back from the bears, takes us at high speed around Sonora Island in a Zodiac boat as we search for a pod of orcas that have been spotted. After a teeth-chattering, high-speed ride we emerge from a bank of thick, low-hanging fog to find about 15, including a recently born calf, just a few hundred metres from the boat. The resort is located on its own island between Vancouver Island and the mainland. It’s this mix of luxurious amenities and unspoilt nature that makes Sonora special. While it can cater to almost every need, I love that you can walk five minutes in any direction from your room and find yourself in cool, lush forest, or on an otherwise deserted headland watching seals and sea lions hunting and playing. Not to mention the way nature comes right into the resort: as we’re eating dinner one evening, an adorable critter – it turns out to be a pine marten – pushes its nose against the windowpane, delighting everyone.



The gateway to all this natural splendour is Vancouver, and it’s well worth a few days of your time. My base in the city before heading to Sonora is the original Fairmont Hotel, in the centre of downtown (though some might prefer its newer, flashier harbourside sisters, Fairmont Waterfront and Fairmont Pacific Rim). Opened in 1939, the Fairmont is classic late-period art deco, with a copper roof, gargoyles and all the amenities you’d expect in a top hotel. I make a second home in its Notch8 restaurant, where I enjoy everything from moules frites at the bar to a full chef’s tasting menu. Related Article Sunday Life What three strangers taught a single mum on a trip to New Zealand The latter is just one of a string of memorable meals in Vancouver, including fantastic fresh sushi at Miku Waterfront, great bistro fare at industrial-chic Nightingale and, best of all, an extravagant tasting menu at the Michelin-starred Published on Main, one of the top restaurants along Vancouver’s “Michelin mile” – Main Street in Mount Pleasant. Here we’re served plate after delectable plate, all showcasing local ingredients, many of them foraged, accompanied by equally fine local wines. With all this culinary temptation, it’s lucky Vancouver is an excellent walking city; on my first day in town, anxious to stave off jet lag, I stroll to Canada Dock, then around the waterfront, and do half a lap of the enormous Stanley Park. And there are other distractions. While I’ve never truly been sold on the benefits of cold-water swimming, the prospect of sharing the water with seals and dolphins is enough for me to be talked into hopping aboard High Tide Sauna’s floating facility, where bouts of sweatiness are interrupted by plunges into Vancouver Harbour (even at the end of summer the water’s a crisp 14 degrees). Afterwards I feel so energised I take myself straight to the Fairmont’s Spa Solea for a hot-stone massage. Even in downtown Vancouver, as urban as it is, nature is never far away. An hour out of town is the Sea to Sky Gondola, where we enjoy mountain-top yoga followed by a gentle guided walk through Squamish Canyon, both led by ex-Sydneysider Nicki, of Wild Vedas. The mountain-top yoga has views to match the moves, and the canyon boasts beautiful mature trees, a spectacular waterfall and lots of cute furry animals – squirrels and chipmunks mostly – and a spectacular waterfall. But no grizzly bears. For that there’s always Sonora.



The writer was a guest of Destination Vancouver and Sonora Resort. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Crime writer Eve Thomson wants readers to know this sobering truth about court cases
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Crime writer Eve Thomson wants readers to know this sobering truth about court cases Mark Dapin November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 15 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

As a sometime crime novelist myself, I do my best to make sure the legal detail in my books is authentic, but authors who also work – or have worked – as lawyers have a bit of a jump on outsiders like me. That said, readers probably expect more of them: their courtroom scenes must be true to life, their legal arguments plausible, and the professional lives of their characters depicted within the bounds of reasonable possibility. Here, three women – two lawyers and a former one – share how their careers have influenced their writing. Eve Thomson, 47 Eve Thomson says some readers’ misapprehensions about the criminal justice system come from watching TV dramas. Ben Clough



“Obviously, when I read crime novels I get frustrated if the legal side of things isn’t right. The novels I love – including the non-crime ones – are those that you can see have been well-researched and you get that sense of truth. At the end of each chapter in my book, Smother, I include a scene from a cross-examination, or an examination, of a witness. You get each character’s and each witness’s perspective, and then the judge’s ruling at the end. It allows the reader to play along and pretend that they’re a juror, and decide whether the conduct of each person is deserving of punishment or not. I put a lot of work into trying to make those [scenes] correct and entertaining but it can be tricky to put forward a set of facts that hooks the reader but is also believable from a lawyer’s perspective. So they’re not going to be 100 per cent accurate. I suspect some misapprehensions have come about from American television series, with lawyers walking around the courtroom and banging on the table in front of the judge – that would never happen in Australia. And, probably, people think it’s a bit more exciting than it really is. Someone who’s watched American courtroom dramas – or even Australian courtroom dramas – might be horrified by the quagmire of procedural issues that happens before a case goes to trial.



It’s often the length of the process that takes its toll on individuals. It’s hard to explain to them why it’s taking so long to resolve what they see as a black-and-white matter. What I’ve tried to transfer into books is how humans immediately react in those moments when something’s happened, but how being ground down in a process can affect them, too. My novels are ‘crime adjacent’ in that often there’s no actual crime committed but they’re about a legal case. I’m interested in how, in civil law in particular, there’s a bit more grey and you can examine the moral choices people make and how the law decides who should be responsible versus who the reader thinks should be responsible. I do all the writing I can in the time I have available: it’s 20 minutes before the kids get up in the morning, it’s being the last person to go to bed at night. It’s not easy but it’s something I’ve always loved. I find it quite relaxing to sit down and do some creative writing, as opposed to writing that’s bound by what’s happening in my case and with my clients.” Joanna Jenkins, 62



Joanna Jenkins says she turned a career of meeting “sociopaths” into material for her books. Helen Henry - Rhubarb Photography “The first book I wrote was How to Kill a Client. I wanted to write about what it was actually like in a law firm. There are such vast amounts of money to be made; you’re sitting in meetings with people who are kind of … sociopathic. I was trying to work out what genre the book should be, then I thought, ‘I know: I’ll kill one of the f---ers!’ I think women probably have more subtle ways of killing people. There’s something very indirect about the way women wreak revenge. That book sparked many conversations. Other lawyers were obsessed with working out who was which character. But in some ways it’s more offensive than that: I was taking a number of people and popping them together into a Frankenstein figure. A lot of very creative people go into law just because they are told by their parents that they’ve got to have a job – and what they really want to do is write a novel or a musical. It gets beaten out of you as you become more grey and besuited. But if you’re really lucky you can break out and do the things you’ve always wanted to do.



Being a lawyer is very stressful. It can be interesting but sometimes it’s not. Writing is a very solitary thing. I do miss the ‘team sport’ associated with being a lawyer. But not enough to want to go back to it. Being a lawyer helps with the practical aspects of the craft of writing. It teaches attention to detail, you write a lot of words and become tolerant of withering criticism – because you get that from clients. So getting edited is a doddle, really! I never write courtroom scenes, mainly because courts are actually quite boring. My central character is a lawyer but she’s into working out what happened in a kind of resigned, obstinate and reluctant way, rather than pursuing it in a courtroom drama. I reckon lawyers on television could sometimes be sued for negligence – they always solve the case by accident, with someone walking in the night before the last day of trial.” Lisa Ellery, 51



Lisa Ellery: “Most people are not criminal masterminds. Most crime isn’t the serial-killing type.” “There are so many things that people don’t realise about crime. Psychopaths are very rare. Most people are not criminal masterminds. Most crime isn’t the serial-killing type. Many people who commit crimes are victims themselves. It wasn’t until I was in my 40s that it occurred to me I could try writing crime. A friend suggested that I read some West Australian crime authors. I read a couple of Alan Carter and Dave Warner books and I thought, gee! I hadn’t realised that West Australians wrote crime; I thought it was Americans! So I started writing a novel, Private Prosecution. I practised criminal law for seven years at the beginning of my career. All the stuff you expect to be the hard part of writing a crime novel – the legal procedure and the tricky terminology – was easy. I knew my knowledge wasn’t up-to-date; I had to look up the legislation a fair bit and I knew what I did and didn’t know. The legal training definitely helped me to structure a crime novel because you can’t have plot holes any more than you can have gaps in the evidence in a real situation.



Editor's pick Sunday Life Infertility can test even the strongest friendships. But it brought Yaelle and Lucy together In Hot Ground the protagonist was a police officer instead of a lawyer – that was not so easy. I had to really brush up on my knowledge of how police do their job. I had to actually ask for help from the police – they said, ‘You’re a defence lawyer and you’d like our help?’ But the Kalgoorlie detectives were really fantastic. There’s a huge appetite for reading about violence from people who are not exposed to it in real life. They’re fascinated by it. Someone described Private Prosecution as ‘cosy crime’, which is a fabulous euphemism for something that softens the impact of real-life violence. I want my writing to be authentic and realistic but I don’t want to portray violence for the sake of people enjoying that – I want them to be horrified and shocked by it. I like to avoid violence against women as well. Female killers are almost invariably victims. There is apparently an equal number of female and male psychopaths. But leaving those people aside, violence wouldn’t have become normalised for violent women if they hadn’t been victims in the first place.



In real life these things are really complex, but no one wants to read about that. When you write a crime novel, everything’s simplified.” Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: We can buy anything we want at the click of a button. But it is costing us more in other ways
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Opinion We can buy anything we want at the click of a button. But it is costing us more in other ways Jane Caro Novelist, author and commentator November 15, 2026 — 5:00am

November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 15 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

My grandfather ran a draper’s shop in Manchester in the UK before, during and after World War II. In those days, retailers had a relationship with those who purchased their wares, particularly if they were regular customers. The people behind the counter gave advice, to those looking to buy, about what would work best for their purposes, and so were often able to sell them a few other items that would make their task easier. The exchange between seller and buyer was not just monetary. It was social, mutually beneficial and human. At some point, retailers turned us from customers into consumers. Getty Images Shopkeeper and customer are both respectful terms, descriptions of roles in society that were important to keep the wheels of commerce turning. In those days, running a successful shop – my grandfather was about to expand his little draper’s empire into three until WWII intervened and put the dampeners on his plans; at the age of 39 he was called up to serve in the Eighth Army – relied on having a wide range of satisfied and regular customers. The customer, as they used to say in those days, was always right, and if you wanted them to return, you had to treat them courteously, no matter what. One of the most important members of any community used to be the bank manager. He is long gone and so are we. JANE CARO Many decades later I can still recall my marketing executive father’s enthusiasm for what he called “self-serve supermarkets” in the 1960s. He also waxed lyrical about things in the United States called hypermarkets. I think they are what became the Kmarts of today. It was right around then that the word “customer” began to be replaced by the word “consumer”, and I suppose that makes sense because supermarkets and hypermarkets were all about streamlining the process of shopping and making it more efficient. Supermarkets would be better, consumers were told, because they would enable retailers to lower prices by buying in bulk and reducing staff. No doubt they were better in many ways, especially at increasing retail profits, but they also began the dehumanisation of the marketplace.



When I think of a customer I think of a person – usually, but not always, a woman with a shopping basket and a list. We still have some shops that sell to customers: bespoke butcher’s, bookshops, expensive delis and patisseries. One of the most important members of any community used to be the bank manager. We accepted less-than-top-notch products from our bank for decades because the manager of our local branch was such a lovely and helpful person. He is long gone and so are we. The job of a customer is to give their custom to the retailers they choose. They make a conscious decision about what they want to buy and who they want to buy it from. When I think of a consumer I do not see a person. I see a worm-like creature with a gigantic open mouth being stuffed full of consumer goods that are being swallowed into a misshapen digestive tract that ends in an anus through which waste is endlessly excreted. The job of a consumer is to consume endlessly and voraciously. Consumers don’t make decisions, they just compulsively serve their own greed and that of the corporations pushing goods into their open maws. There are no individuals really involved in consumption; it is a group activity. It must be if anyone is going to make a profit. Related Article Opinion

David Jones collapse Want to know why DJs went bust? Walk through one of its stores at midday Melissa Singer Associate Editor, Sunday Life The indignity of being a consumer is one thing, and led to a huge fall in the level of service shoppers came to expect or receive, but things are so much worse today. I now find it difficult to think of those of us who buy things (and that’s everybody, I suppose) as much more than prey. We now find ourselves unable to contact any kind of human being if a purchase or transaction goes wrong. I recently bought a new Fitbit from an online retailer. I could not get it to pair with my phone. I even got my IT guy to try to help me get it working – no joy. The only contact I could get with the Australian-based retailer was via an AI chatbot. It gave me endless instructions, none of which helped. In the end, in disgust, I threw the Fitbit in the bin. Every product is a click away, thanks to Amazon, delivery services and streamers, and yet it’s exhausting and joyless. The amount of time it can take to find a TV program you want to watch via a streamer you pay for – passwords, verification numbers, confirmation emails, you name it – makes the whole process the opposite of relaxing. We are bombarded with ads, some selling us legitimate products but many attempting to scam us. I have stopped buying any clothes on the internet. When they arrive they never live up to the picture of the garment I saw online. We are there to be gouged, exploited, conned and ripped off.



I’ll pay a little extra to be treated as a customer. I can put up with being a consumer if there’s no other option, but if I even vaguely suspect I am being regarded as prey, I will take my custom elsewhere.
