World.title: The harsh brow is out. Here is an expert’s tips for keeping them balanced
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Hair trends come and go with the seasons, and the arrival of warmer weather means brows can also use a refresh. Brow queen Amy Jean Linnehan says there is a trend towards “softer, more natural brow tones in taupes, soft ash-browns and neutral brunettes, rather than overly dark, heavy brows”.

When filling in brows, use a powder to create fullness and definition; a fine-tipped pencil for mimicking individual hairs; and gel for hold and to create lift and the appearance of fuller brows. Getty Images

“Summer is the perfect time to reassess your brow colour and shape,” adds Linnehan, who recommends a Mist Brow Tattoo treatment, which she says “can make all the difference to framing up your face. With cosmetic tattooing, there is a preference for sheer washes of colour.”

Brows look best balanced with a subtle, rather than exaggerated, arch. According to Linnehan, the new brow is based around “a pixelated effect. The result should be so subtle that nobody can tell you’ve had your brows tattooed.”

For filling in sparse brows, Linnehan suggests using a powder to create fullness and definition; a fine-tipped pencil for mimicking individual hairs; and gel for hold and to create lift and the appearance of fuller brows.

World.title: Does New Zealand law need a constitutional change?
World.content:
Audio player for " Rethinking the constitution " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2604145%2Fdoes-new-zealand-law-need-a-constitutional-change

Unjust, illegitimate and illegal is how a legal scholar describes New Zealand's constitution in her new book, which calls for fundamental change to constitutional law.

Professor Claire Charters told RNZ's Saturday Morning Aotearoa was unique in that it didn't have a single written constitutional document.

"Very unusual, one of only a couple in the world... our constitution is made up of statutes and conventions and law made by the courts, so that might include statutes like the Human Rights Act."

Another unusual point in the country's legal makeup is that courts cannot overturn legislation that is inconsistent with rights or what could be understood as fundamental constitutional values.

Charters discusses what this means for the country from a Māori perspective, something she said was lacking and necessary for everyone

"I do think that if you're in a nation that doesn't respect Māori rights or the rights of refugees or other groups... I think that's a problem for everyone.

"To live in a state where rights of any group are subject to being overturned is a problem for everyone."

Professor Claire Charters Provided

She argues New Zealand has some of the weakest levels of legal protection globally when it comes to indigenous sovereignty.

"In Canada, in the US, for example, treaties with indigenous peoples have higher law status. They trump or take precedence over legislation that is inconsistent.

"So pretty powerful. I mean, imagine if Te Tiriti o Waitangi had that higher law status, and every law in Aotearoa had to comply with Te Tiriti o Waitangi."

Charters said New Zealand was in breach of indigenous rights in different ways.

She referenced the overturning of activist Mike Smith's case against Fonterra, Z Energy and other major emitters as one example.

"The Treaty Principles Bill, which is clearly a rights breach on some level, to, gosh, the Electoral Act amendments, going back to that, were just so cynical, in my view,

"The government knew, that that would have an incredibly disproportionate impact on Māori voters, and Pasifika voters, and youth, and Asian voters.

"Our institutions like the Waitangi Tribunal, which carry enormous mana and do an incredible job... its recommendations are not binding."

She said it was an "orthodox understanding" in legal circles that Māori did not cede sovereignty in Te Tiriti o Waitangi even if it was not always understood in political, societal circles.

"It astounds me how many people have not sat down and read that very short document, or translations of the Te Reo Māori version.

"We need to have Māori reflected in our constitution. If it's just imposed upon us, and we can't see ourselves in this constitution, that is incredibly divisive."

She proposed several different ways of approaching this including jurisdictional changes, the idea of a Māori senate or having greater rights protection for everyone.

World.title: 111 'solid', 'fragile', 'effective' and a safety risk - all at the same time
World.content:
Police say the 111 emergency call system is "solid" and "effective", despite their own reports to the government calling it "increasingly fragile", and creating safety risks for the public and their own officers.

The system is built on 1990s technology and police are working to find a replacement, but were unable to give a timeline to RNZ for delivering one, after more than four years.

"It is complicated, but we are working on it with urgency," acting director for communications and dispatch Inspector Natasha Rodley said.

RNZ asked how 111 could be both effective and fragile at the same time.

"We actually think they both are true," said Rodley. "There's always opportunities to be better, to make improvements and that's what our new system would look to do, to build on what we've got, which is a solid system, and make it even better, more accessible, and more modern so that it's not reliant on voice calls."

Several times, she emphasised that people would get an effective response by calling 111.

Police reports to the government in 2023 detailed how that was not always the case - they described actual deaths and injury related to constraints or failures in the system, as RNZ revealed in 2024.

Another report on improving the whole of policing in April said: "The system has faced persistent reliability and performance issues, compounded by difficulties in integrating with other agencies, with some faults taking weeks to resolve.

"These outages and planned outages put pressure on call-takers and compromise public safety."

Maintaining 111 presented public safety risks, while its fragility and complicated structure presented a fundamental risk to emergency response, it said.

RNZ: "Does the system present a fundamental risk to emergency response?"

Rodley: "As of today, no."

RNZ: "Why does your report say it does?"

Rodley: "Because there are opportunities to be better always and it is an ageing system."

Police say people will get an effective response if they call 111. 123rf

Police, fire and ambulance share the system, but none is responsible for it all or developing it. To complicate things, the front end is privately run and owned by telecommunications company Spark.

Spark has said it wants that to change.

A police briefing to minister Mark Mitchell a year ago said the current system created safety risks for first responders - police, ambulance and fire staff.

RNZ: "Do you accept that?"

Rodley: "No."

RNZ: "Do you want to explain why you don't agree with the report that went to the minister?"

The inspector then asked RNZ to quote the report, which included outlining "seven key vulnerabilities" that the minister was told in 2025 created the risks.

RNZ: "Has something happened in the intervening year that we have not yet reported on that has changed that situation?"

Rodley: "No, I think I probably am interpreting it differently. I doubt whether that has changed.

"I guess then I have to change my answer to 'yes', because I would be consistent with the report."

The risk to responders was largely about the difficulty sharing information between the front-lines, she said.

"Maybe all three emergency services need to be involved and they are all not able to be contacted at the same time, which is a limitation of our current system."

She added: "It's an ageing system and IT moves quickly, and we want to make sure that we've got a robust system into the future."

When would that happen?

"That is what we are working through currently with the future of the emergency contact system working group to get the right information for the ministers for that decision to be made."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

The aim was to have the next briefing to ministers in February, nine months later than forecast in early 2026.

"As you know, this is complicated and getting all the information together is a lengthy process."

What happened after February would depend on the government, she said.

"It was never going to be a quick process. This is critical infrastructure - we've got to get this right."

The improvement plan in April 2026 said a new 111 system might be in place in the 2027/28 financial year.

Was that still the aim?

"That would be an aspirational date, absolutely," Rodley said.

Had they looked overseas for an idea of the possible cost?

"No, no, we're not at that stage yet, sorry... honestly, we're just not at that stage yet."

The April report called 111 "increasingly unfit for purpose", but Rodley said police's main message was the system "as it stands, is operating effectively".

World.title: Two men reportedly use crowbar to get in to Northland Woolworths
World.content:
Police are investigating a break in at a Northland Woolworths supermarket early on Saturday morning.

Officers were called to Dargaville's Woolworths on Victoria Street at about 5:30am.

"Reportedly two men used a crowbar to gain entry through the store's front entrance. An investigation is in progress," police said.

Woolworths spokesperson Robin Pinner said the store was working with police and had provided CCTV footage of the incident and those involved.

Pinner said the store was open and trading on Saturday with no impact on customers.

"Unfortunately, we continue to see retail crime have a very real impact in our stores, on our team, security guards and customers, and their whānau, despite extensive security measures and efforts individually and working across industry.

World.title: What we've learnt 10 years on from Kaikōura earthquake
World.content:
Audio player for " Ten Years Since the Kaikoura Earthquake " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/science-and-technology/2598860%2Fwhat-we-ve-learnt-10-years-on-from-kaikoura-earthquake

Ten Years Since the Kaikoura Earthquake Saturday Morning Download MP3 21m

Ten years have passed since the devastating Kaikōura earthquake, an event that took the lives of two people, demolished homes and led to changes in the country's seismic modelling.

Earth Sciences New Zealand volcanologist Graham Leonard told RNZ Saturday Mornings there was a lot to learn after the natural hazard struck.

"Global scientists learned a lot from this too. We realised that these large earthquakes can actually be across many faults at the same time."

He explained that earthquakes were typically the result of stress built up for hundreds of years across a plane and across a region.

Once the fault couldn't hold the stress, it began to unzip from a point that was the epicentre, then later transferred that stress onto other fault-lines.

"Our national seismic hazard model underwent a major revision and, globally, our understanding of the way earthquakes rupture and unzip changed with this event."

Immediately after the earthquake Leonard said there were "geological detectives in the air", taking photographs and assessing the damage for clues.

"Those fault cuts are 10-12 metres long. The uplift at the coast was up to eight metres."

Scientists also assessed satellite imagery and put drones in the air to utilise LiDar.

Road damage Kaikōura to Waiau Valley (file image) RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Leanard said, along with land damage, offshore impacts were also significant.

"There was a massive sediment movement in the steep offshore bathymetry that dropped debris flows and sediment into the canyon that flows north from there, the Kaikōura Canyon, and right up through beyond Hawke's Bay off of the eastern North Island, 600-700 kilometres."

He said the earthquake took place on a steep coastal location, where many faults were part of the plate boundary action, bringing mountains out of the water.

"That means it's hard to get roads in and out, hard to have the connection of infrastructure. We saw tens of thousands of landslides in this event, really quite unprecedented."

Leonard said scientists could see it was a widespread earthquake right away from the geonet shake reports, but there were some blank spots.

"There was a dark spot in the middle, where people either didn't have connectivity or they were really busy dealing with something else, and we got no reports in the central area."

A damaged bridge on the road between Waiau and Mt Lyford following the earthquake in 2016. (file image) RNZ / Conan Young

"Throughout that area, there were widespread landslips and earthquake-shaking damage, and people were isolated for a long time."

The lessons learnt from the event were now part of the knowledge helping to prepare for future earthquakes, including a highly likely Alpine Fault quake.

Also known as the AF8, scientists estimate a 75 percent chance of a magnitude 8 or higher earthquake will happen at the southern fault in the next 50 years.

Leonard said, because the fault covered a larger location, the energy released was expected to be much more impactful, with far more landslides across the South Island.

"Directivity will be important. If it unzips again from south to north, that will send energy through to Wellington again.

"It will probably mostly be on land, but there is a chance of it rupturing offshore. In that case, more at the south end, so there's a chance of local tsunami."

He said scientists were coming together with emergency management to plan for the event.

"That's everything from thinking about the changes in engineering, and perhaps the opportunity to engineer buildings that might be more rapidly post-earthquake fixable or even usable.

World.title: Four rescued, one still missing at Kariotahi Beach
World.content:
Four people were rescued and one was still missing, after an incident at an Auckland beach.

Acting Inspector Kuhrt Wieneke said police responded to the "water-related incident" about 6.30pm Saturday.

He said four people were taken out of the water safely.

"One person is in a serious, but stable condition, while the three others are in a minor condition.

"At this stage, one person remains outstanding."

World.title: New Zealand reacts, as US progresses investigation into lamb imports
World.content:
New Zealand is "deeply disappointed" that the US International Trade Commission will move its safeguard investigation into lamb imports to the next stage, Minister for Trade and Investment Todd McClay says.

In May, McClay said he expected the United States government to launch a trade investigation into lamb imports, warning it could result in New Zealand lamb exports to the US facing increased tariffs.

On Saturday, McClay said the commission's vote was equally split, which meant it would now look at possible remedies.

"New Zealand lamb exports do not harm US producers," he said. "Our lamb complements US production and helps meet growing consumer demand.

"Our share of US lamb consumption has stayed stable for the past 20 years. We will keep working closely with industry and dealing directly with our US counterparts.

"I have instructed officials to travel to Washington DC for the commission's remedy hearing on 1 December.

"After the commission makes its recommendations, the US administration will decide whether to impose safeguard measures and what form they would take."

World.title: The 16 MPs (likely) voted out of Parliament
World.content:
Even as Parliament looks likely to grow to 131 MPs, several who have been there for the last term have been saying goodbye this week.

Because they were involuntarily ejected by voters, these 16 departing MPs probably won't get the chance to deliver valedictory speeches - so this will have to do for now.

National

Nicola Willis, the deputy leader and finance minister who also championed National's economic growth and social investment strategies, is the highest-profile exit, and one of National's hardest-working and most effective ministers.

She had worked as a staffer for both John Key and Bill English, and built a reputation as a fierce debater, going on to be a general manager at Fonterra and a director at the New Zealand Initiative, before returning to Parliament as an MP in 2018 on National's list, after the resignation of Steven Joyce.

After previously attempting campaigns in traditionally left-leaning Wellington electorates - against Grant Robertson in Wellington Central in 2017 and 2020, and Ōhāriu's Greg O'Connor in 2023 - she chose not to contest an electorate this time, ending up a victim of National's overhang.

Paul Goldsmith and Nicola Willis were key members of Christopher Luxon's cabinet. Fiona Goodall/Getty Images

At third on the list, Chris Bishop is another victim of National's electorate success, after conceding Hutt South to Labour's Ginny Andersen on election night and acknowledging his chances of returning in the final count were "extremely unlikely".

A former lobbyist for Philip Morris, and staffer for Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce, Bishop entered Parliament in 2014 on National's list, claimed Hutt South in 2017 after the departure of Labour's Trevor Mallard and lost it to Andersen in the 2020 'red wave' election, before winning it back in 2023.

Another of National's hard-working front bench, Bishop has led National's revision and replacement of Labour's Resource Management Act reforms, housing, infrastructure and transport, and became Attorney-General this year, while losing his role as National campaign chair in April, after rumours of an attempted leadership spill.

With National's low polling in 2026, Paul Goldsmith shifted from the one-tick strategy he'd run in Epsom against a succession of ACT leaders since 2011 to an explicit two-tick campaign against David Seymour, but appears to have fallen short, winning 30.5 percent of electorate votes on the night, compared to Seymour's 36.8.

A historian, biographer, pianist and taekwondo black belt, the trusted Luxon loyalist ended up with 10 portfolios (with GCSB and NZSIS being one combined role) - believed to be the most held by a minister this century - after Chris Penk's August attempt to topple the leader and sudden exit.

After being an Auckland councillor criticised for attempts to have homeless people removed from the CBD, he went on to become a National minister under John Key, had a stint as finance spokesperson under Judith Collins, and under Luxon, has led broadcasting, electoral and justice changes, including the move-on orders and removal of same-day voter enrolment.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as the father of the House - the longest continuously serving male MP - and Parliament's Speaker.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as father of the House. VNP / Phil Smith

He became MP for Ilam in the first MMP election of 1996, after unsuccessfully challenging Jim Anderton in '93, holding the seat until the red wave of 2020. He was deputy leader under both Don Brash and Judith Collins, and was a Leader of the House, defence minister, foreign minister, transport minister and led the response to the Canterbury earthquakes under Key.

His past life as a woodwork teacher stood him in good stead in the Speaker's chair, but whether his family's Olympic rowing history had much impact is unclear.

Nancy Lu was National's highest-ranked new MP in 2023, after Andrew Bayly's by-election win in Port Waikato saw him move to an electorate seat, freeing up a spot for a list seat.

Born in Guangzhou, China, she moved to Auckland at age 10 and became a chartered accountant, before becoming the party's only Chinese-heritage candidate in 2020.

Melissa Lee was the first Korean elected to Parliament - and the first Korean-born woman to enter a country's Parliament outside Korea - when she came in on National's list in 2008. She came close to unseating Labour's Helen White from Mt Albert in 2023, falling short by just 18 votes in a judicial recount.

After being a journalist for 23 years, including writing for the NZ Herald and the Listener, she was replaced as media and communications minister, and dumped out of Cabinet in Luxon's first reshuffle in 2024.

Carlos Cheung will hope special votes tip his way in Mt Roskill, with just 262 votes separating him and Michael Wood, who was dumped from cabinet in 2023 for repeatedly failing to declare shares and lost the previously safe Labour seat, as the red tide swept back out.

Cheung was born in Hong Kong and moved to New Zealand as a teenager, he has a PhD in diabetes and cardiac disease, and made it a point of pride to visit every junior, intermediate, secondary and special school in his electorate.

Vanessa Weenink had probably the most explosive comments of any departing MP, saying she would not miss the abuse from members of the public and expressing frustration at National's rightward shift.

A general practitioner for 20 years and an army medical officer for 22 - including deployments to Afghanistan and East Timor - Weenink was a Labour member, until the NZ Medical Association she chaired was disestablished in 2022, after which she joined National, narrowly taking Banks Peninsula in '23, before losing it again to Labour's Tracey McLellan.

Vanessa Weenink switched allegiances to National, after the Labour government disestablished her NZ Medical Association. VNP/Phil Smith

Labour

Deborah Russell was first elected in 2017, as MP for New Lynn, replacing former leader David Cunliffe, but after two terms, had to return on the list in 2023, after losing to Paulo Garcia.

An academic with a PhD in philosophy and co-writer of a book on tax fairness, she was minister of statistics and the Earthquake Commission under Chris Hipkins, and occasionally landed in hot water for expressing tax views out of line with the party's.

Rachel Boyack was an organiser for First Union, before reclaiming the Nelson electorate in the 2020 red wave from National's Nick Smith, who had held the seat since 1996, and narrowly held it in '23 by just 26 votes against National's Blair Cameron, before losing it to him by more than 1200 votes this election.

Her Plain Language Bill that aimed to make government documents easier to understand was reversed by the National-led coalition last term.

Dan Rosewarne was an army mechanic, who attained the rank of captain - with two deployments to Afghanistan, one to Solomon Islands and one responding to the Kaikōura earthquake - and survived leukaemia, before entering Parliament in 2022 on the list, after Kris Faafoi's retirement.

He was ejected again, after losing Waimakariri to National's Matt Doocey in '23, but returned to Parliament briefly this year, after the resignation of Peeni Henare in March.

Georgie Dansey entered Parliament on Labour's list, after Adrian Rurawhe's resignation in February, before the former Speaker's death in September.

Georgie Dansey's stay in Parliament may be brief, unless special votes save her seat. VNP / Phil Smith

She had lost the Hamilton West by-election, caused by Gaurav Sharma's resignation, to National's Tama Potaka in 2022, and fell short in Hamilton East in '23 and '26, but with just 456 votes separating her and incumbent Ryan Hamilton, she'll hope special votes land in her favour.

Green

At 19th on the Greens list in 2023, Mike Davidson never really expected to be an MP, but entered in October 2025, after the resignation of Benjamin Doyle capped off a now well-traversed string of MP replacements for the party in the last term.

A former Christchurch City Councillor who advocated for cycleways and public transport, his 2026 list placing at 20th means a return to Parliament seems very unlikely - almost as unlikely as the first time.

NZ First

Jamie Arbuckle controversially stayed on as a Marlborough district councillor - a role he'd held since 2010 - after coming to Parliament on New Zealand First's list in 2023.

He's 13th on the list - so, next in line - after placing behind rising stars Craig Stobo and Taine Randall, and former National MPs like Alfred Ngaro, Harete Hipango-Brownlie and Michael Laws. He could yet return, if Laws is eventually dumped and the party doesn't lose support in special votes.

Independents

Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris were both removed from Te Pāti Māori during its internal ructions a year ago.

Kapa-Kingi - who had helped develop iwi health services, and worked in homelessness and suicide prevention - had defeated Labour deputy Kelvin Davis and was later re-instated to Te Pāti Māori, after a court battle.

Mariameno Kapa-Kingi's term was tumultuous, after she was banished from and then re-instated to Te Pāti Māori. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

However, she ultimately stood under the banner of her own Te Tai Tokerau party for the election, losing to Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards.

Ferris - nicknamed 'Doc' (Tākuta means 'doctor', he was named for the man who saved his and his mother's life during a difficult birth) never sought a court battle to return to the fold and ran as an independent this year.

An expert in Māori art and design, and mātauranga Māori, he was considered an outside chance to defeat Labour's Rino Tirikatene, who had beat him in 2020, but won in 2023 with a 2800-vote margin, after a campaign where he went toe to toe with the likes of Winston Peters and David Seymour in The Press leaders debate.

Pre-election exits

Lest we forget, some honourable mentions for the MPs that chose to leave on their own terms, resigning within the final six months, so as to not trigger by-elections.

World.title: Motorcyclist dies while fleeing police in Whangārei
World.content:
A man has died in a motorcycle crash in Whangārei, after riding through a red light, while fleeing police.

Northland District Commander Superintendent Matthew Srhoj said, at about 12.50pm Saturday, a motorcyclist was signalled to stop on Kamo Road, after being observed riding in a dangerous manner.

"When he fled from police through a red light, a pursuit was initiated, before being quickly abandoned," he said. "The rider soon after collided with a turning car on the corner of Bank and Grey streets.

"Police immediately after provided medical assistance, however, the rider died at the scene."

Three people in the car received non-serious injuries, Srhoj said.

"The Serious Crash Unit is conducting a scene examination. Enquiries into the circumstances of the crash are ongoing,"

World.title: Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands
World.content:
All four bowlers from the 2018 Cape Town Test spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into ball tampering, the ABC understands, running counter to claims by former opening batter David Warner.

Warner wrote on social media that Cricket Australia's investigation — which saw him and Steve Smith banned for a year, and Cameron Bancroft rubbed out for nine months — was poorly handled and had a pre-determined outcome.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation. If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?" Warner wrote.

But sources connected to the bowling group said Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were interviewed. The other front-line bowler from Cape Town, current Test captain Pat Cummins, said during a marathon press conference on Friday that he spoke to investigators.

Sources close to the bowlers said they all spoke to investigators. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Cricket Australia)

"They were all interviewed. [Warner's] comments are just not true," one source told the ABC.

The ABC also understands Tim Paine was interviewed as part of the investigation.

Cummins is sadly mistaken In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

After Cummins's press conference, Warner said Cummins had "thrown [Usman Khawaja] under the bus" by rejecting Khawaja's claims that more people were responsible for sandpaper entering the field of play than Warner, Bancroft and Smith.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence," Warner said on Fox Sports before Friday's ODI between Australia and England.

"I feel like it was a botched investigation. It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us [Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft] and we had to move on and just accept responsibility."

Usman Khawaja (right) said it wasn't fair for three players to bear all the responsibility for ball tampering. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

And Warner has doubled down on social media.

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that bowlers had no idea," he wrote.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Cricket Australia said in response: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since.

"Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players right to provide their own version of events."

In his new book, Khawaja said he was never spoken to despite sitting next to Cameron Bancroft during discussions about using sandpaper on the ball.

What did Khawaja say about Sandpapergate in his book? Much has been written and said about Usman Khawaja's new book — but what's actually in the pages of Sabr?

Cummins on Friday said he spoke to investigators and there were calls at the time for anyone with more information to come forward.

On Tuesday, Starc was one of the first players to be asked about Khawaja's claims and said there were "differing opinions of eight years ago".

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since," he said.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

In 2021, Bancroft implied in an interview that the bowlers likely knew what was going on.

"Obviously what I did benefits bowlers and the awareness around that, probably, is self-explanatory," he said.

Starc, Cummins, Lyon and Hazlewood released a joint statement in response, saying they were disappointed to have their integrity questioned.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," they wrote five years ago.

World.title: Hauser ends stunning triathlon season with silver
World.content:
Australia's leading triathlete Matt Hauser has claimed a silver medal in the season-ending World Triathlon Championship Series race in Abu Dhabi.

Gold Coast-based Hauser finished 18 seconds behind Brazil's Miguel Hidalgo, with New Zealand's Paris Olympics silver medallist Hayden Wilde in third.

The result confirms Hauser's second place finish in the overall season standings, with newly crowned world champion, Vasco Vilaça of Portugal, not racing in Abu Dhabi.

"I could really feel the legs in the back end of that race, I think I could feel the whole year in the back end of that race to be honest," said Hauser, who won four golds this season, as well as the Noosa Tri earlier this month.

"Miguel had too much out there today, you could tell he was really locked in and credit to him he did a lot of work on the bike as well.

"So all round a really great race and good to see him back on top as well."

The 'world champion persona' didn't come overnight for Matt Hauser Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

The race, originally scheduled for March but postponed due to security concerns in the region, took place after the grand final in Pontevedra.

However, the competition still provided valuable qualifying points for the LA 2028 Olympic Games.

"I always think about LA, it's always in my mind, without overexposing my thoughts. It would be silly not to think about it," Hauser told AusTriathlon in the lead up to the Abu Dhabi event.

"It's a process and journey we've been on since Paris, I'm really focused on performing well at those Games."

The qualification period runs until May 18, 2028, with an athlete's 12 best results until then counting towards their overall ranking.

Fellow Australian Luke Willian came home in fifth place, with Luke Schofield 29th, Brandon Copeland 35th and Cal McClusky 40th.

"[It was good to see] Luke Willian having a sprint finish for fourth and fifth," Hauser said

"I'm just really stoked on the podium, it's been a big year and a long year at that."

Hayden Wilde (right) is shaping up as one of Matt Hauser's biggest challengers for Olympic gold in LA. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

In the women’s race, Matilda Offord was the best placed of the Australians finishing in 35th, with Sophie Malowiecki not finishing.

Russia's Diana Isakova claimed her first World Triathlon Series victory, surging away from Luxembourg's Jeanne Lehair, with American Gwen Jorgensen in third.

The race marks the end of the World Triathlon Series Championship races, as the tour combines with the Professional Triathletes Organisation to form a new Triathlon World Tour.

The new circuit will combined the existing T100 Triathlon World Tour and the World Triathlon Championship Series (WTCS), rebranded as the T100 World Championship Tour and T50 World Championship Tour respectively.

The Professional Triathletes Organisation (PTO) and World Triathlon today announced what the Triathlon World Tour brand will look like to fans and athletes when it starts next year, as well as the initial 2027 T50 and T100 World Championship Tour calendars.

"Our sport was really fragmented from a competition and commercial perspective, which was holding it back," World Triathlon president Antonio Arimany said earlier this year.

"We could have waited until the end of the current Olympic qualification before making the changes, but the changes we're making were too important to wait.

"By introducing the Triathlon World Tour now, we are creating one unified structure and brand, which can unify as many events as possible, creating a win-win situation for all of us in the sport."

World.title: A friendship forged on the rugby league fields of New Zealand a century ago
World.content:
Awhina Hetet and Rita McRae Kingi share a drink on a blistering November day, on the balcony of Awhina's Logan business.

The women and their families met and became close mates in Brisbane, after moving to the city from Rotorua and Marton and in New Zealand.

But the families' close bond was first forged more than a century ago, on the rugby league fields of New Zealand.

Awhina's great-great-great grandfather Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Māori All Stars in 1909.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Rita's great-great grandfather Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae was a coach, captain, and player.

The players had all anglicised their names before making the trip across the ditch for the campaign 117 years ago.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet (far left) was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909 and Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae (far right) was a coach, captain, and player. (Supplied)

"New Zealand was a nation of union players," Awhina says. "When they came over in 1909 to Australia … we brought with us our haka, our culture. They had two guides with them … they came with a campaign to show, 'this is who we are, we're Māori. We love this game.'"

"You see how proud they are and I think our people absolutely displayed that proudness when they put on the shirt."

Rob Hetet, Awhina Hetet, Rita McRae King, Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi and Harley Kingi. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

One of the guides was Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator who was posthumously awarded a Master of Philosophy in Anthropology from the University of Oxford.

Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator, was a guide. (Supplied)

At the time, rugby league was struggling financially in Australia. But the Aussie-Kiwi clashes attracted more than 30,000 to their games.

The Maori side left victorious, taking the cup back to New Zealand. It is now in the care of Awhina's family "in an undisclosed location," she laughs, in New Zealand.

Rob Hetet with the 1909 cup. (Supplied)

"That cup's still standing, it's one of the oldest rugby league cups in existence," she says.

"Beautiful history," adds her father, Rob Hetet. "That's probably why I am really passionate."

The Hetet family also has distant links to star Kiwi player Kalyn Ponga, who is part of the starting side for the World Cup Final in Brisbane this Sunday.

Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi, Harley Kingi and Rob Hetet. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The Hetet and McRae families will be in the stands at Lang Park, with a closer link to the game than most other revellers.

"It's been 13 years since we were in the finals," says Awhina.

"Our boys have been amazing throughout this whole campaign … may the best team win!"

World.title: Australia wins six Youth Olympics medals as African Games hailed
World.content:
Australia has come away from the 2026 Youth Olympic Games with six medals as Senegal held up its hands for the Olympic movement in Africa.

The Dakar Games were the first Olympic event to be hosted in Africa, with organisers hailing the success as further proof of the continent's ability to host major international competitions.

South Africa, which staged the men's FIFA World Cup in 2010, is among countries in talks with the IOC about hosting the 2036 Olympic Games.

Nearly 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 competed across 25 sports and 153 medal events over two weeks in Senegal.

"I think that everyone came here with certain expectations and I think those expectations have been far exceeded," International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said on Thursday.

"It has been an magnificent journey. It has been extremely magical.

"I think we've shown the world the capability that we have and now we need to choose to take that forward," the Zimbabwean two-time Olympic champion added.

Australia's six medals included four silvers and two bronzes.

Boxer Marley Dodd claimed silver in the men's 55kg event, while Mackenzie Macdonald claimed Australia's first ever taekwondo Youth Olympic Games medal in the 49kg category.

Marley Dodd won silver on the penulimate day of the competition. (Supplied: AOC)

Australia's cyclists excelled, with Elsie Apps winning silver and Caleb McKenzie bronze on the same day in the women's and men's road races.

Tasmania's McKenzie, who was diagnosed with the autoimmune illness Hashimoto’s disease earlier this year, led the race via a brave breakaway right up until the final lap before sprinting for bronze.

"I wasn't on the bike for a long time," McKenzie told Olympics.com.

"I couldn't ride my bike, I couldn't train and nothing really went well for me.

Caleb McKenzie rode in the breakaway for the majority of the men's road race. (Supplied: AOC)

"I finally pulled it together at the end of this year and had a really good ride. I had the confidence. We talked about it before we raced about having confidence in yourself, and we said, 'If you believe, you achieve'."

Apps, meanwhile, sprinted to silver.

"I'm so grateful for the opportunity that I was given to be able to go out there and get a medal," Apps said.

"It's been really inspiring. To have a little taste of what it would be like, it really makes you want more and hopefully I can make it there [to Brisbane 2032]."

Elsie Apps came second in the women's road race. (Supplied: AOC)

Queensland's beach volleyball pairing Thomas Turner and Ryan Edgar won bronze, while the women's rugby sevens teams were only denied gold in an extra-time thriller against Kenya, which claimed a first ever Olympic rugby sevens title for the nation.

Apps and Dodd were named as closing ceremony flag bearers, with Chef de Mission Kenny Wallace said the success gave him a lot of positivity heading to Brisbane 2032.

"To summarise the last two weeks … it would come down to being proud," he said.

"I'm inspired by what our Australian sporting ecosystem has in store leading into LA28 and into Brisbane 2032.

"When we came into this campaign, we hoped Dakar would become that important milestone for our emerging athletes with Brisbane 2032 on the horizon.

"It's been incredibly inspiring to see the athletes developing even further here in Dakar and understanding what it means to be part of an Australian team.

"That is what a Youth Olympic Games can do. I really look forward to seeing some of the faces that we've had in the team here in Brisbane."

First African Games hailed but future questioned

Elisabeth Diatta was one of Senegal's gold medal winners at her country's first home Olympic event. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Beach wrestling's Olympic debut brought particular pride to Senegal, where wrestling is a national sport, with 16-year-old Elisabeth Diatta's win the first for the host nation.

Other Youth Olympic debuts included baseball5, a simplified version of baseball, skateboarding, and the Chinese martial art wushu.

China finished with the most gold medals, 18, followed by Japan with 11 and Russia with eight.

Three African countries came next: Egypt with six, and Ethiopia and Senegal with five each.

The IOC staged the first summer Youth Olympic Games in 2010 in Singapore, however it has delayed naming the host for the next event, set to take place in 2030.

Kirsty Coventry hailed Africa's first Olympic event. (Supplied: AOC)

"We took a pause … and we are analysing and that's where we are. We are still analysing. The data we will collect from Dakar will be added," Coventry said.

"As we move forward, the way we want to engage with young people is extremely important. We have to analyse what will be the best way for the movement to continue in the future."

Coventry noted that just 15 per cent of athletes who have competed at the Youth Olympic Games have gone on to compete at the full Olympics.

Jess Fox and Emma McKeown are notable Australians who made the leap, winning gold at the Youth Olympic Games before going on to claim 20 Summer Olympic Games medals between them.

"We have to be very realistic about what we want the Youth Olympics to be," Coventry said.

ABC/wires

World.title: Australian cricket urged to stop 'eating itself' as Sandpapergate rolls on
World.content:
Greg Chappell has urged Australia's past and present cricket stars to end their civil war as the ghosts of Sandpapergate continue to haunt the game.

Usman Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin last week when he claimed the ball tampering scandal in Cape Town in 2018 was everyone in the team's responsibility.

Cameron Bancroft, who was in charge of using sandpaper to roughen up one side of the ball, copped a nine-month ban in the wake of the cheating scandal, while Steve Smith and David Warner were suspended for a year and stripped of their leadership roles.

The fallout continues to this very day.

Test skipper Pat Cummins delivered an extraordinary 70-minute press conference in Sydney on Friday where he provided an open floor for journalists to ask whatever they wanted in regards to Sandpapergate 2018 and ball tampering in general, among other hot topics.

The 33-year-old steadfastly rejected claims he had any prior knowledge of the 2018 plot to use sandpaper on the ball in order to gain reverse swing.

He also hit out at Khawaja, saying the accusations were "complete nonsense" and suggested they were "probably defamatory".

Warner returned serve just hours after the press conference, saying he stood by all of Khawaja's claims and wouldn't rest until the full truth came out.

The former Test opener also accused Cummins of throwing Khawaja under the bus with his sandpaper denials.

Usman Khawaja has stood by his comments. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Chappell knows a thing or two about controversy.

In 1981, and with NZ requiring six runs off the final ball to force a draw in a one-day match at the MCG, then-Australia captain Chappell ordered his younger brother Trevor Chappell to bowl the last delivery underarm.

While technically legal at the time, the move caused a massive backlash and forced a rule change, with the incident still brought up to this very day.

"Good luck with that. I think 45 years tells me it will probably be a while before it gets trumped," Chappell replied when asked if 'Sandpapergate' had finally trumped the underarm controversy.

"Mistakes have been made, I think you have to own them.

Cummins faces the music In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

"It would've been a tough time back in 2018 with all of that going on. I don't think you're always ready for these disasters when they happen, but we all make mistakes and they're all human beings.

"They're going to make mistakes, and I think we have to accept that and own those decisions, as I had to do 45 years ago."

Chappell doesn't want the in-fighting in Australian cricket to continue.

"We don't want to see Australian cricket eating itself and having a little spat within the family," Chappell said.

"Hopefully Pat's put a bit of a line under it and we can start getting on with the summer of cricket.

"It'll be a distraction, but I think they've all had enough experience that when they walk out on the cricket field there's only one thing they're thinking about."

As for Cummins' claims of having no knowledge of the plan to tamper with the ball?

"We have to believe it," Chappell said.

"Pat's a very honourable man and very talented on the field, but I think he's very talented off the field as well.

"I think from a cricket point of view they just need to move on and focus on what's in front of them."

Khawaja was due to make an appearance at a book-signing event in Merrylands on Saturday, but publishers Pelican said it unfortunately had to be postponed.

AAP

World.title: Flag football takes flight as young Aussie athletes compete in China
World.content:
A team of high school athletes has travelled from the Gold Coast to China to compete against some of the world's best NFL flag football players.

The fast-emerging sport is a non-contact take on the United States's most beloved game and looks a bit like OzTag.

Teams of five run plays to pass a football down the field in the hope of scoring touchdowns, pulling flags from the belt of their opponents to stop play.

Khodi Fabian, 15, had spent most of her life excelling at Australian sports, including touch football, before putting on the flag belt.

Khodi plays the role of wide receiver, catching long balls down the field thrown by the quarterback.

"I never thought I'd get into NFL. My life has been all touch," she said.

Despite that, the teen didn't shy away from the new sport, and represented Queensland in a competition earlier this year.

Coco Gillett (left) and Khodi Fabian say playing touch football has opened the door to competing in a future Olympic Games. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Kodhi is among 10 Palm Beach-Currumbin State High School students competing in this weekend's NFL Flag Asia Pacific Championship in Shanghai.

The team is the only Australian side invited to play in the competition.

"It's really fun to do something different, especially since it's a new sport. It's exciting to play," Khodi said.

Rapid growth on way to Olympics

In flag football, teammates work together to pull flags from the belt of their opposition to stop play. (ABC Gold Coast: Emily Dobson)

Flag football will make its Olympic debut in Los Angeles in 2028, generating rapid growth in participation since the move was announced in 2023.

The fast-approaching showcase has prompted major investment by the NFL in Australia, headquartered on the Gold Coast.

A 2022 pilot of 10 local schools helped the sport gather steam, before it was expanded to 750 schools across Australia with free flag kits announced by NFL commissioner Roger Goodell in April.

"There's over 20 million people playing in a very short period of time. By the time we get to [Brisbane] 2032 that number will be exponentially higher," Mr Goodell said.

Bindy McCormack says flag football presents huge career opportunities and professional pathways for her students. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Teacher Bindy McCormack agreed the growth had been rapid.

After first seeing the game three years ago during state championships on the Gold Coast, Ms McCormack said she was hooked.

"We took a team to compete and we'd never played before, we just learnt on the run," the coach said.

"We ended up winning and there were lots of selectors, lots of talk about the opportunities moving forward, so I think that locked me in to embed it within the school."

Fun keeps girls playing sport

A team of 10 Gold Coast students are the only Australians competing at the NFL Flag Asia Pacific Championships in Shanghai. (ABC Gold Coast: Emily Dobson)

NFL Australia and New Zealand general manager Charlotte Offord said the league was footing the bill for the team of 10 plus two coaches to travel and compete in the one-day international event.

She said the investment aimed to break down barriers for women in sport and create more pathways for young people, regardless of the outcome of the China championship.

"There's US colleges for young athletes to go and play flag now," Ms Offord said.

"We've recently announced we'll launch a professional flag league in the next five years … where people will be paid to play in the US."

Charlotte Offord says footing the bill for the trip is an investment by NFL Flag in the future of the game domestically. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Coco Gillett, 13, plays centre for the team heading abroad and said she had been "gobsmacked" to get a call-up to compete internationally.

Despite the difference to her usual sports, Coco said the culture of the game had helped her enjoy playing flag.

"All coming together and scoring and having fun with your friends … there's lots of celebrating," she said.

Unlike some of her teammates, Coco will be too young to qualify for the LA Games in 2028, something she said would drive her to keep her sights set on the big leagues.

"The Olympics would be great … I just want to try and get better each year and progress," Coco said.

World.title: Tears for Pochettino as Man Utd turn to former Spurs boss
World.content:
Tears filled Mauricio Pochettino's eyes as he discussed quitting the US national team for his dream job with Manchester United.

"A decision that in some parts, it's a very sad decision, in other parts, we are professional and we need also to try to find the next step, to try and make your dreams come true," he said.

Just three months after the US Soccer Federation announced his contract to lead the Americans through to the 2030 World Cup, Pochettino said he will depart next week for Old Trafford.

The Argentine will try to revive the 20-time English champions, who sit in the relegation zone after 10 games of the Premier League season.

"They know that there's not too many opportunities [that] can happen in your career like a side of Manchester United and, of course, when that arrives, it's difficult to turn down," Pochettino said during an emotional news conference at the US team training camp.

He signed a two-and-a-half-year contract and will take over on November 18 ahead of a crucial Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield four days later, becoming United's eighth permanent coach or manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino choked up at a news conference, speaking while seated between USSF president Cindy Parlow Cone and chief executive JT Batson.

"One of the most difficult decision in our career," he said, crying and rubbing his hands as Cone put a supportive hand on his back.

He did not want to speak about the state of United.

Mauricio Pochettino has coached from the visitors dug out at Old Trafford in the Premier League. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

The English club said the 54-year-old was "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players".

It said he had "consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues".

Pochettino's appointment came one day after Michael Carrick was fired for overseeing United's worst league start in 40 years.

Manchester United sits in 18th place in the Premier League.

Pochettino and his assistants will remain with the US for the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.

The former Spurs coach took over the US team in 2024 and led the co-host Americans to the round of 16 at this year's World Cup.

The USSF is likely to inquire about Pep Guardiola's interest and also could consider elevating Under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, a former national team defender.

The Americans' next game with the full player pool after Tuesday is likely to be in late March, so the US could take its time with its search.

Going into his final two games, Pochettino led the US to 21 wins, 12 losses and two draws — counting a penalty shootout win over Costa Rica as a draw. He was the first long-term US coach not to win any titles since Steve Sampson from 1995-98.

Pochettino said he told his US players and staff of his decision in a meeting on Thursday.

"I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation," Pochettino said.

"And they know us, how committed we are for the next two games."

Mauricio Pochettino will lead the USA in two more matches against Haiti this international window. (Getty Images: Press Association/PA Images)

After coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in the Premier League, Espanyol in Spain and winning the French title with Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino takes a job that has proved to be too big for a succession of managers since Ferguson led the team to a record 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns during a near 27-year tenure.

United has not won the league since Ferguson's last season in 2013 and has been overtaken by rivals Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Arsenal.

Champions League-winning coaches Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho failed to meet United's expectations, while David Moyes, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Carrick also came up short.

Despite winning the French league with PSG in 2022, arguably Pochettino's greatest achievement was turning Tottenham into a serial title contender in the Premier League and also leading the club to the Champions League final in 2019.

He has never won a major trophy in England, most recently losing the final of the English League Cup with Chelsea in 2024.

It is not known how much Pochettino will earn at United, as typically European soccer teams do not disclose the salaries of coaches and players.

United has spent huge sums on coaches and executives over the past 13 years and paid well in excess of $100 million in severance payments alone.

AP

World.title: McKeown returns, Pallister stars at Swim GP
World.content:
Lani Pallister produced the race of the evening and Kaylee McKeown made a successful return in the opening session of the inaugural Swim GP.

This is McKeown's return to competition after the backstroke star pulled out of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games because of glandular fever.

She won the 50m backstroke skins event, beating Iona Anderson in the last round on Friday night at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre.

Asked if she was having fun immediately after the backstroke skins, a breathless McKeown groaned "no".

Pallister won the 400m freestyle in 3 minutes 53.73 seconds, just two seconds off her personal best.

At the start of next month, the Australian distance freestyle ace will compete at the world short-course championships in Beijing.

Lani Pallister of team KingTide was superb, as ever. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Wahoo team leads on 105 points, 11 ahead of Kraken, with McKeown's Tsunami team next on 77 and Pallister's King Tide scoring 63 and with work to do in Saturday's final session.

Swim GP format Traditional swimming competitions are no longer enough, as Swimming Australia continues to explore alternative formats with the Swim GP in Melbourne, and the return of the International Swimming League in London this December.

Kyle Chalmers is captaining the Kraken team, but he is not competing in the made-for-TV novelty event.

On doctor's orders the 28-year-old is in the midst of a six-week break from swimming after the latest MRI scan on his troublesome back.

Six weeks is manageable, especially with three Olympics under his belt and all the faith that experience brings.

But an injury tweak at the Swim GP could turn that into 10 weeks, with next year's national trials looming large, and the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away.

"Earlier, when I was going through surgeries, I'd always try to force myself back in the pool and set myself back further — taking more anti-inflammatory tablets or getting a cortisone injection as a quick fix," he told AAP.

"But my doctor has advised me to have six weeks of no swimming and it's very important to take that seriously, so I don't push that six weeks out to 10 weeks.

"Then I'm really behind the eight ball of where I need to be."

Kyle Chalmers is resting his back for this event. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

After qualifying for the Paris Olympics two years ago, Chalmers revealed he had needed four epidural injections into his spine. That is as brutal as it sounds and he'd prefer not to go through it again.

"It would have been up there as one of the worst experiences for an athlete," he said.

"At some point you have to step back and say 'I am a human being first, I'm not just a racehorse that needs to be jabbed'.

"I don't want the quick fix, I need the long-term solution so I can run around in the backyard with my daughter — hopefully also future children."

Chalmers also noted that he usually takes time out of the water around this time of year.

He calls this enforced lay-off a small road bump.

But Chalmers was keen to be in Melbourne and lead the Kraken team, calling the Swim GP a great opportunity for the sport.

"I know I could race here and it could be fine, but does it put me back a little bit further in my rehab, and trying to get my body right for what matters most?" he said.

"That's why it's still cool to be able to be here and be part of the team."

Fellow Olympic gold medallist Mollie O'Callaghan also pulled out of the event as she manages a skin infection.

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Tech.title: Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade.

What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. Duffy said that there were “over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” causing disruption to radar feeds and communication with planes.

Secretary Duffy also took the opportunity to call on additional funding from Congress for modernizing the Air Traffic Control system, and to tout the work the FAA has done so far. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work.
